The sentence is about the goodness of his choice, not its size.

example: We gathered shells along the shore.
hook: When the coach shouts "Gather round," the whole team huddles together in one tight circle.

traps.why: Scatter means spread apart, the opposite of gather.
Lather looks like gather but means make soap bubbles.
You might count what you gather, but gather means bring together.

syn1.tip: Think of "gather round" or gathering shells at the beach. Both mean bringing things into one place.

sc1.stem: The teacher asked us to _____ around the fish tank so that everyone could see the baby fish.

traps.why: Scattering spreads people apart, but they needed to come close to see.
The fish swim in the tank, but the students do not.
Wandering is moving around loosely, not coming together in one spot.

sc1.tip: "So that everyone could see" tells you the class came close together around the tank.

decoys.why: Everyone needed to see the baby fish, so running away from the tank makes no sense.
You glance at something, not around it; the teacher wanted everyone to come together.
Students cannot grow larger around a tank; they need to come together.
Nobody is coming out of hiding; the class needs to come together to see.
Falling down around the tank would not help everyone see the baby fish.

traps.why: Spreading apart is the opposite of gathering.
Lining up puts things in a row, not into one group.
You may sort what you gather, but gathering is collecting it.

syn2.tip: A family gathering is when everyone comes together. Look for the choice about coming or bringing together.

sc2.stem: Before the storm, the farmer hurried to _____ his chickens into the barn, because the birds had wandered all over the yard.

traps.why: The chickens were already scattered; the farmer wanted them together.
Farmers feed chickens, but the clue is about bringing them in.
Release means let go, but he wanted them safe inside.

sc2.tip: The birds "had wandered all over the yard," and a storm was coming. He had to bring them together into the barn.

decoys.why: He hurried to bring the chickens into the barn, not leave them behind.
You cannot look closely at chickens into a barn; he needed to bring them together.
With a storm coming, he was moving the scattered birds inside, not admiring them.
Noticing the chickens would not get the wandering birds into the barn.
The farmer was saving the chickens from the storm, not eating them.
Changing the chickens would not move the wandering birds into the barn.

example: The donkey carried a heavy burden up the hill.
hook: Picture a backpack stuffed with bricks: that heavy weight pressing on your shoulders is a burden.

traps.why: Relief is when a weight is taken away, the opposite of a burden.
Border looks a bit like burden but means an edge or line.
A basket can hold a load, but it is not the load itself.

syn1.tip: Think of a pack animal carrying a burden up a hill. It is the heavy thing being carried.

sc1.stem: The donkey trudged up the hill under its _____, a load of firewood so heavy that its back sagged.

traps.why: A donkey may wear a saddle, but the sentence says the load was firewood.
Donkeys can carry riders, but the comma explains it was firewood.
Relief means less weight, but its back sagged from heaviness.

sc1.tip: The words after the comma, "a load of firewood so heavy," tell you exactly what fills the blank: a heavy load.

decoys.why: The sentence says the blank is a load of firewood, not a friend.
The blank is described as a heavy load of firewood, not bravery.
Firewood that makes a back sag is a heavy load, not riches.
The blank is a load of firewood, and a skill cannot make a back sag.
The sentence names a heavy load of firewood, not peaceful agreement.
A load so heavy its back sagged is no safe, comfortable place.

traps.why: A helpful gift makes life easier; a burden makes it harder.
You might carry a burden on a journey, but it means the load.
Small is too weak; a burden is heavy and hard to carry.

syn2.tip: People say something is "a burden on my shoulders." Picture the weight pressing down.

sc2.stem: Carrying the heavy suitcase felt like a _____ at first, but once Dad added wheels to it, pulling it through the airport was easy.

traps.why: A breeze means easy, but "but" shows it only became easy later.
Airports mean journeys, but the clue is about weight.
A prize feels good, but carrying the suitcase felt hard.

sc2.tip: "But once Dad added wheels" it "was easy," so at first it was the opposite: a hard, heavy load.

decoys.why: The suitcase was heavy and hard at first, so it was nothing like a safe place.
The sentence says carrying it was hard at first, not a natural skill.
The suitcase was a heavy thing to carry, not a friend along for the trip.
Carrying a heavy suitcase felt hard, not like a story.
The sentence contrasts hard carrying with easy pulling, not with an old story.
The heavy suitcase was a hardship at first, not good luck.

example: Our generous neighbor shared her tomatoes with everyone.
hook: A generous friend splits her last cookie with you and hands you the bigger half.

traps.why: Stingy means unwilling to share, the opposite of generous.
General looks like generous but means broad or overall.
Rich people can give, but generous means willing to share.

syn1.tip: A "generous helping" of food is a big, kind serving. Generous people give freely.

sc1.stem: Unlike his stingy brother, who never shares a single chip, Leo happily hands out his snacks to the whole bus because he is _____.

traps.why: Greedy describes the brother, but "unlike" shows Leo is the opposite.
Snacks connect to hunger, but a hungry boy would keep them.
Sharing happily is praised here, not called wasteful.

sc1.tip: "Unlike his stingy brother" signals a contrast. Leo "happily hands out his snacks," so he loves to share.

decoys.why: Leo happily hands out snacks, so the sentence is about sharing, not being worried.
Handing out snacks shows sharing, not eagerness to learn something.
The contrast is with his stingy brother, so the word must mean willing to share.
The sentence contrasts Leo with a stingy brother, so it needs a word about sharing.
Nobody accused Leo of anything; he is sharing snacks, so the word must mean giving.

traps.why: Greedy means wanting everything for yourself, the opposite of generous.
Gentle looks a little like generous but means soft and careful.
Wasteful is a negative word for using too much; generous is praise.

syn2.tip: Generous people are happy to give and share. Find the word about giving.

sc2.stem: When the bake sale ran out of money for supplies, a _____ neighbor donated fifty dollars and three dozen cookies without even being asked.

traps.why: A stingy neighbor would never donate money and cookies.
Greedy people keep things; this neighbor gave a lot away.
General looks like generous but means broad, not giving.

sc2.tip: The neighbor "donated fifty dollars and three dozen cookies without even being asked." That example shows someone happy to give.

decoys.why: The neighbor gave money and cookies without being asked, which shows giving, not worry.
Donating fifty dollars and cookies shows a giving person, not someone eager to learn.
The clue is the donation, so you need a word about giving, not accuracy.
Vast describes huge places, and the donation clue asks for a word about giving.
Brief means short in time, which has nothing to do with donating money and cookies.

example: My loyal dog waits for me after school.
hook: A loyal dog waits by the door every afternoon, sticking with you no matter what happens.

traps.why: A false friend turns on you, the opposite of a loyal one.
Royal sounds like loyal but means having to do with kings.
Loyal friends are friendly, but loyal means sticking by someone.

syn1.tip: Think of a loyal pet that always stays by your side. Loyal means you can count on them.

sc1.stem: Even when the team lost every game, Kai stayed a _____ fan, wearing his jersey to every match and never switching teams.

traps.why: A doubtful fan might give up, but Kai never switched teams.
Royal sounds like loyal but means having to do with kings.
Fans can be noisy, but the clue is about never switching teams.

sc1.tip: "Even when the team lost every game" and "never switching teams" show Kai stuck with them. That is faithfulness.

decoys.why: Kai never switched teams even when they lost, so he was a fan for a long time.
Wearing his jersey and never switching teams shows faithfulness, not eagerness to learn.
The clue is that he never switched teams, so the word must mean faithful.
Sticking with a losing team shows faithfulness, not softness or carefulness.
Swift means fast, but the sentence is about Kai staying with his team.

traps.why: Unreliable means you cannot count on someone, the opposite of loyal.
Loyal friends may help, but loyal means staying true to someone.
Stubborn is a negative word for not changing; loyal is praise.

syn2.tip: A loyal fan or friend sticks with you through good times and bad. Pick the word for staying true.

sc2.stem: Some friends drift away when you move to a new school, but Maya stayed _____, writing me a letter every single week for two whole years.

traps.why: Distant fits friends who drift away, but "but" shows Maya was different.
Silent means saying nothing, but Maya wrote every week.
Polite is too weak; weekly letters for years show deep faithfulness.

sc2.tip: "Some friends drift away... but Maya" sets up a contrast. Writing every week for two years means she stayed true.

decoys.why: Writing every week for two years shows faithfulness, not worry.
The contrast is with friends who drift away, so Maya must be faithful.
Nobody blamed Maya for anything; she kept writing, which shows she stayed faithful.
The sentence is about Maya not drifting away, not about her bragging or not.
Friends drifting away is the contrast, so you need a word meaning faithful.

example: The sandcastle collapsed when the wave hit.
hook: Pull one card from the bottom of a card house and watch the whole thing collapse into a flat pile.

traps.why: Stand means stay upright, the opposite of collapse.
Collide looks like collapse but means crash into something.
Things may shake before falling, but collapse means actually falling.

syn1.tip: Picture a sandcastle when a wave hits: it falls in on itself. Topple also means fall over.

sc1.stem: If you pull out the bottom block, the whole tower will suddenly _____ into a heap on the table.

traps.why: Pulling out the base would never make a tower rise.
Wobble is too weak; the tower ends up in a heap.
Collide looks like collapse but means crash into something else.

sc1.tip: "Pull out the bottom block" causes the tower to end up "into a heap." It must fall down suddenly.

decoys.why: A tower losing its bottom block falls into a heap; it does not grow larger.
The tower ends up in a heap, so it falls down rather than comes into view.
A tower cannot run away; pulling the bottom block makes it fall down.

traps.why: Standing firm means staying up, the opposite of collapsing.
Shaking slightly is too weak; collapse means falling all the way.
Sliding moves something over; collapsing makes it fall down.

syn2.tip: A collapsed tent lies flat on the ground. Collapse means fall down suddenly.

sc2.stem: The old wooden bridge looked sturdy from far away, but when the truck rolled onto it, the rotten boards began to _____ beneath its wheels.

traps.why: Hold fits "sturdy," but "but" and "rotten" show the boards gave way.
Rotten boards get weaker under weight, not harder.
Collect looks like collapse but means gather together.

sc2.tip: "Looked sturdy... but" signals a surprise, and the boards were "rotten." Under a heavy truck, they would fall down.

decoys.why: The boards were rotten, so they broke under the truck instead of holding up.
Rotten boards under a heavy truck would fall in, not grow larger.
The boards are giving way under the wheels, not coming out into view.
Boards cannot run away; the rotten wood gives way under the truck.

example: The doctor examined my sore throat.
hook: At a checkup, the doctor shines a little light to examine every corner of your ears.

traps.why: Ignore means pay no attention, the opposite of examine.
Explain also starts with ex but means tell how something works.
A glance is a quick look; examine means a long, close look.

syn1.tip: Picture a doctor examining a sore throat with a light. You look closely at every detail.

sc1.stem: Using a magnifying glass, the young scientist bent down to _____ the beetle's tiny legs one by one.

traps.why: Nobody uses a magnifying glass to ignore something.
Bugs sometimes get squashed, but a scientist studies the legs carefully.
Explain looks like examine but means tell about something.

sc1.tip: "Using a magnifying glass" and looking "one by one" show careful, close looking.

decoys.why: The scientist uses a magnifying glass to look closely, not to build the legs.
A magnifying glass is for looking closely, not for eating a beetle's legs.
She bent down to study the legs one by one, which is the opposite of leaving.
You cannot hug tiny beetle legs; the magnifying glass shows she is looking closely.
A magnifying glass helps you look closely; it does not change the legs.

traps.why: Turning away means not looking, the opposite of examining.
A quick glance is too weak; examining takes a careful look.
Artists study things to draw them, but examine only means look closely.

syn2.tip: An eye exam or a test checks things carefully. Examine means study with close attention.

sc2.stem: Instead of just glancing at the used bike, Dad wanted to _____ it carefully, checking the brakes, the chain, and every tire for leaks.

traps.why: Ignoring the bike means not checking anything, but Dad checked everything.
Skim means a quick look, which is what "instead of just glancing" rules out.
Explain looks like examine but means tell how something works.

sc2.tip: "Instead of just glancing" means the opposite of a quick look. Checking brakes, chain, and tires means looking closely.

decoys.why: Checking the brakes, chain, and tires is careful inspection, not just thinking highly of it.
Dad was checking every part of the bike, so he was not leaving it behind.
The bike was already built and used; Dad was checking it over closely.
Checking brakes and tires for leaks means looking closely, not changing the bike.
The sentence lists things Dad checked, so he looked closely rather than used it up.

example: Use gentle hands when you hold the hamster.
hook: A gentle breeze barely ruffles the leaves, and gentle hands hold a baby bird without squeezing it.

traps.why: Rough means harsh and hard, the opposite of gentle.
Gentle people may move slowly, but gentle means soft and kind.
Weak is a negative word; gentle is soft by choice and kind.

syn1.tip: Think of "gentle hands" holding a hamster. Gentle means soft, kind, and careful.

sc1.stem: The vet was _____ with the scared kitten, stroking it softly and lifting it with great care.

traps.why: Rough is the opposite of stroking softly and lifting with care.
Strict sounds stern, but the vet was soft and kind.
Vets may work quickly, but "great care" shows softness, not speed.

sc1.tip: "Stroking it softly" and "lifting it with great care" describe the blank. You need a word for soft and careful.

decoys.why: Stroking softly and lifting with great care shows softness, not brave confidence.
The vet moved softly and with great care, not very fast.
Lifting the kitten with great care means slow and soft, not quick.
The clues are stroking softly and great care, which describe a soft, kind manner.

traps.why: Harsh means rough or cruel, the opposite of gentle.
Calm things can seem sleepy, but gentle means soft and kind.
Dull is a negative word meaning boring; gentle is a compliment.

syn2.tip: A gentle soap or a gentle breeze is soft, not strong. Look for the word that means soft and calm.

sc2.stem: My little sister plays roughly with her toys, but she is always _____ with our old cat, petting him slowly so she never hurts him.

traps.why: Careless fits the rough play, but "but" shows she acts differently with the cat.
Forceful means using strength, but she pets him slowly to avoid hurting him.
She does play, but the clue is about being soft and careful.

sc2.tip: "Plays roughly... but" signals a contrast. "Petting him slowly so she never hurts him" means soft and careful.

decoys.why: She pets the cat slowly, so swift, meaning very fast, is the opposite.
The sentence says she pets him slowly, and rapid means very fast.
She is careful so she never hurts him, which is soft, not brave and confident.
Petting slowly so she never hurts him shows calm care, not a rush.
The contrast with playing roughly asks for a word meaning soft and careful.

example: The friends embraced at the airport.
hook: Inside embrace is brace, from an old word for arms, so to embrace someone is to take them in your arms.

traps.why: Pushing moves someone away from you; embracing pulls them close.
Embarrass starts like embrace, but it means to make someone feel awkward.
Waving is a way to greet someone, but it uses no arms around them.

syn1.tip: Picture arms wrapping around a friend. Embrace is what you do when you are very happy to see someone you love.

sc1.stem: When Sofia spotted her grandmother at the airport, she ran to _____ her, wrapping her arms around her tightly.

traps.why: She ran, but chasing does not mean wrapping your arms around someone.
Scolding is angry; wrapping arms around someone tightly is loving.
Avoiding someone means staying away, not running to hold them.

sc1.tip: Look at "wrapping her arms around her tightly." That describes a hug, so the blank must mean hug.

decoys.why: She ran toward her grandmother and hugged her, which is the opposite of leaving her.
Fleeing means running away, but Sofia ran to her grandmother and held her.
Wrapping your arms around someone is a hug, not looking closely at them.
The sentence describes wrapping arms around her, which is an action, not thinking highly of her.
She had already spotted her grandmother, and the arms wrapped tightly show a hug.

traps.why: Pushing away is the opposite of pulling someone close in a hug.
A handshake is a greeting too, but it is not a hug.
Brace yourself means get ready, but embrace is not about trouble.

syn2.tip: Embrace has the word brace inside, which comes from an old word for arms. Think arms around someone.

sc2.stem: My little brother usually squirms out of everyone's arms, but after his scary dream he ran to _____ Mom and would not let go of her.

traps.why: Escape fits his usual squirming, but the "but" says this time was different.
Teasing is playful or mean, and it does not fit holding on tight.
Embarrass looks like embrace, but it means make someone feel awkward.

sc2.tip: The word "but" tells you he did the opposite of squirming away, and "would not let go of her" shows a hug.

decoys.why: He would not let go of Mom, so he was hugging her, not leaving her.
He ran to Mom and held on, which is the opposite of running away.
Holding on and not letting go is a hug, not looking closely at someone.
The clue is that he would not let go, which describes hugging, not admiring.
He ran to Mom and held her, so he was hugging, not noticing her.

example: The swift rabbit darted into the bushes.
hook: The swift is a bird so fast that it can catch and eat insects while zooming through the air.

traps.why: Slow is the opposite of swift.
Strong animals can be powerful, but swift is about speed, not strength.
Active just means busy moving; it does not say how fast.

syn1.tip: Think of "swift as the wind." Swift describes something that zooms by quickly.

sc1.stem: The cheetah, the fastest runner on land, is so _____ that it can catch up to a speeding jeep in seconds.

traps.why: A lazy animal could never catch a speeding jeep.
Cheetahs are spotted, but spots do not help them catch a jeep.
Cheetahs can be fierce, but the clue is about running fast.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "fastest runner on land" and "catch up to a speeding jeep." Both point to speed.

decoys.why: Catching a speeding jeep is about speed, not size.
The sentence is about being the fastest runner, and gentle says nothing about speed.
The fastest runner on land is special, not normal.
Catching a speeding jeep shows speed, not bravery.
The clue is the fastest runner on land, which is about speed, not curiosity.
Catching a speeding jeep in seconds is anything but gentle or mild.

traps.why: Sluggish means slow and lazy, the opposite of swift.
Graceful is about smooth, pretty movement, not about speed.
Swollen starts like swift, but it means puffed up.

syn2.tip: A swift runner wins races. Ask yourself which choice describes something that moves quickly.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's old turtle takes all morning to cross the yard, but our new puppy is so _____ that she reaches the fence in two seconds.

traps.why: Slow describes the turtle; the "but" says the puppy is different.
Puppies are playful, but that does not explain reaching the fence in two seconds.
A sleepy puppy would not dash across the yard in two seconds.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the puppy against the slow turtle, and "in two seconds" shows she is very fast.

decoys.why: The puppy is compared to a slow turtle, so the word must describe speed.
Reaching the fence in two seconds is about speed, not faithfulness.
The contrast with the slow turtle shows the puppy is fast, not kind.
Reaching the fence quickly is about speed, not size.
The puppy is new and young, and the sentence is about how fast she moves.
Two seconds compared to all morning makes the puppy unusually fast, not normal.

example: The doctor got an urgent phone call.
hook: An urgent message shouts, "Drop everything and deal with me now," like a fire alarm ringing.

traps.why: Unimportant things can wait; urgent things cannot.
Alarms are loud, but urgent means it must be handled now, not noisy.
Danger can make things urgent, but urgent itself means needing action now.

syn1.tip: You hear urgent in "urgent care," where doctors see you right away. A pressing problem also pushes you to act now.

sc1.stem: The note from the farmer was _____: "Come to the barn right now; the cow is having her calf!"

traps.why: Casual means relaxed, but "right now" shows there is no time to relax.
A calf being born right now is serious news, not a joke.
The note is about a note's message, and this one is short and rushed.

sc1.tip: The farmer says "right now." A note that needs action right away is urgent.

decoys.why: Come right now shows the note needed quick action, not that it was mild.
A cow having her calf right now is an emergency, not something normal.
The words right now show the note demanded quick attention, not that it was soft.
Nothing in the note is strange; it simply needs attention right away.
The farmer is asking for help fast, not being unfriendly.

traps.why: Something that can wait is the opposite of urgent.
Urgent things may come with alarms, but urgent is about timing, not noise.
Urgent looks like urge, but it does not mean wanting something badly.

syn2.tip: Think of an urgent phone call from a doctor. It cannot wait until later.

sc2.stem: Because the water from the broken pipe was quickly flooding the kitchen, Dad said fixing it was _____ and called the plumber before finishing his dinner.

traps.why: Optional means it could wait, but he stopped dinner to call.
Fixing pipes may be boring, but that would not make Dad stop eating.
A flooding kitchen is a problem, not something delightful.

sc2.tip: The cause is "quickly flooding the kitchen," and the effect is calling "before finishing his dinner." It could not wait.

decoys.why: Water quickly flooding the kitchen made Dad stop dinner, so it was not normal.
A flooding kitchen is a serious problem needing attention now, not a mild one.
Dad called right away because of flooding, not because the job was strange.
The clue is that the water was quickly flooding, so the fix needed to happen now.

example: Maya is keen to join the chess club.
hook: A keen kid's hand shoots up first, eager to answer every single question the teacher asks.

traps.why: Bored is the opposite of keen; a keen person is excited to do something.
Clean rhymes with keen, but it means not dirty.
Nervous is a jumpy feeling too, but it means worried, not eager.

syn1.tip: You might hear "keen to help" or "keen on soccer." Both mean really wanting to do it.

sc1.stem: Ravi has always taken a _____ interest in insects, spending every recess searching under rocks for new beetles.

traps.why: Searching every single recess shows much more than a slight interest.
The sentence says "always," so his interest is not sudden.
Someone who hunts beetles every recess truly cares; the interest is real.

sc1.tip: Ravi spends "every recess searching under rocks." That much effort shows a very eager interest.

decoys.why: Searching for beetles every recess shows a strong interest, not a mild one.
A modest interest is small, but Ravi searches every single recess.
Spending every recess hunting beetles shows a very eager interest, not a normal one.
Ravi happily searches under rocks, so he is eager about insects, not worried.
Ravi loves looking for beetles, so his interest is friendly and eager, not unfriendly.

traps.why: Not caring is the opposite of being keen.
Slightly curious is too weak; keen means very interested.
Keen sounds like clean, but it has nothing to do with tidiness.

syn2.tip: A keen fan never misses a game. Keen means strong interest, not just a little.

sc2.stem: Most of the class groaned about the long field trip to the museum, but Jamal was _____ to go and had his lunch packed the night before.

traps.why: Unwilling fits the groaning class, but "but" says Jamal felt differently.
Packing lunch early shows excitement, not fear.
Someone unable to go would not pack lunch the night before.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets Jamal against the groaning class, and packing "the night before" shows he could not wait.

decoys.why: Packing lunch the night before shows Jamal was eager, not worried, unlike his groaning classmates.

example: Use precise measurements when you bake.
hook: A precise cut lands exactly on the line, not a hair to the left or the right.

traps.why: A rough guess is the opposite of a precise answer.
Precious looks like precise, but it means very valuable.
Pre can mean before, but precise has nothing to do with time.

syn1.tip: Think of "precise measurements" in a recipe or science lab. Precise means exactly right.

sc1.stem: The scientist needed a _____ measurement, accurate to a tenth of a millimeter, so she used a special ruler.

traps.why: A rough measurement would never be accurate to a tenth of a millimeter.
Scientists may want speed, but the clue is about accuracy.
Precious looks like precise but means valuable, which does not fit a measurement.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "accurate to a tenth of a millimeter." That is an exact measurement.

decoys.why: Accurate to a tenth of a millimeter is about exactness, not speed.
A tenth of a millimeter is tiny, and the clue is about accuracy, not size.
She needed a special ruler, so the measurement had to be exact, not normal.
The sentence says accurate, so the measurement needed to be exact, not fast.
A generous measurement is a loose, large one, but she needed exact accuracy.
The clue is accurate to a tenth of a millimeter, which calls for exactness.

traps.why: A rough guess is close at best; precise means exactly right.
Precise work can look neat, but precise means exact, not pretty.
Pre often means before, but precise is not about doing things early.

syn2.tip: A precise answer is not just close. Look for the choice meaning exactly right.

sc2.stem: The directions for the model rocket were so _____ that Leo built it perfectly on the first try without guessing where even one tiny screw belonged.

traps.why: Vague directions would force Leo to guess, but he never had to.
Colorful pictures are nice, but color does not explain a perfect first try.
Crumpled paper says nothing about whether the directions were clear and exact.

sc2.tip: Look at the result: Leo built it "perfectly" and "without guessing." Directions that cause that must be exact.

decoys.why: Leo never had to guess, so the directions were exact, not just normal.
Building it without guessing shows the directions were exact, not that they were huge.
The clue is that Leo never guessed where a screw went, which means exact directions.
Knowing where every tiny screw belonged is about exactness, not speed.
Directions that leave no guessing about tiny screws are exact, not mild.

example: The library is my haven on busy days.
hook: A haven was first a harbor, a calm spot where ships hide safely from storms at sea.

traps.why: Danger is the opposite of a haven, which keeps you safe.
People seek a haven during a storm, but the storm is not the haven.
Raven looks like haven, but it is a black bird.

syn1.tip: You may hear "safe haven." A haven is a place you go to be safe and protected.

sc1.stem: During the storm, the old barn became a _____ for the chickens, keeping them warm, dry, and safe.

traps.why: A trap catches animals; the barn kept the chickens safe.
A prison holds you against your will; this barn was a welcome shelter.
Chickens might play there, but the clue is about staying safe from the storm.

sc1.tip: The sentence says the barn kept the chickens "warm, dry, and safe." A place that keeps you safe is a haven.

decoys.why: The barn kept the chickens safe, and a hazard is a danger, the opposite.
The barn helped the chickens by keeping them warm and dry; it was not a heavy load.
A barn is a building that shelters, not a friend who goes along with the chickens.
A barn is not the top of a mountain; the sentence is about staying safe.
The barn was a real place keeping chickens dry, not an old famous story.
A barn is a place, not a clever plan, and the sentence describes shelter.

traps.why: A dangerous place is the opposite of a haven.
Ships run to a haven to escape a stormy sea.
Haven sounds a bit like heaven, but it just means a safe place.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "safe haven." A haven is where you feel protected.

sc2.stem: The school hallway was loud and crowded, but the quiet art room became Mia's _____, a place where she could breathe and draw in peace.

traps.why: A nightmare is scary, but the art room gave Mia peace.
Drawing may be her hobby, but the blank names a place.
Art rooms have lessons, but a lesson is not a peaceful place.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets the art room against the loud hallway, and it is "a place" of peace. That is a haven.

decoys.why: The art room let Mia breathe in peace, so it was not a heavy load.
The sentence calls the room peaceful, and a hazard is a danger.
Mia felt peace in the room, not deep sadness.
The sentence calls it a place, and a companion is a friend, not a place.
Mia may be good at drawing, but the sentence says the blank is a place.
The blank is a place where she found peace, not a secret plan.

meaning: a friend who goes along with you
example: My dog is my favorite hiking companion.
hook: Com means with and pan comes from bread, so a companion is someone you share bread with.

traps.why: An enemy is against you; a companion goes along with you as a friend.
Compass starts like companion, but it is a tool for finding direction.
A leader goes in front of a group; a companion simply goes with you.

syn1.tip: Com means with. A companion is someone who is with you, like a buddy on a trip.

sc1.stem: On the long road trip, our dog Biscuit was a faithful _____, riding beside me in the back seat the whole way.

traps.why: Pest is annoying, but faithful shows Biscuit was a welcome friend.
A stranger is someone you don't know, not your faithful dog.
Road trips need a driver, but Biscuit was riding in the back seat.

sc1.tip: Biscuit is "faithful" and rode "beside me" "the whole way." A friend who goes along with you is a companion.

decoys.why: The road trip was the journey; Biscuit was the one riding beside you.
The car carried them, but Biscuit riding beside you is a friend, not a vehicle.
Faithful and riding beside you show Biscuit was good company, not a heavy load.
A faithful dog riding beside you is not a danger or risk.
Biscuit rode beside you as a friend; a dog is not a safe place.
Biscuit is a real dog riding in the car, not an old famous story.

traps.why: An enemy is the opposite of a friend who keeps you company.
Companion comes from words for sharing bread, but it does not mean baker.
Companion looks like company, but it does not mean a business owner.

syn2.tip: Think of a "travel companion." It is a friend who goes along with you.

sc2.stem: Since Grandpa lives alone and gets lonely, our family adopted a gentle cat to be his _____, and now he always has someone to sit with on the porch.

traps.why: An enemy would not fix loneliness; the cat is a friend.
A chore is a job you dislike; the cat makes Grandpa less lonely.
A guard keeps you safe, but the problem here is loneliness, not danger.

sc2.tip: The cause is that Grandpa "gets lonely," and the effect is he "always has someone to sit with." That is a companion.

decoys.why: The cat was meant to help lonely Grandpa, not be a heavy load for him.
The cat cheered up lonely Grandpa, so it did not bring deep sadness.
A gentle cat to sit with is not a danger or risk.
Grandpa needed someone to sit with, not luck or money.
The cat is someone to sit with on the porch, not a secret plan.
A cat that keeps Grandpa company is not a natural skill.

example: The humble champion thanked her whole team.
hook: A humble hero says, "Thanks, team," instead of "Look at me," even after winning the big game.

traps.why: Proud is the opposite of humble; a humble person does not show off.
Humid looks like humble, but it means damp and sticky air.
Bumbling rhymes with humble, but it means clumsy.

syn1.tip: A humble winner does not brag. Look for the word that means not showing off.

sc1.stem: Even after becoming the most famous scientist in the country, Dr. Lin stayed _____, never acting more important than her helpers.

traps.why: Proud fits fame, but she was "never acting more important."
Famous scientists may be busy, but the clue is about not acting important.
Scientists are curious, but that does not match how she treated her helpers.

sc1.tip: The words "Even after" signal a contrast, and "never acting more important than her helpers" means not proud.

decoys.why: She never acted more important than others, and vital means extremely important.
The clue is that she never acted important, which is about not being proud, not brave.
Treating her helpers as equals is not unfriendly or ready to argue.
Scientists are exact, but the sentence is about her not acting more important.
Nothing in the sentence says she was worried; it says she was not proud.
Never acting more important than her helpers is a good trait, not evil.

traps.why: Acting important is the opposite of being humble.
Humble is a good quality; it does not mean feeling down.
That describes humid, a word that only looks like humble.

syn2.tip: Humble is a compliment for someone who does great things but never brags.

sc2.stem: When reporters asked about her winning goal, the _____ soccer player just pointed to her teammates and said she could not have done it without them.

traps.why: A boastful player would take all the credit, not give it to teammates.
Thanking teammates is kind, not rude.
An injury would not explain why she gave her team the credit.

sc2.tip: Her actions show who she is: she "pointed to her teammates" instead of taking credit. That is humble.

decoys.why: Soccer players can be fast, but the clue is giving her teammates the credit.
Speed is not the point; she gave her teammates credit instead of bragging.
Praising her teammates is friendly, not unfriendly and ready to argue.
Nothing shows anger; she calmly gave credit to her teammates.
The clue is that she did not brag, not that she was nervous.
Her size is not the point; she pointed to her teammates instead of bragging.

example: We had a mild winter with little snow.
hook: Mild salsa barely tickles your tongue, while hot salsa makes your eyes water and your nose run.

traps.why: Harsh is the opposite of mild; mild is soft and gentle.
Wild looks and sounds like mild, but it means untamed.
Mild is not an insult; it just means not too strong.

syn1.tip: Think of "mild salsa" or "mild weather." Both are soft and gentle, not harsh.

sc1.stem: This salsa is so _____ that even little kids who hate spicy food can eat it happily.

traps.why: Fiery salsa is very spicy, and kids who hate spice could not eat it.
Salsa can be chunky, but that has nothing to do with spice.
Being famous would not make spicy food easy for kids to eat.

sc1.tip: The sentence says kids "who hate spicy food" can eat it. So the salsa must be gentle, not hot.

decoys.why: Kids who hate spicy food can eat it, so the flavor is not strong.
Kids who hate spicy food enjoy it, so nothing about it is fierce or angry.
The salsa is easy for picky kids to eat, so it is not harsh.
The sentence is about how spicy the salsa is, not how big it is.
Little kids can eat it happily, so it is not grown-up or strong.
Being exact has nothing to do with whether kids can handle the spice.

traps.why: Very spicy is the opposite of mild.
Too strong a change; mild food still has some flavor, just not much heat.
Mild weather is pleasant, not cold and icy.

syn2.tip: On a menu, mild is the choice that is not hot. It means gentle, not too strong.

sc2.stem: Instead of a bad case of the flu, Tia had only a _____ cold, so she felt well enough to read and play board games in bed.

traps.why: Severe means very bad, but Tia felt well enough to play.
Colds spread, but that does not explain why she felt well enough to play.
Wild looks like mild, but a wild cold makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "Instead of a bad case" and "felt well enough" both show the cold was gentle, not strong.

decoys.why: Tia felt well enough to play games, so her cold was not very bad.
The word only shows her cold was weak, not fierce or extreme.
The sentence compares how bad the illness was, not how fast it moved.
A cold is not grown-up; the sentence is about how weak the cold was.
A cold cannot have honorable qualities; the clue is that it was not bad.
A cold does not share anything; the sentence says it was not severe.

meaning: peaceful agreement; or sounds that blend
example: The neighbors lived in harmony.
hook: In harmony, different voices or people fit together like puzzle pieces into one pleasing whole.

traps.why: Conflict means fighting, the opposite of harmony.
Harmony starts with harm, but it has nothing to do with hurting.
A melody is a tune; harmony is sounds or people blending together.

syn1.tip: People who "live in harmony" get along. Harmony means everyone fits together peacefully.

sc1.stem: The choir sang in perfect _____, their many voices blending together into one beautiful sound.

traps.why: Chaos is a messy jumble, but the voices were blending beautifully.
A choir that sang could not be in silence.
Choirs may wear matching outfits, but the clue is about blending voices.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "voices blending together into one beautiful sound." That is harmony.

decoys.why: The choir may be skilled, but the clue is voices blending into one sound.
The sound was beautiful and blended, not full of deep sadness.
The clue is voices blending together, which has nothing to do with bravery.
Voices blending into one sound describes music, not being careful.
The sentence describes voices blending beautifully, not hard work.
Blended voices make music, not luck or money.

traps.why: An argument is the opposite of harmony.
Harmony is about music, but it needs sounds blending, not one note.
Harmony begins with harm, but it means getting along, not hurting.

syn2.tip: In a choir, harmony is when different voices blend together nicely. Look for a choice about mixing well.

sc2.stem: My two cats used to hiss and swat at each other all day, but now they live in _____, sharing a food bowl and napping side by side.

traps.why: Danger fits the old fighting, but "but now" says things changed.
Cats napping side by side are relaxed, not afraid.
Harmony can be about music, but these cats are getting along, not singing.

sc2.tip: The words "but now" show a change from fighting. "Sharing a food bowl" means they get along peacefully.

decoys.why: The cats now nap side by side happily, which is peace, not deep sadness.
They share a bowl and nap together, so they are not being careful around each other.
The sentence is about the cats getting along now, not about riches.
Napping side by side shows peace between the cats, not hard work.
The change is from fighting to getting along, not about bravery.

example: I had a sudden urge to eat ice cream.
hook: An urge is that tug inside you, like an invisible hand pulling you toward the cookie jar.

traps.why: Reluctance means not wanting to do something, the opposite of an urge.
To urge someone is to advise strongly, but the noun urge is your own desire.
A habit is something you do often, not a sudden strong wish.

syn1.tip: Think of the verb urge, to push someone. An urge is a push from inside you to do something right now.

sc1.stem: Walking past the bakery, I felt a sudden _____ to buy a warm cinnamon roll right that minute.

traps.why: Reluctance means not wanting to buy, but the sentence shows wanting.
A habit is not sudden, and the sentence says sudden.
A suggestion comes from someone else, but this feeling comes from inside you.

sc1.tip: The words "sudden" and "right that minute" show a strong want that pops up fast. That is an urge.

decoys.why: You wanted to buy the roll right that minute, and caution would hold you back.
Smelling a bakery and wanting a cinnamon roll is not a moment of deep sadness.
A heavy load does not make you want to buy a roll right away.
Nothing dangerous happens here; the sentence is about wanting a cinnamon roll.
Buying a roll needs no special skill; the sentence is about a sudden wish.
Nothing was won here; the speaker just suddenly wanted a cinnamon roll.

traps.why: A lack of interest is the opposite of a strong wish.
An urge is strong, so a small wish is too weak.
Fear can come suddenly too, but an urge is wanting, not fearing.

syn2.tip: An urge pulls you toward something, like the urge to scratch an itch. That is a strong desire.

sc2.stem: Although Marcus had promised to save his allowance, he fought a powerful _____ to spend it all on the new video game at the store.

traps.why: He would not need to fight an unwillingness to spend; that matches his promise.
A duty is something you must do, not something you crave.
Permission comes from someone else, and nobody fights against permission.

sc2.tip: "Although he had promised to save" sets up a fight inside him. He had to fight a strong want to spend.

decoys.why: Caution would help Marcus save his money, not push him to spend it all.
Spending money on a game does not take bravery; Marcus was fighting a strong wish.
Marcus was fighting a desire to spend, not a skill he had.
Nothing sad happened; Marcus just badly wanted the new video game.
A heavy load does not tempt Marcus to spend his allowance on a game.
Peaceful agreement does not pull Marcus toward spending all his money.

meaning: a friend or partner who helps you
example: My best friend is my ally in every game.
hook: An ally is the teammate who has your back, like Robin standing beside Batman in every fight.

traps.why: An enemy works against you, the opposite of an ally.
Alley looks like ally, but it means a narrow street.
A leader guides a group, but an ally stands beside you as a helper.

syn1.tip: Countries that join together in a war are called allies. Think of someone who is on your side.

sc1.stem: When the older kids tried to take over the swings, Rosa found an _____ in Tom, who stood beside her and helped.

traps.why: Tom helped Rosa, so he was not her enemy.
An umpire judges fairly and does not take one side.
An audience only watches, but Tom stood beside her and helped.

sc1.tip: Tom "stood beside her and helped." Someone who takes your side and helps is an ally.

decoys.why: Tom stood beside Rosa and helped, so she found a helper, not a wish.

traps.why: A bitter rival competes against you, the opposite of an ally.
A narrow street is an alley, a word that only looks like ally.
A neighbor lives near you but does not have to help you.

syn2.tip: An ally is on your team. When someone sides with you and helps, that person is your ally.

sc2.stem: Because Jada had helped him study for every spelling test, Leo considered her his strongest _____ in the whole class.

traps.why: A rival competes against you, but Jada helped Leo.
A critic points out faults, but Jada was kind and helpful.
Everyone in the class is a classmate, so it misses the helping.

sc2.tip: "Because Jada had helped him" is the cause. Someone who helps you is on your side, your ally.

decoys.why: Jada helped Leo study, so she was a help to him, not a heavy load.
Jada helped Leo with every test, so she was no danger to him.
Jada is a person who helped Leo, not a skill he has.
The sentence describes Jada as a helper, not as bravery.
Jada is a friend who helped Leo study, not a big win.

example: He was anxious about the big spelling test.
hook: Anxious ends in -ous, full of: anxious means full of anxiety, like butterflies before a big test.

traps.why: Calm means peaceful and relaxed, the opposite of anxious.
Angry is a different upset feeling; anxious is about worry.
Terrified means extremely scared, much stronger than anxious.

syn1.tip: Anxious ends in -ous, full of. It means full of anxiety, that nervous worry before something big.

sc1.stem: Waiting all afternoon for the doctor to call with her test results, Hana felt _____ and worried the whole time.

traps.why: Long waits can be boring, but the sentence says she was worried.
Cheerful does not go with worried the whole time.
Waiting all afternoon might make you sleepy, but the clue is worry.

sc1.tip: The sentence says she was "worried the whole time" while waiting. The blank goes with worried, so anxious fits.

decoys.why: The sentence says Hana was worried, and bold means brave and confident.
Hana was worried the whole afternoon, so her feelings were not gentle or weak.
Hana was worried while waiting, not extremely angry at anyone.
Waiting for test results has nothing to do with being faithful to someone.
Hana waited all afternoon, so nothing about her was moving fast.
Hana was not giving or sharing anything; she was worried about her results.

traps.why: Relaxed means at ease, the opposite of anxious.
Cautious ends like anxious, but it means careful.
Ashamed is feeling bad about something you did, not worry about what's coming.

syn2.tip: Picture the jittery feeling before a test or a doctor visit. Anxious and nervous both describe that feeling.

sc2.stem: Ben usually felt calm on the soccer field, but before the championship game his stomach churned and he felt more _____ than ever.

traps.why: The word but shows a change away from calm, so not relaxed.
A churning stomach shows nerves, not confidence.
A churning stomach might seem like hunger, but here it shows nerves.

sc2.tip: "Usually felt calm, but" signals a change to the opposite of calm. A churning stomach before a big game means nervous.

decoys.why: Ben's stomach churned, so he felt nervous, not brave and confident.
The sentence says he usually felt calm but not this time, so mild is backward.
A churning stomach before a big game shows nerves, not extreme anger.
The sentence is about Ben's nerves, not whether he bragged.
Being kind and soft does not explain Ben's churning stomach.
Feeling grown up does not make your stomach churn before a game.

meaning: an old story about gods or heroes
example: We read a Greek myth about Zeus.
hook: Myths are ancient stories, like Zeus hurling lightning bolts or Hercules battling a many-headed monster.

traps.why: A fact is something true, while a myth is an old made-up story.
Moth looks like myth, but it is an insect.
A riddle is a puzzling question, not an old story about gods.

syn1.tip: Think of Greek myths about Zeus and Athena. A myth is an old story passed down for ages, like a legend.

sc1.stem: In the ancient Greek _____, the god Apollo drove a golden chariot that pulled the sun across the sky.

traps.why: Greeks worshiped gods in temples, but a temple is a building, not a story.
A newspaper reports real events, not a god pulling the sun.
Greek is a language, but a language does not tell about Apollo's chariot.

sc1.tip: A god driving "a golden chariot that pulled the sun" could only happen in a story. An old story about gods is a myth.

decoys.why: Apollo driving the sun across the sky happens in a story, not in a ship or jar.
A god pulling the sun across the sky is a story, not a special meal.
The sentence describes a story about Apollo, not the top of a mountain.
Apollo driving the sun is something told in a story, not a great win.
The sentence tells what happens in an old Greek story, not a secret plan.
Apollo's chariot ride is part of a story, not scattered broken pieces.

traps.why: A true report tells real facts, unlike a myth.
Jokes are told aloud too, but a myth is an old tale of gods.
Myths explained nature, like the sun, but they are not science.

syn2.tip: Myths are very old tales about gods and heroes, often explaining things like thunder. Look for the choice meaning an old story.

sc2.stem: Grandpa explained that the tale of a giant who dug the Grand Canyon is only a _____, since scientists know a river carved it.

traps.why: Scientists say a river carved it, so the giant tale is not a fact.
A theory is a science idea, but the giant tale is a story.
Scientists take measurements, but a giant tale is not one.

sc2.tip: "Only a" plus "since scientists know a river carved it" tells you the giant tale is not true. It is an old made-up story.

decoys.why: Grandpa means the giant story is made up, not that it is a secret plan.
A made-up story about a giant is not a danger or risk.
The giant tale is a made-up story, not a long trip.
Grandpa is saying the tale is untrue, not that it is a great win.
The tale is being called a made-up story, not a heavy load.
Grandpa is talking about a story, not a ship or container.

example: She felt grief when her goldfish died.
hook: Grief is the heavy heart you feel when you lose someone you love, like a beloved pet.

traps.why: Joy is great happiness, the opposite of grief.
Anger is a different strong feeling; grief is sadness.
Disappointment is a mild letdown, much weaker than grief.

syn1.tip: Grief has a heavy, sad feeling. You hear it in grieving, which is what people do after someone they love dies.

sc1.stem: When their beloved old horse died, the whole family was filled with _____ and cried for days.

traps.why: Relief is a good feeling, but crying for days shows sadness.
Worry is about what might happen; the horse had already died.
Annoyance is too weak to make a family cry for days.

sc1.tip: The horse was "beloved" and the family "cried for days." That shows deep sadness, which is grief.

decoys.why: The family cried for days after the horse died, so they felt sadness, not success.
Crying for days shows deep sadness, not peaceful agreement.
The family cried for days, which shows sadness rather than bravery.
Losing a beloved horse fills a family with sadness, not carefulness.
Nobody gained riches here; the family was crying over their horse.
Tears are wet, but the family was filled with sadness, not wetness.

traps.why: Great happiness is the opposite of grief.
Mild annoyance is far too weak, and it is not sadness.
Fear is a different feeling; grief is sadness over a loss.

syn2.tip: Grief is what people feel after losing someone they love. It is not a small sadness but a deep one.

sc2.stem: Mia's house had always been full of laughter, but after her grandmother passed away, a quiet _____ settled over the family for months.

traps.why: The word but shows a change from laughter, so not joy.
A quiet house might seem boring, but losing a grandmother brings sadness.
Confusion is not knowing what is happening, not sadness over a loss.

sc2.tip: "Always been full of laughter, but after her grandmother passed away" signals a change to deep sadness. That is grief.

decoys.why: The word but shows the happy house changed to sadness after the grandmother died.
After a grandmother passes away, a family feels sadness, not a great win.
The grandmother's death brought sadness, not luck or money.
A meal does not settle over a family for months after a death.
The top of a mountain cannot settle over a grieving family.

example: The cat gave the new puppy a hostile stare.
hook: A hostile cat arches its back, hisses, and dares anyone to come one step closer.

traps.why: Welcoming means warm and friendly, the opposite of hostile.
Shy people may seem distant, but they are not against you.
Annoyed is only a little bothered, weaker than hostile.

syn1.tip: Picture a hostile crowd booing the other team. Hostile describes someone who acts against you, like an enemy.

sc1.stem: Instead of welcoming the new goat, the older goats were _____, snorting angrily and butting it away from the hay.

traps.why: Instead of welcoming tells you they were not friendly.
They were near the hay, but snorting angrily shows unfriendliness, not hunger.
Butting can be play, but angrily shows a bad feeling.

sc1.tip: "Instead of welcoming" tells you the goats did the opposite of being friendly, and "snorting angrily" confirms it. They were hostile.

decoys.why: The goats were snorting angrily and butting the newcomer, which is the opposite of gentle.
The goats pushed the new goat away from the hay, so they were not sharing at all.
Snorting angrily and butting are harsh actions, not mild ones.
The sentence is about how the goats treated a stranger, not about being faithful.
Butting a newcomer away from food is not an honorable act, so noble does not fit.

traps.why: Acting like a friend is the opposite of hostile.
Shyness is quiet and nervous, not angry and against you.
A bit grumpy is too mild; hostile means ready to fight.

syn2.tip: You may hear about hostile armies facing each other. A hostile person treats you like an enemy.

sc2.stem: After the new kid knocked over his Lego castle on purpose, Jamal gave him a _____ glare and refused to share his blocks for the rest of the day.

traps.why: Nobody is grateful when their castle is knocked over on purpose.
Curious means wanting to know, but refusing to share shows anger.
Playful is a happy feeling, but Jamal was upset.

sc2.tip: The castle was knocked over "on purpose," so Jamal "refused to share." That cause and effect points to an unfriendly, hostile glare.

decoys.why: Jamal was upset and refused to share, so his glare was not kind or soft.
Jamal refused to share his blocks, which is the opposite of generous.
His castle was knocked over on purpose, so his glare was stronger than mild.
The glare shows anger at the new kid, not faithfulness to him.
The sentence is about Jamal being angry, not about him avoiding bragging.

example: The tailor will alter the dress to fit.
hook: A tailor can alter your jeans, shortening the legs so they fit you just right.

traps.why: To keep something the same is the opposite of altering it.
Destroy means wreck completely, much stronger than alter.
Tailors measure before they alter, but measuring changes nothing.

syn1.tip: Think of a tailor who alters clothes to fit. To alter something is to make it different in some way.

sc1.stem: When the rain started, we had to _____ our picnic plans and move the whole party into the garage.

traps.why: They moved the party, so they did not keep the plan the same.
Plans can be written, but moving indoors means the plan changed.
Sharing a plan does not explain moving the party into the garage.

sc1.tip: "Move the whole party into the garage" shows the plan became different because of rain. To make a plan different is to alter it.

decoys.why: Moving the party into the garage changes the plans; it does not make them bigger.
Because of the rain they changed their plans, not remembered them.
Rain ruined the outdoor picnic, so they had to change the plans, not admire them.
You cannot hug picnic plans; the rain forced them to change the plans.
The rain forced a change of plans, not an official announcement of them.
The plans already existed; the rain made them change those plans, not build them.

traps.why: Leaving something the same is the opposite of altering it.
A copy is the same as the original, not different.
Throwing something away is much more than changing it.

syn2.tip: When you alter a plan, you don't throw it out. You just make it different.

sc2.stem: Grandma's famous cookie recipe is perfect just the way it is, so she warned us never to _____ even one ingredient.

traps.why: Measuring keeps a recipe right, so Grandma would not warn against it.
You must mix ingredients to make cookies, so that warning makes no sense.
Cookies need their ingredients, so she would not forbid including them.

sc2.tip: The recipe is "perfect just the way it is," so the warning must be about not making it different. That means alter.

decoys.why: Grandma says the recipe is perfect as is, so the warning is against changing it.
You need to gather ingredients to bake, so Grandma would not warn against it.
Grandma loves her recipe, so she would not warn you against admiring it.
Getting ingredients is needed to bake; the warning is about changing them.
The clue is that the recipe is perfect just the way it is, so never change it.
Noticing an ingredient would not hurt the recipe; changing one would.

example: The judge declared Lily the winner.
hook: In the Declaration of Independence, America declared to the whole world that it was free.

traps.why: To hide something is to keep it secret, the opposite of declaring.
Whispering is quiet and soft, much weaker than a firm declaration.
Decide starts like declare, but it means make up your mind.

syn1.tip: Think of the Declaration of Independence, where the colonies announced their freedom. To declare is to say something out loud, firmly.

sc1.stem: On the morning announcements, the principal will officially _____ a snow day for the whole school district.

traps.why: Kids enjoy snow days, but the principal is making an announcement.
Imagining happens in your head, not on the morning announcements.
Doubt means feeling unsure, the opposite of saying something officially.

sc1.tip: "Officially" and "on the morning announcements" tell you the principal is formally saying something to everyone. That is declare.

decoys.why: The principal is announcing a snow day, not noticing or discovering one.
Morning announcements are for saying things officially, not looking closely at them.
On the announcements the principal says things officially, not thinks highly of them.
You cannot hug a snow day; the principal is officially announcing it.
A snow day is announced, not built.
The word officially tells you the principal is announcing, not bringing things together.

traps.why: Keeping something secret is the opposite of declaring it.
Asking is a question; declaring is a firm statement.
A quiet guess is far weaker than a firm, official statement.

syn2.tip: A referee declares a winner and a judge declares a verdict. Declare is formal and firm, so look for official saying.

sc2.stem: Instead of quietly hinting that he wanted the last slice of pizza, Diego stood up to _____ to the whole table that it was his.

traps.why: Instead of quietly means he was not quiet, so not whisper.
Mumbling is unclear and soft, far weaker than standing up and saying it.
Pretending is acting, but Diego stood up to say it plainly.

sc2.tip: "Instead of quietly hinting" tells you Diego did the opposite: he said it boldly and clearly. That is declare.

example: Dogs can detect smells we cannot.
hook: A detective detects clues, noticing tiny things like a muddy footprint that everyone else missed.

traps.why: To overlook something is to miss it, the opposite of detect.
Protect ends like detect, but it means keep safe.
Detectives solve cases, but detect only means notice or find.

syn1.tip: Detect is inside detective. A detective notices clues others miss, so detect means to notice or discover.

sc1.stem: Our smoke alarm can _____ even a tiny amount of smoke and will beep loudly to warn us.

traps.why: An alarm that misses smoke would not beep to warn us.
A smoke alarm does not make smoke; it senses it.
Protect looks like detect, but nobody protects smoke.

sc1.tip: The alarm will "beep loudly to warn us," so first it must sense the smoke. Sensing or noticing is detect.

decoys.why: A smoke alarm notices smoke so it can beep; it does not collect it.
The alarm warns you about smoke; it does not use the smoke up.
The alarm beeps because it notices smoke, not because it puts up with it.
An alarm that beeps to warn you is noticing smoke, not thinking highly of it.
An alarm cannot hug smoke; it notices the smoke and beeps.
The alarm does not get smoke; it notices smoke and warns you.

traps.why: To ignore something is to pay no attention, the opposite of detect.
Reject sounds like detect, but it means refuse.
Inventing creates something new; detecting finds something already there.

syn2.tip: Smoke detectors and metal detectors find things you can't see. To detect is to discover something that is there.

sc2.stem: Although the sugar was mixed so well into the lemonade that you could not see it, your tongue could easily _____ the sweet taste.

traps.why: Although sets up a contrast, so your tongue did not miss it.
The sugar was hidden from your eyes, but your tongue found it.
A tongue cannot take sugar out of lemonade.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast: you "could not see" the sugar, but your tongue could still notice it. To notice is to detect.

decoys.why: Your tongue noticed the sweetness; it did not change the taste.
A tongue cannot announce anything; the point is that it notices the hidden sugar.
Your tongue does not build a taste; it notices the sugar you cannot see.
The sentence contrasts not seeing the sugar with noticing it by taste.
A tongue cannot hug a taste; it notices the sweetness you could not see.
Your tongue does not make the taste bigger; it notices the sweetness.

meaning: wanting very much to do something
example: The eager students raised their hands at once.
hook: An eager puppy wags its whole body and races to the door the moment it hears the leash jingle.

traps.why: Unwilling means not wanting to, the opposite of eager.
Nervous is also a feeling before an event, but it is worry.
Desperate is much stronger and comes from a bad situation.

syn1.tip: Picture an eager student waving a hand to answer first. Eager means wanting very much to do something, and so does keen.

sc1.stem: Lena was so _____ for the aquarium field trip that she packed her lunch three nights early and could barely sleep.

traps.why: The sentence mentions sleep, but she could barely sleep, so not sleepy.
She packed three nights early, so she was not unprepared.
Packing three nights early is the opposite of being late.

sc1.tip: She "packed her lunch three nights early" and "could barely sleep." Those actions show she wanted to go very much, so she was eager.

decoys.why: Packing lunch three nights early shows excitement, not unfriendliness.
Lena could barely sleep, so her feeling was much stronger than mild.
Lena was so excited she could barely sleep, so the trip was not boring to her.
Packing early and losing sleep show excitement, not being grown up.
The sentence is about how excited Lena was, not about bragging.
Lena's early packing shows she was excited, which has nothing to do with being humble.

traps.why: Bored and slow is the opposite of eager.
Worry is a different feeling before an event, not happy wanting.
Pushy and greedy are negative; eager is a positive kind of wanting.

syn2.tip: Eager has a happy feeling, like an eager beaver or kids rushing to recess. Look for the choice that means excited and ready.

sc2.stem: Most of the class groaned when Mr. Park mentioned the science fair, but Priya was _____ to start, sketching ideas for her volcano that very afternoon.

traps.why: The word but shows Priya felt differently from the groaning class.
Someone afraid to start would not sketch ideas that very afternoon.
Starting that very afternoon is quick, not slow.

sc2.tip: "Most of the class groaned, but Priya" signals she felt the opposite of the class. Sketching ideas that very afternoon shows she was eager.

example: He was modest about winning the prize.
hook: A modest winner just smiles and says thanks instead of shouting that they are the best.

traps.why: Boastful means bragging, the opposite of modest.
Honest rhymes with modest, but it means telling the truth.
Winners may become famous, but modest is about not bragging.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "modest about winning." A modest person keeps quiet about their success, just like a humble person.

sc1.stem: Jamal was _____ about his science-fair win, saying only that he had been lucky and his partner deserved the credit.

traps.why: A boastful winner would brag, not give his partner the credit.
Jealousy fits contests, but Jamal won and shared the praise.
A greedy person keeps the credit, but Jamal gave it away.

sc1.tip: Jamal said "only that he had been lucky" and that "his partner deserved the credit." Someone who won't brag is modest.

decoys.why: Jamal called himself lucky and gave his partner credit, so he was not acting bold and confident.
Nothing shows Jamal wanting something badly; the sentence is about him downplaying his win.
Jamal was not worried; he was playing down his win by giving credit away.
Nothing in the sentence shows anger; Jamal calmly said he was lucky.
Praising his partner is friendly, not unfriendly or ready to argue.

traps.why: Showing off is what a modest person does not do.
Modest people can be skilled, but modest is about how they talk.
This is about manners too, but it is negative and modest is positive.

syn2.tip: Modest is a kind, positive word for someone who does not brag about what they can do.

sc2.stem: Although she scored all three goals in the championship game, Maya stayed _____ and told everyone the whole team deserved the win.

traps.why: A boastful player would take the credit, not give it to the team.
Players get tired, but that does not explain sharing the credit.
Games can make you nervous, but the clue is about sharing credit.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a surprise: she scored every goal, yet she "told everyone the whole team deserved the win." She did not brag.

decoys.why: Maya gave the whole team credit instead of acting confident about her three goals.
Fierce might describe her play, but the sentence is about how she talked afterward.
Speed fits a soccer game, but the clue is that she shared credit with the team.
Maya was not worried; she was giving credit to her team after winning.
Telling everyone the team deserved the win is friendly, not unfriendly.

example: The rain ceased just before the game.
hook: A cease-fire is when both sides in a fight agree to stop shooting.

traps.why: Begin means start, the opposite of cease.
Seize sounds like cease, but it means grab.
Slowing down is too weak; cease means stop completely.

syn1.tip: Think of a cease-fire, when the shooting stops. To cease is to stop.

sc1.stem: The coach blew her whistle and told the players to _____ running and gather around her.

traps.why: Players can't keep running and gather around the coach at once.
Practice fits sports, but the whistle tells them to stop.
Enjoying running does not fit a whistle that calls players in.

sc1.tip: The coach "blew her whistle" so they would "gather around her." To gather, the players must stop running.

decoys.why: The players were told to gather around her, so they had to stop running, not keep going.
Remembering running makes no sense when the coach wants the players to come gather around.
The whistle meant stop and gather, not think highly of running.
The coach wanted the players to stop and gather, not study their running closely.
To gather around her, the players had to stop running completely, not just change it.

traps.why: Keeping on going is the opposite of ceasing.
That means seize, which only sounds like cease.
Slowing down is too weak; ceasing means stopping fully.

syn2.tip: When the rain ceased before the game, it came to an end. Cease means something stops completely.

sc2.stem: Instead of letting the music keep blaring all night, the neighbors agreed to _____ their party at ten o'clock so everyone could sleep.

traps.why: Continuing the party would keep everyone awake.
Parties are planned, but this one had to stop so people could sleep.
Seize sounds like cease but means grab.

sc2.tip: "Instead of letting the music keep blaring" points to the opposite of keep going. They stopped "so everyone could sleep."

decoys.why: Making the party bigger would not let everyone sleep at ten o'clock.
The neighbors wanted quiet so people could sleep, not to bring their party together.
Announcing the party would not help anyone sleep; the music had to stop.
You cannot build a party at ten o'clock so everyone can sleep; it had to stop.
Thinking highly of the party would not end the blaring music so people could sleep.

example: The crew had to abandon the sinking ship.
hook: Picture sailors rowing away from a sinking ship they will never see again: they abandon it.

traps.why: Keeping something is the opposite of abandoning it.
Wandering is roaming around, not leaving something behind for good.
Bandage looks like abandon but means to wrap a wound.

syn1.tip: Think of "abandon ship," when sailors leave a ship forever. To desert something means the same.

sc1.stem: Once the chicks learn to fly, the robins will _____ their nest for good and never come back to it.

traps.why: Robins build nests, but the clue says they never come back.
Defending means staying to protect it, not leaving forever.
Sharing a nest does not match never coming back to it.

sc1.tip: The words "for good and never come back to it" tell you the robins leave the nest forever.

decoys.why: The robins will never come back to the nest, so they are leaving it, not building it.
Making the nest bigger does not match never coming back to it.
The sentence says they leave for good, not that they look at the nest closely.
Thinking highly of the nest does not fit never coming back to it.
The robins already have the nest and are leaving it for good, not getting it.

traps.why: Holding on is the opposite of abandoning.
A break is short; abandoning is leaving for good.
You might pack before leaving, but packing is not leaving forever.

syn2.tip: When you abandon something, you go away and leave it behind, never coming back for it.

sc2.stem: Even when the storm knocked down half of their tent, the campers refused to _____ the trip and kept hiking toward the lake.

traps.why: They kept hiking, so they refused to quit, not refused to continue.
Enjoying fits a trip, but the clue is about not giving up.
The trip was already happening, so planning does not fit.

sc2.tip: "Refused to" and "kept hiking" are opposites of the blank. Since they kept going, the blank means give up and leave.

decoys.why: The campers kept hiking, so refusing to put up with the trip makes no sense.
Refusing to remember the trip has nothing to do with continuing to hike.
They kept hiking, so the point is they did not quit, not whether they admired it.
Refusing to look at the trip closely does not explain why they kept hiking.
Kept hiking shows they did not give up, not that they refused to make the trip bigger.

example: The wicked witch cast a spell on the prince.
hook: Think of the Wicked Witch of the West, cackling as she plots nasty tricks against Dorothy.

traps.why: Kind is the opposite of wicked.
Naughty is too weak; wicked means truly evil.
Wicked witches are magical, but wicked is about being evil.

syn1.tip: Picture the Wicked Witch in fairy tales. Wicked describes someone truly bad, like a villain.

sc1.stem: In the fairy tale, the _____ stepmother made Cinderella scrub the floors while she planned cruel tricks.

traps.why: A gentle stepmother would not plan cruel tricks.
Loving people don't plan cruel tricks.
Naughty is too mild for someone planning cruel tricks.

sc1.tip: She "planned cruel tricks" and made Cinderella scrub floors. That shows a truly evil character.

decoys.why: A stepmother who plans cruel tricks is not kind and soft.
Making Cinderella scrub floors and planning cruel tricks is the opposite of generous.
Cruel tricks show bad character, not good, honorable qualities.
The clue is her cruel tricks, which point to evil, not grace or style.
Nothing in the sentence is about faithfulness; it is about her cruelty.
Someone planning cruel tricks is not described by good manners.

traps.why: Kind and gentle is the opposite of wicked.
Some people use wicked as slang for awesome, but the test means evil.
Silly is far too mild for wicked.

syn2.tip: Wicked has a dark, negative feeling. Think of the villains in stories.

sc2.stem: Unlike the kind old wizard who helped the village, the _____ sorcerer cast spells to ruin the farmers' crops and frighten their children.

traps.why: A helpful sorcerer would not ruin crops.
Both wizards are magical, so this does not show the contrast.
Wise is a positive word, but this sorcerer is cruel.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the kind old wizard" tells you the sorcerer is the opposite of kind. He wants to "ruin" and "frighten."

decoys.why: The sorcerer is unlike the kind wizard and frightens children, so he is not gentle.
Ruining farmers' crops is the opposite of being happy to give or share.
A sorcerer who ruins crops and scares children does not have honorable qualities.
The sentence contrasts kind and cruel, not faithful and unfaithful.
The clue is his harmful spells, which point to evil, not grace or style.
The sentence is about harming the village, not about bragging.

example: Mom was furious when the dog chewed her shoes.
hook: Furious is fury plus -ous, so full of fury you turn red and stamp your feet.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of furious.
Annoyed is too weak; furious means extremely angry.
Curious sounds like furious, but it means wanting to know.

syn1.tip: Furious contains fury, a wild anger. Enraged contains rage. Both mean extremely angry.

sc1.stem: Mr. Park was not just a little annoyed; he was _____, red-faced and stamping his feet, when the puppy chewed his new shoes.

traps.why: Grumpy is only a little upset, but he was more than that.
Cheerful people don't stamp their feet over chewed shoes.
Puzzled is a feeling, but red faces and stamping show anger.

sc1.tip: "Not just a little annoyed" means he was much angrier than annoyed. "Red-faced and stamping his feet" backs that up.

decoys.why: The sentence says he was not just a little annoyed, so mild is too weak.
Being red-faced and stamping his feet shows anger, not worry.
Stamping his feet and turning red is the opposite of gentle.
Stamping his feet red-faced shows rage, not good manners.
A chewed pair of new shoes made him angry, not eager.
The sentence is about his anger over the shoes, not about bragging.

traps.why: Perfectly calm is the opposite of furious.
A bit grumpy is much too weak for furious.
Curious only rhymes with furious.

syn2.tip: Look for fury inside furious. The -ous ending means full of, so furious is full of fury.

sc2.stem: When her little brother spilled grape juice all over her finished art project, Lena was so _____ that she shouted and slammed her bedroom door.

traps.why: Nobody is pleased when their art project gets ruined.
Bothered is too weak for shouting and slamming doors.
Worry is a feeling, but shouting and slamming show anger.

sc2.tip: The spill caused her to have "shouted and slammed her bedroom door." That reaction shows extreme anger.

decoys.why: Shouting and slamming the door show anger far stronger than mild.
Shouting and slamming her door is the opposite of gentle.
Shouting and slamming doors are not good manners.
Her ruined project made her angry, and shouting shows rage, not worry.
The sentence is about her anger at the spill, not about sharing.
Grape juice on her finished project made her angry, not eager.

example: We got lost in the dense fog.
hook: Dense fog is so thick and packed that you can barely see your own hand.

traps.why: Thin is the opposite of dense.
Tense rhymes with dense, but it means stiff or nervous.
Dense forests can be dark, but dense means closely packed.

syn1.tip: Think of "dense fog" or a "dense forest," where everything is packed so thick you can hardly see through.

sc1.stem: The forest was so _____, with trees packed tightly together, that sunlight barely reached the ground.

traps.why: An open forest would let sunlight in.
Forests can be quiet, but quiet does not block sunlight.
Tense sounds like dense but describes a feeling, not trees.

sc1.tip: "With trees packed tightly together" explains the blank. Tightly packed trees block the sun.

decoys.why: The clue is trees packed tightly together, which is about thickness, not huge size.
A spooky forest might sound wicked, but the sentence is about trees packed tightly together.
Nothing here is wild or intense; the trees are simply packed tightly, blocking sunlight.
Trees packed so tightly that sunlight barely gets through is not gentle or weak.
Graceful style would not keep sunlight from reaching the ground; packed trees would.
Modest describes people who don't brag, not trees packed tightly together.

traps.why: Spread far apart is the opposite of dense.
Dense forests may have tall trees, but dense means packed tightly.
Slightly crowded is too weak; dense means very tightly packed.

syn2.tip: Picture a dense crowd squeezed shoulder to shoulder. Dense means lots of things packed into a small space.

sc2.stem: Our backyard grass is thin and patchy, but the grass at the park is so _____ that you can't see any dirt between the blades.

traps.why: Bare grass would show lots of dirt.
Short grass can still have dirt showing between the blades.
Soft grass feels nice, but softness doesn't hide the dirt.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "thin and patchy." Grass with no dirt showing is thick and packed.

decoys.why: The contrast is thin versus thick grass, not small versus huge size.
You can't see dirt because the grass is thick, not because it is stylish.
Boring grass would not hide the dirt; the sentence contrasts thin grass with thick grass.
The park grass is thicker than the thin backyard grass, not weaker or gentler.
Exact grass makes no sense; the clue is that no dirt shows between blades.
Gentle is about being soft and kind, not about grass growing thick enough to hide dirt.

example: Beavers construct dams out of sticks.
hook: Construct holds the root struct, meaning build, just like structure and construction site.

traps.why: Destroy is the opposite of construct.
Instruct looks like construct, but it means teach.
Designing is planning; constructing is actually building.

syn1.tip: Look for struct, meaning build. You see it in construction site, where workers build things.

sc1.stem: For the science fair, our team will _____ a bridge out of popsicle sticks and glue that can hold a brick.

traps.why: You can't destroy a bridge so that it can hold a brick.
