Kim's daily care shows she would not fail to look after it, not hold it.

example: Apples were abundant in the orchard this fall.
hook: Picture an apple tree so abundant that its branches bend under hundreds of shiny apples.

traps.why: Scarce is the opposite of abundant.
Rare things are often valuable, but abundant is about how much there is.
Abandoned looks like abundant but means left behind.

syn1.tip: Think of an abundant harvest, with baskets overflowing with food. Abundant is about having lots of something.

sc1.stem: Last summer blueberries were scarce on the island, but this year they were _____, covering every bush by the thousands.

traps.why: Rare matches last summer, but the word but signals a change.
Abandoned looks like abundant but means left behind, which makes no sense here.
Price is not the point; the sentence is about how many there were.

sc1.tip: Look at "scarce ... but this year" and "by the thousands." The blank must mean the opposite of scarce: a huge amount.

decoys.why: The berries were covering every bush, so the bushes were full, not empty.
The sentence contrasts scarce with thousands of berries, so it is about amount, not breaking.
The clue is about how many berries there were, not whether they were boring.
Berries covering every bush by the thousands is about amount, not about not working.
Berries cannot be careful, and the sentence is about how many there were.
Berries do not want or not want things; the clue is thousands of them.

traps.why: Hard to find is the opposite of abundant.
Worth is about value, but abundant is about amount.
A little extra is too weak; abundant means a large amount.

syn2.tip: Abundant things are everywhere, like leaves in fall. Pick the choice that means a big amount.

sc2.stem: Because the rain had been so _____ this spring, the creek overflowed its banks and the garden grew taller than ever.

traps.why: Scarce rain would never make a creek overflow.
Chilly describes temperature, but an overflowing creek needs lots of rain.
Light rain is too little to flood a creek.

sc2.tip: This is cause and effect: the rain made the creek "overflowed its banks." Only a huge amount of rain could do that.

decoys.why: Rain that held back could not make the creek overflow and the garden grow taller.
An overflowing creek shows there was lots of rain, not rain that breaks easily.
The creek overflowed, which tells you about the amount of rain, not clearness.
Rain cannot have manners, and the clue is the overflowing creek.
The garden grew taller than ever, so the rain was plentiful, not gloomy.
An overflowing creek points to a large amount of rain, not boring rain.

example: The stubborn mule would not move an inch.
hook: Picture a stubborn mule planting its hooves and refusing to budge, no matter how hard you pull.

traps.why: Flexible people change their minds easily, the opposite of stubborn.
Stubby looks like stubborn but means short and thick.
Bossy people tell others what to do; stubborn people refuse to change.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "stubborn as a mule." A stubborn person will not change their mind.

sc1.stem: My little brother is a _____ eater who refuses to try anything green, no matter how much we beg.

traps.why: A willing eater would try green foods, but he refuses.
Hungry fits the word eater, but it says nothing about refusing.
Stubby looks like stubborn but means short and thick.

sc1.tip: The clue is "refuses to try anything green, no matter how much we beg." He will not change his mind.

decoys.why: He refuses no matter how much you beg, which is not about good manners.
A fierce eater would gobble everything, but he refuses to try anything green.
The sentence is about refusing to try food, not about being on time.
Refusing no matter how much we beg is about not changing his mind, not breaking.
Bright and clear does not describe someone who refuses to try new food.
The clue is that he refuses despite begging, which is about not giving in.

traps.why: Quick to agree is the opposite of stubborn.
Stubborn people may get upset, but stubborn means refusing to change.
Being slow to learn is different from refusing to change your mind.

syn2.tip: A stubborn kid digs in their heels. Look for the choice that means not giving in.

sc2.stem: Grandpa usually gives in when we ask for one more story, but tonight he was _____ and would not change his mind about bedtime.

traps.why: Flexible fits his usual habit, but the word but signals a change.
Bedtime suggests sleepy, but the clue is that he would not change his mind.
Generous matches how he usually gives in, not how he acted tonight.

sc2.tip: The contrast "usually gives in ... but tonight" tells you he did the opposite of giving in.

decoys.why: He would not change his mind, so he was firm and clear, not unclear.
The clue is that he would not change his mind, not his manners.
Being full of energy does not explain refusing to change his mind.
He held firm about bedtime, which is not the same as being easily broken.
The sentence is about refusing to give in, not about having nothing to do.
Sticking to bedtime is about not changing his mind, not about being silly.

example: She painted the sunset in vivid oranges and pinks.
hook: Vivid comes from a Latin word meaning alive, so vivid colors and memories feel strong enough to be alive.

traps.why: Dull is the opposite of vivid.
Livid looks like vivid but means furious.
Paintings can be vivid, but painted does not mean bright and clear.

syn1.tip: Think of vivid colors in a box of new markers. Vivid things are bright, clear, and strong.

sc1.stem: Even years later, Omar has a _____ memory of the reef, recalling every bright color of the coral and every fish.

traps.why: A faint memory is weak, but Omar recalls every color.
Nothing in the sentence is sad; it describes a bright, detailed memory.
Livid looks like vivid but means furious, which does not fit a memory.

sc1.tip: The clue is "recalling every bright color of the coral and every fish." A memory that detailed is bright and clear.

decoys.why: Omar recalls every color and every fish, so his memory is clear, not fuzzy.
A memory that lasts years with every detail is strong, not easily broken.
The memory is full of bright coral and fish, not something stern and gloomy.
A memory cannot have manners; the clue is that it is bright and detailed.
The sentence is about how clear the memory is, not whether something is possible.

traps.why: Faded and blurry is the opposite of vivid.
Very angry is livid, a word that only looks like vivid.
New things may look bright, but vivid means clear and strong, not new.

syn2.tip: A vivid dream feels so real you remember every detail. Pick the choice about clearness and strength.

sc2.stem: The old photo in the attic had faded to gray, but the new poster on my wall was _____, full of glowing reds and blues.

traps.why: Dull describes the faded photo, not the glowing poster.
Posters can tear, but the clue is about glowing colors.
Valid looks like vivid but means true or acceptable.

sc2.tip: The contrast "faded to gray, but" tells you the poster is the opposite of faded. "Glowing reds and blues" confirms it.

decoys.why: The clue is glowing colors, which means bright and strong, not unclear.
Glowing reds and blues sound cheerful and bright, not stern or gloomy.
The contrast with the faded photo is about color, not about breaking easily.
A poster full of glowing colors is bright, and honesty has nothing to do with it.
A poster cannot be careful; the clue is its glowing reds and blues.

example: The rigid cardboard would not fold.
hook: A rigid ruler snaps before it bends, while a rubber one wiggles; rigid things hold their shape.

traps.why: Flexible is the opposite of rigid.
Frigid looks like rigid but means very cold.
Rigid things may be heavy, but rigid means unable to bend.

syn1.tip: Think of a rigid board that will not bend at all. Rigid means stiff.

sc1.stem: Unlike the bendy straw, the metal rod was completely _____ and would not bend no matter how hard Ali pushed.

traps.why: Flexible describes the bendy straw, not the rod that would not bend.
Metal can be shiny, but the clue is about bending.
Frigid looks like rigid but means very cold.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the bendy straw" sets up a contrast, and "would not bend" tells you exactly what the rod was like.

decoys.why: The rod would not bend however hard Ali pushed, so it was strong, not easily broken.
The clue is that the rod would not bend, not whether it was empty.
Not bending when pushed is about stiffness, not about not being used.
The sentence compares bending, not color, so bright does not fit.
A metal rod that would not bend is stiff, not full of energy.
A rod cannot have manners; the clue is that it would not bend.

traps.why: Easy to fold is the opposite of rigid.
Very cold means frigid, a word that just looks like rigid.
Slightly firm is too weak; rigid things do not bend at all.

syn2.tip: Rigid cardboard will not fold. Look for the choice that means it cannot bend.

sc2.stem: The glue dried overnight, so the paper mask became _____ and kept its shape even when we dropped it on the floor.

traps.why: A floppy mask would lose its shape, not keep it.
Glue is sticky, but dried glue made the mask hold its shape.
Fragile things break easily, but this mask survived being dropped.

sc2.tip: This is cause and effect: the glue "dried," so the mask "kept its shape." That means it became stiff.

decoys.why: The mask kept its shape even when dropped, so it did not break easily.
Drying glue and keeping its shape is about stiffness, not bright colors.
The clue is that the mask kept its shape, not that it looked bright.
Keeping its shape when dropped is about being stiff, not about being empty.
There was only one mask, and the clue is that it kept its shape.
A mask cannot have manners; the dried glue made it stiff.

example: A cave was the bear's dwelling.
hook: A dwelling is where you dwell, or live, whether it is a castle, a tent, or an igloo.

traps.why: Furniture goes inside a home, but it is not the home itself.
A visitor comes to a dwelling; a dwelling is the place.
Swelling rhymes with dwelling but means a puffy bump.

syn1.tip: Dwelling comes from dwell, which means to live somewhere. Your dwelling is where you live.

sc1.stem: The igloo, built from blocks of snow, was a cozy _____ where the family lived during the long winter.

traps.why: Blankets are cozy, but a family cannot live inside a blanket.
Sleds go with snow, but the igloo is where the family lived.
Swelling sounds like dwelling but means a puffy bump.

sc1.tip: The sentence tells you the answer: "where the family lived." A place where people live is a dwelling.

decoys.why: The igloo was cozy and the family lived there, so it was safe, not a danger.
The family lived in the igloo, so it is a home, not a meal.
The sentence says the family lived there, which makes it a home, not a cure.
The igloo was real and built from snow blocks, not an old story.
The family actually lived in the igloo, so it was a home, not a copy.
The clue is where the family lived, which points to a home, not a win.

traps.why: Work happens at an office or shop, not necessarily where you live.
Dwelling on something means worrying, but a dwelling is a place to live.
A store is a place to shop, not a place to live.

syn2.tip: People dwell in houses, apartments, and tents. Find the choice that means where someone lives.

sc2.stem: The fox spent its days roaming the wide meadow, but at night it slept in its _____, a snug hole dug under the old oak.

traps.why: The fox roamed the meadow by day; but points to a different place.
A path is for traveling, not a snug hole to sleep in.
Swelling sounds like dwelling but means a puffy bump.

sc2.tip: "But at night it slept" contrasts with roaming, and "a snug hole dug under the old oak" describes the fox's home.

decoys.why: The fox slept in a snug hole under the oak, which is a place, not tiredness.
The hole is where the fox sleeps snugly, not something blocking its way.
A snug hole where the fox sleeps is safe, not a danger.
The blank is explained as a snug hole, a place to live, not a feeling.
The hole is the fox's real home, not an exact copy of something.
A snug hole dug under the oak is a home, not a small broken piece.

example: Finishing the puzzle tonight is not feasible.
hook: Feasible comes from a French word meaning to do, so a feasible plan is one you can actually do.

traps.why: Impossible is the opposite of feasible.
A feasible plan can be done, but it may still be hard.
Visible ends like feasible but means able to be seen.

syn1.tip: Feasible ends in -ible, meaning able to be. A feasible plan is able to be done.

sc1.stem: With only one hour left, building a whole treehouse was not _____, so we decided to just paint the sign instead.

traps.why: Not impossible would mean they could build it, so why stop?
Visible looks like feasible but means able to be seen.
A treehouse would be useful; the problem is the short time.

sc1.tip: "With only one hour left" is the cause, and "so we decided to just paint the sign" is the effect. The big job could not be done.

decoys.why: The sentence is about whether building was possible, not whether something was more than enough.
If building were not foolish, there would be no reason to switch to painting the sign.
The problem is too little time to finish, not that the plan was unclear.
Building a treehouse being full of energy has nothing to do with running out of time.
The sentence is about time running out, not about the treehouse being strange.
Stiffness has nothing to do with having only one hour left.

traps.why: Too hard to do is the opposite of feasible.
Able to be seen means visible, which only looks like feasible.
A feasible plan could be done; it has not been done yet.

syn2.tip: The ending -ible means able to be. Ask yourself: able to be what? Feasible plans can be done.

sc2.stem: Swimming across the whole lake seemed scary at first, but with a life jacket and a coach rowing beside her, the plan was _____ for Nora.

traps.why: Impossible matches the scary start, but the word but signals a change.
The life jacket and coach make the swim safer, not dangerous.
Foolish gives the plan a bad feeling, but the help makes it sensible.

sc2.tip: "Seemed scary at first, but" signals a turn. With a "life jacket and a coach," the swim becomes something she can do.

decoys.why: The life jacket and coach make the swim safer, so the plan is not silly.
The lake is big, but the sentence asks whether the plan could be done.
The word but shows the scary feeling went away, so a stern, gloomy word fails.
A plan cannot be easily broken; the sentence is about whether Nora can do it.
A plan cannot be unwilling, and the sentence shows the help made the swim possible.
The sentence is about safety making the swim possible, not about bright colors.

example: We strive to do our best every day.
hook: Strive rhymes with drive: when you strive, you drive yourself to try your very hardest.

traps.why: Quit is the opposite of strive.
Thrive looks like strive but means to grow strong and do well.
Hoping wishes for something; striving works hard for it.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "strive to do your best." Striving means putting in effort.

sc1.stem: Our team will _____ to win the championship, practicing harder than ever and never giving up.

traps.why: A team practicing harder than ever is not refusing to win.
Pretending is not real effort, and this team is practicing for real.
Hesitating means holding back, but they are never giving up.

sc1.tip: The clue is "practicing harder than ever and never giving up." That describes trying very hard.

decoys.why: A team practicing harder than ever is not pausing; it is trying hard.
Practicing harder and never giving up is the opposite of failing to try.
The team is never giving up, so it would not stop.
The sentence shows eager effort, not fear of winning.

traps.why: Giving up is the opposite of striving.
Try a little is too weak; striving means trying very hard.
Grow and do well means thrive, which only looks like strive.

syn2.tip: Strive sounds like drive. When you strive, you push yourself with lots of effort.

sc2.stem: Instead of quitting when her kite kept crashing, Priya continued to _____ to fly it, fixing the tail and trying again until it soared.

traps.why: She kept fixing and trying, so she did not refuse.
Her kite really soared, so her effort was real, not pretend.
Forgetting does not fit someone fixing the tail and trying again.

sc2.tip: "Instead of quitting" sets up a contrast. The blank must mean the opposite of quitting: working hard to succeed.

decoys.why: The sentence says instead of quitting, so Priya did not stop.
Priya kept fixing the kite and trying again, which shows effort, not pausing.
Priya worked on her kite until it soared, so she did not fail to try.
The sentence shows Priya working hard, not fearing the kite.

example: A fallen tree was an obstacle on the trail.
hook: On an obstacle course, every wall, tire, and rope net is something standing in your way.

traps.why: A pathway helps you through; an obstacle blocks you.
Obstacles show up on journeys, but a journey is the trip itself.
Some obstacles are dangerous, but an obstacle is anything that blocks you.

syn1.tip: Think of an obstacle course at field day. Each obstacle is something in your way.

sc1.stem: A huge boulder in the middle of the road was an _____ that kept the truck from moving forward.

traps.why: An engine helps a truck move; the boulder stopped it.
An opening lets you through, but the boulder kept the truck back.
An invitation welcomes you in; the boulder kept the truck out.

sc1.tip: The clue is "kept the truck from moving forward." Something that blocks your way is the answer.

decoys.why: A helper would not keep the truck from moving; the boulder is in the way.
A boulder is not a natural feeling; it is something blocking the road.
A boulder is not a wish or desire; it physically blocks the truck.

traps.why: A clear path is the opposite of an obstacle.
A race course may have obstacles, but it is not one.
A big rock can be an obstacle, but obstacles can be many things.

syn2.tip: An obstacle stops you from getting where you want to go. Pick the choice about blocking.

sc2.stem: Being shy was a big _____ for Mia at first, but she overcame it and made three new friends by the end of camp.

traps.why: You do not need to overcome something that helps you.
A hobby is something you enjoy, not something you overcome.
A reward is a good thing, but shyness was a problem for Mia.

sc2.tip: The words "but she overcame it" tell you shyness was something in her way that she had to get past.

decoys.why: Mia had to overcome her shyness, so it was a problem, not a success.
Mia overcame her shyness, so it was blocking her, not helping her.
Shyness was the problem Mia overcame, not the cure for anything.
Being shy was something real Mia had to overcome, not an old story.
Nobody argued in the sentence; shyness was something standing in Mia's way.

example: There was ample food for every guest.
hook: You hear ample in phrases like ample time and ample room, meaning plenty with some left over.

traps.why: Scarce is the opposite of ample.
Simple rhymes with ample but means easy or plain.
Ample food is about amount, not flavor.

syn1.tip: Think of "ample parking" at a big store, with lots of empty spaces. Ample means plenty.

sc1.stem: We had _____ time, more than enough, so we stopped for ice cream on the way to the game.

traps.why: With little time, you would not stop for ice cream.
Simple rhymes with ample but means easy, which does not describe time.
Losing time would leave less, not more than enough.

sc1.tip: The sentence defines the blank right after it: "more than enough." Having extra time is why they could stop.

decoys.why: The sentence explains it means more than enough, not quick or on time.
The sentence says more than enough time, not a stiff schedule.
The clue more than enough is about amount, not about being unclear.
The sentence defines the blank as more than enough, not possible to do.
Nothing strange about the time is mentioned; the clue is more than enough.

traps.why: Not quite enough is the opposite of ample.
Just barely enough is too little; ample means extra.
Ample food is about how much, not how good it tastes.

syn2.tip: If you have ample snacks, you can share and still have some left. Look for the choice that means extra.

sc2.stem: The tiny tent was cramped for two campers, but the new one had _____ room for all four of us plus our backpacks and sleeping bags.

traps.why: Little room matches the tiny tent, but the word but signals a change.
Tents can get muddy, but the clue is about how much space there is.
Simple rhymes with ample but means plain or easy, not roomy.

sc2.tip: "Cramped ... but the new one" signals a contrast. Fitting four campers "plus our backpacks" means plenty of space.

decoys.why: Tents can get wet, but the sentence is about fitting four campers and gear.
The sentence compares cramped and roomy tents, not breakable ones.
The contrast with cramped shows the new tent had plenty of space, not stiffness.
The sentence is about how much space there was, not about being unclear.
Room cannot be full of energy; the sentence is about enough space for everyone.

example: The machines sat idle over the holiday.
hook: Idle sounds like idol, but an idle car just sits with its engine running, going nowhere.

traps.why: Busy is the opposite of idle.
Ideal looks like idle but means perfect.
Broken machines cannot work; idle ones simply are not working right now.

syn1.tip: Think of a car idling at a red light: running but not going anywhere. Idle means not doing anything.

sc1.stem: All winter the tractors sat _____ in the barn, with no fields to plow and no work to do.

traps.why: The tractors had no work, so they could not be busy.
Ideal looks like idle but means perfect, which makes no sense here.
Running tractors are noisy, but these had no work to do.

sc1.tip: The clue is "with no fields to plow and no work to do." The tractors were not working.

decoys.why: The tractors had no work to do, so they were not full of energy.
Tractors with no work to do all winter were not quick or busy.
Tractors do not have feelings; they sat unused because there was no work.
The tractors were not refusing anything; there were simply no fields to plow.
The sentence is about having no work, not about bright colors.

traps.why: Hard at work is the opposite of idle.
Perfect means ideal, a word that only looks like idle.
An idle machine still works; it just is not being used.

syn2.tip: Idle hands are hands with nothing to do. Pick the choice that means not being used.

sc2.stem: During the school year our playground is packed with kids, but in July the swings hang _____, swaying gently with no one riding them.

traps.why: Crowded matches the school year, but the word but signals a change.
Ideal looks like idle but means perfect, which does not fit.
A packed playground is loud, but July swings have no one riding them.

sc2.tip: "Packed with kids, but in July" sets up a contrast, and "with no one riding them" tells you the swings are not being used.

decoys.why: No one is riding the swings in July, so they are not full of energy.
The empty July swings are the opposite of bright and full of life.
The swings are swaying gently, so they are not stiff.
The crowds are gone in July, and the clue says no one is riding.
The swings sway gently and quietly; nothing suggests they are stern or unsmiling.

meaning: to look steadily for a long time
example: We gazed at the stars all night.
hook: When you gaze at the night sky, your eyes stay fixed on the stars as if glued there.

traps.why: A glance is a quick look, the opposite of a long, steady gaze.
Graze looks like gaze but means to eat grass, like cows do.
Squinting uses your eyes too, but it means narrowing them, not looking long.

syn1.tip: Think of gazing at the stars or out a window: your eyes stay on one thing for a long time.

sc1.stem: Lying on the warm grass, we would _____ up at the drifting clouds for hours without looking away.

traps.why: A glance is quick, but the sentence says for hours without looking away.
Graze looks like gaze but means to eat grass.
You might wave at the sky, but the clue is about looking, not waving.

sc1.tip: The words "for hours without looking away" tell you the missing word means looking steadily for a long time.

decoys.why: The sentence says you looked for hours without looking away, and glance means a quick look.

traps.why: A quick peek is the opposite of a long, steady look.
Eating grass is what graze means, a word that only looks like gaze.
Listening closely is paying attention with your ears, not your eyes.

syn2.tip: Gaze is about your eyes and time. Picture someone gazing dreamily out a window for a long while.

sc2.stem: My little brother usually glances at a picture for a second, but at the aquarium he would _____ at the sharks for twenty minutes, barely moving.

traps.why: A peek is quick, but the sentence says twenty minutes.
A gasp is a quick breath of surprise, not twenty minutes of looking.
Nodding moves your head; the clue is about watching for a long time.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast with "glances for a second." The answer must mean looking for a long time, like "twenty minutes."

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts his usual quick glances with twenty minutes of looking, so glance is backwards.

example: I could not comprehend the hard question.
hook: If you truly comprehend a story, you could explain it to a friend in your own words.

traps.why: To misunderstand is to get the meaning wrong, the opposite of comprehend.
Compare starts like comprehend but means to see how things are alike.
Memorizing stores words in your head; you can memorize without understanding.

syn1.tip: Reading comprehension questions ask whether you understood the passage. That is the same comprehend.

sc1.stem: The instructions were written in Japanese, so I could not _____ a single word of them.

traps.why: You can't misunderstand words you can't read at all; the sentence says you didn't understand.
Complete looks a bit like comprehend but means to finish.
Ignoring is choosing not to pay attention, not being unable to understand.

sc1.tip: Look at "written in Japanese, so." If you don't know Japanese, you cannot understand the words.

decoys.why: Seize means to grab, and you cannot physically grab words printed in instructions.
The problem is reading Japanese, not building words, so construct does not fit.
The sentence is about not understanding a foreign language, not about failing to take care of something.
The clue is that the words were in Japanese, which explains not understanding them, not not loving them.
Nothing in the instructions was hard to put up with; you just could not read them.
Forbid means to not allow, which makes no sense for reading words in another language.

traps.why: Missing the point means not understanding, the opposite of comprehend.
Learning by heart is memorizing, which is not the same as understanding.
Comprehend comes from an old word for grab, but now it means grab an idea.

syn2.tip: Think of "reading comprehension" at school. It checks whether you understood what you read.

sc2.stem: Even though my older sister explained the board game rules three times, my grandpa still could not _____ how the pieces were supposed to move.

traps.why: Compare starts like comprehend but means to see how things are alike.
Ignoring means not paying attention, but Grandpa was listening and still confused.
Saying he could not misunderstand would mean he understood perfectly.

sc2.tip: "Even though" and "still" show a surprise: three explanations, yet Grandpa didn't get it. The word means understand.

decoys.why: The rules were explained three times, which shows Grandpa could not understand them, not admire them.

example: The coach looked grim after the loss.
hook: Picture a referee with a grim face: no smile, tight lips, eyes serious as he holds up a red card.

traps.why: Cheerful means happy and smiling, the opposite of grim.
Grimy looks like grim but means covered in dirt.
Furious is wild anger; grim is just serious and unsmiling.

syn1.tip: Grim has a hard, short sound, like a tight-lipped face. Think of "a grim look" when bad news comes.

sc1.stem: The coach's face was _____, serious and unsmiling, as she announced that practice would run an extra hour.

traps.why: Joyful is happy, but the sentence says serious and unsmiling.
Grimy looks like grim but means dirty.
A puzzled face looks confused, not serious and stern.

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank, "serious and unsmiling," tell you exactly what the missing word means.

decoys.why: The sentence says her face was serious and unsmiling, and lively means full of energy.
A serious, unsmiling face is not bright and full of life.
The sentence describes her face as serious and unsmiling, not strange or unusual.
Vivid describes bright, strong colors or images, not a serious, unsmiling expression.
The clue is serious and unsmiling, which says nothing about her face being wet.

traps.why: Bright and happy is the opposite of a grim, unsmiling face.
Dirty and greasy describes grimy, a word that only looks like grim.
A grim person is quiet and serious, not noisy or rude.

syn2.tip: Imagine a coach after a big loss, saying nothing and not smiling. That face is grim.

sc2.stem: After the team lost the championship by one point, the players walked off the field with _____ faces, and nobody said a word on the long bus ride.

traps.why: Beaming faces are smiling, but the team had just lost.
Grand starts like grim but means large and impressive.
Hopeful is a bright feeling, but losing and silence show a dark mood.

sc2.tip: Losing "by one point" causes the mood, and "nobody said a word" shows it. The faces were serious and unsmiling.

decoys.why: The team just lost and nobody spoke, so their faces were not full of energy.
Players who lost and rode home in silence would not have bright, lively faces.
The sentence is about how the players felt after losing, not the size of their faces.
Vivid means bright and strong, which does not match a silent, defeated team.

example: The soup had a peculiar purple color.
hook: A peculiar sock is the one with polka dots and stripes that never matches anything in your drawer.

traps.why: Ordinary means normal, the opposite of peculiar.
Particular looks similar but means specific or picky.
Strange things aren't always ugly; peculiar just means unusual.

syn1.tip: People say "What a peculiar noise" when they hear something they can't explain. It means strange.

sc1.stem: The soup had a _____ taste, sweet like candy one moment and sour like lemons the next, that no one could describe.

traps.why: A familiar taste would be easy to describe, but no one could.
The taste switched from sweet to sour, so sweet alone doesn't fit.
Popular looks a bit like peculiar but means liked by many.

sc1.tip: A taste that flips from candy to lemon and "that no one could describe" must be strange.

decoys.why: The taste jumped from sweet to sour and could not be described, which makes it strange, not stern.
Sincere means honest, and a taste cannot be honest or dishonest.
Rigid means stiff, which describes objects, not a taste that changes from sweet to sour.
The sentence is about how odd the taste was, not how big it was.
Weary means very tired, and a taste cannot be tired.
Prompt means right on time, which has nothing to do with a strange mix of flavors.

traps.why: Normal is the opposite of peculiar.
Scary goes too far; peculiar things are odd, not frightening.
Hidden things are hard to find, but peculiar things are unusual.

syn2.tip: Think of "a peculiar smell" in the fridge. You don't know what it is; it is strange.

sc2.stem: Most cats run from water, so it seemed _____ when our cat Pepper jumped into the bathtub and splashed around happily.

traps.why: Most cats run from water, so a splashing cat is not expected.
Popular looks a bit like peculiar but means liked by many people.
Gentle describes how Pepper acted, not how unusual it seemed.

sc2.tip: "Most cats run from water" tells you Pepper did something unusual. The blank means strange.

decoys.why: The bathtub is wet, but the sentence says the cat's behavior seemed unusual compared to most cats.
Pepper jumped in and splashed happily, which is the opposite of careful behavior.
Pepper jumped in happily, so nothing about the moment seemed unwilling.
The clue says most cats run from water, so the point is that it was unusual, not possible.
Pepper splashed around happily, so the moment was strange, not serious and stern.

example: The market was full of vibrant colors.
hook: A vibrant room seems to hum with color and energy, as if it were vibrating with life.

traps.why: Dull means flat and boring, the opposite of vibrant.
Violent starts like vibrant but means rough and harmful.
Lively places can be noisy, but vibrant is about energy and color.

syn1.tip: People talk about vibrant colors and vibrant cities. Both are bright and bursting with energy.

sc1.stem: The coral reef was _____, bursting with bright colors and full of darting fish and waving sea plants.

traps.why: Lifeless is the opposite of a reef full of fish and plants.
Violent starts like vibrant but means rough and harmful.
Reefs are near sand, but the clue is about bright colors and life.

sc1.tip: After the blank come "bursting with bright colors" and "full of darting fish." The word means bright and full of life.

decoys.why: The reef was bursting with bright colors, and dim means not bright.
The reef was full of fish and plants, so it was not empty.
The sentence says the reef was full of life, the opposite of hard to find.
Bright colors and darting fish give a cheerful feeling, not a serious, stern one.
A reef full of darting fish is lively, not very tired.

traps.why: Dull and faded is the opposite of bright and lively.
Vibrant shares a root with vibrate, but it means full of life.
Lively things can be loud, but vibrant means bright and energetic.

syn2.tip: Picture a vibrant garden in summer: bright flowers, buzzing bees, everything alive.

sc2.stem: In winter the garden looked gray and bare, but by June it was _____ again, with red roses, yellow sunflowers, and bees buzzing everywhere.

traps.why: Gloomy fits the winter garden, but "but by June" signals a change.
Frozen fits winter, but the sentence is describing the garden in June.
Vacant ends like vibrant but means empty.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts "gray and bare" with June's roses, sunflowers, and bees. The answer means bright and full of life.

decoys.why: By June the garden had red roses and yellow sunflowers, so it was bright, not dim.
The June garden was full of flowers and bees, so it was not empty.
Gray and bare describes winter; June brought color and buzzing bees, which is cheerful, not grim.
Flowers and bees were everywhere in June, the opposite of in short supply.
Bees buzzing everywhere shows a busy garden, not one that is idle.

example: The train will depart at noon.
hook: At the airport, the big board labeled Departures lists the flights about to depart, or leave.

traps.why: Arrive means to come in, the opposite of depart.
Depart has "part" in it, but it means leave, not split into pieces.
Depend starts like depart but means to rely on.

syn1.tip: Think of arrivals and departures at an airport. Departing flights are the ones leaving.

sc1.stem: The ferry will _____ from the dock at exactly three o'clock, so be on time or it will leave without you.

traps.why: Arrive is the opposite, and the sentence says it will leave without you.
Boats drift, but a ferry leaving at an exact time is not drifting.
Depart has "part" in it, but it doesn't mean split into pieces.

sc1.tip: The end of the sentence says "it will leave without you." That restates the blank: the ferry will leave.

decoys.why: The ferry will leave without you, so the blank means leave, not look steadily.
A ferry cannot look quickly; the sentence warns it will leave without you.

traps.why: Coming back is the opposite of departing.
Depart contains "part," but it means leave, not break into pieces.
Travelers wait before trips, but depart means the moment you leave.

syn2.tip: A train that departs at noon pulls away from the station at noon. Departure is the leaving.

sc2.stem: We were going to _____ early in the morning, so we said goodbye to our hosts the night before and packed our bags.

traps.why: Staying is the opposite, and saying goodbye shows they were leaving.
Decide starts like depart but means to make a choice.
Unpacking happens when you arrive, but they packed bags to leave.

sc2.tip: Saying "goodbye" and packing "our bags" are the effects. People do those things because they are about to leave.

decoys.why: You packed and said goodbye to go early, not to pause before acting.
Saying goodbye to hosts and packing bags points to leaving, not coming into view.
Packing bags and saying goodbye show you were leaving, not trying very hard.
Goodbyes and packed bags mean you were leaving, not looking at something for a long time.
Nothing in the sentence is about begging; goodbyes and packed bags mean leaving.

example: Penguins reside in cold southern regions.
hook: Your residence is the place where you reside: your home, the address on your mail.

traps.why: To roam is to wander with no fixed home, the opposite of reside.
Resist starts like reside but means to fight against.
You visit a place for a short time; you reside where you live.

syn1.tip: Reside is the verb inside residence and resident. A resident of a town is someone who lives there.

sc1.stem: Most of my cousins _____ in Texas, where their families have lived in the same town for years.

traps.why: A vacation is short, but their families have lived there for years.
Resist starts like reside but means to fight against.
Wandering means moving around, but they stayed in the same town for years.

sc1.tip: The clue "have lived in the same town for years" restates the blank. It means to live in a place.

decoys.why: The clue says their families have lived there for years, which is about living, not trying hard.
The sentence is about where the cousins have lived for years, not bragging.
Families living in the same town for years means living there, not pausing.
The clue about living in the same town for years points to living, not begging.

traps.why: Moving far away is leaving a home, not living in it.
Reside comes from an old word for sit, but it means live somewhere.
A vacation is a short stay, not where you live.

syn2.tip: Think of the word resident, as in "residents of this building." Residents reside there, which means they live there.

sc2.stem: Some birds only pass through our town each spring, but the cardinals _____ here all year, building nests in our backyard tree.

traps.why: Migrating birds travel away, but these cardinals stay all year.
Visitors stay briefly, but the cardinals are here all year building nests.
Decide looks a bit like reside but means to make a choice.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts birds that "only pass through" with cardinals here "all year, building nests." They live here.

decoys.why: Cardinals staying all year and building nests are living there, not just pausing briefly.
Birds building nests all year are living here, not bragging about themselves.
The contrast with birds passing through shows cardinals live here, not stare here.
Building nests all year means the cardinals live here, not that they beg.
The sentence contrasts passing through with staying all year, so the blank means live.

example: We built a replica of the Eiffel Tower.
hook: A toy race car built to look exactly like a real one, down to the stickers, is a replica.

traps.why: The original is the real thing, the opposite of a copy.
Reply starts like replica but means an answer.
A fake tries to fool you; a replica is an honest copy.

syn1.tip: Replica sounds a bit like repeat. A replica repeats the look of the real thing.

sc1.stem: The model in the museum is a _____ of the Liberty Bell, an exact copy right down to the crack.

traps.why: A relic is a real old object, but this is an exact copy.
Reply starts like replica but means an answer.
A sketch is a rough drawing, not an exact copy right down to the crack.

sc1.tip: The phrase "an exact copy right down to the crack" restates the blank. The word means an exact copy.

decoys.why: The sentence calls the model an exact copy, not a small broken piece.
A museum model that matches the bell exactly is a copy, not an old story.
The clue says exact copy, and a place where someone lives is not a copy.
The sentence says the model is an exact copy, not a great win.
Nothing suggests danger; the sentence explains the model is an exact copy.
A model that matches the bell down to the crack is a copy, not a cure.

traps.why: The real thing is the original, not a copy of it.
A rough sketch is only loosely like something; a replica matches exactly.
Replay looks like replica but means showing a moment of a game again.

syn2.tip: Museums and gift shops sell replicas of famous objects. They look just like the real ones.

sc2.stem: The real dinosaur bones were too fragile to move, so the museum displayed a plastic _____ that looked just like the skeleton instead.

traps.why: The original is the real bones, which were too fragile to move.
Fossils are the real bones, but this one is plastic.
Replay looks like replica but means showing something again.

sc2.tip: The real bones couldn't move, "so" the museum used something "plastic" that "looked just like" them. That is a copy.

decoys.why: The plastic piece looked just like the whole skeleton, so it is a copy, not a broken piece.
The museum showed a plastic object that looked like the skeleton, not an old story.
Something plastic that looks just like the skeleton is a copy, not a home.
The plastic object replaced fragile bones by looking just like them, so it is a copy.
The museum needed something that looked like the skeleton, not a cure.

example: My parents forbid phones at dinner.
hook: In Harry Potter, students are told never to enter the Forbidden Forest: going there is not allowed.

traps.why: Allow means to let something happen, the opposite of forbid.
Forgive starts like forbid but means to stop being angry at someone.
Forbid ends in "bid," but it has nothing to do with offering.

syn1.tip: Think of a sign that says "Forbidden." That means no one is allowed. Forbid means to not allow.

traps.why: Giving permission is the opposite of forbidding.
Advising is too weak; forbidding is a firm no.
Forbid contains "bid," but it doesn't mean offering a price.

syn2.tip: "Forbidden fruit" is something you are not allowed to have. Forbid means saying a firm no.

sc2.stem: The pool has a sign that says no running, because the lifeguards _____ racing on the wet, slippery tiles near the deep end.

traps.why: Permit means allow, but the sign says no running.
Forgive starts like forbid but means to stop being angry.
Cheering is approving, but the sign and slippery tiles show disapproval.

sc2.tip: The sign says "no running" and the tiles are "slippery." That is the cause; the lifeguards do not allow racing.

decoys.why: The sign says no running, so lifeguards do not allow racing; they do not admire it.
A no running sign means lifeguards do not allow racing, not that they love it.
The sign shows lifeguards actively stop racing, not that they fail to take care of it.
The no running sign means lifeguards stop racing, not copy it.
The sign says no running, so the blank means not allow, not understand.

meaning: to fear something that will happen
example: I dread going to the dentist.
hook: That heavy, sinking feeling in your stomach the night before a shot at the doctor is dread.

traps.why: To welcome something is to be glad it's coming, the opposite of dread.
Tread looks like dread but means to step or walk.
Dislike is too weak; dread is real fear of what is coming.

syn1.tip: Dread is inside dreadful, which means terrible. When you dread something, you are scared it will happen.

sc1.stem: Every Sunday night I _____ Monday's math quiz, worrying about it before it has even begun.

traps.why: Celebrating is happy, but the sentence says worrying.
If you forgot the quiz, you wouldn't be worrying about it.
Dream looks like dread but means to imagine while sleeping or wishing.

sc1.tip: The clue is "worrying about it before it has even begun." Worrying about something coming means you fear it.

decoys.why: You are worrying about the quiz, so you fear it rather than love it.
On Sunday night the quiz has not begun, so you cannot put up with it yet.
The sentence says you are worrying about the quiz, not ignoring it.
The clue is worrying before it begins, which means fearing, not understanding.
The sentence is about worrying ahead of time, not hiding the quiz.
You cannot refuse to allow a quiz; the clue says you are worrying about it.

traps.why: Looking forward to something is happy waiting, the opposite of dread.
Anger is a strong feeling too, but dread is fear, not anger.
Boredom is not caring; dread is worrying about what's coming.

syn2.tip: People say "I dread Mondays." They mean they feel afraid and worried as it gets closer.

sc2.stem: My sister loves thunderstorms and watches them from the window, but our dog Max seems to _____ them, hiding under the bed at the first rumble.

traps.why: Adore fits the sister, but "but" shows Max feels the opposite.
A dog ignoring storms wouldn't hide under the bed.
Tread looks like dread but means to step or walk.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the sister who "loves" storms with Max "hiding under the bed." Max is afraid of them.

decoys.why: The sister loves storms, but the word but shows Max feels the opposite and hides.
Max hiding under the bed shows fear, not copying the thunderstorms.
Hiding at the first rumble shows Max fears storms, not that he understands them.
A dog hiding under the bed is scared of storms, not eating them.
Max hides from the storms, so he fears them rather than grabbing them.

example: A gigantic pumpkin won first prize at the fair.
hook: Gigantic has the word giant right inside it, so picture something only a giant could own.

traps.why: Tiny is the opposite of gigantic.
Big things are often heavy, but gigantic is about size, not weight.
Tall is only about height; gigantic means big in every way.

syn1.tip: Look inside the word: gigantic contains giant. Anything giant sized is huge.

sc1.stem: The sunflower was so _____, like something a giant would grow, that it stood taller than the garage roof.

traps.why: A tiny sunflower could never stand taller than the garage roof.
Sunflowers can wilt, but a wilted flower would droop, not tower.
Sunflowers are bright, but brightness doesn't make one taller than a roof.

sc1.tip: Look at "like something a giant would grow" and "taller than the garage roof." Both point to extremely big.

decoys.why: Standing taller than the garage roof is about size, not being bright and full of life.
The clues about a giant and a garage roof point to size, not bright color.
Taller than the garage roof describes size, not a happy, bright look.
Soil can be fertile, but the sentence describes the sunflower's huge size.
The giant and garage roof clues tell you the sunflower is huge, not just strange.

traps.why: Miniature means very small, the opposite of gigantic.
Giants are strong in stories, but gigantic means big, not powerful.
Giants can be scary, but gigantic says nothing about being frightening.

syn2.tip: Think of the giant hiding inside gigantic. You want the choice that means extremely big.

sc2.stem: Our kitten was tiny when we got her, but she has grown into a _____ cat who can no longer squeeze through the pet door.

traps.why: Little is what she used to be; the word but signals a change.
Kittens are playful, but being playful wouldn't stop her fitting through the door.
Cats can be lazy, but laziness doesn't explain being too big for the door.

sc2.tip: The word "but" shows a contrast with "tiny," and "can no longer squeeze through" shows she is now very big.

decoys.why: The cat can no longer squeeze through the door, so the clue is about size, not liveliness.
Being stubborn is about attitude, but the cat can't fit through the door because of size.
A happy mood wouldn't stop a cat from fitting through the pet door.
A tired cat could still squeeze through; the sentence contrasts tiny with big.
The sentence contrasts tiny with something bigger, not something strange.

example: The kids pleaded for one more story.
hook: Picture a puppy at the dinner table, eyes wide, pleading for one scrap of your sandwich.

traps.why: To refuse is to say no, the opposite of begging for something.
Pledge looks like plead, but it means to promise.
Demanding is bossy; pleading is asking humbly and hopefully.

syn1.tip: Think of a kid saying "please, please, please." That is pleading, and it means the same as begging.

sc1.stem: Every night at bedtime, the twins _____ for just one more chapter, saying "Please, please, please!"

traps.why: Kids wait at bedtime, but waiting doesn't involve saying "please, please."
Voting is choosing, but the twins are begging with their words.
You search for something lost, not for a chapter someone reads to you.

sc1.tip: The twins keep saying "Please, please, please!" Saying please over and over is begging.

decoys.why: Saying please again and again is begging, not pausing before acting.
The twins are begging with words, not working hard to reach a goal.
The twins want to stay for one more chapter, not leave.

traps.why: Refusing firmly is saying no, the opposite of pleading.
Pleading is asking very hard, not asking in a relaxed way.
Complaining is grumbling about something, not begging for it.

syn2.tip: Plead sounds a lot like please. When you plead, you ask for something again and again because you want it badly.

sc2.stem: Instead of yelling about a later bedtime, Maya decided to _____ with her parents, softly asking again and again for just ten more minutes.

traps.why: Fighting is angry, but Maya is asking softly instead of yelling.
Agreeing means accepting the rule, but Maya keeps asking for more time.
Visiting is spending time with someone, not asking them for something.

sc2.tip: The phrase "softly asking again and again" tells you what she did, and "instead of yelling" rules out anything angry.

decoys.why: Maya is asking for ten more minutes, not living somewhere with her parents.
Maya stays and keeps asking softly, so she isn't leaving.

example: My socks were still damp from the rain.
hook: Damp is the in-between feeling: not dry, not dripping, like socks still drying after a rainy walk home.

traps.why: Dry means no water at all, the opposite of damp.
Soaked is far too wet; damp is only a little wet.
Damp places can feel chilly, but damp is about wetness, not cold.

syn1.tip: Think of a towel that is almost dry but not quite. That slightly wet feeling is damp, or moist.

sc1.stem: The beach towel wasn't soaking wet, just a little _____ from drying off after the morning swim.

traps.why: A towel just used to dry off after swimming wouldn't be dry.
Drenched means soaking wet, which the sentence says it wasn't.
Beach towels fade in the sun, but drying off doesn't fade them.

sc1.tip: The clue is "wasn't soaking wet, just a little." You need a word for a small amount of wet.

decoys.why: A towel can't be tired; the clue compares it to soaking wet.
The sentence is about how wet the towel is, not how bright it is.
The clue says not soaking wet, so the blank describes wetness, not strangeness.
Bright colors have nothing to do with drying off; the clue is about wetness.

traps.why: Completely dry is the opposite of damp.
Dripping wet is much too strong; damp is just a little wet.
Damp things can feel cold, but damp describes water, not temperature.

syn2.tip: Damp sits between dry and soaked. Pick the choice that means a little bit wet.

sc2.stem: The morning dew had left the grass a bit _____, so our socks felt slightly wet by the time we crossed the field to school.

traps.why: Dry grass wouldn't make your socks feel wet.
Flooded grass would soak you, not leave socks slightly wet.
Grass color has nothing to do with getting socks wet.

sc2.tip: Dew causes the effect: "socks felt slightly wet." The grass must have been a little wet too.

decoys.why: Lively grass wouldn't make your socks wet; the dew made it slightly wet.
The dew affects wetness, not how well the field grows plants.
Bright color wouldn't explain why the socks felt slightly wet.
Stiff grass wouldn't soak socks; the sentence is about dew and wetness.
The grass wasn't hard to find; the dew made it slightly wet.

example: We read by the dim light of a candle.
hook: When you slide the light switch down to dim, the room turns soft and shadowy but not fully dark.

traps.why: Bright is the opposite of dim.
Slim rhymes with dim, but it means thin.
Quiet describes weak sound; dim describes weak light.

syn1.tip: Think of a dimmer switch that turns lights down low. Dim light is weak or faint.

sc1.stem: The flashlight's batteries were nearly dead, so its beam was too _____ to light the path through the woods.

traps.why: Nearly dead batteries make a weak beam, not a bright one.
Flashlights can be heavy, but weight doesn't stop a beam lighting the path.
The batteries are the problem, and a new beam makes no sense.

sc1.tip: The cause is "batteries were nearly dead." Dying batteries make light that is weak, so the beam couldn't light the path.

decoys.why: Nearly dead batteries make a weak beam, and vivid means bright and strong.
The beam couldn't light the path, so it wasn't bright and full of life.
Batteries can run down, but a beam of light can't feel tired.
The beam is on but weak, so the issue is brightness, not being unused.

traps.why: Brightly lit is the opposite of dim.
Totally black means no light; dim still has a little light.
Things may look blurry in dim light, but dim describes the light itself.

syn2.tip: Picture reading by one weak candle. The room is dim because there isn't much light.

sc2.stem: The kitchen was bright and sunny at noon, but by evening the light had grown so _____ that Grandma switched on a lamp to read her book.

traps.why: Glaring light is very bright, so Grandma wouldn't need a lamp.
Evening light can look golden, but that wouldn't make reading hard.
Warm light can still be easy to read by, so no lamp needed.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "bright and sunny," and Grandma needs "a lamp to read." The light was weak.

decoys.why: Grandma needed a lamp, so the light was weak, not bright and strong.
The kitchen was bright at noon but not by evening, so vibrant is backwards.
The light faded so much that Grandma needed a lamp, the opposite of bright.
The blank describes the light, not Grandma, and light can't be tired.
Grandma turned on a lamp because it got dark, not because anything got wet.

example: Farmers grow corn in the fertile valley.
hook: Fertile soil is the kind where you drop in a seed and it seems to sprout overnight.

traps.why: Barren land grows nothing, the opposite of fertile.
Fragile looks a bit like fertile, but it means easy to break.
Plants need sun, but fertile describes the land, not the weather.

syn1.tip: Farmers want fertile fields because lots of crops grow there. Fruitful land gives plenty of food.

sc1.stem: The farmers chose the valley because its _____ soil could grow huge crops of corn, beans, and squash.

traps.why: Rocky soil makes crops hard to grow, not huge.
Price matters to farmers, but cheap soil can't grow huge crops by being cheap.
Dusty soil is too dry to grow huge crops.

sc1.tip: The clue is "could grow huge crops of corn, beans, and squash." You need a word for soil that grows plants well.

decoys.why: Stiff, hard soil wouldn't grow huge crops of corn, beans, and squash.
The farmers chose the valley for its good soil, not because soil was hard to find.
Worn-out soil couldn't grow huge crops, which is why farmers chose it.
Soil isn't described by brightness; the clue is about growing big crops.
Strange soil doesn't explain why it could grow huge crops.
The crops are huge, but the soil itself is described by how well it grows plants.

traps.why: Lifeless land grows nothing, the opposite of fertile.
Farmland is often flat, but flat doesn't mean plants grow well.
Fertile means able to grow plants, not already planted with them.

syn2.tip: You often hear fertile soil or a fertile valley. Ask yourself what farmers want from land: lots of crops.

sc2.stem: Nothing would grow in our shady, rocky backyard, but Aunt Rosa's _____ garden produced so many tomatoes that she gave bags of them to the neighbors.

traps.why: Barren is like our yard, but the word but signals a contrast.
A frozen garden couldn't produce bags of tomatoes.
Fragile looks like fertile, but it means easy to break.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "nothing would grow," and "so many tomatoes" shows her garden grew plenty.

decoys.why: The shady yard grew nothing, so a dim garden wouldn't produce so many tomatoes.
Stiff, hard ground is like the rocky yard, not a garden full of tomatoes.
Aunt Rosa had so many tomatoes she gave them away, the opposite of scarce.
Her garden was busy producing lots of tomatoes, so it wasn't idle.
The sentence describes a garden that grows a lot, not one that seems stern.

example: The weary hikers rested by the stream.
hook: Picture hikers dragging their feet at the end of a long trail: that heavy, worn-out feeling is weary.

traps.why: Energetic means full of energy, the opposite of weary.
Wary looks almost the same, but it means careful or watchful.
Tired hikers may be sore, but weary means tired, not hurting.

syn1.tip: Weary often describes travelers after a long trip. Think of how you feel at the end of a long day.

sc1.stem: After hearing the same song forty times on the car trip, Dad grew _____ of it and begged us to pick another.

traps.why: If Dad were fond of the song, he wouldn't beg for another.
Being proud of a song wouldn't make him beg us to change it.
Jealousy makes no sense here; the repeats are what bothered him.

sc1.tip: Look at "forty times" and "begged us to pick another." Hearing it so often made him tired of it.

decoys.why: Dad wasn't careful about danger; he heard the song forty times and got tired of it.

traps.why: Lively means full of energy, the opposite of weary.
Worried sounds a bit like weary, but it means anxious.
Lazy means not wanting to work; weary people are tired from working hard.

syn2.tip: Picture the weary hikers resting by the stream. They have used up their energy.

sc2.stem: Grandpa usually races us up the hill, but after a whole day of moving furniture, he felt too _____ to climb even the front steps.

traps.why: Being lively would make climbing easy, not impossible.
Excited people are full of energy, but Grandpa can't climb even steps.
He might be hungry after work, but hunger wouldn't stop him climbing steps.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with racing up the hill, and "a whole day of moving furniture" wore him out.

decoys.why: Grandpa could not climb even the steps, and vibrant means full of energy.
Wary looks like weary but means watchful of danger, not tired from moving furniture.
Feeling happy would not stop Grandpa from climbing the front steps.
The sentence is about Grandpa being worn out, not about his mood.
Being clever with words has nothing to do with being too worn out to climb.

meaning: hard to find; in short supply
example: Water is scarce in the desert.
hook: When something is scarce, there is barely any left, like the last cookie in the jar after a party.

traps.why: Plentiful means there is lots, the opposite of scarce.
Scary looks like scarce, but it means frightening.
Scarce things are often valuable, but scarce is about how much there is.

syn1.tip: Think of water in the desert. There is very little of it, so it is hard to find.

sc1.stem: During the long drought, water became so _____ that ten farm families had to share the one well that still worked.

traps.why: Families wouldn't need to share one well if water were plentiful.
Cheap water would be easy to get, not something ten families share.
Cold water doesn't explain why only one well still worked for everyone.

sc1.tip: The cause is "the long drought," and the effect is ten families sharing "the one well." Water was hard to find.

decoys.why: Ten families sharing one well means there was too little water, not more than enough.
Damp is about water, but the sentence is about how little water there was.
Fertile describes land that grows plants, not water that is running out in a drought.
A drought means very little water, so gigantic makes no sense here.
Water cannot be tired; the sentence says there was hardly any water left.

traps.why: In large amounts means plenty, the opposite of scarce.
Scarce things may cost more, but scarce means there is little.
Completely gone is too strong; scarce means a little is left.

syn2.tip: You might hear that food was scarce in winter. That means there wasn't much of it to go around.

sc2.stem: In spring the berry bushes were loaded with fruit, but by late fall berries were so _____ that the birds had to search all day to find a few.

traps.why: Plentiful describes spring; the word but signals a change.
Ripe berries are ready to eat, but that doesn't make them hard to find.
Juicy berries are tasty, but birds wouldn't search all day for plenty.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "loaded with fruit," and birds had to "search all day to find a few."

decoys.why: The birds searched all day to find a few, so there were not more than enough.
Berries can be bright, but the clue says birds could barely find any.
Fertile describes soil that grows plants, not berries that are hard to find.
Bright color would not make birds search all day to find a few berries.
The problem was how few berries there were, not how big they were.
Wet berries would still be easy to find; the birds found only a few.

example: Grandpa always has a cheerful smile.
hook: Cheerful is just what it says, full of cheer, like a friend who whistles while doing chores.

traps.why: Gloomy means sad and dark, the opposite of cheerful.
Careful looks a bit like cheerful, but it means paying close attention.
Happy people can be loud, but cheerful is about mood, not noise.

syn1.tip: Break it apart: cheer plus ful means full of cheer. Merry Christmas is a cheerful greeting.

sc1.stem: The sunny yellow walls and bright curtains made the once-gray waiting room so _____ that even nervous patients smiled.

traps.why: Gloomy fits the old gray room, not sunny yellow walls.
A crowded waiting room wouldn't make nervous patients smile.
Bright colors don't make a room cold, and cold doesn't cause smiles.

sc1.tip: The causes are "sunny yellow walls and bright curtains," and the effect is that "even nervous patients smiled." The room felt happy.

decoys.why: Sunny yellow walls and bright curtains make a room bright, not dim.
The room made nervous patients smile, so it was not gloomy or stern.
A boring room would not make nervous patients smile.
Nothing in the sentence is about wetness; it is about bright colors making people smile.
A room cannot be tired; the bright colors made it happy looking.

traps.why: Grumpy means cranky, the opposite of cheerful.
Funny people make you laugh, but cheerful describes a happy feeling.
Polite means having good manners, which isn't the same as happy.

syn2.tip: The ending ful means full of. Someone cheerful is full of cheer, which is a happy feeling.

sc2.stem: Even though it rained all through our camping trip, my little brother stayed _____, singing silly songs and splashing happily in every puddle.

traps.why: Grumpy fits a rainy trip, but even though signals the opposite.
Splashing in every puddle would not keep him dry.
He was singing silly songs, so he wasn't quiet.

sc2.tip: "Even though it rained" warns you he didn't act sad, and "singing silly songs" and "splashing happily" show his mood.

decoys.why: He was singing silly songs and splashing happily, so he was not stern or gloomy.
Splashing in every puddle shows energy, not being very tired.
Singing silly songs is fun, not long and boring.
Rigid means stiff, but he was happily splashing around in the rain.
He splashed happily in every puddle, so he was not careful about danger.

example: Our gracious host offered us lemonade.
hook: A gracious host makes you feel like the most welcome guest in the world before you even take off your coat.

traps.why: Rude means impolite, the opposite of gracious.
Precious rhymes with gracious, but it means very valuable.
Fancy hosts may be wealthy, but gracious is about kind manners, not money.

syn1.tip: Gracious is full of grace, the kind of good manners a polite host shows. Think of someone who says please and thank you.

sc1.stem: The _____ host greeted every guest warmly at the door, took their coats, and politely offered them lemonade.

traps.why: A grumpy host wouldn't greet every guest warmly.
A stingy host wouldn't happily offer everyone lemonade.
Bossy is pushy, but this host acted warmly and politely.

sc1.tip: The host "greeted every guest warmly," "took their coats," and "politely offered" lemonade. All of these are kind and welcoming.

decoys.why: The host greeted everyone warmly, so he was not stern and unsmiling.
A host who welcomes every guest warmly is not suspicious of them.
The host was busy taking coats and offering lemonade, not doing nothing.
Nothing in the sentence suggests the host was tired; it shows he was warm and polite.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is the host's warm and polite welcome.

traps.why: Rude and unfriendly is the opposite of gracious.
Grace can mean moving smoothly, but gracious is about kindness, not movement.
A party can be fancy, but gracious describes how a person treats others.

syn2.tip: Picture the gracious host offering you lemonade. A gracious person makes others feel welcome.

sc2.stem: Coach Lee's team lost the championship by one point, yet instead of sulking she was _____, shaking hands with the winners and praising their great game.

traps.why: A bitter coach would sulk, but she praised the winners instead.
Jealous is a sour feeling, but she was kind to the winners.
She might be tired, but that doesn't explain shaking hands and praising.

sc2.tip: The words "yet instead of sulking" signal a contrast, and "shaking hands" and "praising their great game" show kind manners.

decoys.why: Instead of sulking, she praised the winners, so she was not stern and unsmiling.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is her kind handshakes and praise.
Shaking hands and praising the winners shows kindness, not watching for danger.
She may be tired, but the clue shows her being kind and polite to the winners.
She was actively shaking hands and praising, so she was not doing nothing.

example: The jolly baker hummed while he worked.
hook: Jolly even sounds bouncy, just like the giggling, belly-shaking happiness it names.

traps.why: Glum means sad and quiet, the opposite of jolly.
Santa is jolly and round, but jolly is about mood, not size.
Jealous starts like jolly, but it means wanting what others have.

syn1.tip: Think of a jolly old man laughing "Ho, ho, ho." Merry and jolly both describe that happy, laughing mood.

sc1.stem: The _____ old man in the red suit laughed "Ho, ho, ho!" and handed every child a candy cane.

traps.why: A grumpy man wouldn't laugh "Ho, ho, ho" and hand out candy.
A sleepy man wouldn't be laughing out loud.
Stern means serious and strict, not laughing.

sc1.tip: He "laughed 'Ho, ho, ho!'" and handed out candy canes. That laughing, happy person is cheerful and merry.

decoys.why: He laughed and handed out candy canes, so he was not stern and unsmiling.
Laughing "Ho, ho, ho" shows a happy man, not a tired one.
Nothing here is about watching for danger; he was laughing and giving out candy.
A laughing man handing out candy canes is fun, not boring.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is his happy laugh.

traps.why: Sulky means pouting and moody, the opposite of jolly.
We often say jolly old man, but jolly doesn't mean old.
Santa gives gifts, but jolly describes his happy mood, not his giving.

syn2.tip: Picture the jolly baker humming while he works. Someone humming happily is in a good mood.

sc2.stem: Our bus driver is so _____ that his loud laugh and silly jokes turn even the rainiest Monday morning into a fun ride.

traps.why: A strict driver wouldn't fill the bus with laughs and silly jokes.
Drivers should be careful, but carefulness doesn't make laughs and jokes.
A sleepy driver wouldn't be laughing loudly and telling jokes.

sc2.tip: The words "so... that" show cause and effect. His "loud laugh and silly jokes" make rides fun, so he is happy and cheerful.

decoys.why: A driver with a loud laugh and silly jokes is not stern and unsmiling.
The driver makes the ride fun, so he is not boring.
Loud laughs and silly jokes show energy and happiness, not tiredness.
Rigid means stiff, but the clue is his laughter and jokes.
Silly jokes and laughing have nothing to do with watching for danger.

example: The deer was wary of the barking dog.
hook: A wary deer freezes with its ears up; wary and beware share a root, and both mean watch out.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite of wary; a wary animal is very careful.
Weary looks like wary but means tired.
Terrified is far too strong; wary means watchful, not frozen with fear.

syn1.tip: Wary is in the word beware. Someone wary is careful and watching for danger.

sc1.stem: The squirrel was _____ of the cat, keeping one eye on it the entire time it nibbled the acorn.

traps.why: An unaware squirrel would not keep one eye on the cat.
Fond is a warm feeling, but watching a cat closely shows worry about danger.
Weary looks like wary but means tired, which the sentence never says.

sc1.tip: The clue is "keeping one eye on it the entire time." Keeping watch on a danger is what a wary animal does.

decoys.why: Weary of means tired of; the squirrel was keeping an eye on the cat for safety.

traps.why: Trusting everyone is the opposite of being wary.
That is the meaning of weary, a word that looks like wary.
Danger can lead to fights, but wary means carefully watching, not attacking.

syn2.tip: Think of a deer lifting its head at a sound. It is not fighting or tired; it is watching for danger.

sc2.stem: Most of the ducks swam right up for bread, but one old duck stayed _____, circling at a distance and watching our hands before it came close.

traps.why: A tame duck would swim right up, but this one kept its distance.
Ducks want bread, but hungry does not explain circling and watching from far away.
An eager duck would rush in; this duck held back and watched.

sc2.tip: The word "but" shows this duck acted differently from the others. "Circling at a distance and watching" means it was careful about danger.

decoys.why: Weary means tired, but the duck was circling and watching your hands, which shows caution.
The duck kept its distance instead of welcoming anyone, so it was not acting kind or welcoming.
Nothing says the duck was happy; it stayed back and watched carefully before coming close.
The sentence describes a duck being careful about danger, not one feeling happy and bright.
The duck was busy circling and watching, so it was not sitting idle.

example: Her witty jokes made the whole class laugh.
hook: A witty person uses their wit, quick clever thinking, to make you laugh with just a few words.

traps.why: Dull is the opposite of witty; witty words are lively and funny.
Wise means smart about life, but witty means clever and funny.
Silly means foolishly funny; witty humor is clever, not foolish.

syn1.tip: Witty comes from wit, which means quick thinking. Witty people are clever in a way that makes you laugh.

sc1.stem: Known for her _____ remarks, Jasmine could make the whole class laugh with one clever line.

traps.why: Dull remarks would not make the whole class laugh.
Rude remarks are unkind; the sentence calls her line clever.
Wordy means too many words, but she needed only one line.

sc1.tip: The clue is "laugh with one clever line." Clever plus funny is exactly what witty means.

decoys.why: Boring remarks would not make the whole class laugh with one clever line.
Stern, unsmiling remarks would not get the class laughing.
Cheerless remarks would not make anyone laugh, and the sentence calls her lines clever.
Wary looks like witty but means careful about danger, which has nothing to do with jokes.
Tired remarks would not be the clever lines that made the class laugh.
The sentence says her lines were clever, not awkward.

traps.why: Boring and slow is the opposite of quick, funny wit.
Witty humor is clever and pleasant, not loud and rude.
Wise is about being smart, but witty also means funny, not serious.

syn2.tip: Look for wit inside witty. Wit is a sharp, quick mind, and witty people use it to be funny.

sc2.stem: The movie's jokes were flat and boring, but the talking parrot's _____ comebacks had everyone in the theater laughing at how clever they were.

traps.why: Boring describes the other jokes; the word "but" signals the parrot was different.
A parrot can be loud, but people laughed because the comebacks were clever.
Mean comebacks hurt; these made people laugh at how clever they were.

sc2.tip: "But" sets the parrot against the "flat and boring" jokes, and "laughing at how clever they were" tells you the comebacks were funny and smart.

decoys.why: Tedious describes the movie's boring jokes, but the parrot's comebacks were the clever contrast.
Stern, unsmiling comebacks would not have the whole theater laughing.
Cheerless comebacks would not make everyone laugh at how clever they were.
Wary means careful about danger, but the sentence is about clever, funny comebacks.
Tired comebacks would not be the clever ones that got the theater laughing.
The audience laughed at how clever the comebacks were, not how awkward.

example: She found a fragment of blue glass.
hook: A fragment is a piece that broke off, like a chip from a dropped plate or part of a sentence.

traps.why: A whole is the complete thing, the opposite of a broken piece.
Figment looks similar but means something imagined, not a broken piece.
A crack is a break in something, not the piece that breaks off.

syn1.tip: Think of a sentence fragment, which is only part of a sentence. A fragment is a small piece of something bigger.

sc1.stem: While digging in the garden, Lucas found a small _____ of a broken clay pot with blue paint on it.

traps.why: A collection is many whole things, not one small piece of a pot.
A copy is made to look like something; Lucas found a real broken bit.
Fragrance looks a bit like fragment but means a smell.

sc1.tip: The clue is "small" and "of a broken clay pot." A small part of something broken is a fragment.

decoys.why: Lucas found a broken piece of a pot, not something blocking his way.
The sentence describes a small piece of a clay pot, not a danger.
A blunder is a mistake, but Lucas found a physical piece of a broken pot.
A small dwelling is a home, not something that comes from a broken clay pot.
A triumph is a win, not a piece of a broken pot you dig up.
Nothing in the sentence is being cured; Lucas found a broken piece of a pot.

traps.why: A complete object is whole, the opposite of a fragment.
Fragments are small bits, not large heavy chunks.
A crack is a line where something breaks, not the piece itself.

syn2.tip: A fragment is what is left after something breaks: just a small part of it.

sc2.stem: When the old plate slipped off the table and shattered, Dad picked up every sharp _____ from the floor so no one would cut a foot.

traps.why: Spills make puddles, but puddles are not sharp and cannot cut feet.
Figment looks similar but means something imagined, which cannot cut.
Plates hold crumbs, but crumbs are soft and come from food.

sc2.tip: The plate "shattered," so it broke into pieces. Something "sharp" that could "cut a foot" must be a broken piece.

decoys.why: Dropping the plate was a mistake, but Dad picked up sharp pieces from the floor.
Dad was picking up sharp broken pieces of the plate, not copies of it.
A remedy is a cure, but Dad was picking up sharp pieces so no one got cut.
An instinct is a feeling, and you cannot pick a feeling up off the floor.
Nobody was arguing; the plate shattered and Dad picked up the sharp pieces.

example: Keep your desk tidy so you can find things.
hook: A tidy room has a place for everything and everything in its place.

traps.why: Messy is the opposite of tidy.
Tiny looks like tidy but means very small.
A tidy sum means a large amount, but tidy here means neat.

syn1.tip: Think of tidying up your room: putting things away so it is neat and in order.

sc1.stem: Unlike her brother's messy room, Jada's room is _____, with books lined up on shelves and clothes folded in drawers.

traps.why: Cluttered means messy, but "unlike" says Jada's room is different from messy.
Tiny looks like tidy, but the sentence describes order, not size.
Rooms can be noisy, but lined-up books and folded clothes show neatness.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her brother's messy room" means Jada's room is the opposite of messy. "Lined up" and "folded" show it is neat.

decoys.why: Books lined up and clothes folded describe neatness, not how dark the room is.
The sentence contrasts her room with a messy one, so it is about neatness, not wetness.
Neat shelves and folded clothes say nothing about size; the clue is the messy room contrast.
Fancy and costly is not the opposite of messy; the details show things are in order.
The sentence praises her neat room, not a cold and cheerless one.
Lined-up books and folded clothes show order, not brightness or liveliness.

traps.why: Scattered things are messy, the opposite of tidy.
New things can look neat, but tidy is about order, not age.
That fits a tidy sum of money, not a tidy room.

syn2.tip: When you tidy up, you put things back where they belong. Tidy means neat and in order.

sc2.stem: Because Grandma likes everything in its place, she keeps her kitchen _____, wiping every counter and putting each spoon back in the same drawer.

traps.why: A crowded kitchen is cluttered, not one where everything is in its place.
Kitchens are often warm, but wiping and putting spoons away shows neatness.
Busy is about activity, but the clue is about keeping things in order.

sc2.tip: "Because Grandma likes everything in its place" causes her to keep the kitchen neat. Wiping counters and putting spoons back are tidy habits.

decoys.why: Wiping counters might leave them wet, but the clue is that she likes everything in its place.
Putting each spoon back in its drawer is about order, not about how bright the kitchen is.
The sentence describes how neat Grandma keeps her kitchen, not how big it is.
Grandma keeps things in their place, which is about neatness, not fancy or costly decoration.
Nothing suggests her kitchen is cold or cheerless; the clues are about keeping things in order.
Wiping counters and putting spoons away make a kitchen neat, not strong and solid.

meaning: to love and care for deeply
example: I cherish the letters my grandpa wrote me.
hook: You cherish what feels like treasure to you, like a favorite stuffed animal you keep safe for years.

traps.why: To neglect means to ignore and not care for, the opposite of cherish.
