Cheer looks a bit like cherish but means to shout or make happy.
Like is too weak; to cherish is to love something deeply.

syn1.tip: Cherish feels warm and loving. Think of something you would never give away because it means so much to you.

sc1.stem: Abuela will always _____ the quilt her mother sewed, keeping it safe and loving it more than anything she owns.

traps.why: You do not forget something you keep safe and love most.
The quilt already belongs to Abuela, so she has no need to borrow it.
Tolerate means just put up with, far too weak for loving it most.

sc1.tip: The clue is "keeping it safe and loving it more than anything." Loving and caring for something deeply is cherishing it.

decoys.why: The sentence says she keeps the quilt safe and loves it, the opposite of neglecting it.
Keeping it safe does not mean hiding it; the sentence stresses that she loves it most.
She loves the quilt more than anything, so she would not fear it.
You endure something hard, but Abuela loves this quilt more than anything she owns.
She keeps the quilt safe, so she is not using it up.
Grabbing something suddenly does not match keeping it safe and loving it.

traps.why: Throwing something away is the opposite of cherishing it.
You might show off things you love, but cherish is about loving them.
Cheer looks a bit like cherish, but cherishing is quiet, deep love.

syn2.tip: Things you cherish are precious to you. You love them deeply and take good care of them.

sc2.stem: Leo thought the old seashell was just junk, but his little sister will _____ it forever because their grandfather found it on his last beach trip.

traps.why: Ignore matches Leo's view, but "but" shows his sister feels the opposite.
People trade shells, but a gift from Grandfather is something to keep.
Notice is far too weak for a special keepsake kept forever.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the sister with Leo, who thought it was "just junk." She sees it as precious because their grandfather found it.

decoys.why: Leo thought it was junk, but the word but shows his sister feels the opposite.
The shell reminds her of their grandfather, so she treasures it rather than fearing it.
The shell is special to her because of Grandpa, not something hard she puts up with.
You cannot eat or use up a seashell, and she wants to keep it forever.
Copying a seashell makes no sense; she loves it because Grandpa found it.

example: She concealed the gift behind her back.
hook: To conceal is to hide something away, like a magician concealing a coin in a closed fist.

traps.why: Reveal means to show, the opposite of conceal.
Cancel looks a bit like conceal but means to call off.
Lost things are out of sight, but concealing is done on purpose.

syn1.tip: Concealed things are kept where no one can see them. Think of a concealed door in a wall that you cannot spot.

sc1.stem: Max tried to _____ the broken lamp by throwing a blanket over it so that no one would see it.

traps.why: Throwing a blanket over the lamp would not show it to anyone.
Broken lamps need repair, but a blanket hides it instead of fixing it.
Cancel looks like conceal but means to call off, not cover.

sc1.tip: The clue is "so that no one would see it." Covering something so it cannot be seen means hiding it.

decoys.why: Max threw the blanket on so no one would see the lamp, which means hiding it.
Max was covering up the broken lamp so no one would see, not showing love for it.
Throwing a blanket over the lamp is about hiding it, not understanding it.
The goal was that no one would see the lamp, so he was hiding it, not grabbing it.
You cannot copy a lamp by covering it; the blanket was to keep it out of sight.
The sentence says the blanket kept anyone from seeing the lamp, which is hiding, not putting up with it.

traps.why: Showing everyone is the opposite of keeping something hidden.
That is seeking, which you do to find hidden things, not hide them.
That means cancel, a word that looks like conceal.

syn2.tip: If you conceal a gift behind your back, no one can see it. Conceal means to hide.

sc2.stem: The magician's sleeve was so wide that she could easily _____ a whole deck of cards inside it, and the audience never once spotted them.

traps.why: Display means show, but the audience never spotted the cards.
Magicians shuffle cards, but the clue is that no one could see them.
Dealing cards puts them out in view, not hidden in a sleeve.

sc2.tip: The wide sleeve causes the result: "the audience never once spotted them." Keeping cards where no one can spot them means hiding them.

decoys.why: The sentence is about keeping cards out of sight, not grabbing them suddenly.
The audience never spotted the cards, so the point is hiding them, not loving them.
The sleeve holds cards so nobody sees them; failing to care for cards makes no sense.
Nothing in the sentence is about fear; the clue is that nobody spotted the cards.
You cannot understand cards inside a sleeve; the clue says she kept them hidden.

example: He likes to boast about his new bike.
hook: A boaster puffs up like a balloon, saying 'I am the best' again and again.

traps.why: Boost looks like boast but means to lift up or increase.
Complaining is also a way of talking, but it means grumbling, not showing off.
Talk is too general; boasting is talking proudly about yourself.

syn1.tip: Boasting sounds proud and a bit annoying. Picture someone saying "I am the best" over and over.

sc1.stem: Kenji likes to _____ about his video game scores, telling everyone again and again how great he is.

traps.why: Worrying about scores would not mean telling everyone how great he is.
Complaining is unhappy talk, but Kenji says how great he is.
He keeps telling everyone about his scores, so he has not forgotten them.

sc1.tip: The clue is "telling everyone again and again how great he is." Talking about how great you are is bragging.

decoys.why: Kenji tells everyone again and again, so he is not pausing at all.

traps.why: Staying humble is the opposite of boasting about yourself.
Cheering others on is kind, while boasting puts the focus on yourself.
That is about how loud you talk, not about praising yourself.

syn2.tip: A person who boasts wants everyone to know how great they are. That is showing off with words.

sc2.stem: Because Theo would _____ about his new sneakers all day long, his friends rolled their eyes and said, 'We get it, your shoes are the best.'

traps.why: His friends answer that his shoes are the best, so he was not complaining.
Worrying about shoes would not make friends say his shoes are the best.
You cannot forget about something all day while talking about it.

sc2.tip: His friends "rolled their eyes" and said "your shoes are the best." That reaction shows Theo kept bragging about them.

decoys.why: Theo talked about his sneakers all day long, which is the opposite of pausing.

example: The pool rules prohibit running.
hook: A sign that says 'No running' prohibits running; prohibited things are not allowed by the rules.

traps.why: Allow is the opposite of prohibit.
Exhibit looks like prohibit but means to show or display.
Breaking a rule may get you punished, but prohibit means not allow.

syn1.tip: Prohibit shows up on signs: "Smoking is prohibited." It means a rule says you may not do it.

sc1.stem: The museum's rules strictly _____ visitors from touching the paintings or taking flash photos.

traps.why: Rules protect paintings, but they do not protect visitors from touching.
Excuse from means let off a duty, but touching is not a duty.
Museums exhibit paintings, but that word looks alike and means show.

sc1.tip: Look at "rules strictly" and "from touching." Strict rules that keep visitors from touching are rules that forbid it.

traps.why: Giving permission is the opposite of prohibiting.
That means exhibit, which only looks like prohibit.
Prohibit is much stronger; it is a rule that says no.

syn2.tip: Think of a pool sign that prohibits running. The rule does not just suggest walking; it does not allow running.

sc2.stem: At home I can eat snacks anywhere, but my school's rules _____ eating in the library, so I always finish my apple before I go inside.

traps.why: Allow matches home, but "but" says school is different.
If eating were encouraged, there would be no need to finish the apple first.
Rules can require things, but nobody finishes eating before a required snack.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts school with home, where you "can eat snacks anywhere." Finishing the apple before going inside shows eating is not allowed.

decoys.why: You finish your apple before going inside, so the rules do not allow eating there.
Rules that ignore eating would let you snack inside, but you finish your apple first.
The rules stop eating in the library; they do not hide it.
Rules cannot fear anything; the sentence shows they do not allow eating in the library.

example: Sorting all the buttons was tedious work.
hook: Tedious work drags on and on, like sorting a thousand buttons one at a time.

traps.why: Exciting is the opposite of tedious.
Hard work is not always boring; tedious means slow and dull.
Hideous looks and rhymes like tedious but means very ugly.

syn1.tip: Tedious has a heavy, dragging feeling. Think of a chore so slow and boring it makes you tired.

sc1.stem: Copying all one hundred spelling words by hand five times was _____, taking hours of slow, boring work.

traps.why: Thrilling work would not be described as slow and boring.
The sentence says it took hours, so it was not quick.
Practice can help, but the clue says boring, not useful.

sc1.tip: The clue is "hours of slow, boring work." Something long, slow, and boring is tedious.

decoys.why: The sentence calls the work slow and boring, which is the opposite of cheerful.
Hours of slow, boring work is not happy and cheerful.
You might feel tired after copying, but the work itself is boring, not tired.
Copying words by hand is boring work, not something clever and funny.
Slow, boring work is the opposite of bright and full of life.

traps.why: Thrilling is full of excitement, the opposite of tedious.
Tedious jobs can be simple, but tedious is about being boring and long.
Tidy starts like tedious but means neat.

syn2.tip: A tedious task drags on with nothing interesting happening. That feeling is dull and boring.

sc2.stem: The first part of the movie was full of car chases, but the last hour was so _____ that my little brother fell asleep on the couch.

traps.why: Thrilling fits the car chases, but "but" signals the last hour changed.
Movies can be loud, but loud scenes keep you awake.
A scary movie would keep a kid awake, not put him to sleep.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the exciting car chases with the last hour. Falling asleep shows that hour was slow and boring.

decoys.why: Your brother fell asleep, so the last hour was dull, not full of life.
Your brother was tired, but the movie itself was boring, not tired.
A clever, funny movie would keep him awake, but he fell asleep.
The clue is that he fell asleep, which points to boring, not happy and bright.

example: The bride had a radiant smile.
hook: Radiant things send out rays of light, like the sun or a huge happy smile.

traps.why: Dim means giving little light, the opposite of radiant.
Rapid starts like radiant but means fast.
Colorful things can be bright, but radiant means giving off light.

syn1.tip: Radiant sends out rays, like the sun. A radiant face seems to shine with joy.

sc1.stem: When she saw her long-lost cousin at the gate, Aisha's face was _____, glowing with happiness like the morning sun.

traps.why: A gloomy face is sad, not glowing with happiness.
Faces can go pale from shock, but hers was glowing like the sun.
A sleepy face is dull and tired, not glowing like morning sun.

sc1.tip: The clue is "glowing with happiness like the morning sun." A face shining with joy is radiant.

decoys.why: Aisha was glowing with happiness, not serious and quiet.
A face glowing like the morning sun is the opposite of cold and cheerless.
The sentence says her face was glowing, and dim means not bright.
She was glowing with happiness at seeing her cousin, not very tired.
Aisha was overjoyed to see her cousin, not watchful about danger.

traps.why: Dull and gloomy is the opposite of shining brightly.
Bright paint is colorful, but radiant things give off their own glow.
Glaring light hurts your eyes; radiant is a warm, pleasant glow.

syn2.tip: Look for ray in radiant: the sun's rays. Something radiant shines brightly and warmly.

sc2.stem: After weeks of gray, rainy skies, the garden looked _____ when the sun finally came out and lit up every wet leaf and petal.

traps.why: Gloomy fits the gray weeks, but the sun finally came out.
Dim means low light, but every leaf was lit up.
Gardens often have shade, but the sun lit up every leaf.

sc2.tip: "After weeks of gray" sets up a change, and "lit up every wet leaf" shows the garden was shining brightly.

decoys.why: Bleak fits the gray weeks, but the sun finally came out and lit everything up.
The sun lit up every leaf, so the garden was bright, not dim.
The sentence is about sunlight making the garden shine, not looking serious and quiet.
The clue is the sun lighting up every leaf, which is about glowing, not neatness.
The garden was lit up by sunshine, not very tired.

meaning: to copy how someone acts or sounds
example: Parrots can mimic human voices.
hook: A mimic octopus copies the shapes of other sea animals, the way a parrot copies a voice.

traps.why: To invent is to make something new, not copy what already exists.
You might memorize words, but mimic means copying how someone acts or sounds.
Mingle starts like mimic but means to mix with a crowd.

syn1.tip: Think of a parrot repeating your words in your own voice. Mimic means to copy.

sc1.stem: The mockingbird can _____ car alarms, other birds, and even barking dogs, copying each sound perfectly.

traps.why: Loud alarms can frighten birds, but the clue says the bird is copying sounds.
You can't copy a sound perfectly while ignoring it.
The bird must hear sounds first, but copying them is much more.

sc1.tip: The words 'copying each sound perfectly' explain the blank. The bird does more than hear the sounds; it copies them.

decoys.why: The sentence says the bird copies each sound perfectly, not that it fears them.
The clue is copying each sound, not understanding car alarms or dogs.
The bird copies the sounds; nothing says it loves car alarms or barking dogs.
The bird copies sounds perfectly, which is the opposite of hiding them.
A bird cannot forbid car alarms by rule; the sentence says it copies them.

traps.why: Creating makes something original, the opposite of copying.
Obeying means doing what you're told, not copying how someone acts.
Copying someone can be used to tease, but tease means to poke fun.

syn2.tip: Parrots mimic voices. Ask what a parrot does with a voice it hears: it copies it.

sc2.stem: Instead of inventing her own dance for the talent show, Lily chose to _____ her favorite pop star, matching every spin and hand wave.

traps.why: She may admire the star, but matching every spin means copying.
You can't match every spin of someone you ignore.
Talking with the star is not the same as matching every move.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of inventing her own' is a contrast clue, and 'matching every spin and hand wave' tells you she copied.

decoys.why: She is matching every spin and hand wave, which means copying, not loving.
Matching someone's dance moves is copying them, not tricking anyone.
She matched every move, so she paid close attention instead of ignoring the star.
Matching every spin shows copying the dance; nothing is being hidden.
The clue is matching every spin and wave, which describes copying, not understanding.

example: The kids shouted with glee at the snow.
hook: Glee is the squeal you let out when you wake up and see snow on a school day.

traps.why: Sorrow is deep sadness, the opposite of great joy.
Glare starts like glee but means an angry stare.
Relief is the feeling when a worry ends, not great joy.

syn1.tip: Glee is a happy word. Picture kids shouting with glee at the snow: that is delight.

sc1.stem: Squealing with _____, the twins raced outside to build their very first snowman.

traps.why: Kids can squeal with fear, but building a snowman is happy.
Snow is cold, but racing out to play shows happiness.
Sad kids don't race outside to build their first snowman.

sc1.tip: The twins are 'squealing' and racing out to build their 'very first snowman.' Those are signs of great joy.

decoys.why: The twins are excited to build their first snowman, so deep sadness is the opposite.
They raced outside full of energy, so being very tired does not fit.
Racing outside to build a snowman shows joy, not careful worry about danger.

traps.why: Deep sadness is the opposite of glee.
Glee is much stronger than a slight pleasure.
A glee club sings, but glee here means great joy.

syn2.tip: Glee is big, bouncy happiness, not just a little. Picture kids squealing when recess begins.

sc2.stem: Mia expected to feel nervous on the roller coaster, but instead she screamed with _____ the whole ride and begged to go again.

traps.why: Terror fits the nervous part, but begging to go again shows joy.
Coasters can make you dizzy, but begging for more shows she loved it.
Miserable riders don't beg to go again.

sc2.tip: 'Expected to feel nervous, but instead' signals a contrast, and 'begged to go again' shows she loved the ride.

decoys.why: The word instead tells you she did not feel nervous, so careful worry is wrong.
She begged to go again, so she felt joy, not deep sadness.
Someone who begs to ride again is having fun, not feeling worn out.

meaning: to gather or pile up over time
example: Dust accumulated on the old books.
hook: Watch snow accumulate: flake by flake it piles up until the whole yard is buried.

traps.why: Scatter means to spread things apart, the opposite of piling them up.
Accelerate starts like accumulate but means to speed up.
You might count what you collect, but accumulate means gather over time.

syn1.tip: Think of cumulus clouds that heap up high. Accumulate means things pile up or are collected bit by bit.

sc1.stem: If you never sweep under the bed, dust bunnies will slowly _____ there, piling higher over the months.

traps.why: Dust that disappears can't be 'piling higher over the months.'
Dust bunnies do hide under beds, but 'piling higher' means gathering.
Shrinking means getting smaller, but the dust is piling higher.

sc1.tip: 'Never sweep' and 'piling higher over the months' tell you the dust keeps gathering.

decoys.why: The dust is piling higher over the months, so it is building up, not disappearing.
Dust bunnies piling higher stay in one spot and grow; they do not wander around.
Piling higher means building up on the floor, not flying high in the air.

traps.why: Spreading out is the opposite of piling up.
Lining up puts things in a row, not in a growing pile.
Dust accumulates when you don't clean up; cleaning removes it.

syn2.tip: Snow that accumulates gets deeper and deeper. Look for the choice that means things gather and grow over time.

sc2.stem: Because Jamal saved every quarter he found for two years, enough coins began to _____ in his jar to buy a new skateboard.

traps.why: Vanishing coins couldn't pay for a new skateboard.
Coins jingle in jars, but saving for years makes them pile up.
Accelerate looks like accumulate but means to speed up.

sc2.tip: 'Because Jamal saved every quarter... for two years' is the cause. The effect is that coins piled up in the jar.

decoys.why: Jamal saved every quarter, so his coins built up instead of disappearing.
Coins in a jar pile up from saving; they cannot wander around freely.
Saving quarters for two years makes coins gather in the jar, not fly high.

example: Buffalo once roamed across the plains.
hook: Picture buffalo roaming the plains, drifting wherever they like with no path and no hurry.

traps.why: Staying put is the opposite of roaming around.
Roar looks like roam but means to make a loud, deep sound.
Racing is fast and has a finish line; roaming is slow and free.

syn1.tip: Roaming has no set path. Think of 'free-roaming' animals that go wherever they please.

sc1.stem: On the big ranch, the horses are free to _____ across hundreds of acres with no fences to stop them.

traps.why: Marching means moving in tidy rows, not wandering freely.
Roar looks like roam, but horses don't roar, and 'free' means wandering.
Tiptoeing is careful and sneaky; nothing here says the horses sneak.

sc1.tip: 'Free' and 'no fences to stop them' tell you the horses can go wherever they like, which is wandering.

decoys.why: Horses move across the land with no fences to stop them; they cannot fly.
Fences stop horses from moving, so the sentence is about wandering, not looking.

traps.why: Staying in place is the opposite of roaming.
Marching follows strict rows; roaming goes anywhere.
Rushing straight somewhere has a goal; roaming has none.

syn2.tip: Roam means free, aimless movement. Animals that roam go wherever they like, with no fences or fixed route.

sc2.stem: At the zoo the lions stay in small pens, but in the wild they _____ for miles across the grassy plains, going wherever they please.

traps.why: Caged lions pace back and forth; free lions wander wherever they like.
Stampeding is a wild, frightened rush, much too strong for free wandering.
Roar looks like roam, but 'going wherever they please' is about moving.

sc2.tip: 'But' sets the wild against 'small pens,' and 'going wherever they please' means wandering freely.

decoys.why: Lions travel across the grassy plains on foot; they do not fly high in the air.
Going wherever they please means moving around, not just looking for a long time.

example: The clumsy puppy tripped over its own paws.
hook: Picture a puppy tripping over its own paws and tipping over its water bowl: that's clumsy.

traps.why: Graceful means moving smoothly, the opposite of clumsy.
Lazy means not wanting to work; clumsy means tripping and bumping.
Crumbly looks a bit like clumsy but means falling into crumbs.

syn1.tip: Think of a clumsy puppy tripping over its paws. Clumsy is about awkward, bumbling movement.

sc1.stem: Usually graceful on the ice, Nora felt _____ in her new skates, wobbling and bumping into the wall all afternoon.

traps.why: Elegant fits 'usually graceful,' but wobbling and bumping are not elegant.
Proud is a happy feeling; wobbling into walls all afternoon is not.
Ice is cold, but wobbling and bumping describe awkward movement.

sc1.tip: 'Usually graceful' sets up a contrast, and 'wobbling and bumping into the wall' shows she moved awkwardly.

decoys.why: Nora was wobbling and bumping the wall, so she was not steady and solid.
Gracious means kind and polite; it only looks like graceful, and she was wobbling.
Wobbling and bumping into the wall all afternoon does not make someone glow brightly.
The sentence describes wobbling and bumping, which is about awkward moving, not mood.

traps.why: Being light on your feet is the opposite of clumsy.
Sleepy people may move slowly, but clumsy means bumping into things.
Clumsy people may get hurt, but clumsy describes how they move.

syn2.tip: Clumsy people drop things and bump into furniture. Pick the choice that describes awkward movement.

sc2.stem: Because his feet had grown so fast that summer, Leo became _____ and kept tripping over chairs and knocking cups off the table.

traps.why: Nimble means quick and sure on your feet, the opposite of clumsy.
Growing kids get hungry, but tripping over chairs shows clumsiness.
Careful people don't keep knocking cups off tables.

sc2.tip: 'Feet had grown so fast' is the cause, and 'tripping over chairs and knocking cups' is the effect. He moved awkwardly.

decoys.why: Leo kept tripping over chairs, so he was not steady and solid.
Knocking cups off the table makes messes, so neat and orderly is backward.
Tripping and knocking things over is about awkward moving, not being funny with words.
Tripping over chairs is accidental, not tricky or sneaky.

example: We built a sturdy treehouse out of thick boards.
hook: A sturdy treehouse won't wobble even when five friends jump around on its thick boards.

traps.why: Flimsy means weak and easy to break, the opposite of sturdy.
Stormy looks a bit like sturdy but describes bad weather.
Sturdy things are often heavy, but light things can be sturdy too.

syn1.tip: Sturdy furniture holds you up without wobbling. Think 'built to last': strong and solid.

sc1.stem: Unlike the wobbly card table, the _____ oak bench held all five of us without a single creak.

traps.why: Shaky is like the wobbly table, but the bench is its opposite.
A fragile bench would break under five people.
Stormy looks like sturdy but describes weather, not benches.

sc1.tip: 'Unlike the wobbly card table' is a contrast, and holding five people 'without a single creak' shows strength.

decoys.why: Clumsy describes awkward people, and the bench is being compared to a wobbly table for strength.
The bench held five people without a creak, which shows strength, not fanciness.
The contrast with the wobbly table is about being solid, not about glowing.
Holding five people without a creak shows the bench is strong, not neat.

traps.why: Easily broken is the opposite of sturdy.
Height says nothing about whether something is strong.
New things aren't always strong; sturdy is about being solid.

syn2.tip: A sturdy chair can hold a grown-up without creaking. Look for the choice about being strong and well made.

sc2.stem: The little bridge over the creek was so _____ that even when the whole class marched across it at once, it never swayed or cracked.

traps.why: A flimsy bridge would sway or crack under a whole class.
Bridges can be slippery, but that doesn't stop swaying or cracking.
Dusty ends like sturdy but means covered in dust.

sc2.tip: 'So _____ that... it never swayed or cracked' links cause and effect. Only something strong and solid stays that still.

decoys.why: The bridge never swayed, and clumsy describes wobbly, awkward movement.
Weary means tired, which explains nothing about a bridge that never cracked.
Being neat would not stop a bridge from swaying under a marching class.
It is over a creek, but being wet does not keep a bridge from cracking.
Fancy and costly does not explain why it never swayed or cracked.
Rough to the touch says nothing about the bridge holding strong under weight.

example: The bleak winter field had no flowers.
hook: Picture a bleak winter field: gray sky, bare trees, biting wind, and not one flower anywhere.

traps.why: Cheerful is bright and happy, the opposite of bleak.
Black looks like bleak but just names a color.
Bleak places can be windy, but bleak means bare and cheerless.

syn1.tip: Bleak describes a gloomy, empty scene, like a gray winter day. Its feeling is sad and cheerless.

sc1.stem: In winter the island is _____, with icy winds, bare gray rocks, and not a single flower to cheer anyone up.

traps.why: Peaceful sounds pleasant; icy winds and no flowers are cheerless.
Nothing on this island cheers anyone up, so it isn't lovely.
Black looks like bleak, but the rocks are gray, not black.

sc1.tip: 'Icy winds,' 'bare gray rocks,' and 'not a single flower to cheer anyone up' all describe a cold, empty, cheerless place.

decoys.why: The island has not a single flower, so it cannot be full of growing plants.
Nothing on the island can cheer anyone up, so cheerful is the opposite.
Icy winds and bare gray rocks are not shining or glowing.
Bare gray rocks are plain and empty, not rich and fancy.
The sentence says nothing there can cheer anyone up, so jolly does not fit.
Icy winds and bare rocks feel cold and empty, not warm and enthusiastic.

traps.why: Bright and lively is the opposite of bleak.
Cozy is a warm, happy feeling; bleak has no cheer at all.
Bleak is much stronger than a little dull.

syn2.tip: A bleak landscape has nothing cheerful in it. Think empty, gray, and sad.

sc2.stem: In June the old park bursts with roses and laughing children, but by January it looks _____, with leafless trees and empty, frozen benches.

traps.why: Cheerful fits June, but 'but' switches to a gloomy January.
Parks are often crowded, but these benches are empty.
Leafless trees and frozen benches are not colorful.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts June's roses and laughter with January's 'leafless trees and empty, frozen benches,' so the blank means cold and cheerless.

decoys.why: In January the park has leafless trees and frozen benches, not a bright glow.
The word but signals a change from the happy June scene, so cheerful is backwards.
Fertile fits the roses of June, but the blank describes the leafless January park.
Empty, frozen benches are bare, not rich and fancy.
The laughing children are gone by January, so jolly is the opposite.
Gracious describes polite, welcoming people, not an empty, frozen park.

example: The queen threw a lavish party.
hook: A lavish party has gold plates, a chocolate fountain, and far more food than anyone could finish.

traps.why: Plain means simple, the opposite of rich and fancy.
Large parties aren't always fancy; lavish means rich and costly.
A lavish party may be crowded, but lavish means rich and fancy.

syn1.tip: Picture a palace feast with gold plates. Lavish means fancy and expensive, the opposite of simple.

sc1.stem: The prince's birthday party was _____, with a chocolate fountain, gold plates, and a hired orchestra that cost a fortune.

traps.why: Gold plates and a hired orchestra are anything but simple.
An orchestra makes noise, but gold plates show richness.
Boring is a negative word; a chocolate fountain sounds rich and fun.

sc1.tip: The examples 'chocolate fountain, gold plates,' and an orchestra 'that cost a fortune' all point to something rich and costly.

decoys.why: Gold plates and a chocolate fountain are the opposite of bare and cheerless.
A party with a fountain and orchestra is not dark or hopeless.
The party had plenty of fancy things, so it was not in short supply.
Rough to the touch has nothing to do with a party that cost a fortune.
The clue is about cost and fanciness, not about being high or towering.
Strong and solid does not describe gold plates and a hired orchestra.

traps.why: Cheap and simple is the opposite of lavish.
Big parties can be loud, but lavish is about rich, costly things.
Lavish is far grander than nice but ordinary.

syn2.tip: Lavish spending means spending lots of money. Look for the choice about costly, fancy richness.

sc2.stem: Our class picnic was usually just sandwiches on a blanket, but this year a parent planned a _____ feast with silver trays, fancy cakes, and a magician.

traps.why: Simple fits the usual sandwiches, but 'but this year' changes things.
Healthy is about good food, not silver trays and a magician.
Lazy starts like lavish but means not wanting to work.

sc2.tip: 'Usually just sandwiches... but this year' signals a contrast. Silver trays and a magician show the feast was rich and costly.

decoys.why: Silver trays, fancy cakes, and a magician are not bare or cheerless.
This feast had more than usual, so it was not in short supply.
Rough to the touch does not describe silver trays and fancy cakes.
A feast with a magician is not dark or hopeless.
The sentence contrasts plain sandwiches with fancy food, not low with high.
The clue is about fancy, costly treats, not about being strong and solid.

example: The blanket was made of coarse wool.
hook: Sandpaper is coarse: rub it and your fingers feel every rough, scratchy grain.

traps.why: Smooth is the opposite of coarse.
Hoarse rhymes with coarse but describes a scratchy voice.
Sharp things cut; coarse things feel bumpy and rough.

syn1.tip: Coarse sand and coarse wool feel rough and scratchy. Don't mix it up with 'course,' like a golf course.

sc1.stem: Unlike the smooth silk scarf, the burlap sack felt _____ and scratchy against Rosa's skin.

traps.why: Soft would match the silk, but 'unlike' means the sack feels different.
Something scratchy against the skin isn't gentle.
Hoarse sounds like coarse but describes a voice, not a sack.

sc1.tip: 'Unlike the smooth silk' sets up a contrast, and 'scratchy' backs it up. The sack felt rough.

decoys.why: Silk sounds fancy, but the blank describes how the burlap felt: scratchy.
The sentence is about how the sack felt on skin, not how it glowed.
A scratchy sack is not kind or welcoming.
The clue is scratchy, which is about touch, not a happy mood.
The sack felt scratchy, which has nothing to do with being tall.
The blank tells how burlap feels, not whether it is hard to find.

traps.why: Silky means very smooth, the opposite of coarse.
Coarse cloth can be heavy, but coarse is about how it feels.
Coarse cloth can be cheap, but coarse describes its rough feel.

syn2.tip: Picture rubbing a burlap sack or sandpaper. Coarse describes that rough, scratchy feel.

sc2.stem: Dad chose the _____ sandpaper for the splintery fence, because its big, gritty grains would scrape the wood down fast.

traps.why: Fine sandpaper has tiny grains, but this one has big, gritty grains.
Price doesn't explain why big, gritty grains scrape fast.
Hoarse sounds like coarse but describes a scratchy voice.

sc2.tip: 'Because its big, gritty grains would scrape the wood' explains the choice. Big, gritty grains make sandpaper rough.

decoys.why: The sandpaper has big, gritty grains, which says rough, not fancy and costly.
Big, gritty grains describe roughness, not neatness.
Sandpaper is chosen for gritty grains, not for shining brightly.
Sandpaper cannot be kind or welcoming; the clue is its gritty grains.
Dad picked it for its gritty grains, not because it was hard to find.
Serious and quiet describes people or events, not gritty sandpaper.

example: The class stood in solemn silence.
hook: Picture a flag ceremony where everyone stands still and silent; that hushed, serious mood is solemn.

traps.why: Playful means silly and fun, the opposite of solemn.
Sullen looks like solemn but means grumpy and sulky.
Solemn moments are quiet, but solemn doesn't mean lonely.

syn1.tip: Solemn moments are serious and hushed, like a 'solemn promise' or a moment of silence.

sc1.stem: The ceremony was _____: no one spoke or smiled as the flag was slowly raised in the quiet morning air.

traps.why: At a joyful ceremony people would smile, but no one did.
No one spoke, so the ceremony wasn't noisy.
Mornings can be sunny, but no smiles show a serious mood.

sc1.tip: 'No one spoke or smiled' and 'quiet morning air' are examples that show a serious, quiet mood.

decoys.why: No one smiled, so the ceremony could not be happy and cheerful.
No one spoke or smiled, which is the opposite of cheerful.
No one spoke, so there were no clever, funny words.
The quiet ceremony had no warm, enthusiastic cheering at all.
The clue is the silence and seriousness, not fancy or costly things.
The flag was raised slowly and quietly, with nothing awkward or bumping.

traps.why: Silly and loud is the opposite of solemn.
Solemn is serious and respectful, not angry.
Sleepy people are quiet too, but solemn means serious.

syn2.tip: Picture people at a memorial standing in silence. Solemn describes that serious, hushed mood.

sc2.stem: During the school's moment of silence for the veterans, the usually giggly kindergartners became _____, standing still with their hands folded.

traps.why: Playful fits 'usually giggly,' but the kids changed and stood still.
Restless kids wiggle, but these children stood still.
Sullen looks like solemn but means sulky, not respectful.

sc2.tip: 'Usually giggly' contrasts with standing 'still with their hands folded' during a 'moment of silence.' The kids became serious and quiet.

decoys.why: Jolly matches usually giggly, but the kids changed and stood still.
During a moment of silence they stopped being giggly, so cheerful is backwards.
The kids were silent, so they were not making clever jokes.
The kids stood still with folded hands, not bumping into things.
Standing silent with folded hands is not warm and enthusiastic.
The moment was serious and quiet, not glowing with happiness.

example: The sly fox fooled the crow.
hook: Picture a sly fox grinning as it tiptoes off with a stolen egg, hoping no one noticed.

traps.why: Honest is the opposite of sly, since sly people hide what they do.
Shy looks like sly but means nervous around others.
Sly people may be unkind, but sly is about tricking, not cruelty.

syn1.tip: Think of the sly fox in stories who tricks the other animals. Sly means sneaky and tricky.

sc1.stem: With a _____ grin, Max sneakily slipped the last cookie into his pocket when no one was looking.

traps.why: Max was sneaking, so his grin was the opposite of honest.
Shy looks like sly, but Max was being sneaky, not nervous.
Max knew exactly what he was doing, so he was not puzzled.

sc1.tip: Look at "sneakily slipped" and "when no one was looking." The grin matches that sneaky action.

decoys.why: Max was grinning while sneaking a cookie, not being serious and quiet.
Sneakily stealing a cookie is not gentle and obedient.
Taking the last cookie in secret is not kind or polite.
A grin while sneaking a treat is not sad or hopeless.
The clue is sneakily, and a grin cannot be high or towering.

traps.why: Truthful is the opposite of sly, which means tricky.
Dry rhymes with sly and looks similar but means not wet.
Wise is a good, admiring word; sly suggests sneaky tricks.

syn2.tip: A crafty person, like a sly one, uses clever tricks to get what they want. Sly has a sneaky feeling.

sc2.stem: Everyone thought the new puppy was too sweet to cause trouble, but it was actually quite _____, secretly hiding shoes whenever we turned our backs.

traps.why: Hiding shoes behind our backs is the opposite of obedient.
A puppy busy hiding shoes is not lazy.
Shy looks like sly, but the puppy was sneaky, not timid.

sc2.tip: The word "but" shows a contrast with "too sweet," and "secretly hiding shoes whenever we turned our backs" shows sneaky behavior.

decoys.why: Meek matches the sweet puppy everyone expected, but the sentence says it was secretly causing trouble.
Gracious means kind and polite, but the puppy was sneakily hiding shoes behind our backs.
Clumsy puppies cause accidents, but hiding shoes secretly is sneaky on purpose, not awkward.
Wary means careful about danger, which has nothing to do with secretly hiding shoes.
Jolly means cheerful, but the clue is about the puppy being sneaky, not happy.
Solemn means serious and quiet, which does not explain secretly hiding shoes.

example: The sailors were in peril during the storm.
hook: Cartoon heroes tied to train tracks are in peril: great danger, with the train coming fast.

traps.why: Safety is the opposite of peril.
Pearl sounds like peril, but it is a shiny gem from an oyster.
Peril can cause fear, but peril is the danger itself.

syn1.tip: You often hear "in peril," like sailors in peril during a storm. That means in great danger.

sc1.stem: When they heard the ice cracking beneath them, the skaters knew they were in _____ and hurried back to shore.

traps.why: Cracking ice is not lucky; it means the skaters were in danger.
With ice cracking beneath them, the skaters were not in control.
Skaters practice, but cracking ice is about danger, not practice.

sc1.tip: The clue is "ice cracking beneath them" and "hurried back to shore." That shows they were in great danger.

decoys.why: Cracking ice is frightening, and the skaters hurried away, so they were not feeling great joy.
Hurrying off cracking ice is escaping danger, not enjoying a great win.
Grief is deep sadness, but cracking ice puts the skaters in danger, not mourning.

traps.why: Protection keeps you safe, the opposite of peril.
Peril is the danger before harm happens, not the accident itself.
An annoyance is a small bother; peril is serious danger.

syn2.tip: Peril is something that could hurt you badly. A hazard sign warns of exactly that kind of danger.

sc2.stem: Unlike the calm pond where we swim safely, the rushing river below the waterfall puts swimmers in real _____, so lifeguards never let anyone go there.

traps.why: The word "unlike" shows the river is the opposite of safe.
Comfort is a pleasant feeling; the rushing river is dangerous.
The river moves, but lifeguards keep people away because of danger.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" contrasts the river with the pond where "we swim safely," and "lifeguards never let anyone go there" shows danger.

decoys.why: Lifeguards keep swimmers away from the river, so it causes danger, not great joy.
The rushing river is contrasted with the safe pond, so it brings danger, not success.

example: The gloomy sky made us stay inside.
hook: Gloomy days have gray skies and gray moods, like Eeyore under his own little rain cloud.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of gloomy.
Roomy rhymes with gloomy but means having lots of space.
Furious is a bad mood too, but it means angry, not sad.

syn1.tip: Gloomy has a dark, sad feeling, like a gray rainy day. Pick the choice with that same dark, sad feeling.

sc1.stem: On that _____ afternoon, dark clouds hid the sun and everyone in the cabin felt sad and hopeless about the canceled hike.

traps.why: Dark clouds hid the sun, so the afternoon was not sunny.
Cozy is a happy feeling, but everyone felt sad and hopeless.
Nothing says the afternoon was busy; the hike was canceled.

sc1.tip: The sentence says "dark clouds hid the sun" and everyone "felt sad and hopeless." That describes a dark, sad afternoon.

decoys.why: Dark clouds hid the sun, so the afternoon was not shining brightly.
Everyone felt sad and hopeless, which is the opposite of happy and cheerful.
Hearty means warm and enthusiastic, but everyone felt sad and hopeless.
Lavish means rich and fancy, which says nothing about dark clouds or sad feelings.

traps.why: Bright and hopeful is the opposite of gloomy.
A bit let down is too mild; gloomy is deeply sad.
A gloomy room may be quiet, but gloomy means sad and dark.

syn2.tip: The word gloom is inside gloomy. Gloom means darkness or sadness, so gloomy means full of dark, sad feelings.

sc2.stem: Even though her best friend was moving away, Lily refused to stay _____ for long; by dinner she was cheerfully planning video calls.

traps.why: Lily refused to stay this way, then became cheerful, so it means sad.
Lily was busy planning calls, so she did not refuse to stay busy.
A friend moving away makes you sad, not proud.

sc2.tip: "Even though her best friend was moving away" suggests sadness, and "refused to stay" contrasts with "cheerfully." The blank is the sad feeling.

decoys.why: Lily ended up cheerful, so she refused to stay sad, not refused to stay happy.
The sentence shows Lily cheering up, so what she refused to stay was sad, not glowing.
Hearty means warm and enthusiastic, which is how she became, not what she refused to be.
Her friend moving away made her sad; being polite and welcoming is not the feeling here.

meaning: to fly high in the air
example: The kite soared above the beach.
hook: An eagle spreads its wings and soars, rising higher and higher into the sky without a single flap.

traps.why: Sink means go down, the opposite of soar.
Sore sounds like soar but means hurting or achy.
Roar looks like soar but means make a loud, deep sound.

syn1.tip: Think of a kite or an eagle soaring high above you. Soar means go up high in the air.

sc1.stem: Hawks _____ high above the canyon, gliding on warm air for hours without flapping their wings.

traps.why: The hawks stay high for hours, so they are not diving down.
Roar looks like soar, but hawks glide silently, they don't roar.
Hawks nest, but "gliding on warm air" means they are flying.

sc1.tip: The clue is "high above the canyon" and "gliding on warm air for hours." That describes flying high.

decoys.why: Gaze means to look steadily, but the clue says the hawks were gliding on warm air.
The hawks stayed gliding for hours, so they did not suddenly disappear.
Hawks gliding on warm air are flying high, not bragging about themselves.

traps.why: Falling down low is the opposite of soaring up high.
Feel achy means sore, which only sounds like soar.
Move around is too general; soar means fly high specifically.

syn2.tip: Picture a hawk soaring above a canyon. It is flying high in the air, rising on the wind.

sc2.stem: Because the wind was strong and steady at the beach, our new kite could finally _____ above the waves instead of crashing into the sand.

traps.why: Plunge means drop fast, like crashing, which the kite stopped doing.
Wobble is too weak; strong wind lets the kite fly high and steady.
Roar looks like soar, but kites don't make loud sounds.

sc2.tip: "Because the wind was strong and steady" is the cause, and "instead of crashing" is a contrast. The kite rose high.

decoys.why: The kite was finally flying instead of crashing, not disappearing from sight.
Mend means to fix something broken, but the strong wind helped the kite fly high.
Kites cannot think carefully; the wind lifted the kite to fly above the waves.

example: The rabbit vanished into the magician's hat.
hook: Poof: in a magic show, a rabbit can vanish, gone so fast you can't see where it went.

traps.why: Appear means come into sight, the opposite of vanish.
Varnish looks like vanish but means coat wood with a shiny finish.
Shrinking makes something smaller; vanishing makes it gone completely.

syn1.tip: Think of magicians making things vanish into thin air. Vanish means to be gone from sight.

sc1.stem: The magician waved his cape, and the white dove seemed to _____ into thin air in an instant.

traps.why: Things appear out of thin air but go "into thin air" when they disappear.
Returning means coming back, but the dove was leaving sight.
Magicians may multiply doves, but "into thin air" means gone.

sc1.tip: The phrase "into thin air in an instant" means gone very fast. That tells you the dove disappeared suddenly.

decoys.why: In an instant the dove was gone, so it did not stay longer than needed.
Roaming takes time, but the dove went into thin air in an instant.
A magic trick makes the dove disappear, not think carefully into thin air.

traps.why: Come into view is the opposite of vanish.
Slowly shrinking is too weak; vanish means gone, and suddenly.
Getting quiet is about sound; vanishing is about being seen.

syn2.tip: When something vanishes, you suddenly can't see it anymore. Picture a ghost vanishing in a movie.

sc2.stem: The moment the lights flipped on, the scary shadows on my bedroom wall seemed to _____, and suddenly my room looked ordinary again.

traps.why: Bigger shadows would not make the room look ordinary again.
Turning on lights makes shadows go away, not get darker.
Moving shadows would still be scary, not ordinary.

sc2.tip: The lights turning on is the cause, and "suddenly my room looked ordinary again" is the effect. The shadows were gone.

decoys.why: The room looked ordinary again, so the shadows were gone, not staying around.
Turning on lights makes shadows go away, not pile up more.
Shadows wandering around would still be scary, but the room suddenly looked ordinary.
The shadows disappeared when the lights came on; they did not fly high in the air.

example: The crowd gave the team a hearty cheer.
hook: A hearty cheer comes from the heart: loud, warm, and full of feeling, like fans cheering a winning team.

traps.why: Unfriendly is the opposite of a warm, hearty greeting.
Hasty looks like hearty but means done in a hurry.
Polite is too mild; hearty means warm and full of energy.

syn1.tip: You may have heard of a "hearty cheer" or "hearty laugh." Both are big, warm, and full of energy.

sc1.stem: Grandpa gave us a _____ welcome, laughing loudly and wrapping each of us in big, warm hugs.

traps.why: Big, warm hugs show the welcome was warm, not chilly.
Polite is too mild for loud laughing and big hugs.
Laughing loudly and hugging everyone is not shy.

sc1.tip: Look at "laughing loudly" and "big, warm hugs." Those examples show a warm, enthusiastic welcome.

decoys.why: Grandpa was laughing loudly and hugging everyone, which is not sad and hopeless.
Laughing loudly is the opposite of a serious and quiet welcome.
Big, warm hugs make the welcome warm, not cold and cheerless.
Grandpa wrapped everyone in hugs, so he was not watchful and careful.
Laughing loudly and giving big hugs is bold and strong, not quiet and gentle.
Serene means calm and peaceful, but Grandpa was laughing loudly with great enthusiasm.

traps.why: Cool and distant is the opposite of hearty.
Hearty contains heart, but it is not about the body part.
Hearty is loud in a friendly way, not a rude way.

syn2.tip: Hearty has a happy, friendly feeling. A hearty welcome makes you feel truly wanted.

sc2.stem: Instead of the weak, mumbled thanks we expected from the grumpy neighbor, he gave us a _____ handshake and a booming laugh.

traps.why: Instead of weak tells you the handshake was strong, not limp.
The word "instead" shows he surprised us by being friendly, not grumpy.
Secret handshakes exist, but the clue is about a warm, strong greeting.

sc2.tip: "Instead of the weak, mumbled thanks" signals a contrast, and "booming laugh" shows strong, warm energy.

decoys.why: The handshake replaced a weak thanks and came with a booming laugh, so it was not weak.
A booming laugh is not quiet or gentle, so a meek handshake does not match.
The neighbor surprised us with a booming laugh, so his handshake was not sad.
Solemn means serious and quiet, but the sentence pairs the handshake with a booming laugh.
Nothing in the sentence suggests the neighbor was being tricky or sneaky.
A handshake is not long and boring; the sentence is about warmth and strength.

example: Dad inquired about the price of the tickets.
hook: Picture a curious detective who inquires everywhere, asking, "Who was here? What did you see?"

traps.why: Answer is the opposite of inquire, which means ask.
Acquire looks like inquire but means get or gain.
Wondering happens in your head; inquiring means actually asking someone.

syn1.tip: Inquire is like the word inquiry, a question. When you inquire, you ask to find something out.

sc1.stem: Mom called the library to _____ whether they had any copies of the new dragon book.

traps.why: Mom wanted to find out, not tell, so announce is the opposite.
Mom can't decide what the library has; she has to ask.
Calling the library is a way to ask, not guess.

sc1.tip: Mom "called the library" to learn "whether they had any copies." Calling to find out means she asked.

decoys.why: Mom called the library, so she was asking them, not just thinking about it.
Calling the library is a way to find something out, not to hide it.

traps.why: Giving answers is the opposite of inquiring.
The in at the start does not mean go inside here.
Demanding loudly is too strong; inquire just means ask.

syn2.tip: Signs that say "inquire inside" mean come in and ask. Inquire means to ask questions.

sc2.stem: Because Sam was curious about how the ancient pyramids were built, he decided to _____ at the museum's front desk during our field trip.

traps.why: Sam was curious, so he needed answers, not to explain.
Being curious makes you ask, not complain.
Waiting at a desk won't answer Sam's question about the pyramids.

sc2.tip: "Because Sam was curious" is the cause. A curious person goes to the front desk to ask questions.

decoys.why: Sam was curious, so he wanted to ask questions, not brag about himself.
Being curious calls for simply asking, not begging at the front desk.
Sam was curious and wanted answers, so leaving the desk would not help him.
Disappearing would not satisfy Sam's curiosity about how the pyramids were built.
Sam was on a field trip and curious, not planning to live at the front desk.
You cannot wander freely while staying at the front desk to learn something.

example: The fox tried to deceive the hens.
hook: Deceive rhymes with believe: when someone deceives you, they make you believe something false.

traps.why: Receive looks like deceive but means get or accept.
Teasing is playful joking; deceiving means making someone believe something false.
People who deceive may get punished, but punish isn't the meaning.

syn1.tip: Think of a magician or a fox in a story who makes others believe something false. That's deceiving.

sc1.stem: The chameleon changes color to _____ hungry birds, tricking them into thinking it is just a leaf.

traps.why: Warning gives a true signal; the chameleon is tricking the birds.
The chameleon wants birds to ignore it, not come closer.
Looking like a leaf doesn't scare birds; it tricks them.

sc1.tip: The sentence says the color change is "tricking them into thinking it is just a leaf." That means fooling the birds.

decoys.why: The chameleon looks like a leaf, not like the birds, so it is not copying them.
The chameleon copies a leaf, not the birds, to fool them.
The chameleon hides itself, not the birds, so conceal does not fit with birds.
The sentence says it is tricking the birds, not loving and caring for them.
Changing color is how it tricks the birds, not how it fears them.

traps.why: To inform is to give true facts, the opposite of deceive.
Deserve looks like deceive but means earn or be worthy of.
Tricksters may steal, but deceive means fool someone, not take things.

syn2.tip: Deceive has a sneaky, untruthful feeling. If you deceive someone, you lead them to believe something that isn't true.

sc2.stem: Grandma is so honest that she would never _____ anyone, even to win a card game or keep a surprise secret.

traps.why: Being honest has nothing to do with refusing to help.
Honest people still thank others; thanking is a kind act.
Receive looks like deceive but doesn't fit the clue about honesty.

sc2.tip: "So honest" plus "would never" tells you the blank is something an honest person refuses to do, like tricking people.

decoys.why: You cannot hide a person by being dishonest; the clue honest points to tricking.
Copying someone has nothing to do with being honest or winning a card game.
Grandpa's honesty is the clue, and copying someone is not a dishonest act.
An honest grandma would surely love people, so never cherishing anyone makes no sense.
Fearing someone has nothing to do with honesty or keeping a secret.

example: Discard the moldy bread in the trash.
hook: In card games you discard a card you don't want by throwing it away onto the pile.

traps.why: Keep is the opposite of discard.
Discover starts like discard but means find something new.
Discard contains card, but it doesn't mean hand out cards.

syn1.tip: In card games, the discard pile holds cards players threw away. Discard means get rid of something.

sc1.stem: Please _____ your empty juice boxes in the recycling bin instead of leaving them on the lunch table.

traps.why: You don't save empty boxes in a recycling bin; you get rid of them.
Empty boxes go in the bin; they are not filled there.
Decorating doesn't belong with a recycling bin; the boxes are trash.

sc1.tip: The clue is "empty juice boxes" going "in the recycling bin." Putting trash in a bin means throwing it away.

decoys.why: You do not lovingly keep empty juice boxes; the recycling bin means throwing them away.
Putting boxes in the recycling bin is throwing them away, not hiding them.
Empty juice boxes going into the recycling bin do not need fixing.
You put juice boxes in the bin; you do not break them into pieces.
Demolish means tearing down something big, not putting boxes in a bin.

traps.why: Hold on to is the opposite of discard.
Setting something aside is for later; discarding gets rid of it.
You may sort things before discarding, but sorting isn't throwing away.

syn2.tip: Dis can mean away or apart. To discard is to put something away from you, like trash.

sc2.stem: Mia usually saves every drawing she makes, but this year she decided to _____ the old ones to make room in her drawer for new treasures.

traps.why: The word "but" means Mia did the opposite of keep.
Rereading old drawings wouldn't make room in her drawer.
Discover looks like discard, but she already knew about her drawings.

sc2.tip: "Usually saves" and "but" signal a contrast, and "to make room" shows she got rid of the old drawings.

decoys.why: Mia wants to make room, so she is getting rid of drawings, not piling them up.
The word but shows she is changing her habit of saving drawings.
Fixing old drawings would not make room in her drawer.
Copying the old drawings would add more, not make room.
Just thinking about the drawings would not clear space in her drawer.

example: The twins are always up to mischief.
hook: Mischief is the playful kind of trouble, like a puppy grabbing your sock and racing off with it.

traps.why: Obedience means doing as you're told, the opposite of mischief.
Misfortune starts like mischief but means bad luck.
Crime is far too serious; mischief is playful bad behavior.

syn1.tip: You hear "up to mischief" about kids or pets causing small, playful trouble. That's naughtiness.

sc1.stem: While we were out, the kittens got into _____, playfully unrolling the toilet paper and knocking pens off the desk.

traps.why: Kittens unrolling toilet paper are wide awake, not in bed.
Unrolling toilet paper is naughty play, not something dangerous.
Getting into line means behaving; the kittens were making a mess.

sc1.tip: The examples "playfully unrolling the toilet paper" and "knocking pens off the desk" show playful bad behavior.

decoys.why: The kittens were playfully unrolling paper, which is naughty fun, not great danger.
The kittens made a mess, but they got into playful trouble, not broken pieces.
Nothing in the sentence is about water; the kittens were playing and knocking things over.
Unrolling toilet paper is playful bad behavior, not something costly and pleasant.
Knocking pens off the desk is the opposite of being careful.

traps.why: Good manners are the opposite of mischief.
Both start with mis, but mischief is on purpose, not an error.
Violence is much too strong; mischief is playful and harmless.

syn2.tip: Mischief has a playful but naughty feeling, like hiding someone's shoes as a joke.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's eyes twinkled with _____ as he hid the TV remote under Dad's pillow and then pretended to help search for it.

traps.why: Twinkling eyes and a playful trick show fun, not sorrow.
Pretending to search is not honest; it's part of the trick.
Grandpa hid the remote himself, so he wasn't worried.

sc2.tip: The twinkling eyes give the playful tone, and hiding the remote and "pretended to help" show a naughty joke.

decoys.why: Grandpa was playing a sneaky prank, not being careful to avoid danger.
Twinkling eyes and a playful prank do not show great tiredness.
Eyes can be wet, but the sentence is about Grandpa's playful prank.
Hiding the remote is a harmless joke, not great danger.
Grandpa planned his playful trick; his twinkling eyes show fun, not a natural feeling.

example: She pondered the puzzle for an hour.
hook: Picture Winnie the Pooh tapping his head saying think, think, think: that is pondering.

traps.why: Ignore means to pay no attention, the opposite of thinking carefully.
Wander rhymes with ponder but means to walk around.
You ponder before you decide, but deciding is making the choice.

syn1.tip: Picture someone with a hand on their chin, thinking hard. That is pondering, so look for the word about careful thought.

sc1.stem: Before choosing a move, the chess player sat silently to _____ every possible choice for ten minutes.

traps.why: Skipping choices is the opposite of studying them for ten minutes.
Announcing means speaking aloud, but the player sat silently.
Skimming is a quick look; ten silent minutes means much deeper thought.

sc1.tip: The clues are "sat silently" and "for ten minutes." Someone quiet for that long before a move is thinking very carefully.

decoys.why: The player sat silently to think about each move, not to fear it.
Before choosing a move, a player thinks carefully, not lovingly cares for choices.
Sitting silently for ten minutes before a move is thinking, not hiding choices.
The player was deciding on a move, not copying how someone acts.
You cannot eat chess choices; the player was thinking hard before moving.

traps.why: Forgetting about something is the opposite of thinking it over.
Talking over is discussing out loud; pondering happens quietly in your head.
Glancing is a quick look, much weaker than careful thinking.

syn2.tip: When you ponder a puzzle, you turn it over and over in your mind. Choose the phrase that means slow, careful thinking.

sc2.stem: Instead of answering right away, Maya took a long walk to _____ whether she should join the soccer team or the school band.

traps.why: Forgetting the question is the opposite of thinking it through.
Announcing tells others; a long walk alone is for thinking.
Ignoring the choice would not need a long walk at all.

sc2.tip: "Instead of answering right away" shows Maya slowed down. A long walk before choosing means she wanted to think carefully.

decoys.why: Maya is trying to make up her mind, not hide her choice from anyone.

example: Lofty mountains rose above the village.
hook: A loft is a high space under a roof, and lofty things are high up like that.

traps.why: Low is the opposite of lofty.
Mountains are often rocky, but lofty is about how high something is.
Steep tells how sharply a slope rises, not how high it reaches.

syn1.tip: Lofty starts like loft, the high room under a roof. Think of something that rises far above you.

sc1.stem: The eagle built its nest on a _____ cliff, so high above the valley that clouds sometimes drifted below it.

traps.why: A low cliff could not have clouds drifting below it.
A short cliff is the opposite of one high above the valley.
Crumbling tells the cliff's condition, but the clue is about height.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: "so high above the valley that clouds sometimes drifted below it." Pick the word meaning very high.

decoys.why: The clue is height, since clouds drifted below the nest, and sturdy describes strength instead.
Nothing says the cliff was cheerless; the sentence stresses how high it was.
The sentence describes height, with clouds below the nest, not a dark or sad mood.
Clouds drifting below the nest show the cliff was high, not rough to the touch.
An eagle would not build its nest on a weak cliff, and the clue is about height.
The sentence explains how high the cliff was, not how peaceful it felt.

traps.why: Deep goes down; lofty goes up.
Wide is about side to side, not how high something rises.
Slightly raised is far too small; lofty means towering.

syn2.tip: Picture lofty mountains rising above a village. The answer should describe great height.

sc2.stem: Unlike the short little houses along the street, the city's newest tower was so _____ that its top floors disappeared into the morning fog.

traps.why: A tiny tower's top floors could not vanish into the fog.
New towers are often modern, but the clue is about height.
Narrow is about width, not how high the tower rises.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the short little houses" sets up a contrast, so the tower must be the opposite of short. Its top "disappeared into the morning fog."

decoys.why: The tower is compared to short houses, so the point is height, not fanciness.
Top floors vanishing into fog shows the tower is tall, not just strong.
A glowing tower would stand out, but its top floors disappeared into the fog.
The fog is there to show height, and the contrast is with short houses.
The sentence contrasts the tower with short houses, so it is about height, not mood.
Being neat would not make the top floors disappear into the fog.

example: The empty house was eerie at night.
hook: Eerie sounds like the long eee of a creaky door slowly opening in a dark, empty house.

traps.why: Cozy means warm and comfortable, the opposite of creepy.
Airy sounds a bit like eerie but means light and breezy.
Eerie places are often dark, but eerie means strange and spooky.

syn1.tip: Think of an eerie silence in a haunted house. The word gives you shivers, so pick the spooky feeling.

sc1.stem: At dusk, the empty fairground had an _____ quiet, strange and a little spooky, as the Ferris wheel creaked in the wind.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of strange.
Inviting is a warm, happy feeling; the quiet here is spooky.
Early looks like eerie but is about time, not feeling.

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank define it: "strange and a little spooky." Choose the word that means exactly that.

traps.why: Warm and welcoming is the opposite of a spooky feeling.
Eerie is a little scary, not deadly or terrifying.
Light and breezy means airy, which only sounds like eerie.

syn2.tip: Eerie things feel odd and give you a small chill, not a full scream. Look for strange plus a little scary.

sc2.stem: The old lighthouse was so _____ after dark, with its broken windows and strange tapping sounds, that even my brave cousin refused to go inside.

traps.why: A cozy place would not scare a brave cousin away.
Airy sounds like eerie but means breezy, which would not scare anyone.
Peaceful places are calm, not full of strange tapping sounds.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: "even my brave cousin refused to go inside." With "strange tapping sounds," the place must feel spooky.

decoys.why: Broken windows and strange tapping scared even a brave cousin, so the lighthouse was not peaceful.
The lighthouse was dark and broken, not shining brightly.
Broken windows show the lighthouse was not neat and in order.
Nothing here is fancy or costly; the details are spooky and broken.
The cousin refused to go in because it was scary, not because it was solid.
Strange tapping sounds make a place frightening, not boring.

meaning: to fix something broken or torn
example: Grandma will mend the hole in my jeans.
hook: Picture Grandma with a needle and thread, mending the hole in your favorite jeans so they're good as new.

traps.why: Breaking something is the opposite of fixing it.
Lend rhymes with mend but means to let someone borrow.
You might clean old clothes too, but mending means fixing them.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "mend a fence" or "mend a sock." Both mean fixing something that is broken or torn.

sc1.stem: Instead of throwing out the torn fishing net, the fisherman sat down to _____ it with new string.

traps.why: Cutting would make the torn net worse, not better.
Washing a net needs no new string; he is fixing the tear.
Selling the net would not need new string.

sc1.tip: "Instead of throwing out the torn fishing net" means he keeps it. Using "new string" on a torn net means he fixes it.

decoys.why: The sentence says instead of throwing out the net, so discarding it is the opposite.
He used new string to fix the net, not to tear it apart.
The net was already torn; new string is for fixing it, not breaking it.
New string is for repairing a torn net, not hiding it.
You cannot love something with new string; the string is used to fix it.
The fisherman was repairing the net with string, not eating it.

traps.why: Tearing apart breaks things; mending fixes them.
Throwing away is what you do instead of mending something.
Send rhymes with mend but means to make something go somewhere.

syn2.tip: When something broken is mended, it works properly again. Pick the phrase that means fixing.

sc2.stem: My bike chain snapped on the way to school, so after class Dad showed me how to _____ it so I could ride home.

traps.why: The chain was already broken; breaking it would not let you ride.
Painting the chain would not make the bike work again.
Bend rhymes with mend, but bending a chain does not fix it.

sc2.tip: The chain "snapped," and afterward "I could ride home." Something broken that works again must have been fixed.

decoys.why: Throwing the chain away would not let you ride home.
The chain was already snapped, so tearing it down would not get you home.
Breaking the chain more would not help you ride home.
Hiding a snapped chain would not let you ride your bike home.
Copying a chain makes no sense; Dad was showing how to fix it.
A snapped chain needs fixing so you can ride, not sending away.

example: The meek lamb followed the shepherd.
hook: Meek rhymes with squeak: picture a meek little mouse squeaking softly and doing whatever it's told.

traps.why: Bossy people give orders; meek people quietly follow them.
Sleek looks like meek but means smooth and shiny.
Meek animals may be small, but meek is about behavior, not size.

syn1.tip: Think of the meek lamb following the shepherd. It is quiet, soft, and does what it is told.

sc1.stem: The _____ new puppy never barked back at the bossy cat; it quietly and gently did whatever the cat wanted.

traps.why: A fierce puppy would bark back, not quietly obey.
Stubborn means refusing to go along, the opposite of obeying.
Puppies are often fluffy, but the clue describes behavior.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: the puppy "never barked back" and "quietly and gently did whatever the cat wanted."

decoys.why: The puppy quietly did whatever the cat wanted, which is gentle, not sneaky.
The puppy is described as quiet and gentle, not quick and full of energy.
A puppy that never barks back is gentle and obedient, not strong and enthusiastic.
The sentence is about obeying the cat, not about bumping into things.
The clue is that the puppy obeyed quietly, which has nothing to do with being strong.
Nothing says the puppy was boring; it was quiet and obedient.

traps.why: Loud and bossy is the opposite of meek.
Weak and sickly describes health, not how someone behaves.
Sleek looks like meek but describes smooth fur or hair.

syn2.tip: A meek person never argues back and follows what others say. Pick the phrase about calm, obeying behavior.

sc2.stem: Although her twin brother argued with every rule, Lena was _____ and always did what the teacher asked without a single complaint.

traps.why: Stubborn fits her brother, but "although" shows Lena is different.
Sleek looks like meek but means smooth, which says nothing about obeying.
Tiny is about size; the clue is about obeying without complaint.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with the brother who "argued with every rule." Lena does the opposite: she quietly obeys.

decoys.why: Lena simply did what she was asked, so she was obedient, not sneaky.
The sentence is about obeying without complaint, not about doing things too quickly.
The clue is that Lena obeyed quietly, not that she was quick and energetic.
Following rules without complaint has nothing to do with bumping into things.
Nothing says Lena was sad; she just obeyed without complaint, unlike her brother.
Lena is being contrasted with a brother who argues, so the point is obedience, not fanciness.

example: The smell of popcorn lingered in the room.
hook: When the smell of popcorn lingers, it hangs around the room long after the movie ends.

traps.why: Leaving is the opposite of staying longer.
Hurrying is rushing off, the opposite of lingering.
Wandering is moving around; lingering is staying in one place.

syn1.tip: Think of a smell that lingers after cooking. It stays around longer than you expect.

sc1.stem: After the concert ended, the fans chose to _____ near the stage for another hour, hoping to meet the band.

traps.why: Scattering means spreading out and going away, not staying near the stage.
The band performs; the fans are staying to meet them.
A pause is brief; another hour is much longer.

sc1.tip: The clues are "after the concert ended" and "for another hour." Staying after it's over means staying longer than needed.

decoys.why: The fans stayed another hour to meet the band, so they did not disappear.
People cannot fly high in the air; the fans waited near the stage.
The fans were hoping to meet the band, not shaking from fear or cold.
The sentence is about staying longer to meet the band, not bragging.

traps.why: Rushing away is the opposite of staying longer.
Line up starts like linger but means to stand in a row.
Lingering is staying a bit longer, not forever.

syn2.tip: People linger after a party when they don't want to leave yet. Pick the phrase about staying past the end.

sc2.stem: Most kids rush out the moment the last bell rings, but my best friend and I like to _____ in the empty classroom, chatting with our teacher.

traps.why: Hurrying matches the other kids, but "but" shows we do the opposite.
You can't vanish and still be chatting with your teacher.
Lunge looks a little like linger but means to jump forward suddenly.

sc2.tip: "Most kids rush out ... but" sets up a contrast. If others rush away, we stay behind longer.

decoys.why: The friends stay behind chatting with the teacher, so they do not disappear at all.
Nobody flies high in a classroom; the sentence is about staying late to chat.
They are happily chatting with their teacher, not shaking from fear or cold.
The sentence contrasts rushing out with staying behind, not with bragging.

example: The brothers had a quarrel over the remote.
hook: Two squirrels fighting over one acorn are having a squirrel quarrel.

traps.why: An agreement is the opposite of an angry argument.
Quarter starts like quarrel but means one fourth or a coin.
A conversation is any talk; a quarrel is an angry one.

syn1.tip: Picture brothers fighting over the TV remote with raised voices. That angry back and forth is a quarrel.

sc1.stem: The sisters had a loud, angry _____ over who would get the top bunk in their new room.

traps.why: A hug is friendly, but the sentence says loud and angry.
A giggle can be loud, but it is happy, not angry.
A deal settles who gets what; loud and angry signal a fight.

sc1.tip: The words "loud, angry" come right before the blank, and they disagree "over who would get the top bunk."

decoys.why: The sisters are angry with each other, which describes an argument, not a careless mistake.
A loud, angry fight over a bunk is not a great win or success.
The sisters are arguing over the top bunk, not eating a special meal.
Loud and angry describe an argument between the sisters, not a difficult situation.
The sentence describes an angry argument, not something blocking their way.
An angry fight over the bunk is a problem, not a cure or fix.

traps.why: A friendly chat is the opposite of an angry fight.
A polite debate is calm; a quarrel is angry.
A battle is a big fight with weapons, much stronger than a quarrel.

syn2.tip: A quarrel uses words, not fists, and the people are upset. Pick the phrase with both angry and disagreeing.

sc2.stem: After their _____ about whose turn it was on the swing, Mia and Jada refused to speak to each other for the rest of recess.

traps.why: Friends who agree would not stop speaking to each other.
A joke is lighthearted; this ended with the girls not speaking.
Quarter looks like quarrel but means one fourth or a coin.

sc2.tip: Look at the result: they "refused to speak to each other." Something about "whose turn it was" made them angry.

decoys.why: They refused to speak to each other afterward, so they were not feeling great joy.
Two girls who stop speaking to each other did not share a great success.
The disagreement was about whose turn it was on the swing, not a special meal.
Something that made them stop speaking caused a problem; it was not a fix.
Nothing is being copied here; the girls argued about whose turn it was.

meaning: done too quickly, without enough care
example: His hasty answer had a silly mistake.
hook: Haste makes waste: a hasty job done in a rush often has to be done all over again.

traps.why: Careful is the opposite of hasty.
Tasty looks and sounds like hasty but describes good food.
Busy people may rush, but busy means having lots to do.

syn1.tip: Hasty comes from haste, as in "haste makes waste." Haste means hurry, so look for a hurrying word.

sc1.stem: Tom's _____ drawing, scribbled in ten seconds just before the bell, was too messy for anyone to recognize.

traps.why: Ten seconds of scribbling is not careful work.
Colorful is about the drawing's look, not how fast it was made.
Beautiful is praise, but the drawing was too messy to recognize.

sc1.tip: The clues are "scribbled in ten seconds" and "too messy." Rushing caused the mess, so pick the word for done too fast.

decoys.why: The drawing took only ten seconds, so it was not long and slow.
A messy scribble done in ten seconds is not rich and fancy.
The sentence calls the drawing too messy to recognize, not shining or glowing.
Strong and solid does not describe how quickly or carelessly a drawing was scribbled.
A drawing rushed out just before the bell is not calm and peaceful.
Very high or towering has nothing to do with a drawing scribbled in ten seconds.

traps.why: Done with care is the opposite of hasty.
On time is about the deadline, not about rushing carelessly.
Done very well is praise; hasty work usually has mistakes.

syn2.tip: A hasty answer often has a silly mistake because it was rushed. Pick the phrase about too much speed.

sc2.stem: Instead of making a _____ choice at the pet store, Ben spent a whole week reading about each kind of lizard before picking one.

traps.why: Ben was careful, so careful is what he did, not what he avoided.
Reading for a week was wise, so it can't be what Ben avoided.
Tasty looks like hasty but describes food, not a choice.

sc2.tip: "Instead of" means Ben avoided the blank. He took "a whole week," so he avoided a choice made too fast.

decoys.why: The contrast is with spending a whole week reading, which is about speed, not sneakiness.
The sentence contrasts careful research with a rushed choice, not with a sad one.
A choice is not strong and solid; the clue is the week Ben spent reading.
Very high or towering does not describe a choice made at a pet store.
The sentence contrasts a slow, careful choice with a rushed one, not an enthusiastic one.

example: My little brother imitates everything I do.
hook: A copycat imitates: when your little brother repeats every word you say, he is imitating you.

traps.why: Inventing makes something new; imitating copies what exists.
Irritate looks like imitate but means to annoy.
You may copy someone you admire, but admiring is just liking them.

syn1.tip: Think of a copycat little brother who does everything you do. That is imitating.

sc1.stem: Little kids often _____ their older siblings, copying the way they dress, talk, and play.

traps.why: Kids who ignore their siblings would not copy how they dress.
Invite starts like imitate but means asking someone to come.
Older siblings teach younger ones; here the little kids copy them.

sc1.tip: The words after the blank explain it: "copying the way they dress, talk, and play." Pick the word that means copy.

decoys.why: The sentence explains the blank as copying how siblings dress and talk, not loving them.
Copying the way someone dresses and talks is not tricking them.
Kids who copy their siblings want to be like them, not send them away.
The sentence is about copying siblings, not hiding them.
Copying how siblings dress and play is the opposite of throwing them away.
Kids do not eat their siblings; the sentence says they copy them.

traps.why: Doing the opposite is the reverse of imitating.
You might look up to someone you copy, but that's respecting, not copying.
Make angry means irritate, which only looks like imitate.

syn2.tip: Imitation means acting just like someone else, like a parrot repeating words. Pick the phrase about copying.

sc2.stem: Rather than _____ her favorite singer's style, Priya wanted a look all her own, so she designed her outfits from scratch.
