traps.why: Priya does invent, but you can't invent a style that already exists.
Irritate looks like imitate but means annoy, which makes no sense here.
Ignoring the style fits what Priya does, not what she avoids.

sc2.tip: "Rather than" sets up a contrast with "a look all her own." The opposite of your own look is copying someone else's.

decoys.why: Throwing away the singer's style would match wanting her own look, so rather than makes no sense.
Priya wanted a look all her own, so the contrast is with copying, not hiding.
You cannot tear down a style; the contrast is with designing her own.
Priya cannot forbid a singer's style; the sentence contrasts copying with making her own.
Nothing is broken here; the clue is that she wanted a look all her own.
You cannot eat a style; the sentence is about copying versus creating.

example: My frail great-grandmother still loves to garden.
hook: Frail and fragile come from the same Latin word, and both describe things that break easily.

traps.why: Sturdy means strong and solid, the opposite of frail.
Fair shares letters with frail but means just or light colored.
Many frail people are old, but elderly is about age, not weakness.

syn1.tip: Frail sounds like fragile, the word stamped on boxes that break easily. Look for the word meaning easily hurt.

sc1.stem: At ninety-five, Mrs. Ortiz looks _____, thin and easily hurt, yet she still walks her tiny dog every morning.

traps.why: Sturdy is the opposite of thin and easily hurt.
Fair looks a bit like frail but doesn't mean easily hurt.
Cheerful describes mood, but the clue describes her body.

sc1.tip: The blank is explained right after it: "thin and easily hurt." The "yet" only shows she stays active anyway.

decoys.why: The sentence explains the blank as thin and easily hurt, which is the opposite of strong.
Thin and easily hurt describes someone weak, not someone strong and full of energy.
The sentence says she looks thin and easily hurt, not quick and energetic.
Towering has nothing to do with being thin and easily hurt.
The words thin and easily hurt describe her body, not a sneaky personality.
Rough to the touch does not match thin and easily hurt.

traps.why: Strong and healthy is the opposite of frail.
Being a little tired is much milder than being frail.
Old and wise describes age and mind, not a weak body.

syn2.tip: A frail person might break a bone from a small fall. Choose the phrase about a weak body.

sc2.stem: The baby bird was too _____ to fly on its own, so we kept it warm in a shoebox until its wings grew stronger.

traps.why: Being too healthy would never stop a bird from flying.
Lazy is about not wanting to; the bird's wings needed to grow stronger.
Fair looks a bit like frail but makes no sense for a bird.

sc2.tip: Look at cause and effect: it couldn't fly "until its wings grew stronger." So the bird must have been weak.

decoys.why: The bird needed its wings to grow stronger, so it was weak, not strong.
A bird that cannot fly until its wings grow stronger is not strong and energetic.
The bird was too weak to fly, not quick and full of energy.
Being high up would not stop a bird from flying; weak wings would.
The problem was that the bird's wings were weak, not that it acted carelessly.
Rich and fancy has nothing to do with a bird too weak to fly.

example: Locked out without a key was a predicament.
hook: Stuck up a tree with the ladder gone, that's a predicament, a tricky spot that's hard to get out of.

traps.why: A solution gets you out of trouble; a predicament is the trouble itself.
Prediction looks similar but means a guess about the future.
An adventure sounds fun; a predicament is an unpleasant spot.

syn1.tip: Picture someone stuck and saying, "What a predicament!" The word names a tricky, unpleasant spot.

sc1.stem: Locked out in the rain with no key and a dead phone, Ava was in quite a _____.

traps.why: Prediction looks like predicament but means a guess about what will happen.
Paradise is a perfect place, the opposite of being stuck in the rain.
Shelter is about rain too, but Ava is locked outside with none.

sc1.tip: The clues "locked out," "no key," and "a dead phone" all describe trouble. You need a word for a hard situation.

decoys.why: Being locked out in the rain with a dead phone is unpleasant, not costly and pleasant.
Ava has a problem with no key and no phone, not a cure or fix.
Ava is alone and locked out, so there is no one to argue with.
Ava is locked out of her home, so she is not in a dwelling at all.
Being stuck in the rain with a dead phone has nothing to do with a meal.

traps.why: A lucky break is good fortune, the opposite of a tough spot.
Pre- seems to mean before here, but predicament has nothing to do with warnings.
A mistake can cause a predicament, but the word names the situation.

syn2.tip: Words like plight and jam fit too. If you are in a predicament, you are stuck in a tough spot.

sc2.stem: Maya thought skipping her homework would give her a fun, free evening, but it turned into a real _____ when the teacher called on her to explain the answers.

traps.why: Treat fits the fun evening, but "but" shows things went badly.
Prediction looks similar but means a guess, not a tough situation.
Skipping work feels like a vacation, but the teacher put her on the spot.

sc2.tip: The word "but" flips the fun evening into trouble. Being called on with no homework done is a tough spot.

decoys.why: Being called on without doing homework is stressful, not a moment of great joy.
Maya hoped for a fun evening, but the word but shows things went badly, not pleasantly.
Nothing in the sentence is about a meal; Maya ended up in a tough spot.
Being called on without answers created a problem rather than fixing one.

example: The garden felt serene in the early morning.
hook: Picture a lake at sunrise, still as glass, with not a sound anywhere; that scene is serene.

traps.why: Frantic means wild and panicked, the opposite of serene.
Sincere sounds a bit like serene but means honest.
Sleepy people may be calm, but serene is about peace, not tiredness.

syn1.tip: Serene sounds soft and smooth, like a quiet lake. Think of a "serene sunset": calm and peaceful.

sc1.stem: Even during the noisy thunderstorm, Grandma's face stayed _____, calm and peaceful, as she knitted by the window.

traps.why: Frightened fits a thunderstorm, but the sentence says her face stayed calm.
Stormy matches the weather, not Grandma's calm and peaceful face.
Gloomy is quiet but sad; the sentence says calm and peaceful.

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank, "calm and peaceful," tell you the meaning. "Even during" shows the storm didn't upset her.

decoys.why: The sentence says her face stayed calm and peaceful, not frightened by the storm.
The storm may be gloomy, but her face is described as calm and peaceful.
Thunderstorms can feel eerie, but the sentence describes her face as calm and peaceful.
Brisk means quick and energetic, but her face stayed calm and peaceful.
Nothing suggests sneakiness; the sentence says her face was calm and peaceful.
Hearty means strong and enthusiastic, but the sentence describes a calm and peaceful face.

traps.why: Nervous means worried and jumpy, the opposite of serene.
Bored is calm in a dull, unhappy way; serene is calm in a pleasant way.
Scenic looks like serene but means having a pretty view.

syn2.tip: Feel the word's mood: gentle and pleasant. Serene people and places are untroubled and at peace.

sc2.stem: Unlike the crowded, noisy cafeteria at lunch, the school library was _____, with only the soft turning of pages breaking the silence.

traps.why: Chaotic describes the cafeteria, and "unlike" says the library is different.
Scenic looks like serene but means having a pretty view.
Boring is a negative feeling; the clue is about calm and quiet.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" signals the library is the opposite of crowded and noisy. "Soft" and "silence" point to a calm, peaceful word.

decoys.why: The library is contrasted with the noisy cafeteria, so it is quiet, not full of energy.
Hearty means warm and enthusiastic, but the library is described by its silence.
The sentence is about quiet versus noise, not about how fancy the library is.
A room cannot be sneaky; the clue is the silence and soft turning of pages.
Sharp edges have nothing to do with the quiet the sentence describes.
The sentence compares noise levels, not how rough something feels.

example: The timid kitten hid under the bed.
hook: A timid mouse peeks out, squeaks, and darts back into its hole at the smallest sound.

traps.why: Bold means brave and daring, the opposite of timid.
Timid creatures are often small, but timid is about fear, not size.
Humid rhymes with timid but means damp and sticky air.

syn1.tip: Think of a "timid puppy" hiding behind its owner. Timid people hang back because they are a little afraid.

sc1.stem: Our new kitten is so _____, or easily frightened, that even the click of the toaster sends her under the sofa.

traps.why: Fearless means not afraid, the opposite of easily frightened.
Kittens are often curious, but hiding at a click shows fear.
Size isn't the point; "easily frightened" tells you the word.

sc1.tip: "Or easily frightened" right after the blank defines the word. Hiding under the sofa at a toaster click shows fear.

decoys.why: A calm kitten would not hide from a toaster click; the sentence says easily frightened.
The sentence defines the blank as easily frightened, and a quiet, calm kitten would not hide.
Hearty means strong and bold, but this kitten runs from a tiny click.
Hiding under the sofa here comes from fear, not from being sneaky.
The sentence explains the word as easily frightened, not awkward or bumping into things.
The kitten is scared, not strange or scary itself.

traps.why: Full of courage means brave, the opposite of timid.
Frozen with terror is far too strong; timid is just easily scared.
Both describe a quick feeling, but timid is about fear, not anger.

syn2.tip: A timid person shies away from new things. If you see a word about being easily scared, that's the match.

sc2.stem: Although Sam was loud and silly with his family at home, he was _____ on the first day of school, barely whispering his name when the teacher asked.

traps.why: Rowdy fits Sam at home, but "although" shows school was different.
Cheerful is a happy feeling; barely whispering shows he was nervous.
Talkative people speak a lot, but Sam barely whispered.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets home behavior against school behavior. "Barely whispering his name" shows he was shy and nervous.

decoys.why: Sam is loud at home but barely whispers at school, so he is not enthusiastic there.
Barely whispering his name shows shyness, not quick energy.
Whispering his name shows Sam was shy, not tricky or sneaky.
The sentence is about how quietly Sam spoke, not about bumping into things.
Barely whispering his name shows nervousness, not cleverness.
Lavish describes costly, fancy things, not a shy boy whispering his name.

example: The vase shattered on the floor.
hook: Drop a glass on a tile floor and hear it shatter into a sparkling spray of pieces.

traps.why: Repair means to fix, the opposite of shatter.
Scatter sounds like shatter but means to spread things around.
A crack is too weak; shatter means breaking into many pieces.

syn1.tip: Hear the crash in the word shatter. Glass that shatters ends up in lots of pieces.

sc1.stem: If the baseball hits the window, the glass will _____ into a hundred tiny pieces all over the floor.

traps.why: Glass that holds stays in one piece, not a hundred.
Chatter sounds like shatter but means to talk fast.
A dent is a small dip, not a hundred tiny pieces.

sc1.tip: "Into a hundred tiny pieces" tells you exactly what happens. You need a verb that means to break apart completely.

decoys.why: The glass ends up in a hundred pieces, which is breaking, not fixing.
The pieces end up all over the floor, so the glass did not disappear.
The baseball might fly high, but the glass breaks into pieces on the floor.
Shaking would not leave a hundred tiny pieces all over the floor.
The glass is breaking apart into pieces, not piling up over time.

traps.why: Fixing with glue puts things back together, the opposite of shatter.
That means chatter, which only sounds like shatter.
A small crack is too weak; shatter breaks into many pieces.

syn2.tip: Think of "shattered glass" after an accident: lots of tiny bits. To shatter is to break into many pieces at once.

sc2.stem: Mia hoped her phone would survive the fall, but the moment it hit the sidewalk, she watched its screen _____, sending bits of glass across the pavement.

traps.why: Survive is what Mia hoped for, but "but" shows it didn't happen.
Screens glow, but bits of glass flying means it broke.
A smudge is far too weak to send bits of glass flying.

sc2.tip: "But" warns that the phone did not survive. "Sending bits of glass" shows the screen broke into pieces.

decoys.why: Bits of glass flew across the pavement, so the screen broke instead of being fixed.
The screen sent bits of glass everywhere, so it broke rather than disappeared.
The phone fell and hit the sidewalk; nothing flew high in the air.
Just shaking would not send bits of glass across the pavement.
The clue is bits of glass flying, which shows breaking, not staying around.

example: The baby bird gave a feeble chirp.
hook: A feeble kitten too weak to stand, or a feeble excuse nobody believes, both are sadly weak.

traps.why: Mighty means very strong, the opposite of feeble.
Lazy is about not wanting to try; feeble is about lacking strength.
Gentle is soft in a good way; feeble is weak in a bad way.

syn1.tip: Feeble is often said of a "feeble voice" or a "feeble old dog." It describes very little strength.

sc1.stem: The sick puppy could manage only a _____ wag of its tail, far weaker than its usual happy thumping.

traps.why: Powerful fits the usual thumping, but this wag was far weaker.
Joyful is a happy word; the puppy is sick and weak.
Wags are friendly, but the clue is about how weak it was.

sc1.tip: "Only" and "far weaker than its usual happy thumping" tell you the wag was very weak.

decoys.why: The wag was far weaker than usual, so it was not strong and enthusiastic.
A sick puppy's wag far weaker than usual is not quick and full of energy.
The sentence is about how weak the wag was, not about sneakiness.
The clue is far weaker, which has nothing to do with being high or towering.
A tail wag cannot have sharp edges; the sentence is about weakness.
Nothing about a sick puppy's tail is rich or costly; the clue is weakness.

traps.why: Full of power is the opposite of feeble.
Slightly tired is too mild; feeble means very weak.
Feeble things are often small, but feeble is about strength, not size.

syn2.tip: Think of a "feeble attempt" that barely tries. Feeble means having almost no strength at all.

sc2.stem: After a week in bed with the flu, Jada felt so _____ that she needed both hands just to lift her backpack.

traps.why: Strong is the opposite; she could barely lift her backpack.
A week in bed is boring, but boredom doesn't make lifting hard.
Cheerful is a happy feeling and doesn't explain struggling to lift.

sc2.tip: "So _____ that she needed both hands just to lift her backpack" shows cause and effect. The flu left her very weak.

decoys.why: Needing both hands to lift a backpack shows weakness, not strength.
After a week of flu, Jada had no energy, so brisk is the opposite.
Being sick can feel sad, but needing both hands points to weakness, not sadness.
Feeling calm would not explain why she needed both hands to lift her backpack.
The sentence is about Jada's weak body, not about being sneaky.
Being tall would not make a backpack hard to lift; the clue points to weakness.

example: We took a brisk walk around the park.
hook: A brisk walk on a chilly morning means quick steps, cold cheeks, and lots of energy.

traps.why: Sluggish means slow and tired, the opposite of brisk.
Risky looks like brisk but means dangerous.
Frantic is too wild and panicked; brisk is quick but in control.

syn1.tip: Brisk sounds quick, like a short snap. A "brisk walk" is fast and full of energy.

sc1.stem: On the cool morning, Grandma set a _____ pace, walking so quickly and energetically that we had to jog to keep up.

traps.why: Leisurely means slow and relaxed, but we had to jog to keep up.
Risky looks like brisk but means dangerous.
The morning was cool, but the blank describes how fast she walked.

sc1.tip: "Walking so quickly and energetically" restates the blank. "Had to jog to keep up" proves the pace was fast.

decoys.why: We had to jog to keep up, so her pace was strong, not weak.
The sentence says she walked quickly and energetically, not quietly and calmly.
A calm, peaceful pace would not make the others jog to keep up.
The pace is described as quick and energetic, which has nothing to do with shyness.
The sentence is about speed and energy, not a sad or dark mood.
A dull, gray pace would not make you jog to keep up with Grandma.

traps.why: Slow and lazy is the opposite of brisk.
Rushed and careless sounds bad; brisk is fast in a good way.
Lively things can be loud, but brisk is about speed and energy.

syn2.tip: Picture a "brisk pace" in a walking race. Brisk always moves quickly, with energy and purpose.

sc2.stem: On lazy Sundays we stroll slowly to the bakery, but on school mornings Dad leads us at a _____ pace so we can catch the bus.

traps.why: Relaxed fits Sundays, but "but" shows school mornings are different.
Mornings can feel sleepy, but catching the bus needs speed.
Careless is a bad kind of rushing; Dad's pace is simply quick.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts slow Sunday strolls with school mornings. "So we can catch the bus" shows the pace is quick.

decoys.why: Dad hurries so you can catch the bus, and a weak pace would be slow.
The calm, slow walk is the Sunday stroll, not the rush to the bus.
The sentence contrasts slow Sundays with school mornings, so a calm pace is backward.
A shy, hesitant pace would make you miss the bus, not catch it.
The clue is about speed, and dull and gray says nothing about moving fast.
A serious, quiet pace sounds slow, but Dad needs to hurry for the bus.

example: Workers will demolish the old barn.
hook: Watch a wrecking ball swing into an old building and knock it down; that's how crews demolish it.

traps.why: Build means to put up, the opposite of demolish.
Polish looks like the end of demolish but means to shine.
Damage is too weak; demolish means tear down completely.

syn1.tip: Think of a "demolition crew" knocking down a building. De- can mean down; to demolish is to tear something down.

sc1.stem: Next week, the workers will _____ the crumbling old mall, knocking it down completely to make room for a park.

traps.why: Crumbling might suggest repair, but they're knocking it down completely.
Polish looks like demolish but means to make shiny.
A scratch is far too small; the mall is knocked down completely.

sc1.tip: "Knocking it down completely" explains the blank. "To make room for a park" shows the mall will be gone.

decoys.why: The workers are knocking the mall down completely, and mend means to fix it.
Thinking about the mall would not knock it down to make room for a park.
Forbidding a building by rule does not knock it down completely.
Copying the mall makes no sense when the workers are knocking it down.

traps.why: Putting back up is building, the opposite of demolish.
That means polish, which only looks like the end of demolish.
A slight dent is far too weak; demolish leaves nothing standing.

syn2.tip: Picture what's left after a building is demolished: just rubble. Nothing is left standing.

sc2.stem: The town wanted to save the old lighthouse, but storms had cracked its walls so badly that the mayor finally decided to _____ it before it fell on someone.

traps.why: Restore fits wanting to save it, but "but" shows that was impossible.
Inspecting checks the cracks but won't stop the walls from falling.
A patch is too small a fix for walls cracked so badly.

sc2.tip: "But" shows the town couldn't save it. "Before it fell on someone" means the mayor chose to bring it down on purpose.

decoys.why: The town wanted to save it, but the mayor gave up and removed it instead.
Just thinking about the lighthouse would not stop it from falling on someone.
Copying a cracked lighthouse would not keep it from falling on anyone.
You send away people as punishment, not a cracked building.

example: The hungry boys devoured the pizza.
hook: A hungry wolf doesn't nibble its dinner; it devours it in big, greedy gulps.

traps.why: Nibble means to take tiny bites, the opposite of devour.
Devote looks like devour but means to give your time to something.
Cooking is about food too, but devour means eating it fast.

syn1.tip: Picture someone who "devoured the whole pizza." Devour means eating fast and hungrily, like a starving animal.

sc1.stem: After a long soccer practice, the starving team can _____ six large pizzas in under ten minutes.

traps.why: A starving team would not refuse pizza.
Baking is about pizza, but no one bakes six in ten minutes after practice.
Sampling is just a taste, too weak for six whole pizzas.

sc1.tip: "Starving" and "six large pizzas in under ten minutes" show eating fast and hungrily.

decoys.why: A starving team would eat the pizzas, not throw them away.
Starving players eat pizza fast; piling it up over time misses the hunger clue.
The team is starving, so they eat the pizzas instead of throwing them.
Thinking carefully about pizza does not fit a starving team in under ten minutes.
Copying pizzas makes no sense for hungry players after practice.

traps.why: Tasting a little is the opposite of gulping everything down.
Hunger makes you devour, but devour is the eating, not the feeling.
Skipping a meal is about food, but it means not eating at all.

syn2.tip: Devour is a strong eating word. A starving dog will devour its food, gulping it down greedily.

sc2.stem: My little sister usually picks at her vegetables for an hour, but when Mom serves her favorite macaroni, she will _____ the whole bowl in two minutes.

traps.why: Nibble matches picking at vegetables, but "but" shows macaroni is different.
Stirring is about food, but it doesn't finish a bowl in two minutes.
She may admire macaroni, but "in two minutes" shows she eats it.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts picking at vegetables with her favorite food. "The whole bowl in two minutes" means eating fast and hungrily.

decoys.why: It is her favorite food, so she eats it fast instead of throwing it away.
Slowly thinking about food is like picking at vegetables, the opposite of two minutes.
She loves macaroni, so she eats the bowl instead of throwing it.
Copying a bowl of macaroni has nothing to do with finishing it quickly.

example: We floated on the tranquil pond.
hook: A tranquil pond is so still it mirrors the sky, with no wind, waves, or noise.

traps.why: Stormy means wild and rough, the opposite of tranquil.
Transparent starts the same way but means see-through.
Lonely is quiet but sad; tranquil is quiet in a pleasant way.

syn1.tip: Think of a "tranquil lake" or tranquil music for falling asleep. Tranquil feels soft and still.

sc1.stem: The pond was _____, with no ripples on the water and only soft birdsong in the air, so Noor read there for hours.

traps.why: Choppy water has waves, but the pond had no ripples.
Gloomy is sad; Noor happily read there for hours.
Ponds can be shallow, but the clues describe calm, not depth.

sc1.tip: "No ripples" and "only soft birdsong" describe a quiet, calm place. "So Noor read there for hours" shows it was peaceful.

decoys.why: Soft birdsong and reading for hours show a peaceful place, not a scary one.
Noor happily read there for hours, so the pond was not sad and dark.
A dull, gray place would not invite Noor to stay and read for hours.
No ripples on the water means stillness, not quick energy.
The clue is about stillness and quiet, not sharp edges.

traps.why: Loud and wild is the opposite of tranquil.
Dull and boring sounds negative; tranquil is calm in a pleasant way.
Ponds can be deep and clear, but tranquil is about calm.

syn2.tip: Tranquil places have no rush and no noise. A word meaning calm, quiet, and peaceful is your match.

sc2.stem: After the screaming crowds and blaring music of the county fair, our campsite in the woods, with only crickets chirping, felt wonderfully _____ as we fell asleep.

traps.why: Noisy describes the fair, not the campsite with only crickets.
The fair had crowds, but the campsite had only crickets.
Dreary is gloomy, which clashes with "wonderfully."

sc2.tip: "After" sets the loud fair against the campsite. "Only crickets chirping" and "wonderfully" point to a calm, peaceful word.

decoys.why: Wonderfully and fell asleep show a pleasant calm, not something strange and scary.
The word wonderfully tells you the campsite felt good, not sad and dark.
Wonderfully signals a happy feeling, but dreary means dull and gloomy.
The campsite is the quiet contrast to the noisy fair, not full of energy.
The contrast is noise versus quiet, not plain versus fancy and costly.

example: Forgetting the cake was a big blunder.
hook: Blunder sounds clumsy, like someone bumping into furniture; a blunder is a big, careless mistake.

traps.why: A success goes right; a blunder goes wrong.
Thunder rhymes with blunder but is the boom in a storm.
You might give an excuse after a blunder, but it isn't the mistake.

syn1.tip: Blunder sounds heavy and clumsy, like "blundering" around in the dark. A blunder is a careless mistake.

sc1.stem: Forgetting to add flour to the cake was a careless _____ that turned it into a gooey mess.

traps.why: A triumph is a big success, not something that makes a gooey mess.
A recipe is about cakes, but forgetting flour is a mistake.
Treat is a happy word; a gooey, ruined cake is bad news.

sc1.tip: "Careless" and "forgetting" point to a mistake. "Turned it into a gooey mess" shows the result of the error.

decoys.why: Forgetting flour ruined the cake, so it was a mistake, not a fix.
Something that made a gooey mess was not useful or valuable.
The gooey mess is the situation; forgetting the flour was the mistake that caused it.
Forgetting an ingredient is a slip, not a risky project or trip.
Leaving out flour is a careless error, not something costly and pleasant.

traps.why: A clever move is smart, the opposite of a blunder.
That describes thunder, which only rhymes with blunder.
A total disaster is too strong; a blunder is a careless mistake.

syn2.tip: People say "a big blunder" about a silly, avoidable error, like a player kicking the ball into his own net.

sc2.stem: The spelling bee champion had answered every hard word perfectly, so everyone gasped at her _____ when she misspelled the easy word 'cat' in the final round.

traps.why: Victory fits a champion, but misspelling 'cat' is a mistake.
Talent is positive; misspelling an easy word is not.
Trophies go with spelling bees, but nobody gasps at a trophy for misspelling.

sc2.tip: "Perfectly" contrasts with "misspelled the easy word." Getting 'cat' wrong is a careless, surprising mistake.

decoys.why: Everyone gasped because she misspelled an easy word, not because she was joyful.
The crowd gasped at a surprising mistake, not at her strength and energy.
Misspelling cat was an error, not a cure or fix.
Missing an easy word hurt her, so it was not something valuable.

example: The jagged rocks scraped my boots.
hook: Picture a jagged lightning bolt or the zigzag edge of a broken saw blade.

traps.why: Smooth is the opposite of jagged.
Jagged rocks can be dangerous, but jagged describes the shape of an edge.
Jagged peaks may be steep, but steep is about slope, not edges.

syn1.tip: Think of a jagged lightning bolt drawn as a zigzag. Its edges go up and down, never smooth.

sc1.stem: The mountain's _____ peaks looked like the sharp, uneven teeth of a giant saw.

traps.why: Smooth peaks would not look like sharp saw teeth.
Jaded looks like jagged but means tired and bored.
Flat peaks could not look like sharp, uneven teeth.

sc1.tip: The words "sharp, uneven teeth of a giant saw" tell you the peaks have sharp, uneven edges.

decoys.why: Peaks can be tall, but the clue is sharp, uneven teeth, which describes shape.
Calm says nothing about sharp, uneven edges like the teeth of a saw.
The sentence compares the peaks to sharp saw teeth, not to something calm.
Mountain peaks are not thin and easily broken, and the clue is about sharpness.
The saw teeth comparison is about sharp, uneven shapes, not a sad mood.

traps.why: Sleek means smooth and shiny, the opposite of jagged.
Jaded looks like jagged but means tired and bored.
Jagged peaks can be tall, but tall is about height, not edges.

syn2.tip: Jagged and ragged both describe rough, uneven edges, like a torn piece of paper.

sc2.stem: Unlike the smooth, rounded pebbles on the beach, the broken seashell had a _____ edge that scratched my finger when I picked it up.

traps.why: A polished edge is smooth and would not scratch your finger.
"Unlike the rounded pebbles" tells you the shell's edge was not rounded.
Seashells often look faded, but that is about color, not a scratchy edge.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the smooth, rounded pebbles" signals the opposite, and "scratched my finger" shows the edge was sharp and uneven.

decoys.why: The edge scratched your finger, but tranquil means calm, like the smooth pebbles it is contrasted with.
Placid means calm, which does not describe an edge sharp enough to scratch a finger.
Serene means peaceful; the sentence needs a word for a rough edge that scratches.
A very weak edge would not scratch you; the sentence describes a sharp, uneven edge.
Dreary describes gloomy weather or moods, not the shape of a seashell's edge.
Timid means shy, which describes people or animals, not a scratchy seashell edge.

meaning: clever and good at judging things
example: The shrewd shopper found the best deal.
hook: A shrewd fox in a fable sees through every trick and always judges the deal just right.

traps.why: Foolish is the opposite of shrewd.
Rude sounds like the end of shrewd but means impolite.
Shrewd traders may get rich, but shrewd is about smart judging.

syn1.tip: A shrewd person is hard to trick. Think of a shrewd shopper who always spots the best deal.

sc1.stem: As a _____ trader of baseball cards, Malik could always judge which cards were worth the most and never got a bad deal.

traps.why: A careless trader would get bad deals, not always good ones.
Luck can bring good deals, but the sentence says he could judge well.
Rude sounds like shrewd but has nothing to do with judging value.

sc1.tip: "Could always judge which cards were worth the most" and "never got a bad deal" show Malik was clever at judging.

decoys.why: Malik always judged well and never got a bad deal, so he was careful, not hasty.
Being shy does not explain why Malik always knew which cards were worth the most.
Meek means gentle and obedient, but the clue is about judging card values well.
Shyness has nothing to do with judging which baseball cards are worth the most.
A sleepy trader would not always judge card values correctly and avoid bad deals.
Feeble means physically weak; the sentence praises Malik's good judgment in trading.

traps.why: A shrewd person is hard to trick, so this is the opposite.
Shrewd looks like shrew, an old word for a mean person.
Too narrow; shrewd people judge many things well, not only shopping.

syn2.tip: Shrewd people size things up well. They can judge what something is worth and who is telling the truth.

sc2.stem: Although the salesman tried to trick her with a fake discount, the _____ shopper checked the real price and walked away with her money still in her pocket.

traps.why: A foolish shopper would fall for the trick, not check the real price.
A trusting shopper would believe the fake discount instead of checking it.
Having money is not the same as being smart about spending it.

sc2.tip: "Although" he tried to trick her, she "checked the real price" and kept her money. That shows she was clever and judged well.

decoys.why: She took time to check the real price, so she was careful, not hasty.
A meek, obedient shopper would go along with the salesman instead of outsmarting his trick.
Being shy does not explain how she saw through the fake discount and kept her money.
A sleepy shopper would likely miss the trick; she was alert enough to check prices.
Shyness has nothing to do with catching the salesman's fake discount.
Frail means physically weak; the sentence is about her clever judgment, not her body.

example: The flimsy umbrella flipped inside out in the wind.
hook: A flimsy paper plate folds in half the second you pile spaghetti on it.

traps.why: Sturdy is the opposite of flimsy.
Flashy starts like flimsy but means bright and showy.
Flimsy things are often cheap, but cheap is about cost, not strength.

syn1.tip: Think of a flimsy umbrella flipping inside out in the wind. Flimsy things are thin and break easily.

sc1.stem: The _____ tent, made of thin plastic and bendy poles, tore apart the moment the wind picked up.

traps.why: A sturdy tent would not tear apart in a little wind.
Cost does not explain why thin plastic tore apart.
Roomy is about size, but the clue is about thin, weak material.

sc1.tip: "Thin plastic and bendy poles" and "tore apart the moment the wind picked up" describe something thin and easily broken.

decoys.why: Hearty means strong, but the tent tore apart as soon as the wind picked up.
Lofty means very tall; the clue is thin plastic and bendy poles that tore easily.
Shrewd means clever, which describes people, not a thin tent that tears in wind.
Tranquil means calm; the sentence needs a word for a tent that breaks easily.
Glum means sad, which describes a person, not a tent made of thin plastic.
Meek describes a gentle person, not a tent that tore apart in the wind.

traps.why: Thick and strong is the opposite of flimsy.
Too strong; flimsy things break easily but are not broken yet.
A soggy box can be weak, but soggy means wet.

syn2.tip: Flimsy describes things that are thin and weak, like a paper cup that crumples when you squeeze it.

sc2.stem: Grandpa's old wooden chair has lasted fifty years, but the _____ plastic chair we bought last week already snapped when my little brother sat on it.

traps.why: A sturdy chair would not snap under a little kid.
Tough is the opposite of flimsy; this chair snapped.
Trusty is a warm, positive word, but this chair let everyone down.

sc2.tip: "But" sets the new chair against one that "lasted fifty years," and "already snapped" shows it was weak and easily broken.

decoys.why: Hearty means strong, but the plastic chair snapped after only one week.
Lofty means very tall; the clue is that the chair broke easily, unlike Grandpa's.
Shrewd means clever, which cannot describe a plastic chair that snapped.
Nimble means quick in movement, but chairs do not move; this one simply broke.
Serene means peaceful; the sentence contrasts a lasting chair with one that broke quickly.
Bashful means shy, which describes people, not a chair that snapped.

example: It was a dreary, rainy Monday.
hook: Dreary days are the gray, drizzly ones when even the dog does not want to go outside.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of dreary.
Dreamy looks like dreary but means soft and pleasant, like a dream.
Rainy days are often dreary, but dreary means dull and gloomy.

syn1.tip: You hear it in "a dreary, rainy Monday." It has a heavy, gray, sad feeling.

sc1.stem: The sky had been a _____ gray for a week, and the dull, gloomy weather made everyone want to stay in bed.

traps.why: A bright sky would not make the weather dull and gloomy.
Dreamy looks like dreary but means pleasant, not gloomy.
Cheery weather would not make everyone want to stay in bed.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "the dull, gloomy weather." The word must mean dull and gloomy.

decoys.why: The weather was dull and gloomy, but serene describes a pleasant, peaceful feeling.
Tranquil sounds peaceful and nice, but this gray sky made everyone feel gloomy.
Hearty means warm and enthusiastic, the opposite of weather that made people stay in bed.
Brisk means full of energy, but the gloomy sky made everyone want to stay in bed.
Jagged describes sharp edges, not a dull gray color in the sky.
Shrewd means clever, which cannot describe the color of a gloomy sky.

traps.why: Bright is the opposite of dreary.
Teary rhymes with dreary but means full of tears.
A dreary place may feel sad, but scary means frightening, not dull.

syn2.tip: Dreary things are dull and gray. Picture a cloudy sky that never clears up.

sc2.stem: Our trip to the beach was supposed to be sunny and fun, but instead we spent a _____ afternoon stuck inside watching cold rain drip down the windows.

traps.why: "But instead" tells you the afternoon was not cheerful.
Watching rain drip while stuck inside is not exciting.
Staying in could be relaxing, but "stuck" gives it an unhappy feeling.

sc2.tip: "But instead" sets the afternoon against "sunny and fun," and "stuck inside" watching "cold rain" sounds dull and gloomy.

decoys.why: The trip was ruined by cold rain, so the afternoon was not warm and enthusiastic.
Nimble describes quick movement, not a gloomy rainy afternoon spent stuck inside.
Shrewd means clever, which does not describe a dull, rainy afternoon.
Lofty means very high, which makes no sense for a rainy afternoon indoors.
Jagged describes sharp edges, not an afternoon of watching cold rain.
Timid describes a shy person, not a gray afternoon stuck inside.

example: The nimble goat climbed the rocky hill.
hook: Jack be nimble, Jack be quick: the nursery rhyme shows nimble means quick and light on your feet.

traps.why: Clumsy is the opposite of nimble.
Humble rhymes with nimble but means not proud.
Athletes may be strong, but nimble is about quick, light movement.

syn1.tip: Think of "Jack be nimble, Jack be quick" jumping over the candlestick. Nimble means moving quickly and lightly.

sc1.stem: The pianist's _____ fingers danced quickly and lightly across the keys during the fastest part of the song.

traps.why: Clumsy fingers would not dance quickly and lightly.
Stiff fingers move slowly, not quickly and lightly.
Humble rhymes with nimble but describes a person's attitude, not movement.

sc1.tip: The words "danced quickly and lightly" tell you exactly how the fingers moved, so the blank means quick and light.

decoys.why: The fingers danced quickly during the fastest part, so they were not weak.
Sleepy fingers would not dance quickly and lightly through the fastest part of the song.
Placid means calm and not easily upset; the clue is quick, light movement.
Shyness does not describe fingers that danced quickly and lightly across the keys.
Jagged means having sharp, uneven edges, not moving quickly and lightly.
Glum means sad, but the sentence describes how fast and lightly the fingers moved.

traps.why: Slow and heavy is the opposite of nimble.
Nimble animals may be small, but nimble is about how they move.
Reckless is a negative word; nimble praises careful, light movement.

syn2.tip: Picture a goat hopping up a rocky hill without slipping. Nimble describes that quick, light way of moving.

sc2.stem: Because the cat was so _____, she leaped from the counter to the top of the bookshelf without knocking over a single vase.

traps.why: A clumsy cat would knock things over.
A heavy cat would not land so lightly.
Hunger might make her jump, but not land without knocking anything over.

sc2.tip: "Because" shows cause and effect: she leaped "without knocking over a single vase," so she must move quickly and lightly.

decoys.why: A hasty, careless cat would knock things over, but this cat touched no vase.
A very weak cat could not leap all the way to the top of the bookshelf.
A sleepy cat would not make a quick, careful leap to the top of a bookshelf.
Being calm does not explain how the cat leaped so lightly without knocking anything over.
A weak, easily hurt cat would struggle to make such a big leap.
Frank means honest and direct, which has nothing to do with leaping gracefully.

example: The king banished the dragon from the land.
hook: In fairy tales, kings banish villains, sending them far away and ordering them never to return.

traps.why: Welcome is the opposite of banish.
Vanish rhymes with banish but means to disappear.
Too broad; banishing is one kind of punishment, sending someone away.

syn1.tip: Kings in stories banish villains from the kingdom. Banish means to send someone away as a punishment.

sc1.stem: As punishment for spoiling the royal feast, the king decided to _____ the jester from the castle forever.

traps.why: A king would not welcome someone as punishment.
Rescuing is kind and helpful, but this is a punishment.
The sentence already says punishment; "from the castle forever" needs sending away.

sc1.tip: "As punishment" and "from the castle forever" show the king sends the jester away for good.

decoys.why: Scolding is a punishment, but you cannot scold someone from the castle forever.
Copying the jester is not a punishment that keeps him away from the castle forever.
The king is punishing the jester by sending him away, not tricking him.
Mend means to fix something broken, which does not send the jester away forever.
Scaring the jester suddenly is not a punishment that removes him from the castle forever.
The king spoiled feast is the topic, but the king sends the jester away, not eats him.

traps.why: Inviting someone back is the opposite of banishing them.
That is what vanish means; banish means to send someone away.
Too weak; banishing is much harsher than scolding.

syn2.tip: When someone is banished, they are forced to leave and stay gone, like a villain sent out of the kingdom.

sc2.stem: Grumpy Mr. Hale wanted to _____ every noisy kid from his quiet street, so he put up a sign that read 'Go play somewhere else.'

traps.why: A sign saying go somewhere else is not a welcome.
Mr. Hale wanted kids to leave, not come.
Rescue is a kind word, but grumpy Mr. Hale wanted kids gone.

sc2.tip: The sign tells kids "Go play somewhere else," and "Grumpy" sets the tone. He wanted to send them away.

decoys.why: The sign tells kids to go play somewhere else, which sends them away rather than scaring them.
His sign honestly tells the kids to leave, so he is not tricking anyone.
Mr. Hale wants the noisy kids gone from his street, not to copy them.
The sign shows he wants the kids to go elsewhere, not to eat them.

meaning: to shake from fear or cold
example: My hands trembled before the race.
hook: Picture a scared puppy in a thunderstorm, trembling from its nose to the tip of its tail.

traps.why: Relaxing is calm and still, the opposite of trembling.
Tumble looks like tremble but means to fall.
Fear can make you scream, but tremble means to shake.

syn1.tip: Think of your hands trembling before a big test. Tremble means shaking a little from fear or cold.

sc1.stem: Standing in the snow without a coat, Maya began to _____ from the cold, her teeth chattering.

traps.why: You sweat from heat, not from standing in the snow.
Chattering teeth show she was not relaxed.
Tumble looks like tremble but means to fall down.

sc1.tip: "In the snow without a coat" causes the blank, and "her teeth chattering" shows her body was shaking from cold.

decoys.why: Cold can break glass, but Maya's chattering teeth show she is shaking, not breaking.
Maya is still standing in the snow with chattering teeth, so she has not disappeared.
Chattering teeth from the cold mean shaking, not speaking softly.
The clue is her teeth chattering from the cold, which describes shaking, not staying.
She is standing still in the snow, and chattering teeth point to shaking.

traps.why: Resting means staying still, the opposite of trembling.
Rumble sounds like tremble but means to make a deep rolling sound.
Too strong; trembling is shaking, not falling down.

syn2.tip: When you are cold or scared, your body shakes in small quick movements. That is trembling.

sc2.stem: Kayla acted brave as she stepped onto the stage, but her knees began to _____ so badly that everyone could see them shaking.

traps.why: Settled knees are still, but everyone could see hers shaking.
Nervous knees might ache, but nobody could see an ache.
Frozen knees would be still, not visibly shaking.

sc2.tip: "Acted brave ... but" signals she was really scared, and "everyone could see them shaking" tells you her knees were shaking.

decoys.why: Everyone could see her knees shaking, not breaking into pieces.
Her knees could not disappear if everyone could see them shaking.
The sentence says her knees were visibly shaking, and linger means to stay too long.

example: The team played with new vigor after halftime.
hook: Picture a dog full of vigor, tugging the leash and racing ahead with strength and energy to spare.

traps.why: Weakness is the opposite of vigor.
Victory starts like vigor but means a win.
Energetic people can be fast, but vigor means strength and energy.

syn1.tip: You hear it in "played with new vigor." It describes doing something with lots of strength and energy.

sc1.stem: Even at eighty, Grandma swims laps with such _____ that she leaves the younger swimmers far behind.

traps.why: Weakness would not let her leave younger swimmers behind.
Slowness could never let her pass the younger swimmers.
Patience is about waiting calmly; it does not make you swim faster.

sc1.tip: She "leaves the younger swimmers far behind" even at eighty. That shows great strength and energy.

decoys.why: Grandma leaves younger swimmers behind, so she has energy, and fatigue means great tiredness.
Making loud noise would not explain why she swims faster than everyone else.
Total confusion would not help her leave the younger swimmers far behind.
Everyone in a pool is wet, so wetness cannot explain why Grandma is faster.
The sentence is about how strongly she swims, not something costly she owns.

traps.why: Laziness is the opposite of vigor.
Courage means bravery, not physical strength and energy.
Anger can feel powerful, but vigor is healthy, positive strength.

syn2.tip: Someone with vigor is full of power, like a team that comes back strong after halftime.

sc2.stem: Sam usually moved slowly in the morning, but after a big breakfast he raked the whole yard with such _____ that he finished before lunch.

traps.why: Laziness would not get the whole yard raked before lunch.
"But" tells you he was no longer slow and sleepy.
Raking can be boring, but boredom would not make him finish so fast.

sc2.tip: "Usually moved slowly ... but" signals a change, and "finished before lunch" shows he worked with lots of energy.

decoys.why: Sam finished before lunch after a big breakfast, so he had energy, not tiredness.
Total confusion would slow him down, but he finished the whole yard quickly.
Making loud noise would not explain why he finished raking before lunch.
Raking the yard is a helpful chore, not playful bad behavior.
The sentence is about how hard he worked, not something costly and pleasant.

example: The placid lake looked like a mirror.
hook: Picture a placid pond so still that the ducks' reflections look like a perfect mirror.

traps.why: Nervous is the opposite of placid.
Plastic looks like placid but is a material, not a mood.
Lazy is a negative word; placid means pleasantly calm.

syn1.tip: Think of "the placid lake looked like a mirror." A placid thing is still and calm, not easily stirred up.

sc1.stem: Our old horse Daisy is so _____ that even fireworks and barking dogs do not upset her one bit.

traps.why: A jumpy horse would be upset by fireworks.
A nervous horse would be scared by barking dogs.
Playful is about loving fun, not staying calm around loud noises.

sc1.tip: "Even fireworks and barking dogs do not upset her" shows Daisy is calm and not easily upset.

decoys.why: Fireworks and barking dogs do not upset Daisy, but a timid horse frightens easily.
Daisy stays calm through loud noises, while bashful means shy and easily embarrassed.
The sentence is about Daisy staying calm, not about her being weak or easily hurt.
Not being upset by fireworks is about calmness, not being quick and full of energy.
The clue is that loud noises do not upset her, which is about calm, not quickness.

traps.why: Excitable means easily stirred up, the opposite of placid.
A sleepy animal may be still, but placid means calm, not tired.
Bored is an unhappy, dull feeling; placid is a pleasant calm.

syn2.tip: Placid describes someone or something calm and hard to upset, like a gentle old horse or a still lake.

sc2.stem: The river roared and splashed over the rocks upstream, but down by our cabin it widened into a _____ pool where we could float without a single ripple.

traps.why: "But" sets the pool against the roaring water, so it was not wild.
Choppy water has waves, but this pool had no ripples.
Plastic looks like placid, and a river cannot widen into a plastic pool.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the pool with the river that "roared and splashed," and "without a single ripple" shows the pool was calm.

decoys.why: The pool has not a single ripple, so it is calm, not quick and energetic.
The rocks upstream may be sharp, but the clue is that the pool has no ripples.
A pool you float in without ripples is calm, not towering high.
The river widened into this pool, so it is not extremely small.

example: The sailor yearned to see home again.
hook: Think of a dog at the window all day, yearning for its owner to come home.

traps.why: Earn is hiding inside yearn, but it means to work for something.
Dislike is the opposite of yearn.
Learn rhymes with yearn but means to gain knowledge.

syn1.tip: You often hear "yearn for home." To yearn is to want something so much that you ache for it.

sc1.stem: Away at camp for the whole summer, Leo would _____ for his mom's cooking, wanting it more than anything.

traps.why: You pay for food, but the sentence is about wanting it badly.
Leo is away at camp, so he is not cooking for her meals.
Apologizing is negative here, but Leo wanted the cooking more than anything.

sc1.tip: The phrase "wanting it more than anything" restates the blank, so it must mean to want something very much.

decoys.why: Leo wants his mom's cooking more than anything, which is longing, not shaking.
The sentence says he was wanting it more than anything, not simply asking about it.
The clue is that Leo wants the cooking badly, and linger means to stay too long.

traps.why: Not caring is the opposite of yearning.
That is close to earn, a different word hiding inside yearn.
Too weak; yearning is wanting something very much.

syn2.tip: A sailor who yearns for home wants it with his whole heart. Yearn is a strong, aching kind of wanting.

sc2.stem: The new video game was fun at first, but after a whole week of rainy days stuck indoors, the twins began to _____ to run outside in the sunshine.

traps.why: After a week stuck inside, the twins wanted to go out, not refuse.
Learn rhymes with yearn, but the twins already know how to run.
Hesitating means holding back, but they badly wanted to get outside.

sc2.tip: "Fun at first, but" signals a change, and a "whole week" "stuck indoors" would make anyone want sunshine very much.

example: The children murmured during the movie.
hook: Murmur even sounds soft: say mur-mur slowly and you hear the low hum of quiet voices.

traps.why: Shout is the opposite of murmur; it means speaking very loudly.
Singing uses your voice too, but murmur is about speaking softly.
Stuttering is about repeating sounds, not about speaking softly.

syn1.tip: Murmur sounds like what it is. Say it slowly: mur-mur, a low, soft sound you can barely hear.

sc1.stem: In the quiet library, we could only _____ to each other so we wouldn't disturb anyone reading.

traps.why: Shouting would disturb the readers, the opposite of what the sentence says.
Singing in a library would bother readers, so it does not fit.
Arguing is about disagreeing, and it usually gets loud.

sc1.tip: The clues are "quiet library" and "so we wouldn't disturb anyone." You need a word for very soft talking.

traps.why: Yelling loudly is the opposite of murmuring.
Listening goes with talking, but murmur means doing the talking softly.
Murmuring is about volume, not about being rude.

syn2.tip: Think of a quiet room where people murmur. The word is all about low, soft voices.

sc2.stem: Instead of shouting the answer like the other kids, Priya leaned close and began to _____ it in my ear so nobody else could hear.

traps.why: The sentence says "instead of shouting," so shout is the opposite of what she did.
Announcing tells everyone, but she wanted nobody else to hear.
Broadcasting spreads words widely, not quietly into one ear.

sc2.tip: "Instead of shouting" signals a contrast, and "so nobody else could hear" means very soft speaking.

decoys.why: Priya whispered so nobody could hear, and hurl means throwing something hard, which is loud and forceful.
Pondering happens silently in your head, but Priya was saying the answer in my ear.
Nothing is being copied here; Priya was quietly telling me the answer so others couldn't hear.
You cannot break an answer into pieces in someone's ear; she was speaking softly.
Throwing the answer away makes no sense; she was sharing it quietly with me.

example: He hurled the ball across the field.
hook: Picture a pitcher hurling a fastball so hard it whistles past the batter.

traps.why: Catching is the opposite of hurling; you stop the ball instead of throwing it.
Hurt looks like hurl, but it means to cause pain.
Kicking sends things flying too, but with your foot, not by throwing.

syn1.tip: Think of hurling a snowball as hard as you can. Hurl is a strong, forceful throw.

sc1.stem: To reach the far end of the field, the outfielder had to _____ the ball as hard as he could.

traps.why: Catching the ball would not get it to the far end of the field.
A toss is too gentle for "as hard as he could."
Holding the ball keeps it in his hand, so it never reaches the far end.

sc1.tip: "As hard as he could" and "far end of the field" tell you he needed a powerful throw.

decoys.why: Discard means throwing something away as trash, not throwing a ball hard across a field.
He wants the ball to travel far, not break into pieces.
Tearing down the ball would not get it to the far end of the field.
Giving up is the opposite of throwing as hard as he could.
Thinking about the ball will not send it to the far end of the field.
Nobody eats a ball; the sentence is about throwing it hard and far.

traps.why: Catching is the opposite of throwing.
Tossing lightly is too gentle; hurling uses great force.
Hurled things travel far, but you throw them, not carry them.

syn2.tip: Hurl is a big, powerful word. Picture an arm swinging back and launching something with all its strength.

sc2.stem: Grandma gently tossed the beanbag, but my little brother liked to _____ it with all his might so it smacked against the back fence.

traps.why: Toss is gentle, but "but" shows the brother did something much stronger.
Catching it would not make it smack against the fence.
Hurt looks like hurl, but you cannot hurt a beanbag into a fence.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "gently tossed," and "with all his might" means a very hard throw.

decoys.why: Copying Grandma would mean a gentle toss, but he used all his might.
Discard means throwing something away as trash, not throwing it hard against a fence.
A beanbag that smacks the fence was thrown hard, not broken into pieces.
Tearing down the beanbag would not make it smack against the back fence.
Eating the beanbag makes no sense; he threw it so it hit the fence.

example: The warm car ride made me drowsy.
hook: Picture a drowsy kitten on a sunny windowsill, blinking slowly, then curling up for a nap.

traps.why: Alert means wide awake and watchful, the opposite of drowsy.
Rowdy looks like drowsy, but it means loud and rough.
Lazy means not wanting to work; drowsy means ready to fall asleep.

syn1.tip: Think of a long car ride when your head starts nodding. That heavy, yawning feeling is drowsy.

sc1.stem: The warm sun and the hum of the fan made Ella so _____ that her eyelids kept drooping during the afternoon story.

traps.why: An alert person's eyelids would not keep drooping.
Warm sun can make you sweaty, but sweat does not make eyelids droop.
Rowdy looks like drowsy, but rowdy kids are loud, not drooping.

sc1.tip: "Her eyelids kept drooping" is what happens when you are sleepy, and a "warm sun" adds to it.

decoys.why: Her eyelids kept drooping, so she was sleepy, not quick and full of energy.
Drooping eyelids show sleepiness, not quick and light movement.
Warm sun and a humming fan make you sleepy, not sad.
Nothing in the sentence is embarrassing; the sun and fan made her eyes droop.
Being clever would not make her eyelids droop during the story.
Being honest has nothing to do with drooping eyelids on a warm afternoon.

traps.why: Wide awake is the opposite of drowsy.
Fast asleep goes too far; a drowsy person is still awake, just barely.
Boredom can make you sleepy, but drowsy means sleepy itself.

syn2.tip: Drowsy describes heavy eyelids and yawns. You are almost asleep but not quite.

sc2.stem: Max was full of energy at breakfast, but by the end of the long bus ride home he felt so _____ that he napped on Mom's shoulder.

traps.why: Lively matches breakfast, but "but" shows he changed, and he napped.
Hunger after a long ride makes sense, but it does not cause a nap.
A noisy boy would not be napping on Mom's shoulder.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "full of energy," and "napped on Mom's shoulder" shows he was sleepy.

decoys.why: The sentence says by the end he napped, so he was sleepy, not full of energy.
He napped on Mom's shoulder, so he was not feeling quick and light.
Nothing scared him; a long bus ride made him sleepy enough to nap.
Being shy would not make him nap; the long ride made him sleepy.
Feeling clever has nothing to do with napping after a long bus ride.
Being honest would not cause him to fall asleep on Mom's shoulder.

meaning: to speak angrily to someone who misbehaved
example: Mom scolded us for tracking in mud.
hook: Picture a mom, hands on hips, scolding the dog that just tracked mud across the clean carpet.

traps.why: Praise means saying nice things, the opposite of scolding.
Scald looks like scold, but it means to burn with hot liquid.
Arguing is two people disagreeing; scolding is one person correcting another.

syn1.tip: Think of being scolded for a mess. Look for the word that means telling someone off for doing wrong.

sc1.stem: The teacher had to _____ the boys for throwing paper airplanes, telling them sternly that it must stop.

traps.why: Nobody praises kids while telling them sternly that it must stop.
Excusing them would let them off, not tell them sternly to stop.
Scald looks like scold, but it means to burn with hot water.

sc1.tip: "Telling them sternly that it must stop" shows the teacher spoke angrily about the misbehavior.

decoys.why: The teacher spoke sternly to stop bad behavior, not softly.
The boys were throwing things, but the teacher was speaking to them, not throwing them.
The teacher wanted the airplanes to stop, not to copy the boys.
Telling them sternly to stop is honest correction, not tricking them.
The teacher was correcting misbehavior, not trying to amaze the boys.
A stern warning to stop is clear, not meant to confuse the boys.

traps.why: Speaking kindly is the opposite of scolding.
Scolding can be loud, but it is about being angry, not just loud.
Speaking secretly is about privacy, not anger at bad behavior.

syn2.tip: You get scolded when you misbehave. The word is about angry words aimed at someone.

sc2.stem: Dad usually laughs off small spills, but when Rufus chewed up his new shoes, Dad had to _____ the puppy in a loud, cross voice.

traps.why: You would not praise a puppy in a cross voice for chewing shoes.
Comforting is kind and gentle, but Dad's voice was loud and cross.
Petting is something you do with a puppy, but not in a cross voice.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with laughing things off, and "a loud, cross voice" shows Dad spoke angrily.

decoys.why: The sentence says a loud, cross voice, and murmur means speaking very softly.
Dad was angry about the shoes, not copying the puppy.
Dad was correcting Rufus in a cross voice, not tricking him.
The puppy chewed the shoes; Dad did not eat the puppy.
You might mend the shoes, but Dad spoke crossly to the puppy.

example: The loud thunder startled the baby.
hook: Startle has start inside it: a startled person starts, or jumps, in sudden surprise.

traps.why: Calming someone is the opposite of startling them.
Startle has "start" in it, but it does not mean to begin.
Terrify is too strong; startle is a quick jolt of surprise.

syn1.tip: Think of a door slamming and making you jump. Startle means a sudden little scare.

sc1.stem: Be careful not to _____ the sleeping cat, or she'll jump straight up in the air in surprise.

traps.why: Soothing the cat would keep her calm, not make her jump.
Lulling means making calm and sleepy, so she would not jump.
Feeding goes with cats, but it would not make her leap in surprise.

sc1.tip: "She'll jump straight up in the air in surprise" tells you the word means to give a sudden scare.

decoys.why: Comforting the cat would not make her jump straight up in surprise.
Copying a sleeping cat would not make her jump up in surprise.
The cat is not broken; the warning is about surprising her awake.
Getting a cat has nothing to do with making her jump in surprise.
The warning is about surprising the cat, not throwing her away.

traps.why: Soothing someone slowly is the opposite of a sudden scare.
Startle contains "start," but it has nothing to do with beginning again.
Confusing someone is about puzzling them, not making them jump.

syn2.tip: Picture someone jumping when a balloon pops. Startle is a quick, surprising jolt.

sc2.stem: Leo hid behind the door hoping to _____ his sister, but she spotted his shadow and didn't even flinch when he jumped out.

traps.why: You do not hide and jump out to soothe someone.
Finding goes with hiding games, but the hider is not the one finding.
Cheer is a happy feeling; jumping out is meant to make her flinch.

sc2.tip: "Hid behind the door," "jumped out," and "didn't even flinch" show he wanted to give her a sudden scare.

decoys.why: He jumped out to scare her, and comforting her is the opposite.
Hiding and jumping out is meant to scare someone, not to scold them.
Jumping out from behind a door is about scaring her, not copying her.
Nothing is broken; he hoped she would flinch when he jumped out.
You do not get a sister by jumping out; he wanted to scare her.
He wanted her to flinch in surprise, not to send her away.

example: The clamor of the crowd filled the stadium.
hook: Clamor sounds like clanging, clattering, and hollering all mashed together into one big noise.

traps.why: Silence means no sound, the opposite of clamor.
Glamor looks like clamor, but it means fancy beauty.
Crowds often make a clamor, but a crowd is people, not noise.

syn1.tip: Clamor sounds like clang and clatter. Think of a noisy lunchroom where everyone talks at once.

sc1.stem: The _____ of fifty geese honking all at once was so loud and confused that it woke the whole campground.

traps.why: Silence could not be loud enough to wake the campground.
A murmur is soft and low, not loud enough to wake everyone.
Grace is a pleasant word; the sentence describes loud, confused noise.

sc1.tip: "Honking all at once" and "so loud and confused" describe exactly what the missing word means.

decoys.why: The sentence is about loud, confused noise, not a feeling of joy.
The sentence describes a loud, confused sound, not playful bad behavior.
Danger is not loud; the honking was a confused noise that woke everyone.
An exact copy cannot be loud and confused like fifty honking geese.
A home does not wake a campground; the honking noise did.
Tiredness is not loud; the sentence is about noise that woke everyone.

traps.why: Peaceful quiet is the opposite of clamor.
A large crowd can make clamor, but clamor is the noise itself.
Music is pleasant and orderly; clamor is loud and messy.

syn2.tip: Picture a stadium when everyone yells at once. Clamor is that loud, jumbled racket.

sc2.stem: The cafeteria was usually calm, but when the fire drill bell rang, a _____ of shouting kids and scraping chairs filled the room.

traps.why: A hush is quiet, but shouting and scraping are loud.
A hum is too soft for shouting kids and scraping chairs.
Glamor looks like clamor, but it means fancy beauty, not noise.

sc2.tip: "But" shows a change from "calm," and "shouting kids and scraping chairs" describe loud, messy noise.

decoys.why: The kids are shouting because of a fire drill, not arguing with each other.
It was only a drill, and the blank names a noise, not a danger.
The room filled with noise, so a small broken piece makes no sense.
Nothing is being copied here; the room filled with loud noise.

example: The bashful boy blushed when called on.
hook: Bashful is one of Snow White's seven dwarfs, the one who blushes and hides his face.

traps.why: Bold means daring and confident, the opposite of bashful.
Boastful looks like bashful, but it means bragging about yourself.
Bashful has "bash" in it, but it has nothing to do with hitting.

syn1.tip: Think of Bashful, the dwarf who blushes and hides. Bashful means shy.

sc1.stem: Whenever someone praised her drawings, _____ Keiko turned bright red and hid her face behind her sketchbook.

traps.why: A bold person would not hide behind a sketchbook when praised.
Praise might make you proud, but proud people do not hide their faces.
Anger can turn you red, but you would not hide from praise.

sc1.tip: "Turned bright red" and "hid her face" when praised show someone shy and easily embarrassed.

decoys.why: Keiko turned red and hid her face, so she was clearly upset, not calm.
Hiding behind a sketchbook shows embarrassment, the opposite of peaceful calm.
Being honest and direct would not make her hide her face from praise.
She was praised, so she felt embarrassed, not sad.
Turning red from praise shows shyness, not physical weakness.
Being clever does not explain why she blushed and hid her face.

traps.why: Outgoing people love meeting others, the opposite of bashful.
Shy people may be alone, but lonely means sad about being alone.
Bashful kids may be quiet, but polite is about good manners.

syn2.tip: A bashful kid blushes and looks at the floor. Look for a word about being shy and nervous.

sc2.stem: Her twin brother loves telling jokes on stage, but _____ Maya would rather hide backstage than have a whole audience staring at her.

traps.why: Outgoing describes her brother; "but" shows Maya is different.
Funny fits the joke telling, but Maya wants to hide, not perform.
Boastful looks like bashful, but braggers want people looking at them.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Maya with her joke-telling brother, and "rather hide backstage" shows she is shy.

decoys.why: Maya hates an audience staring at her, so she is easily upset, not calm.
Wanting to hide backstage shows nervousness, not peaceful calm.
The sentence is about Maya fearing attention, not about her being sad.
Her brother is the lively one; Maya would rather hide.
Being honest and direct has nothing to do with fearing a staring audience.
The contrast is about shyness on stage, not about being clever.

example: He looked glum after the game was canceled.
hook: Picture Eeyore from Winnie the Pooh, head drooping, sighing quietly: that is one glum donkey.

traps.why: Cheerful means happy, the opposite of glum.
Glossy starts like glum, but it means shiny.
Angry is a bad mood too, but glum means quietly sad.

syn1.tip: Glum and gloomy both start with gl and both feel gray and sad, like a rainy day.

sc1.stem: After his kite snapped loose and blew away, Theo sat _____ on the bench, chin in hands, not saying a single word.

traps.why: Losing his kite would not make Theo cheerful.
Restless means fidgety, but Theo sat still with his chin in his hands.
Proud is a good feeling; losing a kite is sad.

sc1.tip: His kite "blew away," and he sat "chin in hands, not saying a single word." That is quiet sadness.

decoys.why: Theo just lost his kite, so he is upset, not calm and untroubled.
Losing his kite would leave Theo sad, not peaceful.
Nothing embarrassed Theo; he is quiet because his kite blew away.
Theo is sad about his kite, not frightened.
Chin in hands after losing his kite shows sadness, not sleepiness.
Theo is sitting still and silent, not quick and full of energy.

traps.why: Loud and cheerful is the opposite of glum.
Heartbroken is too strong; glum is a quiet, low mood.
Calm and relaxed are pleasant feelings; glum is unhappy.

syn2.tip: Think of someone sitting with a frown and saying nothing after bad news. That is glum.

sc2.stem: Usually Ava hums and chatters all the way to school, but this morning, after losing her favorite bracelet, she walked beside me looking _____ and silent.

traps.why: Cheerful fits her usual mood, but "but" shows today was different.
Chatty matches her usual habit, but she was silent this morning.
Busy says nothing about the sadness of losing her bracelet.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with her usual humming, and "losing her favorite bracelet" points to quiet sadness.

decoys.why: Ava just lost her favorite bracelet, so she would not look peaceful.
Losing her favorite bracelet upset Ava, so she is not calm.
Ava is quiet because she lost her bracelet, not because she is embarrassed.
Ava is sad about her bracelet, not scared.
Her usual humming is gone, so she is not full of energy today.
Being honest and direct does not describe how losing a bracelet made her look.

example: The magic trick astonished the audience.
hook: Picture a magician pulling an elephant out of a top hat while the crowd sits astonished, mouths hanging open.

traps.why: Boring someone is the opposite of astonishing them.
Finish ends with the same sound, but it means to complete.
Confusing leaves you puzzled; astonishing leaves you amazed.

syn1.tip: Think of a magic trick that makes your jaw drop. Astonish means to amaze.

sc1.stem: Her ten-foot jump is sure to _____ the judges, who have never seen anything so amazing in their lives.

traps.why: Judges who see something amazing are not bored.
Disappoint is a let-down feeling, but the jump is amazing.
Watching a jump will not tire the judges.

sc1.tip: The judges "have never seen anything so amazing," so the jump will surprise them greatly.

decoys.why: The judges are amazed by the jump, not confused by it.
An amazing jump would impress the judges, not make anyone speak angrily.
The judges are not sad, so they need no comfort.
The judges watch the jump; they are not copying it.
An amazing jump would never send the judges away as punishment.

traps.why: Boring someone is the opposite of astonishing them.
Mildly interesting is far too weak; astonish is a huge surprise.
Confusion is not the same as being amazed.

syn2.tip: Astonish is a big surprise word. Picture wide eyes and an open mouth.

sc2.stem: Everyone expected the tiny puppy to be scared of the big dogs, so it may _____ you to learn that she bosses around the whole dog park.

traps.why: A tiny puppy bossing big dogs is not boring news.
Hearing a short fact will not tire you out.
Disappoint is a sad feeling; a brave puppy is fun, surprising news.

sc2.tip: "Everyone expected" her to be scared, so learning she is the boss would greatly surprise you.

decoys.why: Learning the puppy is bossy is a surprise, not something that comforts you.
The surprising news about the puppy does not speak angrily to you.
Learning a fact cannot send you away as punishment.
The sentence is about being surprised, not about copying anyone.

example: The tricky riddle bewildered the whole class.
hook: Bewilder hides the word wild inside: picture a hiker lost in the wild, turning in confused circles.

traps.why: Explaining makes things clear, the opposite of bewildering.
Bewilder has "wild" in it, but it does not mean to make wild.
Amazing someone surprises them; bewildering leaves them confused.

syn1.tip: Think of a riddle so tricky you have no idea where to start. Bewilder means to confuse.

sc1.stem: The hallways of the fun house all looked exactly alike, which seemed to _____ visitors, who had no idea which way to go.

traps.why: Guiding visitors would help them know where to go.
A fun house might delight people, but these visitors felt lost.
Hurrying is about speed, not about not knowing which way to go.

sc1.tip: The hallways "all looked exactly alike," and visitors "had no idea which way to go." They were completely confused.

decoys.why: Visitors had no idea which way to go, so they were confused, not amazed.
Identical hallways leave you lost, not suddenly scared.
Being lost in alike hallways would upset visitors, not comfort them.
The hallways cannot chase anyone; they make visitors lost.
Hallways cannot speak angrily; the clue is that visitors were lost.
The hallways keep visitors lost inside, not send them away.

traps.why: Explaining clearly is the opposite of bewildering.
Slightly distracting is too weak; bewilder means completely confused.
Confusion can be annoying, but bewilder is about being lost, not mad.

syn2.tip: A bewildered person scratches their head and does not know which way to turn.

sc2.stem: The math riddle seemed simple, but its strange twists would _____ even my older sister, who scratched her head for an hour and still could not solve it.

traps.why: Twists that help would let her solve it, but she could not.
Please is a happy feeling, but she scratched her head in confusion.
Bewilder has "wild" inside, but the twists confused her, not excited her.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "seemed simple," and "scratched her head for an hour" shows she was completely confused.

decoys.why: She scratched her head and could not solve it, so she was confused, not amazed.
An hour of head scratching shows confusion, not a sudden scare.
A riddle she could not solve would frustrate her, not comfort her.
A riddle cannot speak angrily; the clue is that she could not solve it.
The riddle does not copy your sister; it confuses her.
A riddle cannot send anyone away; it stumped her for an hour.

example: A minute bug crawled on the leaf.
hook: Said my-NOOT, a minute crumb is so tiny you might need a magnifying glass to spot it.

traps.why: Enormous means huge, the opposite of minute.
A minute of time is brief, but my-NOOT minute is about size.
Mute looks a bit like minute but means silent.

syn1.tip: When it is said my-NOOT, minute describes size, not time. Picture something you would need a magnifying glass to see.

sc1.stem: The microscope revealed _____ creatures swimming in the pond water, far too tiny to see with the eye alone.

traps.why: Giant is the opposite; the creatures were too tiny to see.
The sentence is about seeing, but the creatures could not be seen by eye.
Brief fits the time meaning of minute, not the size meaning.

sc1.tip: The words "far too tiny to see with the eye alone" describe the blank. You need a word meaning extremely small.

decoys.why: The creatures were in the pond water, just too tiny to see.
The clue says far too tiny to see, which is about size, not edges.
The creatures were too tiny to see, not strong or extreme.
You needed a microscope because they were tiny, not because they were shy.
The creatures were swimming and too tiny to see, which is about size, not sleepiness.

sc2.stem: Although the elephant left huge footprints in the mud, the ant's tracks beside them were so _____ that we needed a magnifying glass to find them.

traps.why: Massive matches the elephant, but "although" sets the ant's tracks against it.
Footprints can be deep, but depth would not need a magnifying glass.
Brief is about time, but tracks are measured by size.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets the ant against the huge elephant, and "needed a magnifying glass" shows the tracks were extremely small.

decoys.why: Strong, intense tracks would be easy to see, but you needed a magnifying glass.
Jagged describes sharp edges, not the tiny size that called for a magnifying glass.
Flimsy means easily broken, which would not explain needing a magnifying glass.
The tracks were right beside the elephant's, so they were not far away.
Ants may be nimble, but the magnifying glass points to the tracks being tiny.

example: Let me be frank: your room is messy.
hook: A frank friend tells it straight, like saying "Your shoe is untied" without any sugarcoating.

traps.why: Secretive people hide things; frank people say things plainly.
Frank can be blunt, but it is not meant to be mean.
Frantic looks like frank but means wildly worried.

syn1.tip: You may have heard "Let me be frank" right before someone tells the plain truth. Frank means honest and direct.

sc1.stem: When Kai asked whether his science poster was any good, his sister was _____: she told him directly that it was too crowded.

traps.why: Vague means unclear, but she told him directly.
Her feedback was honest, not cruel; nothing shows she wanted to hurt him.
Silent is about speaking, but she did speak and told him directly.

sc1.tip: After the colon, "told him directly" explains the blank. A word meaning honest and direct fits.

decoys.why: She told him directly, which is the opposite of being shy and embarrassed.
A timid sister would hold back, but she spoke directly about the poster.
Nothing says she was sad; the clue is that she spoke directly.
Being calm does not explain why she told him directly what was wrong.
Sleepiness has nothing to do with telling him directly that the poster was crowded.

traps.why: Hiding the truth is the opposite of being frank.
Frank is honest, not unkind; harsh and mean is too negative.
Frank is about what you say, not how loudly you say it.

syn2.tip: A frank person says what they really think, plainly. It is about honesty, not about being unkind.

sc2.stem: Most of the judges gave polite, fuzzy comments, but Ms. Ortiz was _____ and told each baker exactly what was wrong with their cakes.

traps.why: Vague fits the fuzzy comments, but "but" shows Ms. Ortiz was different.
Frantic looks like frank but means wildly worried.
Shy is about speaking up, but she told everyone exactly what was wrong.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Ms. Ortiz with the fuzzy comments, and "told each baker exactly what was wrong" shows she was honest and direct.

decoys.why: Ms. Ortiz told bakers exactly what was wrong, which a timid judge would avoid.
A shy judge would not tell each baker exactly what was wrong.
Her comments were strong and clear, not weak, unlike the fuzzy ones.
Being sleepy does not contrast with the other judges' polite, fuzzy comments.
The sentence is about her honesty, not about her feeling sad.

example: She had a novel idea for the science fair.
hook: A novel idea is one nobody has had yet, like a backpack with built-in snack drawers.

traps.why: Familiar means well known, the opposite of novel.
A novel is a book, but the describing word novel means new.
Noble looks like novel but means honorable.

syn1.tip: Think of "innovation" and "novice," which share novel's start. Both point to something new.

sc1.stem: Using drones to deliver library books was a _____ idea, new and unusual, that no town nearby had ever tried before.

traps.why: Common is the opposite; no nearby town had tried it.
