Novels are fiction, but this idea was new, not made up.
Noble looks like novel but means honorable, not new and unusual.

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank, "new and unusual," restate its meaning. "No town nearby had ever tried" backs it up.

decoys.why: The sentence calls the idea new and unusual, not dull and gloomy.
The sentence says the idea was new and unusual, not weak or easily broken.
Nothing says the idea was weak; it says no nearby town had tried it.
Real is not the same as new and unusual, which the sentence spells out.
The clue is that no town had tried it, not that it was enough.
Drones may fly far, but the sentence says the idea was new and unusual.

traps.why: Old and ordinary is the opposite of novel.
That describes the book called a novel, not the describing word.
Novel things are unusual, but novel does not mean scary.

syn2.tip: A novel idea has never been tried before. Here novel is a describing word, not the book.

sc2.stem: Grandpa expected the same old plain cake, so he was surprised when Mia served a _____ dessert: pickle ice cream that no one had ever tasted.

traps.why: Familiar fits "same old," but Grandpa was surprised by something never tasted.
Bookish connects to novel the book, which has nothing to do with dessert.
Stale means old, but no one had ever tasted this dessert.

sc2.tip: "Same old" sets up a contrast with "surprised," and "no one had ever tasted" shows the dessert was new and unusual.

decoys.why: Grandpa expected something plain, and pickle ice cream was the surprising opposite of dull.
The surprise was that no one had ever tasted it, not that it was real.
Having enough dessert would not surprise Grandpa; something never tasted before would.
The dessert was not far away; it was a brand new kind of treat.
Nothing says the dessert was easily broken; it was unlike anything tasted before.

example: Sleep is essential for good health.
hook: The essential things are the ones you cannot do without, like water on a hot hike.

traps.why: Optional means you can skip it, the opposite of essential.
Helpful is too weak; essential means you cannot do without it.
Essential oils smell nice, but essential means absolutely needed.

syn1.tip: Essential holds the word "essence," the heart of something. If it is essential, you cannot leave it out.

sc1.stem: Water is an _____ supply for any desert hike; without it, you simply cannot go at all.

traps.why: Optional is the opposite; without water you cannot go.
Supplies can cost money, but the clue is about needing it.
Icy relates to water, but the clue says you cannot go without it.

sc1.tip: The clue is "without it, you simply cannot go at all." Something you cannot go without is absolutely necessary.

decoys.why: The sentence says you cannot go without water, so it must be necessary, not strong.
Without water you cannot go at all, which means necessary, not easy to see.

traps.why: Something extra can be skipped; essential things cannot.
Somewhat useful is far too weak for essential.
Needed things can cost a lot, but essential is about need, not price.

syn2.tip: Picture a packing list: the essential items are the ones that must go. Absolutely needed is the match.

sc2.stem: Glitter pens are fun extras for art class, but scissors are _____, because almost every project requires cutting paper.

traps.why: Optional matches "fun extras," but "but" shows scissors are different.
Fragrant fits essential oils, not scissors that every project needs.
Colorful fits art class, but the clue is that every project requires cutting.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts scissors with "fun extras," and "every project requires cutting" explains why scissors are absolutely necessary.

decoys.why: Scissors are contrasted with extras because every project needs them, not because they are enough.
Scissors are needed for almost every project, not new and unusual.
Scissors cut paper, but the sentence is about them being needed, not their edges.
The because clause says projects require cutting, so scissors are necessary, not easy to see.
Nothing says the scissors break easily; the point is that every project needs them.

meaning: having the skill to do something
example: She is capable of running a mile.
hook: A capable kid can handle the job, like packing her own lunch without any help.

sc1.stem: Even at age four, my little sister was _____ of tying her own shoes and pouring her own cereal.

traps.why: Afraid is a negative feeling, but the sentence shows something she could do.
Tired of chores is about feelings, but the sentence praises her skill.
Ashamed is negative, but "even at age four" praises what she could do.

sc1.tip: "Even at age four" sets up a surprising skill, and tying shoes and pouring cereal are things she could do herself.

traps.why: Not up to it means unable, the opposite of capable.
Eager is about wanting to, but capable is about being able to.
That is far too strong; capable means skilled enough, not the best.

syn2.tip: Being capable is about having the skill, not about wanting to. Look for the choice that means able.

sc2.stem: Dad worried the new babysitter was too young, but she turned out to be very _____ and handled dinner, homework, and bedtime without a single problem.

traps.why: Helpless fits Dad's worry, but "but" shows the worry was wrong.
Youthful connects to "too young," but the clue is how well she handled everything.
Nervous is negative, but she handled everything without a single problem.

sc2.tip: "But" tells you Dad's worry was wrong, and "handled dinner, homework, and bedtime without a single problem" shows she had the skill.

decoys.why: Being sleepy would not explain how she handled every task without a single problem.
The sentence is about her skill, not about her being sad.
Shyness does not explain why she handled everything without a single problem.
Dad worried about her age, but the sentence shows she was skilled, not tiny.

meaning: far away and hard to reach
example: They live on a remote island.
hook: A remote control works from across the room; a remote island sits far across the sea, hard to reach.

traps.why: Nearby means close, the opposite of remote.
A TV remote controls things, but remote places are far away.
Remote places can feel lonely, but remote is about distance.

syn1.tip: Think of a remote control, which works from far away. Remote places are far off and hard to get to.

sc1.stem: The research cabin is so _____ that scientists must hike for two days and then take a boat to reach it.

traps.why: Convenient means easy to reach, but this takes two days and a boat.
Cabins can be cozy, but coziness doesn't explain a two-day trip.
A cabin could be modern, but that wouldn't make it hard to reach.

sc1.tip: "Hike for two days and then take a boat" shows the cabin is far away and hard to reach.

decoys.why: The long hike and boat ride show the cabin is far away, not sharp edged.
Being important does not explain needing two days and a boat to reach it.
The trip is long because the cabin is far away, not because it is necessary.
A cabin that takes two days and a boat to reach is hard to get to, not easy.
The clue is the long journey, which shows distance, not gloominess.
A tiny cabin would not take two days of hiking and a boat to reach.

traps.why: Close by is the opposite of remote.
Some remote places are snowy, but remote means far away.
That describes a TV remote, not a remote place.

syn2.tip: Remote places are far off, like a cabin deep in the mountains. Don't let the TV remote pull you toward buttons.

sc2.stem: Our old apartment was right next to the school, but our new farmhouse is so _____ that the bus ride takes almost an hour each way.

traps.why: Close fits the old apartment, but "but" shows the farmhouse is different.
Farmhouses can be big, but size doesn't make a bus ride long.
Farms are often quiet, but quiet doesn't cause an hour-long bus ride.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the new home with one "right next to the school," and the hour-long bus ride shows it is far away.

decoys.why: Minute means tiny, but a small farmhouse would not make the bus ride take an hour.
The farmhouse is new to the family, but being unusual does not make the bus ride long.
A gloomy house would not explain why the bus ride takes almost an hour.
A farm may feel calm, but the clue is the long bus ride, which means distance.
A weak, thin house has nothing to do with a long bus ride to school.

example: The intense heat melted my popsicle.
hook: Intense heat, intense focus, an intense game: whatever it is, intense turns it all the way up.

traps.why: Mild means gentle, the opposite of intense.
Noticeable is too weak; intense means very strong.
Heat can be intense, but intense describes many strong things, not just heat.

syn1.tip: Intense heat, intense practice: intense turns things way up. Look for the choice that means very strong.

sc1.stem: Liam felt an _____ wave of excitement, so strong and extreme that he could barely stand still in line.

traps.why: Ordinary is far too weak for excitement "so strong and extreme."
Awful is negative, but excitement is a happy feeling here.
Empty means nothing there, but the feeling was strong.

sc1.tip: Right after the blank, "so strong and extreme" restates the meaning. Pick the word that means very strong.

decoys.why: The sentence says the excitement was strong and extreme, not necessary.

traps.why: Barely felt is the opposite of intense.
Fairly strong is too weak; intense is very strong.
"In tents" sounds like intense but has nothing to do with strength.

syn2.tip: Intense means the strength is turned all the way up, not just a little. "Very strong" is the match.

sc2.stem: The sun was so _____ at the beach that my sandals got too hot to touch and I needed sunscreen every hour.

traps.why: Weak sun would not make sandals too hot to touch.
Cloudy is about weather, but clouds would block the heat, not add to it.
Pleasant sounds nice, but too-hot sandals show the sun was extreme.

sc2.tip: The effects tell you: sandals "too hot to touch" and sunscreen "every hour" mean the sun was very strong.

decoys.why: A gloomy, gray sun would not make your sandals too hot to touch.
The sun is far away, but the sentence is about how hot and strong it felt.
Tiny is the opposite of a sun strong enough to heat sandals.
Calm does not explain sandals too hot to touch and sunscreen every hour.
The sun cannot be sad, and the clue is about strong heat.

example: This ring is made of genuine gold.
hook: A genuine smile reaches your eyes; a fake one stops at your mouth.

traps.why: Fake is the opposite of genuine.
Generous looks like genuine but means giving.
Real gold is valuable, but genuine means real, not worth a lot.

syn1.tip: Genuine leather, genuine gold: the phrase means the real thing. Check by thinking of its opposite, fake.

sc1.stem: Unlike the fake plastic pearls from the toy store, Grandma's necklace is made of _____ pearls from the sea.

traps.why: Imitation means fake, but "unlike" shows Grandma's pearls are different.
Plastic matches the toy store pearls, but "unlike" sets Grandma's apart.
Generous looks like genuine but means giving, which pearls cannot be.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the fake plastic pearls" sets up a contrast, so Grandma's pearls must be the opposite of fake: real.

decoys.why: Thin and easily broken describes the plastic toy pearls, not the real ones.
The sentence contrasts fake with real, not old with new.
The pearls came from the sea, but the clue is unlike the fake ones.
Pearls do not have names, and the sentence contrasts fake with real.
Gloomy does not contrast with fake plastic pearls the way real does.

traps.why: A copy is the opposite of something genuine.
That describes generous, which looks like genuine.
Real things may be costly, but genuine means real, not expensive.

syn2.tip: A genuine painting is the real one, not a copy. If something is genuine, nobody faked it.

sc2.stem: The expert checked the signature carefully and found it was _____, so the old baseball card really had been signed by the famous player.

traps.why: A fake signature means the player did not really sign it.
Signatures can smudge, but that wouldn't prove the player signed it.
Generous looks like genuine but means giving, which makes no sense here.

sc2.tip: "So the card really had been signed" is the result, which means the signature was real, not fake.

decoys.why: The card was signed by a famous player, so the name was known.
The card might be thin, but the expert was checking if the signature was real.
Frank means honest in speech, and a signature cannot speak.
The card is old, and the sentence is about whether it was really signed.
Far away has nothing to do with the player really signing the card.

meaning: something costly and pleasant, not needed
example: A hot bath felt like a luxury.
hook: A luxury is a fancy extra you want but don't need, like a limousine ride to school.

sc1.stem: A hot tub is a _____, not a need; it is pleasant and costly, but people can live without one.

traps.why: A necessity is a need, but the sentence says "not a need."
A chore is unpleasant work, but a hot tub is pleasant.
Appliance is too general and doesn't capture costly and not needed.

sc1.tip: "Not a need" and "people can live without one" tell you it is a pleasant, costly extra.

decoys.why: A hot tub may feel soothing, but the sentence says pleasant and costly, not a cure.
A hot tub is not a place where people live.
Nothing in the sentence says the hot tub is a copy of something.
The sentence calls the hot tub pleasant, not a careless mistake.
The sentence calls the hot tub pleasant, so it is not an unpleasant situation.
A hot tub is not a risky trip or project.

traps.why: A basic need is the opposite of a luxury.
Luxuries are pleasant extras, not something bad or useless.
Rich people enjoy luxuries, but a luxury is a thing, not a person.

syn2.tip: Luxuries cost a lot and feel great, but you don't need them. "Costly" and "extra" are both key.

sc2.stem: After a week of cold camp showers, a long, steaming bath at home felt like a real _____ that Rosa wanted to enjoy slowly.

traps.why: A chore is unpleasant, but Rosa wanted to enjoy the bath.
Shower is about washing, but a bath can't feel like a shower she enjoys.
The cold showers were the hardship; the steaming bath was the treat.

sc2.tip: After a hard week of "cold camp showers," the steaming bath was something Rosa "wanted to enjoy slowly," a pleasant treat.

decoys.why: Rosa wanted to enjoy the bath slowly, so it was not an unpleasant situation.
A warm bath Rosa enjoys is not great danger.
Rosa enjoyed the bath, so it was not a careless mistake.
A bath is not an angry argument, and Rosa was enjoying it.
Rosa was at home, but the bath itself is not a place to live.

example: We have sufficient snacks for the trip.
hook: Sufficient snacks means nobody goes hungry, but there isn't a mountain left over either.

traps.why: Lacking means not enough, the opposite of sufficient.
Excessive means too much, more than sufficient.
Efficient sounds like sufficient but means working without waste.

syn1.tip: Sufficient sounds like "suffice," as in "that will suffice," meaning that is enough. Not too little, not too much.

sc1.stem: We packed a _____ supply of water for the hike, exactly as much as we would need and no more.

traps.why: Huge is too much; the sentence says "no more" than needed.
A tiny supply would not be as much as they needed.
Water can be frozen, but the clue is about the amount.

sc1.tip: The phrase "exactly as much as we would need and no more" restates the blank. That is enough, nothing extra.

decoys.why: A tiny supply would not be exactly as much as you need.
The sentence is about how much water, not whether it was new.
The hike may be far away, but the clue is about the amount of water.
Calm describes moods, not exactly as much water as needed.
Gloomy does not describe an amount of water packed for a hike.

traps.why: Too little is the opposite of sufficient.
That is too much; sufficient is just enough.
That describes efficient, which sounds like sufficient.

syn2.tip: Sufficient is just the right amount for the job. More than needed is too much; less is not sufficient.

sc2.stem: Last year the class ran out of paint halfway through the mural, but this year the art teacher made sure the supply was _____ for every student to finish.

traps.why: Short fits last year, but "but" shows this year was different.
Paint is colorful, but the clue is about having enough to finish.
Efficient sounds like sufficient but means working without waste.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts this year with running out, and "for every student to finish" shows there was enough paint.

decoys.why: A tiny supply would run out again, but the teacher made sure everyone could finish.
The problem last year was running out, not the paint being far away.
New paint does not matter here; the clue is having enough for every student.
Easily harmed does not tell you there was enough paint for everyone.
Frank means honest in speech, which paint cannot be.

example: It was apparent that she was tired.
hook: Apparent has the word appear inside it: something apparent appears plainly, so everyone can see it.

traps.why: Hidden is the opposite of apparent; apparent things are easy to see.
Parental looks like a parent, but it means having to do with parents.
Apparent contains appear, but it doesn't mean appearing quickly.

syn1.tip: Look for the word appear inside apparent. Something apparent appears clearly to anyone looking, so it is obvious.

sc1.stem: From the mud on his shoes and his wet hair, it was _____ to everyone that Sam had been playing outside.

traps.why: Muddy shoes and wet hair make it certain, not doubtful.
The clues show it plainly, so it was not unknown to anyone.
Nothing was puzzling; the mud and wet hair explain everything.

sc1.tip: The sentence starts "From the mud on his shoes and his wet hair." That evidence makes it easy for everyone to see what Sam did.

decoys.why: The mud and wet hair show it was easy to see, not extremely important.
The clues made it easy to tell, not absolutely necessary.
Sam playing outside is not new and unusual; the clues just made it clear.
The mud and wet hair made the answer close at hand, not far away.
Frank describes a person speaking honestly, not something shown by mud and wet hair.

traps.why: Hard to find is the opposite; apparent things are easy to notice.
Apparent only looks like a parent; it has nothing to do with families.
Big things are easy to spot, but apparent means clear, not large.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "it was apparent that she was tired." Everyone could see it clearly, so apparent means easy to see.

sc2.stem: Maya tried to hide her disappointment with a smile, but her sadness was _____ to her friends, who could see the tears in her eyes.

traps.why: She tried to hide it, but "but" shows her friends saw it.
Her friends saw her tears, so her sadness was not unknown.
Tears made her sadness plain, not a mystery.

sc2.tip: The word "but" flips the idea of hiding. Her friends "could see the tears," so her sadness was easy to see.

decoys.why: Her friends could see the tears, so her sadness was easy to see, not tiny.
Her friends saw the tears right there, so her sadness was not far away.
Anonymous describes an unknown name, but her friends could clearly see her sadness.
The sentence is about whether her sadness could be seen, not whether there was enough.
Nothing says her sadness was new or unusual; the clue is that friends could see it.
The tears show her sadness was easy to see, not that it was necessary.

example: There was a distinct smell of smoke.
hook: A distinct smell of smoke is one you notice right away, sharp and clear, not faint or mixed in.

traps.why: Faint means barely noticed, the opposite of distinct.
Extinct rhymes with distinct, but it means no longer living.
A distinct sound is easy to pick out, but it need not be loud.

syn1.tip: Think of "a distinct smell of smoke." You notice it clearly, not dimly, so distinct means clear.

sc1.stem: Even in the noisy gym, Nora's voice was _____, clearly heard above everyone else's shouting.

traps.why: A muffled voice is hard to hear, but hers was clearly heard.
Hoarse is about a voice, but a rough voice isn't clearly heard.
Distant looks like distinct, but a faraway voice wouldn't be clearly heard.

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank, "clearly heard above everyone else's shouting," tell you what the blank means.

decoys.why: Her voice was clearly heard above the shouting, so it was not tiny.
A shy voice would get lost, but hers was clearly heard over everyone.
A faraway voice would be hard to hear, but hers was clearly heard.
The sentence is about her voice being clearly heard, not about being sleepy.
Nothing says Nora was sad; the clue is that her voice was clearly heard.
The clue is that her voice could be heard clearly, not that she was calm.

traps.why: Hard to notice is the opposite; distinct things stand out.
That is distant, which looks like distinct but means something else.
Bright colors can stand out, but distinct isn't about color.

syn2.tip: Something distinct stands apart clearly from what is around it, like a voice you can pick out of a crowd.

sc2.stem: Although the twins look almost alike, Jamal has a _____ freckle on his left cheek that makes it easy to tell them apart.

traps.why: A faint freckle would be hard to see, not easy.
A hidden freckle couldn't help anyone tell the twins apart.
The twins are similar, but the freckle is what makes them different.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with "look almost alike," and "easy to tell them apart" shows the freckle is clearly noticed.

decoys.why: A tiny freckle would be hard to spot, but this one makes telling them apart easy.
A freckle on his cheek cannot be far away and hard to reach.
A freckle does not bend; the clue is that it is easy to notice.
A freckle cannot be shy; the sentence is about something easy to notice.
A freckle cannot feel sad; the clue is that it helps tell the twins apart.
The freckle helps because it is easy to see, not because it is new.

example: Practice is crucial before a big game.
hook: A crucial moment is the one everything depends on, like the last kick that decides the whole championship.

traps.why: Minor means small and unimportant, the opposite of crucial.
Cruel starts like crucial, but it means mean and unkind.
Crucial tasks are often hard, but crucial means very important.

syn1.tip: Think of "Practice is crucial before a big game." It means you really need it, so crucial means extremely important.

sc1.stem: The final penalty kick was a _____ moment, because the whole championship depended on whether it went in.

traps.why: The whole championship depended on it, so it was not minor.
A kick that decides a championship is far from pointless.
A moment that decides everything is tense, not relaxing.

sc1.tip: Look at "because the whole championship depended on whether it went in." A moment everything depends on is extremely important.

decoys.why: The whole championship depended on the kick, so the moment was huge, not tiny.
A championship-deciding kick is tense and important, not sleepy.
The sentence says everything depended on the kick, which is about importance, not sadness.
The moment was right there on the field and mattered a lot; nothing was far away.
A moment cannot be shy; the clue is that the whole championship depended on it.
The sentence is about how much the kick mattered, not about bending.

traps.why: That is the opposite of crucial, which means it matters most.
A little useful is far too weak; crucial means extremely important.
Crucial looks a bit like cruel, but it has nothing to do with meanness.

syn2.tip: When something is crucial, everything depends on it. Ask yourself whether things would fall apart without it.

sc2.stem: Most of the recipe steps were simple, but adding the baking soda was _____, since leaving it out would make the cake flat and heavy.

traps.why: Leaving it out ruins the cake, so it is not optional.
A step that ruins the cake if skipped is not unimportant.
Easy fits the simple steps, but "but" signals this step is different.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts this step with the simple ones, and "since leaving it out would make the cake flat" shows how much it matters.

decoys.why: Leaving the baking soda out ruins the cake, so the step is big, not tiny.
The cake fails without it, so the step is much more than just good enough.
The sentence is about how important the step is, not whether there was enough.
A flexible step could be skipped, but skipping this one makes the cake flat.
The clue is that the cake fails without it, not that the step was new.

example: The kitchen was in chaos after the party.
hook: Picture a hamster loose in class: kids shrieking, chairs falling, paint everywhere. That total confusion is chaos.

traps.why: Calm is peaceful and quiet, the opposite of chaos.
Chorus starts like chaos, but it is a group of singers.
Chaos is often noisy, but it means confusion, not just sound.

syn1.tip: Think of "The kitchen was in chaos after the party." Nothing was in its place, so chaos means disorder.

sc1.stem: The messy closet was in total _____, with shoes, toys, coats, and games all jumbled together with no order at all.

traps.why: The closet had "no order at all," so order cannot fit.
Jumbled shoes and toys are the opposite of neatness.
A closet may be quiet, but the clue is about messiness, not sound.

sc1.tip: The sentence says everything was "jumbled together with no order at all." That describes total confusion.

decoys.why: A closet full of jumbled things is messy, but it is not making a loud noise.
A closet cannot behave badly; the sentence describes things with no order.
Shoes and toys jumbled together with no order is a mess, not something fancy.
A messy closet is disorganized, not in great danger.
The sentence describes a jumbled mess, not great joy.
The closet has no order at all, which has nothing to do with energy.

traps.why: Perfect order is the opposite of chaos.
A little untidiness is too weak; chaos is complete confusion.
Crowds can cause chaos, but chaos is the confusion itself.

syn2.tip: Chaos is the word for when everything is mixed up and no one can find order, like a room after a wild party.

sc2.stem: When the class hamster escaped during art time, the room fell into _____ as kids shrieked, chairs tipped over, and paint spilled across the floor.

traps.why: Shrieking kids and tipping chairs are the opposite of silence.
Spilled paint and shrieks show the room was anything but calm.
An escaped hamster broke the usual routine; nothing went normally.

sc2.tip: The escape caused the effects listed after "as": "kids shrieked, chairs tipped over, and paint spilled." That is total confusion.

decoys.why: Shrieking, tipped chairs, and spilled paint show confusion, not great joy.
Spilled paint and tipped chairs describe a wild mess, not something pleasant and costly.
The scene is about total confusion, not strength and energy.
Spilled paint and shrieking kids have nothing to do with value or excellence.

example: The dog pursued the ball across the yard.
hook: A puppy racing after butterflies across the yard is pursuing them: it follows wherever they go.

traps.why: To flee is to run away, the opposite of pursue.
Persuade looks like pursue, but it means to talk someone into something.
Pursuing comes before catching; you can pursue without ever catching.

syn1.tip: Think of police cars "in hot pursuit." They are racing after someone, so pursue means chase.

sc1.stem: Our playful puppy loves to _____ butterflies across the yard, racing after them wherever they fly.

traps.why: The puppy races after the butterflies, so it doesn't avoid them.
Racing after something is the opposite of ignoring it.
The puppy does more than watch; it races after them.

sc1.tip: The sentence says the puppy is "racing after them wherever they fly." The blank must mean chase.

decoys.why: The puppy is racing after the butterflies wherever they fly, not eating them.
Racing after the butterflies means chasing them, not copying them.
A puppy cannot speak angrily; it is racing after the butterflies.
The puppy races after the butterflies, so it is chasing them, not throwing them.
The puppy is racing after butterflies, not comforting them.
You can't tear down a butterfly; the sentence says the puppy races after them.

traps.why: Running away is the opposite of pursuing.
That is persuade, which only looks like pursue.
Capturing is the end of a chase; pursue is the chasing part.

syn2.tip: When you pursue something, you go after it. People even pursue goals, which means going after them.

sc2.stem: My cat usually hides from loud noises, but when the toy mouse squeaked, she leaped up to _____ it down the hallway.

traps.why: Avoid fits "hides," but "but" shows she did something different.
She leaped up and went down the hallway, so she didn't ignore it.
Escaping means getting away; "but" shows she went toward the mouse.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "hides from loud noises." She "leaped up" and went "down the hallway," so she chased the mouse.

decoys.why: The cat leaped up and went down the hallway after the mouse, so she chased it.
A cat cannot speak angrily; she leaped up and went after the toy.
A toy mouse is not sad; the cat leaped up to go after it.
The cat went down the hallway after the mouse, not breaking it into pieces.
The cat was going after the mouse, not sending it away as punishment.
The cat leaped up to go after the toy down the hallway, not confuse it.

example: Their lemonade stand was a successful venture.
hook: Opening a lemonade stand with all your savings is a venture: a bold try that might pay off or might not.

traps.why: A routine is a safe everyday habit; a venture is a risky new try.
Denture rhymes with venture, but it means a set of false teeth.
A venture can fail, but venture means the attempt, not the result.

syn1.tip: Think of a "business venture," like starting a lemonade stand. It is a new project that takes some risk.

sc1.stem: Opening a lemonade stand was Kai's first business _____, and he worried he might lose all his savings.

traps.why: Business card is a real phrase, but a lemonade stand isn't a card.
He only worried he might lose, so it wasn't a loss yet.
Business suit is a phrase, but opening a stand isn't clothing.

sc1.tip: Opening a stand is a "business" project, and "he worried he might lose all his savings" shows it was risky.

decoys.why: Kai worried he might lose his savings, so this was a risky project, not something valuable.
A lemonade stand is a project Kai started, not someone against him.
Nothing says the stand was a copy; the clue is the risk of losing savings.
A lemonade stand is not where Kai lives; it is a risky project.
Kai feared losing his savings, so the stand was a risk, not a costly treat.
Opening a stand is a project Kai tried, not a final decision.

traps.why: A sure thing has no risk, the opposite of a venture.
You might lose money on a venture, but venture means the project.
Chores are safe and regular; a venture is new and risky.

syn2.tip: The phrase "nothing ventured, nothing gained" means if you never take a risk, you never win. A venture is a risky try.

sc2.stem: Building a treehouse with no plans was a bold _____, but Mia and her dad were willing to risk a few smashed thumbs to try it.

traps.why: They hadn't tried yet, so it couldn't already be a failure.
They were only about to try, so it wasn't a success yet.
A habit is something you do often; this was a new, risky try.

sc2.tip: Look at "bold," "willing to risk," and "to try it." Those words describe a risky project they were starting.

decoys.why: Mia and her dad chose to try the project, and nobody plans a careless mistake.
A predicament is a mess you get stuck in, not a project you decide to try.
They built with no plans, so the treehouse was not an exact copy of anything.
The sentence is about taking a risk, not about something costly and pleasant.
Nothing in the sentence shows Mia and her dad arguing; they are trying a risky project.

example: His speed is an asset to the team.
hook: If your fast feet help your team win, your speed is an asset: something useful you bring to the group.

traps.why: A burden weighs you down, the opposite of an asset.
Assistant starts like asset, but it means a helper person.
Both are money words, but an expense costs you money.

syn1.tip: Think of "His speed is an asset to the team." His speed helps them win, so an asset is an advantage.

sc1.stem: Because Marco speaks three languages, he is an _____ to our travel club, helping everyone talk with locals.

traps.why: He is helping everyone, so he isn't an obstacle.
Someone who helps everyone talk is welcome, not an annoyance.
He is part of the club and helps it, so not an outsider.

sc1.tip: "Because Marco speaks three languages" and is "helping everyone talk with locals," he is something valuable to the club.

decoys.why: Marco helps everyone talk with locals, so he does not block the club's way.
Marco helps the club, so he is on their side, not against them.

traps.why: Worthless is the opposite of valuable.
Something owed is a debt; an asset is something good you have.
Harmful things hurt you; assets help you.

syn2.tip: Ask whether the thing helps. An asset is anything useful or valuable you have, like a skill, a tool, or savings.

sc2.stem: Jake thought his long arms were awkward, but on the volleyball team they turned out to be a real _____, helping him block every shot at the net.

traps.why: Problem fits "awkward," but "but" shows his arms turned out helpful.
His arms help him block shots, so they aren't a burden.
Blocking every shot is something to be proud of, not embarrassed by.

sc2.tip: "But" flips "awkward" into something good, and "helping him block every shot" shows his arms were very useful.

decoys.why: Jake worried his arms were awkward, but the sentence says they ended up helping him.
His arms help him block every shot, which is the opposite of a careless mistake.
The sentence says his arms turned out helpful, not a difficult situation.
His arms are truly useful for blocking shots, not something costly and unneeded.

example: Baby turtles are vulnerable on the beach.
hook: A hermit crab out of its shell is vulnerable: soft, unprotected, and easy for a hungry bird to grab.

traps.why: Protected means kept safe, the opposite of vulnerable.
Valuable ends like vulnerable, but it means worth a lot.
A vulnerable animal may feel scared, but vulnerable means easily harmed.

syn1.tip: Think of "Baby turtles are vulnerable on the beach." They can't protect themselves, so vulnerable means defenseless.

sc1.stem: Without its hard shell, the hermit crab is _____, easily harmed by any hungry bird that spots it.

traps.why: Without its shell, the crab is easily harmed, not safe.
It has lost its hard shell, so it isn't protected.
Valuable looks like vulnerable, but the sentence is about danger.

sc1.tip: "Without its hard shell" tells you it has no protection, and "easily harmed" restates what the blank means.

decoys.why: The crab is easily harmed without its shell, so it is not skilled at protecting itself.
Hermit crabs may hide, but the clue is easily harmed, not shy.
The sentence is about being easily harmed, not about bending easily.
The sentence describes danger from birds, not the crab's mood.
Whether the crab is real has nothing to do with being harmed by birds.

traps.why: Well protected is the opposite of vulnerable.
Vulnerable only looks like valuable; it is about danger, not worth.
Vulnerable means could be hurt, not already hurt.

syn2.tip: The ending -able hints at "able to be." Vulnerable means able to be hurt, or easily hurt.

sc2.stem: Inside the castle walls the soldiers felt safe, but the farmers living outside were _____ whenever an enemy army marched across the open fields.

traps.why: Secure matches the soldiers, but "but" shows the farmers were different.
The farmers lived outside the walls, so they weren't protected.
Victorious is a battle word, but farmers in open fields were in danger.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the farmers with the soldiers who "felt safe." Living outside the walls in "open fields" left them easily harmed.

decoys.why: The farmers lived just outside the walls, and the point is that they were unprotected.
The farmers are contrasted with the safe soldiers, so they were in danger, not skilled.
The sentence contrasts safe soldiers with farmers exposed to attack, not good enough ones.
The farmers were unprotected from the army, not important or worth noticing.
An enemy army marching toward you is a danger, nothing extremely good.

meaning: someone against you in a contest
example: My opponent shook my hand after the match.
hook: In chess, your opponent sits across the board from you, trying to win the game you are trying to win.

traps.why: A teammate plays on your side, the opposite of an opponent.
Component ends like opponent, but it means one part of something.
A referee is in the game, but judges it instead of playing against you.

syn1.tip: Think of "My opponent shook my hand after the match." That is the person you played against, a rival.

sc1.stem: Before the chess tournament began, Ravi politely shook hands with his _____, the player sitting across the board.

traps.why: In chess the player across the board is against you, not your teammate.
A coach doesn't sit across the board playing you.
Chess has no partners; the player across the board plays against you.

sc1.tip: The words "the player sitting across the board" in a "chess tournament" describe the person playing against Ravi.

decoys.why: Ravi shook hands with a player, and a quarrel is an argument, not a person.
The player across the board is a real rival, not an exact copy.
The tournament had not begun, and you shake hands with a player, not a decision.
The blank names the player sitting across the board, not a risky project.
The blank is a person playing against Ravi, not a safe place.

traps.why: Someone on your side is a teammate, the opposite of an opponent.
A scorekeeper is part of the game but isn't trying to beat you.
A coach helps you win; an opponent tries to beat you.

syn2.tip: Opponent sounds like it is related to oppose, which means to be against. Your opponent is the person against you in a contest.

sc2.stem: Even though Priya and Jen are best friends off the court, in tomorrow's tennis final each girl will be the other's _____, trying hard to win.

traps.why: Teammate fits "best friends," but each girl is trying to beat the other.
Partners play together; in this final they play against each other.
A fan cheers from the stands; each girl is playing to win.

sc2.tip: "Even though" sets up a contrast with "best friends." In the "tennis final" each is "trying hard to win" against the other.

decoys.why: Each girl is trying to win against the other, so she is not helping her.
Off the court they are friends, but in the final each is the other's rival.
The girls are playing against each other, not copying each other.
They are still best friends, just competing; a quarrel is an angry argument.
The sentence is about trying hard to beat each other, not about joy.

example: An anonymous donor gave books to our school.
hook: An anonymous gift arrives with no name on it, so you never learn who sent it.

traps.why: Famous people are known by name, the opposite of anonymous.
Unanimous looks like anonymous, but it means everyone agrees.
Anonymous notes can be kind; anonymous is about the name, not mood.

syn1.tip: Think of "an anonymous donor" who gives a gift. Nobody knows the donor's name, so anonymous means unnamed.

sc1.stem: An _____ letter arrived praising our class garden, but nobody ever learned who had written it.

traps.why: An autographed letter is signed, so people would know who wrote it.
The letter was praising the garden, so it wasn't angry.
Official letters show who sent them, but nobody learned the writer here.

sc1.tip: The sentence ends "nobody ever learned who had written it." A letter whose writer's name is unknown is anonymous.

decoys.why: Nobody learned who wrote it, so the writer was hidden, not easy to see.
The clue is that nobody learned who wrote it, not how strong the letter was.
The sentence is about an unknown writer, not something sure to happen.
The but clause points to a missing name, not a letter that was good enough.
The sentence stresses that the writer was unknown, not that the letter was necessary.

traps.why: Being known by everyone is the opposite of anonymous.
That is unanimous, which only looks like anonymous.
Anonymous notes are often letters, but neat writing doesn't hide a name.

syn2.tip: When someone stays anonymous, their name is never given. Ask yourself whether you know who it is.

sc2.stem: Because the class wanted honest answers, the teacher made the survey _____, so no one had to write their name on the paper.

traps.why: A public survey would show who answered, not hide their names.
Unanimous looks like anonymous, but it means everyone agrees.
Surveys can be required, but that doesn't explain why names were left off.

sc2.tip: The result follows "so": "no one had to write their name on the paper." A survey without names is anonymous.

decoys.why: The class wanted honest answers, but the clue is that no one wrote their name.
Students' answers might be honest, but the survey itself had no names on it.
No one wrote their name, so who answered was hidden, not clearly noticed.
The sentence is about leaving off names, not about bending or changing easily.
Nothing says the survey was tiny; the clue is that no names were written.

meaning: to give up or give way
example: The team would not yield, even when behind.
hook: A yellow YIELD sign on the road tells drivers to slow down and give way to other cars.

sc1.stem: Drivers must _____ to people in the crosswalk, stopping and giving way so they can cross safely.

traps.why: Drivers may wave, but the clue says stopping and giving way.
React is too general; the sentence names a specific action, giving way.
Objecting means pushing back, the opposite of giving way.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: "stopping and giving way." Pick the word that means letting others go first.

decoys.why: The sentence says drivers stop and give way, not speak softly to walkers.

traps.why: Standing firm means not giving way, the opposite of yield.
A field can yield crops, but that is a different meaning.
Yield signs make drivers slow, but yield means letting others go first.

syn2.tip: Think of the road sign. Yield means you let the other person have their way.

sc2.stem: Even though the other team scored three goals in a row, our captain refused to _____ and kept cheering everyone on until the final whistle.

traps.why: He did keep going, so refusing to continue makes no sense.
Scoring is about the game, but the clue is about not giving up.
Produce matches yield as in crops, not yield as in giving up.

sc2.tip: "Even though" and "refused to" show the captain would not give up. The blank means to give up.

decoys.why: The captain kept cheering loudly, and murmur means speaking softly, which has nothing to do with not giving up.
Nobody bargains with the other team during a game, and the sentence is about not giving up.
Refusing to want something makes no sense here; the clue is that the captain kept going.
The sentence is about not giving up when losing, not about changing completely.

example: A flexible straw bends without breaking.
hook: A gymnast doing the splits and a bendy straw are both flexible: they bend without breaking.

traps.why: Rigid means stiff and hard to bend, the opposite of flexible.
Breakable is about snapping; flexible things bend instead of breaking.
You flex muscles, but flexible means able to bend, not strong.

syn1.tip: Flex means bend, and -ible means able to be. Flexible is able to bend.

sc1.stem: Unlike a stiff wooden ruler, the rubbery plastic one was _____ enough to bend into a full circle without snapping.

traps.why: Stiff describes the wooden ruler; this ruler is unlike it.
Brittle things snap, but this ruler bends without snapping.
Weight has nothing to do with bending into a circle.

sc1.tip: "Unlike a stiff" ruler signals a contrast, and "bend into a full circle without snapping" shows it bends easily.

decoys.why: Tense means nervous, and a plastic ruler cannot feel nervous or bend because of it.
The ruler bends without snapping, so it is not easily harmed; easily hurt misses the point.
Being tiny does not let a ruler bend into a circle; the clue is about bending.
Being new and unusual has nothing to do with bending without snapping.
Being far away does not help a ruler bend into a full circle.

traps.why: Stiff and hard is the opposite of flexible.
Breaking is the opposite of what flexible things do when bent.
Flexing muscles sounds close, but flexible means bending easily.

syn2.tip: Think of a flexible straw. It bends without snapping.

sc2.stem: Because gymnasts stretch every day, their bodies become so _____ that they can touch their toes and twist into shapes most people cannot.

traps.why: Stretching makes bodies less stiff, and stiff bodies cannot twist.
Stretching can feel sore, but soreness does not help you twist.
Flexing hints at muscles, but touching toes needs bending, not strength.

sc2.tip: "Because" they "stretch every day," they can "touch their toes and twist." That shows bodies that bend easily.

decoys.why: Tense people are tight and nervous, but stretching makes gymnasts loose enough to twist into shapes.
The sentence is about bending and twisting easily, not about being easily hurt.
Stretching does not make bodies tiny; it lets them touch their toes.
Whether people know a gymnast's name has nothing to do with touching toes.
Bodies do not become far away from stretching; the clue is about twisting into shapes.
Intense means strong or extreme, but the clue is specifically about bending easily.

example: She acquired a new stamp for her collection.
hook: When you acquire something, you get it, like adding a rare new card to your collection.

traps.why: Lose is the opposite of acquire, which means to get.
Inquire looks like acquire, but it means to ask.
Require rhymes with acquire, but it means to need.

syn1.tip: Think of a collector who acquires new stamps. Acquire means to get or gain.

sc1.stem: At first Omar hated olives, but after a summer in Greece he began to _____ a taste for them.

traps.why: He started out hating olives, so he gained a taste, not lost one.
Require looks like acquire but means need, which does not fit.
Forgetting is about memory; the clue shows Omar gained a liking.

sc1.tip: "At first Omar hated olives, but" signals a change. You gain a taste for something over time.

decoys.why: You eat olives, but you cannot eat a taste; the sentence means he came to like them.
He went from hating olives to liking them, so he gained a taste rather than sending one away.
The sentence says he started to like olives, so nothing was torn down.
You cannot throw a taste; the sentence is about slowly coming to like olives.

traps.why: Giving away is the opposite of getting something.
You may want something first, but acquire means actually getting it.
Ask about is what inquire means, a word that looks like acquire.

syn2.tip: If you acquire a skill or a toy, you end up having it.

sc2.stem: Mia saved her allowance for months so she could finally _____ the skateboard she wanted, and she proudly carried it home from the store.

traps.why: She carried it home, so she got it rather than sold it.
Require looks like acquire but means need, not get.
You can admire something without saving money; she bought it.

sc2.tip: "Saved her allowance" is the cause and "carried it home from the store" is the effect. She got the skateboard.

decoys.why: She proudly carried the skateboard home, so she did not break it into pieces.
She carried the skateboard home proudly; she saved money to get it, not to throw it.
Saving for months to tear down the skateboard she wanted makes no sense.
She wanted the skateboard and took it home, so she did not send it away.
You cannot eat a skateboard; she saved her allowance to get one.

example: Rain was inevitable with those dark clouds.
hook: Inevitable is in (not) plus evitable (avoidable): something you cannot avoid, like tomorrow arriving.

traps.why: Optional means you can skip it, the opposite of inevitable.
The in- does not mean it won't happen; it surely will.
Invisible looks like inevitable, but it means cannot be seen.

syn1.tip: In- means not, and evitable means avoidable. Inevitable means not avoidable.

sc1.stem: Growing older is _____; no matter what we do, nobody can avoid having another birthday.

traps.why: Preventable means it can be stopped, but nobody can avoid aging.
Birthdays can be exciting, but the clue is that nobody can avoid them.
Invisible looks like inevitable but means cannot be seen.

sc1.tip: The part after the semicolon restates the blank: "nobody can avoid" it. Pick the word meaning cannot be avoided.

decoys.why: The sentence says nobody can avoid it, so growing older cannot bend or change.
Everyone has birthdays, so growing older is not new and unusual.
The clue says nobody can avoid it, not that growing older is silly.
The sentence is about something no one can avoid, not about something extremely good.
Growing older is not far away; the clue says nobody can avoid it.

traps.why: Inevitable things definitely happen, so this is the opposite.
Too weak: inevitable means it will happen, not just might.
Inevitable is about what will surely happen, not what is over.

syn2.tip: You often hear "it was inevitable" about something everyone saw coming. It is sure to happen.

sc2.stem: Since Max left his ice cream cone in the hot sun for an hour, a sticky, melted mess was _____ by the time he came back.

traps.why: Ice cream always melts in hot sun, so a mess was very likely.
Invisible looks like inevitable, but a sticky mess is easy to see.
Nobody would be surprised; hot sun always melts ice cream.

sc2.tip: "Since" shows cause and effect: "hot sun for an hour" always melts ice cream. The mess was sure to happen.

decoys.why: A melted ice cream mess is the opposite of strong and healthy.
A sticky, melted mess is not extremely good; the clue is that it had to happen.
The mess was not far away; the hot sun made it certain to happen.
A mess does not have an unknown name; the sentence is about what was sure to happen.
Calling the mess enough misses the clue that an hour in the sun made it unavoidable.

meaning: to comfort someone who is sad
example: I consoled my friend after she lost.
hook: When you console a crying friend, you comfort them; that is the verb, not the game console.

traps.why: Teasing makes a sad person feel worse, the opposite of consoling.
Counsel sounds like console, but it means to give advice.
Praise is for doing well; console is for someone who is sad.

syn1.tip: You console someone who is sad or hurt. Think of a consolation prize that cheers up the losers.

sc1.stem: When Rosa's goldfish died, her friends tried to _____ her by drawing pictures and sharing happy memories of it.

traps.why: Sharing happy memories is kind, not teasing.
Blame is about whose fault it was, but the friends were being kind.
Drawing pictures for Rosa is paying attention to her, not ignoring her.

sc1.tip: Her goldfish "died," so Rosa is sad. Friends "sharing happy memories" are trying to make her feel better.

decoys.why: Her friends drew pictures and shared happy memories, so they were being kind, not angry.
Friends sharing happy memories are staying close to Rosa, not sending her away.
Drawing pictures for a sad friend is meant to comfort her, not scare her.
Sharing happy memories helps Rosa feel better; it is not meant to confuse her.
Her friends were on her side, helping her through sadness, not against her.

traps.why: Annoying someone bothers them, the opposite of consoling.
Conceal starts like console, but it means to hide.
Pity is feeling sorry for someone; consoling means helping them feel better.

syn2.tip: Console has a gentle, kind feeling. It means calming someone who is upset.

sc2.stem: Instead of laughing when his little sister fell off her bike, Leo knelt beside her to _____ her, wiping her tears and promising she would be okay.

traps.why: Mocking is like laughing at her, which Leo did not do.
Scolding is harsh, but Leo was gentle and kind.
A warning comes before trouble; Leo was helping after she fell.

sc2.tip: "Instead of laughing" sets up a contrast, and "wiping her tears" shows Leo is comforting his sad sister.

decoys.why: Leo wiped her tears and promised she would be okay, which is kind, not angry.
Kneeling and wiping tears is gentle; Leo was not trying to scare his sister.
Leo knelt beside his sister, so he was not chasing her.
Leo stayed beside his sister to help her, so he did not send her away.
Promising she would be okay is meant to calm her, not confuse her.

example: Each idea has some merit.
hook: Scouts earn merit badges by showing real skill, so merit means true worth that someone earned.

traps.why: A flaw is a weak spot, the opposite of merit.
Merit can earn a reward, but merit is the worth itself.
Mercy looks like merit, but it means kindness or forgiveness.

syn1.tip: Think of a merit badge, earned for doing something well. Merit is the good value something has.

sc1.stem: Each project will be judged on its _____, or real value, not on how fancy the poster looks.

traps.why: The sentence says "real value," and flaws are bad points.
The sentence says not to judge by how fancy it looks.
Neatness is about looks, but the clue says "real value."

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank, "or real value," tell you the meaning. "Not on how fancy" warns against looks.

decoys.why: The sentence says fancy looks do not count, and luxury is about costly, fancy things.
The sentence defines the blank as real value, not a careless mistake.
The phrase or real value tells you the word means value, not total confusion.
The sentence explains the blank as real value, not a strong wish to succeed.
Judging leads to a verdict, but the blank is defined as real value, not a decision.
The sentence says the blank means real value, and glee means great joy.

traps.why: A weakness is a bad point, the opposite of merit.
A merit badge is a prize; merit itself means worth.
Being popular is not the same as having real worth.

syn2.tip: "That idea has merit" means the idea is good and worth something.

sc2.stem: The judges ignored the singer's famous last name and picked her only for her talent and hard work, so she knew the win came from real _____.

traps.why: Talent and hard work are strengths, not flaws.
The judges ignored her famous name, so fame did not win it.
Mercy looks like merit, but she won by talent, not kindness.

sc2.tip: "Picked her only for her talent and hard work" is the cause. A win earned by talent comes from real worth.

decoys.why: The judges ignored her famous name, so the win came from earned value, not costly privilege.
She won for talent and hard work, so the win did not come from a careless mistake.
Nothing in the sentence describes confusion; the judges chose her carefully for her talent.
Playful bad behavior has nothing to do with winning through talent and hard work.
She may have felt joy, but the win came from her talent, not from joy.
Thankfulness may come after winning, but the win itself came from her talent and work.

example: The town's most notable building is the clock tower.
hook: Notable has note inside it: something notable is worth taking note of, like a record-breaking jump.

traps.why: Ordinary means plain and common, the opposite of notable.
Noble looks like notable, but it means honorable or royal.
Note can mean a musical sound, but notable means worth noticing.

syn1.tip: Notable is note plus -able: able to be noted. Something notable makes you take note.

sc1.stem: The most _____ moment of our whale-watching trip, worth noticing above all, was seeing a humpback leap completely out of the water.

traps.why: The moment was worth noticing above all, so it was unforgettable.
Noble looks like notable but means honorable, which fits no whale.
A whale leaping out of the water is exciting, not calm.

sc1.tip: The phrase "worth noticing above all" restates the blank. Pick the word that means worth noticing.

decoys.why: The sentence says worth noticing above all, and adequate means only good enough.
A moment worth noticing above all is far more than just enough.
The clue is about being worth noticing, not about being sure to happen.
A moment cannot have an unknown name; the clue asks for worth noticing.
The whale bends as it leaps, but the clue asks for a moment worth noticing.
Nothing says the moment was easily harmed; the clue says worth noticing above all.

traps.why: Notable things stand out, so they are hard to forget.
You write notes, but notable means worth noticing, not written.
Too weak: notable things really stand out.

syn2.tip: Take note means pay attention. A notable thing deserves your attention.

sc2.stem: Most of the rocks Ava found at the beach were plain gray pebbles, but one _____ stone sparkled with purple crystals and made everyone stop to look.

traps.why: The other rocks were ordinary; this stone was different.
Noble looks like notable but means honorable, not eye-catching.
Beach stones are often smooth, but the clue is that it stood out.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the "plain gray pebbles" with one stone that "made everyone stop to look," so it was worth noticing.

decoys.why: The stone stood out from plain pebbles, so it was more than just good enough.
The stone made everyone stop to look, which is about standing out, not being unavoidable.
A stone having an unknown name does not explain why everyone stopped to look.
Stones do not bend; the sentence is about one stone standing out.
A stone cannot feel nervous; the sentence says it sparkled and drew attention.
A stone has no skills; the sentence is about it being worth noticing.

meaning: what happens because of an action
example: Missing the bus had a consequence.
hook: A consequence comes in sequence after an action: first you make a choice, then its consequence follows.

traps.why: A cause comes first; a consequence is what comes after.
Too narrow: a consequence can be good or bad, not only punishment.
Conference looks like consequence, but it is a meeting.

syn1.tip: Consequence contains sequence, things in order. A consequence comes after an action as its result.

sc1.stem: One _____ of staying up too late is feeling tired and grumpy the next morning at school.

traps.why: Feeling tired is caused by staying up; it is not the cause.
A reason explains why; feeling tired comes after staying up.
A benefit is good, but feeling tired and grumpy is bad.

sc1.tip: Feeling tired "the next morning" happens because of "staying up too late." The blank names what results from an action.

decoys.why: Feeling tired and grumpy is not a good quality of staying up late.
Feeling tired and grumpy is a bad result, not something useful.
Staying up may feel like a treat, but being tired and grumpy is no luxury.
Feeling tired is not a wish to succeed; it is what happens afterward.
No one makes a final decision here; the sentence describes what happens after staying up.

traps.why: A cause comes before; a consequence follows after.
Too narrow: consequences are not always penalties.
Consequence contains sequence, but it means a result, not a list.

syn2.tip: Adults say "actions have consequences." A consequence is whatever follows from what you did.

sc2.stem: Kim learned that every choice has a _____, something that happens afterward because of it, when skipping practice meant sitting on the bench.

traps.why: The sentence describes what happens afterward, not what comes before.
A purpose is a goal; the clue is about what happens afterward.
Sitting on the bench is a bad result, not a reward.

sc2.tip: The words after the comma restate the blank: "something that happens afterward because of it." That is a result.

decoys.why: The sentence defines the word as something that happens afterward, not value or excellence.
Sitting on the bench is a result that happens afterward, not a final decision about a choice.
Sitting on the bench is a bad result, not a pleasant treat.
The sentence says something that happens afterward, not a risky project.
No one argues here; skipping practice simply led to sitting on the bench.
A safe place is not something that happens afterward because of a choice.

example: We had adequate time to finish.
hook: Adequate means just enough: not a gold medal, but a passing grade that gets the job done.

traps.why: Lacking means not enough, the opposite of adequate.
Too strong: adequate is just okay, not excellent.
Accurate looks like adequate, but it means correct.

syn1.tip: "Adequate time" means enough time. Adequate is okay, not amazing.

sc1.stem: Jon's poster was not great, but it was _____, just good enough to earn a passing grade.

traps.why: The sentence says the poster was "not great," so not excellent.
A terrible poster would not earn a passing grade.
Accurate looks like adequate but means correct, not good enough.

sc1.tip: "Not great, but" tells you it was okay, and "just good enough" restates the blank.

decoys.why: The sentence says the poster was not great, so it was not extremely good.
A poster that is just good enough to pass is not worth special notice.
The poster earned a passing grade, so it was not silly or senseless.
Just good enough is the opposite of very strong or extreme.
The sentence is about the poster's quality, not whether it bends.
We know it is Jon's poster, and the clue is about being good enough.

traps.why: Adequate means there is enough, so this is the opposite.
Too strong: adequate is just good enough, not the best.
Adequate sounds like equal, but it means good enough.

syn2.tip: Adequate is a middle word. It means it does the job, nothing more.

sc2.stem: We packed only one sandwich each, which was _____ for a short hike, so nobody got hungry before we returned home at lunchtime.

traps.why: Nobody got hungry, so the sandwiches did their job.
Taste is not the point; the clue is that it was enough.
Accurate looks like adequate but means correct, which fits no sandwich.

sc2.tip: "So nobody got hungry" is the effect: one sandwich was enough. "Only" hints it was just enough, not a feast.

decoys.why: Nobody got hungry, so one sandwich made sense for a short hike.
The sandwich was enough food; nothing about it being easily harmed.
The hike was short and they got home by lunch, so nothing is far away here.
Nothing says the sandwiches were unusual; the clue is that nobody got hungry.
A sandwich cannot be nervous; the sentence says it was enough food.
One plain sandwich each was just enough, not worth special notice.

meaning: to follow a rule or request
example: Please comply with the library rules.
hook: Comply rhymes with reply: when the teacher asks you to sit, you comply by sitting down.

traps.why: Defy means to refuse to obey, the opposite of comply.
Complain starts like comply, but it means to grumble.
Reply rhymes with comply, but it means to answer.

syn1.tip: Signs say "please comply with the rules." Comply means do what the rule or request says.

sc1.stem: All visitors must _____ with the zoo's rules, so Jamal obeyed the sign and kept his hands out of the tank.

traps.why: Jamal obeyed the sign, so he did not argue with the rules.
Compete starts like comply, but you cannot compete with rules.
Messing with rules is naughty, but Jamal followed them.

sc1.tip: "So Jamal obeyed the sign" shows what visitors must do with the rules. The blank means to follow them.

decoys.why: Jamal simply obeyed the sign; he did not discuss the rules to make a deal.

traps.why: Refusing to listen is the opposite of complying.
Rule makers are on the other side; complying means following rules.
That is a compliment, a word that looks like comply.

syn2.tip: You comply with a rule or request. It means you follow it.

sc2.stem: Most of the class lined up quietly when the fire alarm rang, but two boys refused to _____ and kept chatting by the window until the teacher called them.

traps.why: The boys did disobey, so refusing to disobey makes no sense.
Complain looks like comply, but the clue is about following the rule.
Reply rhymes with comply, but nobody asked the boys a question.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the boys with the class that "lined up quietly." They refused to follow the rule, so the blank means obey.

decoys.why: The boys kept calmly chatting, and the clue is that they did not follow the class.
The boys kept chatting, so the word must mean following the rule, not speaking softly.
They were not discussing a deal; they ignored the fire drill rules.
The sentence contrasts them with classmates who lined up, so it means following the rule.

example: Fresh herbs enhance the soup's flavor.
hook: On TV, a detective says 'enhance' and a blurry photo suddenly gets sharper and better.

traps.why: Worsen means make worse, the opposite of enhance.
Enchant looks similar but means to cast a spell or delight.
Perfect means make flawless; enhance just means make better.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase 'enhance the flavor.' Something enhanced ends up better than it was before.

sc1.stem: A pinch of cinnamon will _____ the flavor of the apple pie, making it taste even better than before.

traps.why: Spoiling the flavor would not make the pie taste better.
You measure cinnamon, but measuring doesn't make the pie taste better.
Enchant looks like enhance but means to put under a spell.

sc1.tip: The sentence tells you: 'making it taste even better than before.' Pick the word that means make better.

decoys.why: The pie tastes even better, so the cinnamon does not send the flavor away.
Cinnamon does not check the flavor; it makes the pie taste better.
The sentence says the pie tastes better, not that the flavor gains or gets something.
A flavor cannot be confused; the cinnamon makes it taste better.
You might be surprised, but the flavor itself is made better, not surprised.

traps.why: Make worse is the exact opposite of enhance.
Enhance is about quality, not size.
Making something brand new goes further than just making it better.

syn2.tip: Enhance is a positive word. Ask which choice adds something good to what is already there.

sc2.stem: The plain cupcakes looked boring, but adding rainbow sprinkles and swirly frosting helped _____ them, and soon every kid in class wanted one.

traps.why: Ruined cupcakes would not make every kid want one.
Weighing cupcakes doesn't change how they look.
Sprinkles don't make cupcakes bigger; they make them look better.

sc2.tip: Look at 'boring, but.' The sprinkles changed boring cupcakes into ones everyone wanted, so they made them better.

decoys.why: Every kid wanted a cupcake, so the sprinkles did not send them away.
Sprinkles and frosting made the cupcakes better, not confusing.
You cannot speak angrily to cupcakes, and the sentence is about making them better.
The cupcakes looked boring, not sad, so they did not need comfort.
Kids wanted to eat the cupcakes, so nobody threw them.
The decorations helped the cupcakes become popular, not work against them.

example: A caterpillar transforms into a butterfly.
hook: Trans means across and form means shape: a caterpillar crosses over into a whole new form as a butterfly.

traps.why: Preserve means keep the same, the opposite of transform.
Perform also ends in form but means act or do.
Adjust means a small change; transform means a complete change.

syn1.tip: Think of a caterpillar that transforms into a butterfly. Which choice means change something into something else?

sc1.stem: In one weekend, the volunteers will completely _____ the empty, weedy lot into a colorful garden full of flowers.

traps.why: Neglecting the lot would leave it weedy, not make a garden.
You divide into parts, but a garden is a whole new thing.
Perform looks like transform but means act on a stage.

sc1.tip: The clue words are 'completely' and 'into.' A weedy lot becoming a garden is a complete change.

decoys.why: Volunteers cannot throw a whole lot; the sentence says they turn it into a garden.
A weedy lot cannot be scared; the sentence is about changing it into a garden.
You cannot confuse an empty lot; the volunteers are changing it into a garden.

traps.why: Staying the same is the opposite of transforming.
Transform is a total change, not a small one.
Trans can mean across, but transform is about changing form.

syn2.tip: Split it: trans plus form. The form, or shape, of something gets totally changed.

sc2.stem: Mom used paint, glue, and paper windows to _____ an old cardboard box into a castle, and nobody could tell it had once held a refrigerator.

traps.why: Preserving the box would keep it looking like a box.
Repairing fixes a box; it doesn't turn it into a castle.
Measuring the box wouldn't hide what it used to be.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: 'nobody could tell it had once held a refrigerator.' The box changed so completely it was unrecognizable.

decoys.why: Mom used paint and glue to change the box, not throw it.
A cardboard box cannot be scared; Mom changed it into a castle.
A box cannot be confused; the sentence says it became a castle.

example: The judges announced their verdict.
hook: Verdict contains dict, meaning say: it is what a judge or jury finally says.

traps.why: A doubt is uncertainty; a verdict settles the question.
A trial happens in court, but the verdict is the decision at its end.
Verb starts the same way but is an action word.

syn1.tip: You hear 'verdict' at the end of a courtroom show, when the jury announces its final decision.

sc1.stem: After tasting all the pies, the judges announced their _____: Grandma's peach pie had won first place.

traps.why: Pies have recipes, but a recipe doesn't say who won.
A question asks; the judges here are giving an answer.
Judges tasting pies have appetites, but announcing one doesn't name a winner.

sc1.tip: After the colon comes what was announced: 'Grandma's peach pie had won first place.' That is a final decision.

decoys.why: The judges announced a winner together, not an angry argument.
What follows the colon is who won, which is a decision, not thanks.
The judges were not announcing a wish to succeed; they named the winner.
Naming the winning pie is a final decision, not a careless mistake.
The judges announced which pie won, not someone they competed against.
The colon shows the judges announced who won, which is a decision, not value.

traps.why: A first guess is unsure; a verdict is final.
Dict means say, but verdict means a decision, not any word.
A hearing happens in court; the verdict is what it decides.

syn2.tip: A verdict ends things. Choose the phrase that sounds settled and done.

sc2.stem: Unlike a guess, which can change, the teacher's _____ on who won the science fair was final, so nobody could argue about it.

traps.why: A question isn't final; it still needs an answer.
Science fairs have posters, but a poster doesn't decide who won.
A hint is only a small clue, not a final answer.

sc2.tip: The word 'Unlike a guess' sets up a contrast, and 'was final' finishes it. You need a word for a final decision.

decoys.why: The sentence says the decision was final and unarguable, not a careless mistake.
Nobody could argue about it, so it was not an angry argument.
The sentence is about a final decision on who won, not a wish to succeed.
The teacher made a final decision about the winner, not a result of an action.
The teacher was judging the fair, not competing against anyone.

meaning: to discuss to reach an agreement
example: We negotiated a later bedtime.
hook: Picture two kids trading lunch: 'I'll give you my chips for your cookie.' They are negotiating.

traps.why: Refusing ends the talk; negotiating keeps talking toward a deal.
Demanding is one side insisting, not both sides working out a deal.
Neglect starts with neg but means fail to take care of.

syn1.tip: You may hear 'negotiate a deal' or 'negotiate a price.' Both sides talk and give a little.

sc1.stem: The two sisters sat down to _____ a deal: Ana would wash the dishes if Bea walked the dog.

traps.why: Breaking a deal ends it; the sisters are making one.
Neglect looks a bit like negotiate but means ignore.
The sentence describes a deal being made, not canceled.

sc1.tip: The colon shows the deal they worked out: 'Ana would wash the dishes if Bea walked the dog.' Each sister gives something.

decoys.why: The sisters agreed on a trade, so they did not work against the deal.
The sentence is about working out an agreement, not speaking softly.
You cannot throw a deal; the sisters were talking out a trade.
The sisters were making a new deal, not checking that one was true.

traps.why: Negotiating means talking it through, not refusing to talk.
An order comes from one side; negotiating needs both sides to agree.
Negotiating is calm give and take, not a loud fight.

syn2.tip: Think of a trade where both people get something. That back and forth is negotiating.

sc2.stem: Instead of shouting at each other over the last slice of pizza, the twins decided to calmly _____, and they agreed to split it in half.

traps.why: Quarreling is fighting, but the twins chose not to shout.
Refusing wouldn't lead them to agree on splitting it.
Eating comes later; first they had to agree how to share.

sc2.tip: 'Instead of shouting' tells you they did something calm, and 'they agreed' shows the result. That is talking to reach a deal.

decoys.why: Wanting the pizza badly would not lead them to agree to split it.
Speaking softly is not the same as discussing until you reach an agreement.

meaning: to change to fit new conditions
example: Animals adapt to their surroundings.
hook: Polar bears adapt to the Arctic with thick fur; living things change to fit where they live.

traps.why: Adopt differs by one letter and means take as your own.
Resisting change is the opposite of adapting to it.
Animals adapt in order to survive, but survive means stay alive.

syn1.tip: Think of 'animals adapt to their surroundings.' They change a little to fit in.

sc1.stem: When the family moved from sunny Florida to snowy Maine, the kids needed a few months to _____ to the cold.

traps.why: Adopt looks like adapt but means take in as your own.
They already moved; the months were for getting used to the cold.
Objecting to the cold is complaining, not getting used to it.

sc1.tip: Moving 'from sunny Florida to snowy Maine' causes a big change. The kids needed time to fit the new weather.

decoys.why: The kids needed time to get used to the cold, not to speak softly.

traps.why: Adapting means changing; staying the same is the opposite.
That is what adopt means, a word that looks like adapt.
Moving can create new conditions, but adapting is fitting into them.

syn2.tip: When you adapt to a new school, you slowly get comfortable there. Pick the choice that means that.

sc2.stem: At first the new puppy whined every night in its crate, but after a week it began to _____ and slept quietly until morning.

traps.why: Complaining fits 'at first,' but 'but' signals the puppy changed.
Adopt looks like adapt but means take in as your own.
Barking is a dog sound, but the puppy ended up quiet.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' shows a contrast: whining 'at first,' then sleeping 'quietly.' The puppy got used to its crate.

decoys.why: The puppy stopped making noise and slept quietly, so it did not keep murmuring.
The puppy calmed down and slept quietly, so it did not get scared suddenly.

example: The chef made a superb dinner.
hook: Superb starts with super: a superb dinner is so good it seems above all the others.

traps.why: Awful means very bad, the opposite of superb.
Okay is only so-so; superb means extremely good.
Superb things can be fancy, but superb means very good.

syn1.tip: Superb begins with super, as in 'super good.' Choose the word for the very best.

sc1.stem: The gymnast's _____ routine, extremely good from start to finish, earned a perfect score from every single judge.

traps.why: A sloppy routine wouldn't earn a perfect score.
Average is ordinary; this routine was extremely good.
Gymnasts may feel nervous, but that doesn't describe how good the routine was.

sc1.tip: The sentence says it outright: 'extremely good from start to finish' and 'a perfect score.' Pick the word that means that.

decoys.why: A perfect score means extremely good, not just good enough.
The clue says extremely good from start to finish, which is more than competent.
Gymnasts bend, but the clue says the routine was extremely good.
The routine earned a perfect score, so nothing points to nervousness.
A routine with a perfect score was not silly and senseless.

traps.why: Very poor is the opposite of superb.
Fairly good is too weak; superb is extremely good.
Super can mean above, but superb describes quality, not height.

syn2.tip: Superb is a word of strong praise. Look for the choice that says something is top quality.

sc2.stem: The first batch of cookies burned, but the second batch was _____, so golden and delicious that Dad ate six before dinner.

traps.why: Ruined fits the first batch, but 'but' shows the second was different.
Decent is only fine; Dad eating six shows they were amazing.
Smoky goes with burning, but these cookies were golden, not burned.

sc2.tip: 'Burned, but' sets up a contrast, and 'golden and delicious' tells you the second batch was wonderful.

decoys.why: Dad ate six golden, delicious cookies, so they were far better than just good enough.
The sentence praises how delicious the cookies were, not whether there were enough.
Golden, delicious cookies are not silly or senseless; the sentence is praising them.
Nothing in the sentence says the cookies could be hurt; it says they were delicious.
The sentence is about how tasty the cookies were, not whether they could bend.
Cookies are not sharp or dull here; the clue is golden and delicious.

example: The room felt tense before the results.
hook: Picture the last seconds of a close game, when everyone holds their breath and grips their seats.

traps.why: Calm means relaxed, the opposite of tense.
Dense rhymes with tense but means thick or packed tight.
Past is a verb tense from grammar, a different meaning of tense.

syn1.tip: Think of a tense moment in a movie, when you are worried about what happens next.

sc1.stem: Waiting for the spelling bee results, Mia was so _____ that her shoulders tightened and she could not relax at all.

traps.why: A calm person could relax, but Mia could not.
Cheerful is happy; tight shoulders show worry.
Waiting can be boring, but boredom doesn't tighten your shoulders.

sc1.tip: The clue is 'her shoulders tightened and she could not relax at all.' Choose the word for that worried feeling.

decoys.why: Her shoulders tightened and she could not relax, which is the opposite of loose and bendy.
The sentence is about nerves, not about Mia being strong and healthy.
Tight shoulders and not relaxing show nerves, not skill at spelling.
Nothing silly is happening; Mia is nervous while waiting for results.
The sentence describes how nervous Mia felt, not how good she was.
Mia's name being unknown has nothing to do with tight shoulders and not relaxing.

traps.why: Relaxed is the opposite of tense.
Terrified is extreme fear; tense is uneasy and unable to relax.
