Anger is another strong feeling, but tense means worried and uneasy.

syn2.tip: Your muscles feel tight when you are tense. That tight, worried feeling before a test is the meaning.

sc2.stem: Before the big soccer final, the locker room felt _____, but as soon as Jada scored the first goal, everyone laughed and finally loosened up.

traps.why: If they were relaxed already, they wouldn't need to loosen up.
Joyful is the feeling after the goal, not before.
A locker room can be crowded, but 'loosened up' is about feelings.

sc2.tip: 'But' shows a change, and 'finally loosened up' tells you the room felt tight and nervous before.

decoys.why: Everyone loosened up only after the goal, so before it the room was not loose.
The laughing came after the goal; before it, the room was nervous, not silly.
The word but shows the mood changed for the better, so it started out bad.
The sentence is about the team's nervous mood, not how far away the room was.
Nothing suggests the locker room was unusual; the clue is that everyone later loosened up.
The contrast with loosening up points to nerves, not to the room being good enough.

example: A fish riding a bike is absurd.
hook: A fish riding a bicycle or a cat doing taxes: anything that silly and senseless is absurd.

traps.why: Sensible means it makes sense, the opposite of absurd.
Absent starts with abs but means not present.
Absurd things can be funny, but absurd means making no sense.

syn1.tip: Absurd ideas make people say 'That's crazy.' Choose the word for something so silly it makes no sense.

sc1.stem: Wearing a snowsuit and mittens to the beach in July is an _____ idea that makes no sense at all.

traps.why: An excellent idea would make sense, but this one doesn't.
Absent looks like absurd but means not there.
Exciting is positive; the sentence calls the idea senseless.

sc1.tip: The sentence gives the meaning: 'an idea that makes no sense at all.' Snowsuits at a July beach are silly.

decoys.why: The idea makes no sense at all, so it is not good enough.
The sentence says the idea makes no sense, not that it is easy to see.
Nobody has to wear a snowsuit to the beach; the clue says it makes no sense.
Whose idea it is does not matter; the sentence says it makes no sense.
The clue is that the idea makes no sense, not that it is very strong.

traps.why: Perfectly reasonable is the opposite of absurd.
Slightly unusual is too mild; absurd is completely senseless.
Careful plans make sense; absurd ideas don't.

syn2.tip: Picture a fish riding a bike. That kind of silly nonsense is absurd.

sc2.stem: My little cousin claimed his goldfish could do his math homework, a story so _____ that the whole family burst out laughing.

traps.why: A goldfish doing math is not believable at all.
A sad story wouldn't make the whole family laugh.
Boring stories don't make people burst out laughing.

sc2.tip: The cause is a goldfish doing homework, and the effect is everyone 'burst out laughing.' The story was silly nonsense.

decoys.why: A goldfish doing homework is not real, and the family laughed at it.
The family burst out laughing, so the story was silly, not serious and strict.
Laughing shows the story was silly, not that anyone felt nervous.
A goldfish doing math is not important; the family found it ridiculous.
A goldfish doing homework is impossible, not sure to happen.

example: The robust oak survived the storm.
hook: Picture a thick old oak that stands tall after a storm while thinner trees snap: robust.

traps.why: Feeble means weak, the opposite of robust.
Rusty has similar letters but means covered in rust.
Robust things may be big, but robust means strong and healthy.

syn1.tip: Think of 'the robust oak survived the storm.' Pick the word for full of strength and energy.

sc1.stem: Grandpa is _____ for his age, strong and healthy enough to chop firewood and swim laps every morning.

traps.why: A frail grandpa couldn't chop firewood every morning.
Age is mentioned, but 'old for his age' makes no sense.
Rusty looks a bit like robust but means covered in rust.

sc1.tip: Right after the comma, the sentence explains: 'strong and healthy enough to chop firewood.' That restates the missing word.

decoys.why: Grandpa is strong and healthy, so he is not easily hurt.
The sentence describes his strength and health, not a strict personality.
Chopping firewood and swimming laps show strength, not hopeful thinking.
Nothing about Grandpa is silly; the sentence praises how strong and healthy he is.
The sentence is about his strength and health, not nerves.
Grandpa's name is not the point; the clue is strong and healthy.

traps.why: Weak and sickly is the opposite of robust.
Size and weight aren't the same as strength and health.
Robust is a compliment; rough and rude is an insult.

syn2.tip: Robust is a positive word for something sturdy that holds up well, like a healthy athlete or a strong tree.

sc2.stem: Most of the tomato plants wilted during the dry summer, but the one by the fence stayed _____, with thick green stems and dozens of fat red tomatoes.

traps.why: Droopy fits the wilted plants, but 'but' shows this one was different.
Dry summers make plants thirsty, but this plant was thriving.
Thick stems and dozens of tomatoes don't describe a tiny plant.

sc2.tip: 'Wilted... but' sets up a contrast, and 'thick green stems' shows the plant stayed strong and healthy.

decoys.why: The other plants wilted, but this one thrived, so it was not easily harmed.
The clue is thick stems and lots of tomatoes, which show strength, not bendiness.
Nothing says the plant came from far away; it stayed healthy in the dry summer.
Plants do not feel nervous; the sentence is about this plant staying healthy.
A healthy tomato plant is not silly; the sentence contrasts it with wilted ones.
A plant cannot be strict; the clue is thick stems and fat tomatoes.

example: Many parents opposed the new rule.
hook: In a tug of war, the two teams oppose each other, each pulling against the other.

traps.why: Support means be for something, the opposite of oppose.
Suppose rhymes with oppose but means guess or think.
People discuss rules they oppose, but discuss just means talk about.

syn1.tip: Oppose is inside opponent, the player on the other side. To oppose is to stand against.

sc1.stem: Most students _____ the plan to shorten recess, so they signed a letter against it.

traps.why: Supporters wouldn't sign a letter against the plan.
Suppose rhymes with oppose but means guess.
Students who enjoy a plan don't write letters against it.

sc1.tip: The clue is 'signed a letter against it.' The students were against the plan.

decoys.why: They signed a letter against the plan, so they did not want to improve it.
You cannot go along with a plan you signed a letter against.
The letter was against the plan, not a check of whether it was true.
The students were against the plan, not trying to make it clearer.
Students cannot get a plan they are signing a letter against.
You cannot throw a plan; the clue is the letter against it.

traps.why: Being in favor is the opposite of opposing.
Opposite can mean across from, but oppose means be against.
Being unsure is too weak; opposing means clearly being against.

syn2.tip: Think of your opponent in a game. They are against you, and that is what oppose means.

sc2.stem: The mayor wanted to close the town pool, but the swim team and dozens of families _____ that idea and packed the meeting to argue for keeping it open.

traps.why: People who approve wouldn't argue to keep the pool open.
Propose looks like oppose but means suggest; it was the mayor's idea.
Ignoring is too weak; they packed the meeting to fight it.

sc2.tip: 'But' shows the families disagreed with the mayor, and 'argue for keeping it open' proves they stood against closing it.

decoys.why: The families argued to keep the pool open, so they did not improve the closing idea.
The families argued against closing the pool, not passing along the mayor's idea.
They packed the meeting to argue against the idea, not to check if it was true.
Arguing to keep the pool open is the opposite of going along with closing it.
The families were fighting the idea, not trying to get it.
The families wanted the idea stopped, not made clearer.

example: The rocky terrain was hard to cross.
hook: Terrain comes from terra, the Latin word for earth, so it means the ground you travel over.

traps.why: Weather is also outdoors, but it is about the air, not the land.
Train sounds like the end of terrain, but a train runs on tracks.
Terror starts the same way but means great fear.

syn1.tip: Terrain starts like terra, which means earth, as in terrarium. Think of the ground under your feet.

sc1.stem: The rocky, hilly _____ made the bike ride difficult, with steep slopes and loose stones everywhere.

traps.why: Weather can make a ride hard, but weather is not rocky or hilly.
Traffic slows riders, but slopes and stones describe the land, not cars.
A terrace is a flat patio, not rocky, hilly land.

sc1.tip: The words "rocky, hilly" and "steep slopes and loose stones" all describe the land itself, so you need a word for the ground.

decoys.why: Steep slopes and loose stones describe the land, not a safe place for animals.
Rocky, hilly land that made the ride hard is not a safe shelter.
Loose stones that make riding difficult are not something costly and pleasant.
The rocky land made the ride difficult, so it was not useful or valuable.
There is no contest here; rocky and hilly describe the land itself.
Rocky and hilly describe the land, not the trip, which is already called the bike ride.

traps.why: Terrace looks similar but means a flat patio or raised level area.
A map shows the land, but it is not the land itself.
A trail is just one narrow path, not all the land and its features.

syn2.tip: Picture a hiker asking what the terrain is like. The answer describes the ground: rocky, flat, or hilly.

sc2.stem: Unlike the flat, smooth sidewalks in town, the _____ on the mountain trail was full of tree roots, sharp rocks, and muddy dips that slowed our hike.

traps.why: Roots, rocks, and dips are parts of the land, not the weather.
A crowd could slow a hike, but a crowd is not full of tree roots.
Train sounds like terrain, but there is no train on a hiking trail.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the flat, smooth sidewalks" sets up a contrast about the ground. Roots, rocks, and dips describe the land you walk on.

decoys.why: Roots, sharp rocks, and muddy dips are not costly comforts, so luxury does not fit.
The sentence describes the land under your feet, not a difficult situation someone is in.
Clamor is a noise, and a noise cannot be full of tree roots and rocks.
The trail's roots and rocks slowed the hike, so they were not something useful.
An opponent is a person you compete against, but the sentence describes ground covered with rocks.

meaning: a safe place, especially for animals
example: The bird sanctuary protects herons.
hook: Sanctuary comes from a Latin word for holy, and holy places were once spots where no one could be harmed.

traps.why: Danger is the opposite of a safe place.
A cage holds animals in, but a sanctuary is a place where they are safe.
Hunters are kept out of a sanctuary; the word means the safe place.

syn1.tip: Think of a "bird sanctuary" or "wildlife sanctuary." Both are places where animals are kept safe from harm.

sc1.stem: The bird _____ by the lake protects herons and ducks, giving them a safe place where no one may hunt them.

traps.why: A feeder gives birds food, but it does not keep hunters away.
A hunter is the danger, not the safe place that protects the birds.
A bird market sells birds; it does not give them a safe home.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains itself: "giving them a safe place where no one may hunt them." You need a word for a protected place.

decoys.why: Terrain is just land, but the sentence says this place protects birds from hunters.
The sentence describes a safe, protected place, and chaos means total confusion.
The birds are given a safe place, not put into a difficult situation.
The place is described as safe from hunters, not as costly or fancy.
Clamor is a loud noise, and a noise cannot protect herons and ducks.

traps.why: A dangerous place is the opposite of a sanctuary.
The word part sanct does mean holy, but a sanctuary is a place, not a song.
An animal doctor helps animals, but a sanctuary is a place, not a person.

syn2.tip: A sanctuary protects whoever is inside it. If you know refuge or haven, sanctuary belongs with them.

sc2.stem: Because hunting and fishing are not allowed there, the forest _____ has become a home where deer, foxes, and owls can live without fear.

traps.why: A danger is the opposite of a home where animals live without fear.
A campsite is for people, not a protected home for animals.
A highway runs through forests, but it is no safe home for deer.

sc2.tip: "Because hunting and fishing are not allowed" is the cause. Animals living "without fear" is the effect, so the forest is a protected place.

decoys.why: Animals live there without fear, so the place is calm and safe, not total confusion.
The sentence says animals live without fear, which is not a difficult situation.
A loud noise cannot become a home where deer and owls live.
A venture is a risky trip or project, but the sentence describes a safe home.
The forest is described as a protected home, not as something costly and fancy.

example: She is a competent swimmer.
hook: A competent cook can follow a recipe and make a good meal, even if she is no famous chef.

traps.why: Unskilled is the opposite of competent.
Competitive looks similar but means eager to win, not able to do well.
Brilliant is much stronger; competent just means good enough to do it well.

syn1.tip: Competent is about having enough skill to do a job well. Think of a "competent driver," one you would trust to drive safely.

sc1.stem: Omar is no champion, but he is _____ at the piano, playing most songs well and without many mistakes.

traps.why: Hopeless fits "no champion," but Omar plays most songs well.
Brilliant is too strong, since the sentence says Omar is no champion.
Competitive means eager to win, but the clue is about playing well.

sc1.tip: "Playing most songs well and without many mistakes" explains the blank. "No champion" rules out a word that is too strong.

decoys.why: The sentence says Omar is no champion, so extremely good is too strong.
Omar plays most songs well, which is not silly or senseless.
The sentence is about how well Omar plays, not about being easily hurt.
Strong and healthy describes his body, but the sentence is about his piano skill.
Being direct or not sharp has nothing to do with playing songs well.

traps.why: Helpless means unable to do things, the opposite of competent.
Complete looks a bit like competent but means finished or whole.
Confident is feeling sure of yourself, not actually having the skill.

syn2.tip: If someone is competent, you can trust them to get the job done. Ask yourself which choice describes real ability.

sc2.stem: Since Maya had practiced first aid all summer, the camp director knew she was _____ enough to help a younger camper bandage a scraped knee.

traps.why: Practice makes Maya skilled, the opposite of clumsy.
Being nervous would not make a director trust her to help.
Competitive looks similar but means eager to win, not able to help.

sc2.tip: "Since Maya had practiced first aid all summer" is the cause. Practice makes you able to do something well.

decoys.why: Maya practiced all summer and can help others, so she is skilled, not easily harmed.
Her summer of practice suggests she has skill, not that she is nervous.
Nothing about practicing first aid makes Maya silly or senseless.
The director knows Maya, and her name has nothing to do with helping bandage a knee.
The sentence is about Maya's skill, not something sure to happen.

example: We wrote cards to show our gratitude.
hook: Gratitude shares a Latin root with gracias, the Spanish word for thank you.

traps.why: Attitude rhymes with gratitude but means the way you think or act.
A gift often earns gratitude, but gratitude is the feeling, not the present.
A complaint reacts to what you got, but with an unhappy feeling.

syn1.tip: Gratitude is close to the word grateful. When you feel grateful, you are full of thanks.

sc1.stem: To show her _____, Lena wrote a thank-you card to the firefighters who had rescued her cat from a tree.

traps.why: A thank-you card shows a happy feeling, not anger.
Attitude sounds like gratitude, but a thank-you card shows thanks.
Lena may have been surprised, but a thank-you card shows thankfulness.

sc1.tip: The words "thank-you card" are the clue. A thank-you card shows that you are thankful.

decoys.why: A thank-you card shows thankfulness, not a strong wish to succeed.
Writing a thank-you card shows thanks, not strength and energy.
The card thanks the firefighters, so it shows her thanks, not her own value.
A thank-you card has nothing to do with showing success and wealth.
The cat was already rescued, and a thank-you card shows thanks, not a problem.

traps.why: Envy is wanting what others have, a bad feeling, not a thankful one.
Politeness covers all good manners; gratitude is the feeling of thanks.
Gravity looks a bit similar but is the force that pulls things down.

syn2.tip: Think of the word grateful. Gratitude is the feeling of being grateful, so look for the choice that means valuing what you were given.

sc2.stem: Instead of complaining about the scratchy sweater from his grandma, Theo hugged her and smiled, filled with _____ for the gift she had knitted by hand.

traps.why: Disappointment fits a scratchy sweater, but Theo smiled instead of complaining.
The sweater may be itchy, but itchiness is not a feeling about a gift.
Envy means wanting what others have, but Theo already has the gift.

sc2.tip: "Instead of complaining" signals a contrast. Theo "hugged her and smiled," so he felt thankful, not upset.

decoys.why: Theo hugged and smiled about a gift, which shows thankfulness, not strength and energy.
Being glad about a handmade gift is thankfulness, not a wish to succeed.
Theo calmly hugged his grandma, so he was not filled with total confusion.
Theo chose to smile instead of complain, so he was not feeling trapped in a problem.
Theo hugged and smiled quietly, and you cannot be filled with loud noise for a gift.

example: The zoo has many exotic birds.
hook: Exotic comes from a Greek word meaning outside, so exotic things come from outside your own land, like a toucan from Brazil.

traps.why: Native means from right here, the opposite of exotic.
Exact starts like exotic but means perfectly correct.
Exotic things can cost a lot, but exotic means from far away.

syn1.tip: Exotic things come from far away and seem unusual to you. Think of "exotic fruits" like dragon fruit sold far from where they grow.

sc1.stem: The pet store sold an _____ parrot from a faraway rain forest, with feathers unlike any bird we had ever seen.

traps.why: An ordinary parrot would not have feathers unlike any bird we had seen.
It may cost a lot, but the clue is about coming from far away.
Exact looks like exotic but means correct; it does not describe a parrot.

sc1.tip: "From a faraway rain forest" and "unlike any bird we had ever seen" both describe something from far away and unusual.

decoys.why: The clue is that the parrot came from far away, not that its name is unknown.
Unusual feathers make the parrot rare and faraway, not silly or senseless.
The parrot has feathers unlike any bird seen before, so it is special, not just good enough.
Sure to happen describes events, not a parrot from a faraway rain forest.
Expecting good things is a feeling, and the sentence describes where the parrot came from.
The clue is the faraway rain forest, so easy to see misses the point.

traps.why: Ordinary is the opposite of exotic.
Some exotic animals are dangerous, but exotic means strange and faraway.
Many exotic things are tropical, but exotic just means from far away.

syn2.tip: If something is exotic, it seems different from what you see every day. Choose the word that means out of the ordinary.

sc2.stem: Our garden is full of common daisies and dandelions, but my aunt's greenhouse holds _____ orchids that came all the way from the islands of Southeast Asia.

traps.why: Local means from nearby, but these orchids came from far away.
Nothing in the sentence says the orchids are drooping or dying.
Excited looks a bit like exotic, but flowers cannot feel excited.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a contrast with "common daisies." The orchids "came all the way from" far islands, so they are the opposite of common.

decoys.why: The orchids are contrasted with common daisies, so they are special, not merely good enough.
The sentence stresses that the orchids came from far away, not that they survive hard conditions.
The contrast is common versus faraway flowers, not whether the orchids have names.
Flowers from distant islands are unusual, not continuing firmly despite problems.
Orchids cannot be nervous, and the clue is that they came from far away.
The sentence contrasts common and faraway flowers, so not sharp or direct makes no sense.

example: Her ambition is to become an astronaut.
hook: Ambition is the fire inside that makes a kid practice free throws every day, dreaming of the big leagues.

traps.why: Laziness means not wanting to work, the opposite of ambition.
Ambulance starts the same way but is a vehicle for sick people.
Talent helps you succeed, but ambition is the wish to succeed.

syn1.tip: Ambition is a strong wish to achieve something big. Think of a person with "big ambitions" who dreams of becoming a doctor.

sc1.stem: Sofia's greatest _____ is to become an astronaut, and she works hard in science class to reach that goal.

traps.why: Sofia works hard to reach this goal, so it is a wish, not a fear.
A talent is something you can do now, not a goal to reach.
A hobby is fun to do now; becoming an astronaut is a future goal.

sc1.tip: "To become an astronaut" and "reach that goal" show the blank is something Sofia strongly wants to achieve.

decoys.why: Becoming an astronaut is a goal she works toward, not something useful she owns.
The sentence calls becoming an astronaut a goal, which is a wish, not her value.
She works hard to reach a goal, which shows a wish to succeed, not thankfulness.
A goal she works hard to reach is a wish, not something costly and pleasant.
Becoming an astronaut is her goal, not a careless mistake.
Becoming an astronaut is a goal, and an opponent is a person you compete against.

traps.why: Not caring is the opposite of ambition.
Ambitious people may fear failing, but ambition is the wish to succeed.
Love of money is greed, a darker feeling than ambition.

syn2.tip: An ambitious person works hard to get somewhere. Pick the choice that shows wanting to achieve something.

sc2.stem: Lazy Leo was happy to sit on the couch all summer, but his twin sister was full of _____ and spent every day training to make the swim team.

traps.why: Laziness describes Leo; "but" shows his sister is the opposite.
A bored person would not train every day to make a team.
Envy is wanting what others have, not working toward your own goal.

sc2.tip: "But" sets up a contrast with "lazy Leo." His sister "spent every day training," which shows a strong drive to succeed.

decoys.why: She trained every day to make the team, which shows drive to succeed, not thankfulness.
Training every day is focused and organized, not total confusion.
The sentence is about her drive to succeed, not a loud noise.
Lazy Leo is the one enjoying comfort; his sister is working hard to succeed.
She is working toward a goal, not already enjoying success and wealth.

example: The new factory brought prosperity to the town.
hook: Picture a town with busy shops, new houses, and plenty of paychecks; that town is enjoying prosperity.

traps.why: Poverty means being poor, the opposite of prosperity.
Property looks similar but means things you own, like land or a house.
Prosperity can bring happiness, but it means success and wealth.

syn1.tip: Prosperity is the noun for prosperous. Think of the wish "peace and prosperity," which means safety and plenty of money.

sc1.stem: After the new factory opened, the town enjoyed years of _____, with good jobs, busy shops, and plenty of money.

traps.why: Good jobs and plenty of money are the opposite of poverty.
Factories can cause pollution, but no one enjoys years of it.
Property looks similar, but the clue describes success and money.

sc1.tip: "Good jobs, busy shops, and plenty of money" describe the blank. You need a word for success and wealth.

decoys.why: Good jobs and plenty of money describe success, not total confusion.
Busy shops might be noisy, but the sentence is about jobs and money.
The clues are jobs, shops, and money, which point to wealth, not thankfulness.
The town already had good jobs and money, so this is success, not a wish.

traps.why: Hardship means hard times, the opposite of prosperity.
Savings is just money put away; prosperity is doing well all around.
Popularity looks a bit similar but means being liked by many people.

syn2.tip: A country in a time of prosperity is doing well. Look for the choice that means things going well, especially with money.

sc2.stem: During the drought, the farmers struggled to pay their bills, but when the rains returned and the crops grew tall, a time of _____ came to the valley.

traps.why: Hardship fits the drought, but "but" shows things got better.
Rain can cause floods, but tall crops show good times, not disaster.
Priority looks similar but means something that matters most.

sc2.tip: "But" shows a contrast with farmers who "struggled to pay their bills." When crops grew tall, the farmers did well and had money.

decoys.why: The rains ended the hard times, so the valley got success, not confusion.
The valley is land, but a time of land makes no sense here.
The sentence contrasts unpaid bills with good times, not quiet with noise.
The farmers could pay bills again, which is wealth, not a wish to succeed.

example: The barn was a refuge from the rain.
hook: Refuge shares a root with refugee, a person who flees danger to find a safe place.

traps.why: Danger is the opposite of a safe place.
Refund looks similar but means money given back.
People take refuge from a storm, but the storm is not the safe place.

syn1.tip: Think of "take refuge," which means find a safe place. People take refuge from storms, danger, or noise.

sc1.stem: When the rain began to pour, the hikers took _____ under a rocky ledge until the storm passed.

traps.why: Taking chances means risking danger, but the hikers were staying safe.
Refund looks like refuge but means money back, which makes no sense here.
To take flight means to run off, but the hikers stayed under the ledge.

sc1.tip: "When the rain began to pour" and "until the storm passed" show the hikers needed protection. Taking it "under a rocky ledge" means finding shelter.

decoys.why: The ledge is rocky land, but the hikers took shelter there, not land.
They waited safely under the ledge, which is shelter, not confusion.
You take shelter from rain, not thankfulness, under a ledge.
A rocky ledge in a storm is a plain shelter, not something costly.
The hikers were hiding from rain, so they needed shelter, not energy.

traps.why: A place of danger is the opposite of a refuge.
That is refuse, a lookalike word; refuge means a safe place.
You seek refuge from stormy weather, but refuge is the shelter.

syn2.tip: A refuge is where you go to get away from trouble. Picture a cozy library as a refuge from a noisy, crowded house.

sc2.stem: The noisy cafeteria gave Mia a headache, so the quiet school library became her _____, a peaceful spot where she could read and escape the crowd.

traps.why: A prison is a place you cannot escape, not a peaceful spot.
The cafeteria gave her a headache; the library is where she escaped it.
A chore is a task, not a peaceful spot to escape the crowd.

sc2.tip: The phrase after the comma restates the blank: "a peaceful spot where she could read and escape the crowd." That describes a safe place.

decoys.why: The library is quiet and peaceful, while clamor is the loud noise she escaped.
The sentence calls the library a peaceful spot, the opposite of confusion.
The library is a place she escapes to, not a hard choice.
A library is a peaceful spot, not someone against her in a contest.
The blank is renamed as a peaceful spot, so it must be a place.

example: This blunt knife can't cut the bread.
hook: A blunt pencil needs sharpening, and a blunt friend tells you straight out that your shirt is on backward.

traps.why: Sharp is the opposite of blunt.
Blurry looks similar but means hard to see clearly.
A blunt knife still works a little; broken means it does not work.

syn1.tip: Blunt describes an edge or point that is not sharp. Think of a "blunt pencil" that needs sharpening before you can write neatly.

sc1.stem: Kindergarten safety scissors have _____, rounded tips instead of sharp points, so no one can get poked.

traps.why: Pointed is the opposite of the rounded tips the sentence describes.
Kids' scissors are often colorful, but the clue is about the tips' shape.
Blurry looks like blunt but means hard to see, not rounded.

sc1.tip: "Instead of sharp points" tells you the blank is the opposite of sharp. "Rounded tips" also points to an edge that is not sharp.

decoys.why: The tips are made so no one gets hurt; they are not easily hurt themselves.
The clue is rounded instead of sharp, which has nothing to do with faraway places.
Rounded tips for safety make sense, so silly does not fit.
The sentence describes the shape of the tips, not an unknown name.
Scissor tips cannot be nervous; the clue is rounded instead of sharp.

traps.why: Gentle words soften the truth, the opposite of blunt words.
Cruel is too strong; a blunt person is honest, not trying to hurt.
Blunt words are often short, but blunt means direct, not brief.

syn2.tip: Blunt also describes how people talk. A blunt person says exactly what they think without softening it, like "That drawing is messy."

sc2.stem: Grandpa is always _____; when I asked how my cookies tasted, he said plainly that they were burned and too salty.

traps.why: A gentle grandpa would soften the news about burned cookies.
Dull matches blunt's knife meaning, but here Grandpa speaks plainly.
The sentence is about cookies, but it shows how Grandpa talks, not eats.

sc2.tip: "He said plainly that they were burned and too salty" shows Grandpa speaks directly without softening the truth.

decoys.why: He plainly said the cookies were burned, which is direct, not hopeful.
He spoke plainly, which is clear and direct, not hard to understand.
We know he is Grandpa, so his name is not unknown.
The clue is that he spoke plainly, not that he bends easily.
Grandpa is the one giving harsh truth, not the one easily hurt.

example: The persistent woodpecker kept tapping.
hook: Persistent comes from persist, meaning to keep going, so a persistent puppy keeps nudging your hand until you pet it.

traps.why: Lazy people give up easily; persistent people keep going.
Personal starts the same way but means private or about one person.
Persistence can annoy people, but persistent mostly praises steady effort.

syn1.tip: Persistent contains persist, which means to keep going. A persistent person does not give up, even when things get hard.

sc1.stem: Even after her robot failed nine times, the _____ inventor kept fixing it until it finally worked on the tenth try.

traps.why: A lazy inventor would not keep fixing the robot ten times.
A hopeless inventor would stop, but this one kept fixing the robot.
Personal looks like persistent but does not describe someone who keeps trying.

sc1.tip: "Kept fixing it until it finally worked on the tenth try" shows an inventor who would not give up after failing.

decoys.why: She kept fixing the robot carefully after each failure, which shows she never quit, not carelessness.
The clue is that she kept trying after nine failures, not that her name is unknown.
Nine failures did not stop her, so she was not easily harmed.
Fixing a robot until it works makes sense, so silly does not fit.
The sentence is about her not giving up, not where she comes from.

traps.why: Quick to quit is the opposite of persistent.
Being on time is a good habit, but persistent means not giving up.
Pushy is a negative word; persistent is mostly a compliment.

syn2.tip: Think of a "persistent cough" that will not go away. Persistent people and things keep on going and do not stop.

sc2.stem: Most of the kids gave up on the tricky jigsaw puzzle after ten minutes, but _____ Jamal kept working on it all afternoon until every piece fit.

traps.why: Impatient kids gave up quickly, but Jamal stayed with it all afternoon.
A bored kid would quit, but Jamal kept working until the end.
Lazy describes quitting, but "but" shows Jamal was different.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Jamal with the kids who "gave up." He "kept working on it all afternoon," so he refused to quit.

decoys.why: Jamal stuck with the puzzle all afternoon, which is about not quitting, not bending.
Jamal is named, and the clue is that he kept working while others quit.
A jigsaw puzzle is not dangerous; the clue is that he never gave up.
Finishing a puzzle is not silly; the sentence praises him for not quitting.
This describes events, not a boy who kept working when others gave up.
The sentence contrasts quitters with Jamal's effort, not with being unknown.

example: The stern librarian asked us to whisper.
hook: Picture a stern judge peering over her glasses: no smile, no jokes, just strict rules and a serious face.

traps.why: Gentle is the opposite of stern; a stern person is firm, not soft.
The stern is the back of a boat, but a stern person is strict.
Furious is far too strong; a stern person is serious, not raging.

syn1.tip: Think of a stern teacher's look when the class gets noisy. It feels serious and firm, like someone enforcing rules.

sc1.stem: With a _____ look and a serious, strict voice, the coach told the team that nobody would skip practice again.

traps.why: A friendly look clashes with the serious, strict voice.
Worried is a feeling on a face, but the clue says strict.
Bored describes a face, but nothing in the sentence shows boredom.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "a serious, strict voice." The look should match that voice.

decoys.why: The coach was warning the team with a strict voice, not giving an excellent look.
Saying nobody would skip practice again is strict, not easygoing or bending.
The coach was firm and in charge, not easily hurt.
The sentence says serious and strict, which is the opposite of careless.
The clue says serious and strict, which tells you the kind of look, not just a noticeable one.

traps.why: Playful is the opposite of stern, which means serious and strict.
Cruel goes too far; stern people are strict but not meant to hurt.
A stern voice may be loud, but stern is about being serious.

syn2.tip: Stern goes with words like warning and look. Ask yourself what face fits a stern warning: a serious one.

sc2.stem: Our new principal seemed friendly in the hallway, but in assemblies she was _____, never smiling and insisting that every rule be followed.

traps.why: Relaxed fits the hallway, but "but" tells you assemblies were different.
Playful people smile, and she was "never smiling."
Nervous is a feeling, but nothing says she was afraid or uneasy.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast with "friendly." Then "never smiling" and "every rule be followed" describe a strict, serious person.

decoys.why: She insisted every rule be followed, so she was not flexible at all.
Someone who insists on following every rule is careful, not reckless.
The sentence is about her never smiling and being strict, not about expecting good things.
Nothing says she was silly; she was serious and strict about rules.
Everyone knows who the principal is, so she is not anonymous.
The sentence describes a strict leader, not someone easily hurt.

example: The prince was heir to the throne.
hook: Heir sounds just like air because the h is silent; an heir is next in line to inherit the crown.

traps.why: An ancestor came before you; an heir comes after.
Air sounds the same as heir but means what you breathe.
An heir may rule someday, but is not the ruler yet.

syn1.tip: Heir is inside the word inherit. An heir is the one who takes over next, so think of who comes after.

sc1.stem: As the king's only child, the young prince was the _____ to the throne and would one day rule.

traps.why: Air sounds like heir, but you cannot be the air to a throne.
A servant works near the throne but would not one day rule.
An ancestor came before the king, not after him.

sc1.tip: The clues are "the king's only child" and "would one day rule." The blank names the person who will take over the throne.

decoys.why: The king's only child will inherit the throne, not fight against it.
The sentence says he would one day rule, which means he will inherit the throne.
A prince who will rule is a person in line for the throne, not a symbol.
The prince is a person who will rule, not a safe place.
The sentence is about who will inherit the throne, not about value.
The prince is not a result of an action; he is next in line to rule.

traps.why: That describes an ancestor, the opposite of an heir.
An heir will rule later; someone else rules now.
Heir looks a bit like hire, but heirs inherit, they are not hired.

syn2.tip: Look inside inherit and you will find heir. An heir is the person who will receive something from someone else.

sc2.stem: Because Grandpa wanted his old stamp collection to stay in the family, he named me his _____, so the albums will be mine someday.

traps.why: Grandpa is the ancestor here; you are the one coming after.
A customer buys things, but the albums will be given, not sold.
A neighbor lives nearby, which does not keep the stamps in the family.

sc2.tip: Follow the cause and effect: Grandpa wants it "to stay in the family," so "the albums will be mine someday." The blank names who receives them.

decoys.why: Grandpa is giving you his albums, so you are not someone against him.
The albums will be yours someday, which means you will inherit them.
Grandpa named a person to get his albums, not a final decision.
You are the person who will receive the albums, not a symbol.
The sentence is about who gets the albums, not a safe place.
You are a person inheriting albums, not a costly pleasure.

meaning: to check that something is true
example: Verify your answers before you turn it in.
hook: Verify starts like very, which once meant true; to verify is to make sure something is true.

traps.why: Disprove means show something is false, the opposite of verify.
Vary looks like verify but means to change.
Guessing is about facts too, but verify means checking for sure.

syn1.tip: The ending -ify means to make. Verify starts like very, an old word for true, so verify means make sure it is true.

sc1.stem: Before adding the fact to her report, Ava checked an encyclopedia to _____ that it was actually true.

traps.why: Deny means say it is not true, but Ava wanted to use the fact.
Imagining does not need an encyclopedia and does not check facts.
Hoping a fact is true is not the same as checking it.

sc1.tip: The clue is "checked an encyclopedia" to see "that it was actually true." The blank means to check that something is true.

decoys.why: Ava checked an encyclopedia to test the fact, not to tell it to others.
She was checking whether the fact was true, not arguing against it.

traps.why: Telling a lie spreads falsehood; verifying finds the truth.
Guessing is not checking; verify means you make sure.
Writing something down does not prove it is true.

syn2.tip: You might hear "verify your password" on a computer. The computer is checking that it is really true and correct.

sc2.stem: Instead of just believing the rumor that school was canceled, Marcus called the office to _____ it, and learned classes were still on.

traps.why: People spread rumors, but Marcus called to check, not to tell others.
Calling the office is the opposite of ignoring the rumor.
Marcus did not make up the rumor; he checked it.

sc2.tip: "Instead of just believing" sets up a contrast. Marcus did not just believe it; he called to check whether it was true.

decoys.why: Marcus called to check the rumor, not to spread it to others.
He called to find out if the rumor was true, not to argue against it.
Marcus wanted to check the rumor, not make it better.
He called to learn the truth, not to change the rumor a little.
Marcus wanted to check whether the rumor was true, not change it completely.

example: We were optimistic about winning.
hook: Optimistic comes from the Latin word optimus, meaning best; optimistic people expect the best and see the glass half full.

traps.why: Gloomy people expect bad things, the opposite of optimistic.
Optical starts the same way but means having to do with eyes.
Certain is too strong; optimistic people hope, they are not sure.

syn1.tip: Optimistic starts like optimum, the best. An optimistic person has a bright, positive feeling about what is coming.

sc1.stem: Even after losing three games in a row, Zoe stayed _____, sure that her team would win the next one.

traps.why: Discouraged fits the losses, but Zoe is "sure that her team would win."
Worried people expect trouble, but Zoe expects a win.
Losing might tire her, but the clue is about her expectations.

sc1.tip: "Even after losing" signals a contrast. Despite the losses, she was "sure that her team would win," so she expected good things.

decoys.why: Zoe was sure her team would win, so she was hopeful, not nervous.
The sentence is about her feeling sure of a win, not about her quality.
Being sure of a win is about hope, not about ignoring danger.
The clue is that she expected to win, not that she was unknown.
Nothing says her name was unknown; she was expecting a win.
Zoe was hopeful about the next game, not from a faraway place.

traps.why: Expecting the worst is pessimistic, the opposite of optimistic.
Optim means best, but optimistic is about expecting, not choosing.
Hard work may help, but optimistic describes a hopeful attitude.

syn2.tip: Think of a glass half full. An optimistic person looks ahead and expects good things to happen.

sc2.stem: The weather report showed sunshine all week, so Dad felt _____ that our camping trip would be dry and fun.

traps.why: Sunshine all week gives no reason to doubt a dry trip.
A sunny report would cheer Dad up, not make him gloomy.
Uneasy means worried, but the good forecast removes any worry.

sc2.tip: Look at cause and effect: "sunshine all week, so" Dad expected the trip "would be dry and fun." Good news leads to a hopeful feeling.

decoys.why: Sunshine all week gave Dad good hopes, so he was not nervous.
The sentence is about Dad expecting a fun trip, not being strict.
A sunny forecast made Dad hopeful; it says nothing about lower quality.
Dad was hopeful about the weather, not careless about danger.

meaning: strong enough to survive hard conditions
example: Hardy plants survive the cold winter.
hook: Hardy plants are survivors: a cactus in scorching desert heat and a pine on a frozen mountain are both hardy.

traps.why: Delicate things break easily, the opposite of hardy.
Tardy rhymes with hardy but means late.
Hardy contains hard, but it means strong, not difficult.

syn1.tip: Gardeners call plants hardy when they survive frost. Think of something that can handle tough conditions without dying.

sc1.stem: Only _____ pine trees could survive the freezing winds and thin soil high on the rocky mountaintop.

traps.why: Weak trees could not survive freezing winds and thin soil.
Decorative is about looks, not about surviving harsh weather.
Potted trees do not grow in mountaintop soil and wind.

sc1.tip: The clue is "could survive the freezing winds and thin soil." Only strong trees could do that.

decoys.why: Trees that survive freezing winds and thin soil are tough, not lower in quality.
The clue is surviving harsh conditions, not coming from a faraway place.
Trees cannot expect good things; the sentence is about surviving harsh weather.
The sentence is about trees surviving cold winds, not lacking experience.
Nothing silly is described; the trees are tough enough to survive.
Trees are not done on purpose; the clue is surviving hard conditions.

traps.why: Fragile things break easily; hardy things hold up.
Big things are not always tough; hardy is about surviving.
Harsh describes the conditions; hardy describes what survives them.

syn2.tip: Picture a hardy weed growing through a crack in the sidewalk. It is strong and survives where other plants cannot.

sc2.stem: Most of Grandma's flowers wilted during the dry, scorching summer, but her _____ cactus kept growing as if nothing had happened.

traps.why: A delicate plant would wilt like the others, but "but" shows contrast.
Thirsty fits a dry summer, but the cactus kept growing fine.
Tardy means late, which says nothing about surviving heat.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cactus with the flowers that "wilted." It "kept growing as if nothing had happened," so it was strong.

decoys.why: The cactus survived when other flowers wilted, so it was tougher, not worse.
The cactus kept growing in the heat; the sentence says nothing about nervousness.
A cactus cannot expect good things; the clue is that it survived the heat.
The sentence is about the cactus surviving heat, not lacking experience.
A cactus is not strict; it is tough enough to survive dry heat.
Nothing silly happens; the cactus just survives the scorching summer.

meaning: not well known; or hard to see
example: He collects songs by obscure bands.
hook: An obscure band is one hardly anyone has heard of, and an obscure path is half hidden in shadow.

traps.why: Famous means known by many, the opposite of obscure.
Secure rhymes with obscure but means safe.
Obscure things may seem strange, but obscure means little known.

syn1.tip: Think of "an obscure fact" in a trivia game: one hardly anyone knows. The word feels hidden or out of sight.

sc1.stem: Mia loves an _____ band so little known that none of her friends has ever heard of it.

traps.why: Obvious means easy to notice, the opposite of little known.
An international band is known around the world, not little known.
An overplayed band is heard everywhere, so her friends would know it.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "so little known that none of her friends has ever heard of it."

decoys.why: The clue is that nobody has heard of the band, not that it is bad.
The sentence says the band is little known, not that it expects good things.
The band is described as little known, not silly.
The clue is that none of her friends has heard of it, not that it is good enough.
The band is little known; nothing says it is sure to happen.

traps.why: Easy to spot is the opposite of obscure.
Kept safe means secure, which only sounds like obscure.
Old things can be forgotten, but obscure does not mean old.

syn2.tip: Obscure has two meanings: little known, or hidden from view. Fog can obscure a road, making it hard to see.

sc2.stem: Everyone knew the famous facts about George Washington, but the fact Ben shared was so _____ that even our teacher had never heard it.

traps.why: A familiar fact is one people know, but the teacher never heard it.
Popular facts are widely known, which does not fit "never heard it."
Being important would not explain why the teacher never heard it.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Ben's fact with the "famous facts." The result, "even our teacher had never heard it," shows the fact was little known.

decoys.why: Notable facts are famous ones, but the sentence says even the teacher had never heard it.
Being extremely good would not explain why the teacher had never heard the fact.
A fact that is just good enough would not be unknown even to the teacher.
A fact cannot be sure to happen, and this says nothing about it being unknown.
Hardy describes things that survive hard conditions, not facts nobody has heard.

example: Can you clarify the directions?
hook: Clarify shares its start with clear: to clarify is to make things clear, like wiping fog off a window.

traps.why: Confuse means make less clear, the opposite of clarify.
Classify looks similar but means sort into groups.
Repeating something does not make it any clearer.

syn1.tip: Clarify starts like clear, and -ify means to make. So clarify means to make clear.

sc1.stem: Because the game's directions were confusing, Mr. Park took a moment to _____ them so everyone understood.

traps.why: Complicating confusing directions would not help everyone understand.
Skipping the directions would not make everyone understand them.
Classify looks like clarify but means sort, which does not help here.

sc1.tip: The directions "were confusing," and afterward "everyone understood." The blank is what turns confusing into clear.

decoys.why: Mr. Park wanted everyone to understand, and bewilder means to confuse them more.
Checking that the directions are true would not help confused players understand them.
Being against the directions would not make everyone understand them.
Expecting the directions would not clear up the confusion the sentence describes.
Using up or tiring out the directions makes no sense and does not help understanding.

traps.why: Making something cloudy is the opposite of making it clear.
Louder does not mean easier to understand.
That means classify, which only looks like clarify.

syn2.tip: Look for clar, as in clear, plus -ify, meaning to make. Put them together and you get make clear.

sc2.stem: At first nobody understood Ms. Lee's riddle, but after she drew a picture on the board to _____ it, the whole class finally got the joke.

traps.why: Making the riddle harder would not help the class finally get it.
Decorating a riddle would not help anyone understand it.
Hiding the riddle would stop the class from getting the joke.

sc2.tip: "At first nobody understood," "but" after the picture, "the whole class finally got the joke." The picture made the riddle clear.

decoys.why: The picture helped the class finally get the joke, so it did not confuse them.
A riddle does not need checking for truth; the picture helped the class understand it.
Ms. Lee drew the picture to help with her riddle, not to be against it.
A riddle cannot be comforted; the picture made the riddle clear.
Ms. Lee already had the riddle; the picture was to make it clear.

example: Her smile conveyed how happy she was.
hook: A conveyor belt carries groceries to the cashier; to convey means to carry something, even a feeling or a message.

traps.why: Hide means keep something secret, the opposite of convey.
Convince looks similar but means persuade someone to agree.
Survey ends the same way but means look over or question.

syn1.tip: Think of a conveyor belt that carries things along. When you convey a message, you carry it to someone else.

sc1.stem: Without saying a single word, the actor used only his face to _____ how sad his character felt.

traps.why: The actor was "without saying a single word," so he could not shout.
You cannot measure sadness with your face.
Using his face to forget sadness makes no sense in a performance.

sc1.tip: "Without saying a single word" and "used only his face" tell you he showed the feeling to the audience.

decoys.why: The sentence is about showing sadness with his face, not comforting someone who is sad.
The actor was showing the feeling, not checking that it was true.
Using his face to be against the sadness does not match showing how the character felt.
The actor was expressing a feeling with his face, not expecting it.
He said not a single word, and nobody was reaching an agreement.

traps.why: Drop means let fall, the opposite of carrying something along.
Lifting raises something, but convey means move it somewhere.
Storing keeps things in place; conveying moves them.

syn2.tip: Convey can mean carry as well as communicate. A conveyor belt at the store carries your groceries.

sc2.stem: The pipes in our school are so old that they can no longer _____ water to the fountains, so we have to bring water bottles.

traps.why: Pipes cannot drink water; they move it.
Freezing water to the fountains makes no sense.
Wasting water would not explain why fountains have no water.

sc2.tip: Follow the cause and effect: the old pipes fail, "so we have to bring water bottles." The pipes no longer carry water.

decoys.why: Pipes do not go along with water as a companion; they carry it to the fountains.
Pipes do not chase water; the sentence is about carrying water to the fountains.
Old pipes failing means they cannot carry water, not that they cannot check it.
Pipes do not comfort water; the problem is that water no longer reaches the fountains.

example: That was a deliberate push, not an accident.
hook: A deliberate foul is no accident: the player planned it and meant to do it.

traps.why: Accidental means by mistake, the opposite of deliberate.
Delicate starts the same way but means easily broken.
A deliberate act can be calm; deliberate means planned.

syn1.tip: You often hear "a deliberate mistake" or "that was deliberate" when someone did something on purpose.

sc1.stem: It was no accident: Leo's choice to skip the hard question was _____, since he planned to come back to it later.

traps.why: The sentence says "it was no accident."
Leo had a plan, so his choice was not careless.
Delicate looks similar but means fragile, which does not describe a choice.

sc1.tip: "It was no accident" and "he planned to come back to it" both tell you the choice was made on purpose.

decoys.why: Leo planned to come back to the question, so his choice was not unplanned.
Leo had a careful plan to return to the question, so he was not careless.
Skipping a hard question to return later is sensible, not silly.
The sentence is about Leo planning his choice, not about it being unknown.
Skipping a test question is not dangerous; the clue is that he planned it.

traps.why: Done by mistake is the opposite of deliberate.
Set free means liberate, which only looks like part of deliberate.
Deliberate acts are planned, not necessarily angry.

syn2.tip: Ask: was it an accident or a plan? A deliberate act is one the person meant to do.

sc2.stem: Maya had spent all week practicing the trick, so when she dropped the ball behind her back, the move was _____, meant to fool her opponent.

traps.why: "Dropped" sounds clumsy, but she practiced it and meant to fool someone.
Luck is not planned, and she practiced all week.
The move was "meant to fool her opponent," so not an accident.

sc2.tip: She "spent all week practicing," so the drop was part of the plan. "Meant to fool her opponent" confirms it was on purpose.

decoys.why: Maya practiced all week, so the move was planned, not sudden.
A practiced move meant to fool someone is clever, not innocent or inexperienced.
Hardy means able to survive hard conditions, which does not describe a planned trick.
The sentence stresses that the move was planned to fool, not hopeful.

example: Reckless biking can cause accidents.
hook: Reck is an old word for care, so reckless means without care, like riding a bike downhill with no brakes.

traps.why: Cautious people watch for danger, the opposite of reckless.
Restless looks similar but means unable to sit still.
Brave sounds admiring; reckless is negative, ignoring danger foolishly.

syn1.tip: The ending -less means without. Reckless means without care, the way a reckless driver ignores danger.

sc1.stem: Racing his bike downhill with no helmet and no brakes, Jake was _____, paying no attention to the danger.

traps.why: No helmet and no brakes is the opposite of cautious.
Racing downhill might tire him, but the clue is about danger.
Nothing says Jake did not know where he was.

sc1.tip: "No helmet and no brakes" and "paying no attention to the danger" describe someone who ignores danger.

decoys.why: Jake paid no attention to danger, so he was not nervous about it.
Riding with no helmet or brakes shows carelessness, not skill.
Stern means serious and strict, which has nothing to do with ignoring danger.
Durable describes long-lasting things, not a boy ignoring danger on a bike.
Calling Jake good enough misses that he was ignoring danger.

traps.why: Very careful is the opposite of reckless.
Courage is praised; reckless is a criticism of foolish risk.
That describes restless, which only looks like reckless.

syn2.tip: You may hear "reckless driving" in news stories. It describes someone who acts without caring about danger.

sc2.stem: Mom calls my older sister a careful driver who always checks her mirrors, but she says my cousin is _____ because he texts while driving.

traps.why: Cautious fits the sister, but "but" shows the cousin is different.
Skillful is praise, and texting while driving deserves none.
Patience is not the issue; texting while driving is dangerous.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cousin with the "careful driver." "Because he texts while driving" shows he ignores danger.

decoys.why: The cousin is contrasted with a careful driver, so he is careless, not purposeful.
Texting while driving is not a sign of driving well.
Mom contrasts him with a careful driver, so she is not praising him.
Durable describes things that last long, not a driver who texts.
Being strict has nothing to do with texting while driving.

example: I persuaded Dad to get pancakes.
hook: Picture a kid persuading Mom with a long list of reasons why the family needs a puppy.

traps.why: Discourage is the opposite: it talks someone out of doing something.
Pursue looks like persuade, but it means to chase.
Forcing gives no choice; persuading wins someone over with words.

syn1.tip: When you persuade someone, you talk them into it, the way you might convince a friend to play your favorite game.

sc1.stem: With a strong speech full of facts, Liam managed to _____ the class to vote for a museum field trip.

traps.why: Forbid means to not allow, the opposite of getting them to vote.
A classmate can't order the class; a speech full of facts wins them over.
Allowing is giving permission, but Liam is changing minds, not giving permission.

sc1.tip: Look at "a strong speech full of facts." Facts and speeches are used to win people over, so Liam talked the class into it.

decoys.why: His speech full of facts talked the class into voting; it did not go along with them.
Liam did not carry the class anywhere; his speech talked them into a choice.
A strong speech wins people over; it does not chase them.

traps.why: Talking someone out of something is the opposite of persuading.
You may argue to persuade, but arguing with someone doesn't mean they agree.
Chase after means pursue, a word that only looks like persuade.

syn2.tip: Think of a salesperson trying to persuade you to buy something. They are trying to talk you into it.

sc2.stem: No matter how many reasons I gave, I could not _____ my little brother to try the spinach, so he pushed his plate away.

traps.why: You give reasons to get someone to try something, not to forbid it.
Allowing is giving permission, but reasons are for changing his mind.
Reminding only brings something to mind; reasons are meant to change his mind.

sc2.tip: The clue is "no matter how many reasons I gave" and "pushed his plate away." You tried to talk him into it and failed.

decoys.why: Consoling comforts someone who is sad, but you were giving reasons to get him to try spinach.
Going along with your brother would not get him to eat spinach, and your reasons failed.

meaning: a sign or symbol of something
example: He gave her a flower as a token of thanks.
hook: A token of friendship, like a bead bracelet, is a small thing that stands for a big feeling.

traps.why: An arcade token is a coin, but here token means a sign of something.
A prize is won; a token stands for a feeling.
A token shows a feeling openly; a secret stays hidden.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "a token of thanks." The gift isn't the thanks itself; it stands for the thanks, like a symbol.

sc1.stem: As a _____ of their thanks, the class gave their teacher a handmade card signed by every student.

traps.why: A lack of thanks would mean no thanks, but they made a card.
Tokens can be used like tickets, but a card isn't a ticket.
You may owe someone thanks, but the card shows thanks rather than owing it.

sc1.tip: The phrase is "as a _____ of their thanks." The card is something that shows their thanks, so it is a sign or symbol.

decoys.why: A handmade card of thanks shows respect, not shame.
A card is not a final decision; it is a sign of the class's thanks.
Nobody faced a hard choice; the card simply showed the class's thanks.
A signed card is not a risky project; it stands for their thanks.
A card is not a safe place; it is a sign of thanks.
An heir is a person who inherits things, but the class gave a card.

traps.why: Ride tokens work like tickets, but this token means a sign of something.
You can say thanks in a speech, but a token is a thing that shows it.
A token of thanks doesn't pay someone back; it just shows how you feel.

syn2.tip: A token stands for something else, the way a heart stands for love. That makes it a sign.

sc2.stem: The small shell bracelet was a _____ of their friendship; it was not worth much money, but it stood for everything the two girls shared.

traps.why: The sentence says it was not worth much money, so it isn't about price.
A lack of friendship would mean no friendship, but they shared everything.
Some tokens are coins, but a bracelet isn't a coin.

sc2.tip: The second half explains the blank: "it stood for everything the two girls shared." Something that stands for a feeling is a token.

decoys.why: The bracelet stood for everything the girls shared, so it shows friendship, not shame.
The bracelet stood for their friendship; it was not a final decision.
A bracelet that stands for friendship is not a hard choice.
The sentence is about a bracelet standing for friendship, not a lack of food.
A bracelet is not a risky project; the sentence says it stood for their friendship.
An heir is a person, but the bracelet is an object that stood for friendship.

example: The cheap glue was inferior to the brand name.
hook: Inferior sits below: a knockoff sneaker that falls apart in a week is inferior to the real thing.

traps.why: Superior means better, the opposite of inferior.
Interior looks like inferior, but it means inside.
Inferior is about being worse in quality, not smaller in size.

syn1.tip: Inferior and superior are a pair. Superior is above and better; inferior is below and not as good.

sc1.stem: Our homemade kite was _____ to the store-bought one, which flew higher, looked nicer, and lasted much longer.

traps.why: The store kite flew higher and looked nicer, so the homemade one wasn't better.
The kites weren't equal; the store kite did everything better.
No one would prefer the kite that flew lower and broke sooner.

sc1.tip: The clue is "which flew higher, looked nicer, and lasted much longer." That describes the store kite, so the homemade one was worse.

decoys.why: Nothing says the kite was dangerous; the store kite simply flew higher and lasted longer.
The sentence compares quality, saying the store kite was better, not that ours was unknown.

traps.why: Higher in quality means superior, the opposite of inferior.
That describes interior, a word that only looks like inferior.
Inferior things are just not as good; they aren't completely useless.

syn2.tip: When something is inferior to something else, it is not as good. Think "below" in quality or rank.

sc2.stem: Although the copycat cereal cost less, its flakes turned soggy in seconds, so most kids agreed it was _____ to the famous brand.

traps.why: Soggy flakes make the copycat cereal worse, not better.
The cereals weren't the same; one went soggy in seconds.
Kids can be loyal to a brand, but this is about the cereal's quality.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast: it was cheaper, but "turned soggy in seconds." That makes it worse than the famous brand.

decoys.why: Soggy flakes make the cereal worse, not dangerous to the famous brand.
The kids judged the cereal lower in quality because of soggy flakes, not unknown.

meaning: to use up completely; or to tire out
example: The long hike exhausted our water supply.
hook: Ex- means out: to exhaust a water bottle is to draw out every last drop until nothing is left.

traps.why: Refresh means to give new energy, the opposite of exhaust.
Exhale looks like exhaust, but it means to breathe out.
Car exhaust is smoke, but the verb exhaust means to use up.

syn1.tip: Think of being "exhausted" after a long day: all your energy has been used up, or drained out of you.

sc1.stem: Running laps in the hot sun for an hour seemed to _____ the players, who flopped onto the grass, completely worn out.

traps.why: The players flopped down worn out, so they weren't given energy.
Entertaining is fun; the players ended up worn out, not amused.
The laps might annoy them, but the clue says they were worn out.

sc1.tip: Look at what happened: the players "flopped onto the grass, completely worn out." The laps tired them out.

decoys.why: The players were completely worn out, and revive means to bring back strength.
The players flopped onto the grass worn out, so the laps did not make them stronger.
The players ended up worn out, so the laps did not make them better.
Running laps in the hot sun does not comfort anyone; it wore the players out.
The sentence is about the players being worn out, not about something going along with them.
Laps cannot be against the players; the clue is that they were completely worn out.

traps.why: Saving up keeps things, the opposite of using them all.
Warming up comes before exercise; exhausting is what tires you out.
Slowing down is milder; exhausting means nothing at all is left.

syn2.tip: When you exhaust a supply of snacks, there are none left. You have used them all up.

sc2.stem: We had to be careful not to _____ our supply of firewood on the first night, or there would be nothing left to burn by Saturday.

traps.why: Gathering adds wood, so it wouldn't leave you with nothing.
Stacking wood doesn't make it disappear by Saturday.
Hidden wood would still be there to burn later.

sc2.tip: The effect is "nothing left to burn." The blank must mean using all the firewood up too early.

decoys.why: Getting more firewood would not leave you with nothing to burn by Saturday.
Making the supply stronger would not leave nothing left to burn.
Making the supply better would not cause you to run out by Saturday.
Checking the supply would not leave nothing to burn; using it all up would.
Carrying the firewood does not burn it up, so you would still have some Saturday.
Changing the supply a little would not leave you with nothing left to burn.

example: My aunt will accompany us to the zoo.
hook: Accompany has the word company inside it: when you accompany someone, you keep them company along the way.

traps.why: Abandon means to leave someone behind, the opposite of going with them.
Accomplish looks like accompany, but it means to finish a goal.
Visiting means stopping by, not traveling along with someone.

syn1.tip: Find the word company inside accompany. When you accompany people, you keep them company as they go.

sc1.stem: Mom will _____ the class on the field trip, riding the bus with the students and staying by their side all day.

traps.why: Mom stays by their side all day, so she isn't leaving them.
Accomplish looks similar, but you can't finish a class like a task.
Mom rides the bus with them, so she doesn't need to call.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank: "riding the bus with the students and staying by their side all day." Mom is going along with them.

decoys.why: Mom stays by the students' side all day, so she is with them, not against them.
The sentence says Mom rides the bus and stays by their side, not that she tires them.
Nobody in the sentence is sad; Mom is simply going along on the trip.
Mom is not tempting the class; she rides with them and stays by their side.
Mom is not talking anyone into anything; she is going along on the trip.

traps.why: Leaving someone behind is the opposite of going with them.
Get done means accomplish, a word that only looks like accompany.
Accompany contains company, but it has nothing to do with businesses.

syn2.tip: A piano player who accompanies a singer plays along with them. To accompany is to go along with someone.

sc2.stem: My little sister was too scared to walk into her new school alone, so Dad offered to _____ her all the way to her classroom door.

traps.why: Sending her would leave her alone, which is what scared her.
Dragging is rough; Dad is being kind by going along.
Chasing her wouldn't help a scared kid feel less alone.

sc2.tip: The cause is "too scared to walk... alone." So Dad helps by going along with her.

decoys.why: Dad is not tempting her; he offers to walk with her so she is not alone.
Dad wants to help his scared daughter, not be against her.
Dad offered to walk with her because she was scared, not to tire her out.

example: I caught a glimpse of a deer.
hook: A glimpse is gone in a blink, like spotting a shooting star from a car window before it disappears.

traps.why: A stare is a long look, the opposite of a quick glimpse.
Glimmer looks like glimpse, but it means a faint flicker of light.
A photo shows what you saw, but a glimpse is the look itself.

syn1.tip: People say they "caught a glimpse" of something that went by fast. A glimpse is a quick look, just like a glance.

sc1.stem: We caught only a quick _____ of the deer before it darted back into the woods.

traps.why: The deer ran off fast, so there was no time for a stare.
Glimmer looks like glimpse but means a flicker of light.
"A quick bite" is about food, not seeing the deer.

sc1.tip: The words "only a quick" and "darted back into the woods" tell you the look was very short.

decoys.why: The deer darted away fast, so you only had a quick look, not a safe place.
The woods are the deer's shelter, but you caught a quick look at the deer.
You saw the deer for a moment; nothing here is a sign or symbol.
You did not make a final decision about the deer; you saw it briefly.
Nobody ate a meal; you just saw the deer for a moment before it ran.
The sentence describes a brief sight of the deer, not a risky trip.

traps.why: A long stare is the opposite of a glimpse.
Faint light means glimmer, which only looks like glimpse.
Eyesight is your ability to see, not one quick look.

syn2.tip: If you only got a glimpse of a famous person, you saw them for just a second. That's a quick look.

sc2.stem: Unlike the long, close look we got at the zoo's lions, we got only a _____ of the cheetah as it raced past.

traps.why: A study is a long, careful look, which the word "unlike" rules out.
A portrait is a picture, not a look at a racing cheetah.
A sniff uses your nose; the sentence is about looking.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the long, close look" sets up a contrast. The cheetah "raced past," so you saw it only for a moment.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts a long look with a quick one, and a token is a sign, not a look.
A sanctuary is a safe place for animals, but the sentence needs a kind of quick look.
The cheetah raced over land, but you got a quick look at it, not its terrain.
A verdict is a final decision, and nothing here is being decided about the cheetah.
The sentence is about how briefly you saw the cheetah, not a result of an action.

example: Is there a park in the vicinity?
hook: Vicinity comes from the Latin word for neighbor, so the vicinity is the neighborhood all around you.

traps.why: Distance is far away; vicinity is close by.
Vicinity ends in city, but it means the nearby area, not a city.
Victory starts like vicinity, but it means a win.

syn1.tip: People ask, "Is there a store in the vicinity?" They mean close by, in the neighborhood.

sc1.stem: Is there a library in the _____ of our school, or do we have to drive all the way across town?

traps.why: The question is about something close, not far, since the other choice is across town.
Victory looks a bit like vicinity but means a win.
A schedule is about time; the sentence is about a place nearby.

sc1.tip: The contrast is with "drive all the way across town." The blank must mean the area close to the school.

decoys.why: The question asks whether a library is nearby, not about the land's physical features.
A glimpse is a quick look, but the sentence asks about the area near the school.
The contrast with driving across town shows the blank means nearby, not success and wealth.
Nothing here is a result of an action; the question is about what is close by.
A school has no strong wish here; the sentence is asking about the nearby area.

traps.why: A faraway place is the opposite of the vicinity.
The ending city is a trick; vicinity means the area near you.
An address is one exact spot; vicinity is the whole area around it.

syn2.tip: Vicinity comes from the Latin word for neighbor. Your neighbors live in the nearby area.

sc2.stem: When our dog ran off, we searched the whole _____ of our house, checking every yard and street within a few blocks.

traps.why: The interior is inside the house, but you checked yards and streets.
The roof is too small an area; you searched several blocks.
A house's value is its price, not the streets around it.

sc2.tip: The sentence restates the blank: "every yard and street within a few blocks." That is the area near your house.

decoys.why: You search an area, not a quick look; the sentence mentions yards and streets nearby.
Searching yards and streets within a few blocks describes a nearby area, not a hard choice.
Bounty means plenty, but the sentence describes the area close to the house.
A banquet is a big meal, not the streets and yards within a few blocks.
The family searched the nearby streets, not a result of some action.

example: We modified the recipe to use less sugar.
hook: Gamers talk about a mod: that's short for modification, a small change someone makes to a game.

traps.why: Preserve means to keep something the same, the opposite of changing it.
Model looks a bit like modify, but it means to show or pose.
Destroying is far too strong; modifying is only a small change.

syn1.tip: A modified bike has had a few parts changed. To modify is to alter something a little.

sc1.stem: Instead of building a brand-new treehouse, the kids decided to _____ the old one a little by adding a rope ladder.

traps.why: "Instead of building a brand-new treehouse" means they did not replace it.
Demolishing knocks it down; they only changed it "a little."
You can't paint something "by adding a rope ladder."

sc1.tip: The signal words are "instead of building a brand-new" and "a little." They changed the old treehouse slightly.

decoys.why: The kids changed it only a little, and transform means to change completely.
Adding a rope ladder does not use up or tire out the treehouse.
The kids are improving the treehouse, not being against it.
You cannot go along with a treehouse; the kids are changing it a little.
Adding a ladder changes the treehouse; it does not check whether something is true.
The treehouse is not sad; the kids are making a small change to it.

traps.why: Keeping it the same is the opposite of modifying it.
Modifying is a small change, not wrecking the whole thing.
An exact copy has no changes at all.

syn2.tip: Think of a "mod" in a video game. It changes a game slightly without building a new one.

sc2.stem: Because the lemonade tasted too sour at yesterday's stand, Maya chose to _____ her recipe by adding one more spoonful of sugar.

traps.why: Repeating the recipe would keep it sour; she wanted it different.
Memorizing a recipe doesn't change how the lemonade tastes.
Throwing it out is too much; she only added one spoonful.

sc2.tip: The cause is "too sour," and the fix is "adding one more spoonful." That's a small change to the recipe.

decoys.why: One more spoonful of sugar is a small change, and transform means a complete change.
Adding sugar changes the recipe; it does not check whether the recipe is true.
The recipe was not confusing; the lemonade was too sour, so Maya changed it slightly.
Maya is not carrying or communicating the recipe; she is adjusting it with sugar.
Maya is fixing her own recipe, not being against it.
Adding a spoonful of sugar does not use up the recipe.

example: The naive puppy chased a skunk.
hook: A naive kid believes a classmate who says the cafeteria will serve free ice cream every day forever.

traps.why: Experienced is the opposite; naive people haven't seen much yet.
Native looks like naive, but it means born in a place.
Stupid is a harsh insult; naive just means lacking experience.

syn1.tip: A naive person trusts too easily because they haven't learned better yet, like a young child. Think innocent.

sc1.stem: Having never camped before, Ella was _____ about the woods and packed no bug spray, no flashlight, and no rain jacket.

traps.why: She had "never camped before," so she was not experienced.
Stubborn means refusing to change; the clue is that she lacked experience.
Nothing in the sentence shows a bad mood, only a lack of know-how.

sc1.tip: The cause is "having never camped before," and the proof is everything she forgot. She didn't know what the woods require.

decoys.why: She had never camped and forgot everything, so she was not skilled at all.
Packing no flashlight or rain jacket shows she did not plan carefully.
A doubtful camper would pack more supplies, but Ella packed almost nothing.
A nervous camper would bring extra gear, but Ella brought none.
The sentence is about Ella's lack of experience, not about her being strict.
Only one person is described, so nothing could be agreed on by everyone.

traps.why: Hard to trick is the opposite of naive.
That's the meaning of native, which only looks like naive.
Naive people lack experience, not the ability to learn.

syn2.tip: Someone naive believes things too quickly, so they are easy to trick. Picture a newcomer falling for an April Fools joke.

sc2.stem: My older brother laughed at how _____ I was to believe that the tooth fairy really left me a gold coin, but I was only five.

traps.why: He laughed at you for believing it, so you weren't being clever.
Native looks like naive but means born in a place.
Believing a story isn't brave, and he was laughing at you.

sc2.tip: The clues are "laughed at," "to believe," and "only five." A young child believes stories too easily.

decoys.why: You believed the tooth fairy story, and skeptical means doubting it.
Your brother laughed at your innocence at age five, not at your skill.
Believing in the tooth fairy shows innocence, not being serious and strict.
The sentence is about how easily you believed, not about doing something on purpose.
Nothing in the sentence shows nervousness; it shows a young child believing a story.
Being strong and healthy has nothing to do with believing in the tooth fairy.

example: This is a potent cleaner, so wear gloves.
hook: Potent shares its root with potential: both are about power, and a potent hot sauce packs huge power into one drop.

traps.why: Weak is the opposite of potent.
Patient looks a bit like potent, but it means calm while waiting.
