Ava was not tricking anyone; the sentence says her choice was careful and sensible.
Packing extra supplies shows Ava cared, so she was not indifferent.
Packing supplies is not about honesty; the sentence calls it careful and sensible.

traps.why: Careless means not paying attention, the opposite of prudent.
Stingy is selfish about money; prudent is sensible, which is a good thing.
Rude is hiding inside prudent, but it means impolite.

syn2.tip: Think of saving money or packing a raincoat just in case. A prudent person thinks ahead and avoids trouble.

sc2.stem: Instead of spending all his birthday money on candy right away, Leo made the _____ decision to save most of it for the new bike he wanted.

traps.why: Hasty means rushed; spending it all right away would be hasty.
Greedy is negative, but saving for a bike is a smart choice.
Costly means expensive, but saving money isn't costly.

sc2.tip: "Instead of spending all" his money right away, Leo saved it. The blank describes a smart choice that plans ahead.

decoys.why: Leo chose to save instead of spending, and extravagant means spending too much.
Saving for a bike is smart, but Leo is not tricking anyone.
Saving money for a bike can work, so the decision is not useless.
Leo clearly cares about getting the bike, so he is not indifferent.
The sentence is about a careful choice with money, not about being honest.

example: Our new kitchen is spacious.
hook: Spacious is space plus -ous, full of space, like a gym big enough for the whole school.

traps.why: Cramped means squeezed with too little room, the opposite of spacious.
Special starts like spacious but means unusual or important.
Spacious is about room inside, not outer space and stars.

syn1.tip: Look inside the word: space plus -ous, full of space. Pick the choice that means having lots of room.

sc1.stem: The new tent is so _____ that all six of us can lie down inside with plenty of room to spare.

traps.why: Cramped means too tight, but there is "plenty of room to spare."
Waterproof is a good tent feature, but the clue is about room.
A tent can cost a lot, but "plenty of room" is about size.

sc1.tip: The clue is "all six of us can lie down inside with plenty of room to spare." The blank is about size.

decoys.why: The clue is plenty of room for six people, not how costly or fancy the tent is.
Sticky air does not explain why six people fit with room to spare.
Being pretty does not give a tent room for all six of you.
The sentence is about how much room is inside, not how bright the tent looks.
How ugly the tent is has nothing to do with fitting six people.

traps.why: Tightly packed means no room, the opposite of spacious.
Neat is about being clean, not about how much room there is.
This means gracious, which rhymes with spacious but means something else.

syn2.tip: Spacious is full of space. A spacious car or room has lots of room inside.

sc2.stem: Our old apartment was so crowded that we bumped elbows at dinner, but the new house is _____, with a huge kitchen and a bedroom for each of us.

traps.why: Tiny describes the old apartment; "but" means the new house is different.
Noisy is about sound; the clue is a huge kitchen and many bedrooms.
Messy is about clutter, not about how much room there is.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the new house with the "crowded" apartment, and "a huge kitchen and a bedroom for each" shows lots of room.

decoys.why: The contrast is crowded versus roomy, and damp air says nothing about room.
A huge kitchen and separate bedrooms show lots of room, not prettiness.
The sentence compares crowding to room, not ugly to pretty.
A house cannot be wild and stormy; the clue is about having more room.
Being asleep or inactive does not describe a house with a huge kitchen.

example: He contemplated which book to read next.
hook: When you contemplate something, you turn it over slowly in your mind, like studying a tricky puzzle piece.

traps.why: Ignore means to pay no attention, the opposite of thinking deeply.
Complete looks a bit like contemplate but means to finish.
Deciding comes after thinking; contemplate is the slow thinking itself.

syn1.tip: Picture someone staring at a sunset, lost in thought. Contemplate means to think about something slowly and deeply.

sc1.stem: Lying on the grass at night, Mateo liked to _____ the stars for hours, thinking deeply about how far away they were.

traps.why: Mateo spent hours thinking about the stars, so he did not ignore them.
A glimpse is a quick look, but Mateo looked and thought for hours.
Describing tells about something in words; Mateo was quietly thinking.

sc1.tip: The sentence tells you: "for hours, thinking deeply about how far away they were." The blank means to think deeply.

decoys.why: Mateo is thinking deeply, not feeling sad over losing the stars.
You cannot call stars to come; Mateo is just thinking about them.
Mateo is lying on the grass, so he does not live in the stars.
Stars already shine; Mateo is thinking deeply, not setting anything on fire.
Mateo spends hours with the stars, so he is not avoiding them.
Mateo is not trying to beat the stars; he is thinking about them.

traps.why: Paying no attention is the opposite of thinking deeply.
A quick glance is far too little; contemplate means long, deep thought.
Contemplate contains "template," but it has nothing to do with copying.

syn2.tip: Contemplate is a slow, quiet word. It describes long, careful thinking, not a quick look.

sc2.stem: The puzzle was so tricky that Grandma sat still for a long time to _____ her next move before she finally placed a single piece.

traps.why: She sat still for a long time, so she did not rush.
Guessing takes little thought; sitting still a long time shows deep thinking.
Announcing tells others; Grandma was quietly thinking first.

sc2.tip: "So tricky that" explains why she "sat still for a long time." She needed to think hard before acting.

decoys.why: Grandma did make her move, so she did not give it up.
Grandma sat still to plan her move, not to get in its way.
You cannot end a move like a law; Grandma was thinking it over.
Grandma was thinking hard about a tricky puzzle, not feeling sad over a loss.
Sitting still for a long time shows careful thought, not doing better than a move.

example: As a novice skier, I stayed on easy slopes.
hook: Novice shares a Latin root with novel and nova, all about new: a novice is new at something.

traps.why: An expert is highly skilled, the opposite of a novice.
Novel looks like novice but means a long made-up story.
Coaches teach beginners, but a novice is the one just starting.

syn1.tip: Novice comes from the same root as new. A novice is someone new at an activity.

sc1.stem: Unlike his sister, a skilled figure skater, Owen was a _____ who had never even worn ice skates before.

traps.why: A champion is skilled, but Owen "had never even worn ice skates."
A skating coach would have worn skates, but Owen never had.
A rival competes; Owen had never even put on skates.

sc1.tip: "Unlike his sister, a skilled figure skater" shows Owen is the opposite of skilled. "Had never even worn ice skates" confirms it.

decoys.why: The contrast is skilled versus never skating, so Owen is a beginner, not annoying.
Never having worn skates makes Owen new, not dangerous.
Owen is a person who has never skated, not a complete failure of an event.
Owen is one person, so he cannot be a very large number.
A formal meal cannot be a person who has never worn skates.

traps.why: Someone highly skilled is an expert, the opposite of a novice.
Novices can be any age; it means being new at something.
Novice comes from "new," but it is a person, not a new thing.

syn2.tip: Think of "novice level" in a game or sport: the easiest level, for people who are new.

sc2.stem: Because Jada had only started guitar lessons last week, the teacher gave her easy songs that a _____ could play with just three fingers.

traps.why: A master is highly skilled, but Jada only started last week.
A composer writes music; easy songs for a new player point to a beginner.
A critic judges music; the clue is that Jada "only started" lessons.

sc2.tip: "Because Jada had only started... last week" explains why she got "easy songs." The blank names someone new.

decoys.why: Jada just started lessons, so the songs suit a beginner, not an annoying person.
Easy songs are for someone new, not someone dangerous.
The songs are for one new player using three fingers, not a huge crowd.
A meal cannot play guitar; the sentence is about someone just starting out.
A failure cannot play songs; the clue is that Jada only started last week.

example: Nothing grew in the barren field.
hook: Picture a barren desert: cracked dirt, no grass, no trees, nothing growing for miles.

traps.why: Fertile land grows plants well, the opposite of barren.
Barren land can be sandy, but barren means nothing can grow there.
Hilly is about the shape of land, not whether plants grow.

syn1.tip: Barren land is bare: nothing grows. Look for the word with "in-," meaning not, before a word for good, growing land.

sc1.stem: Unlike the rich garden soil out front, the sandy patch behind the shed was _____, and no seed Dad planted there would ever sprout.

traps.why: Blooming means full of flowers, but no seed there would ever sprout.
Sun helps plants grow, so it doesn't explain why nothing sprouts.
Damp soil helps seeds grow, so it doesn't explain why nothing sprouts.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the rich garden soil" shows a contrast, and "no seed... would ever sprout" tells you the patch can't grow anything.

decoys.why: Dormant means alive but resting, but here no seed would ever sprout.
Soil that bounces back would grow plants, but nothing sprouts in this patch.
The patch is unlike the rich soil, so it is not healthy or good.
The patch is sandy and grows nothing, which damp air does not explain.
The clue is that no seed would sprout, not how much room the patch has.
A sandy patch where nothing grows is not pretty as a picture.

traps.why: Full of plants is the opposite of barren land.
Barren sounds like baron, a nobleman, but means unable to grow plants.
Snowy land looks bare, but barren means nothing can grow there.

syn2.tip: Think of a barren field or barren desert where nothing grows. Barren and bare even start the same way.

sc2.stem: After the wildfire swept through, the hillside was _____: no grass, no bushes, and not a single tree was left standing.

traps.why: Green means full of plants, but nothing was left on the hillside.
Steep is about the slope of a hill, not what grows on it.
Peaceful is a pleasant word, but the burned hillside is bleak and empty.

sc2.tip: The words after the colon explain the blank: "no grass, no bushes, and not a single tree." The hillside is bare.

decoys.why: With no grass, bushes, or trees left, the burned hillside is not pretty.
A burned hillside with nothing left is not healthy or good.
Dormant plants are still there resting, but here nothing was left standing.
After a wildfire the land is bare, and damp air does not describe that.
The colon lists everything that is missing, so the hillside is bare, not impressive.
The fire is over; the sentence describes a bare hillside, not a stormy one.

example: An extravagant cake had ten layers.
hook: An extravagant party goes way overboard: ten-layer cakes, gold balloons, and a bill much bigger than it needed to be.

traps.why: Thrifty means careful with money, the opposite of extravagant.
Elegant is tasteful praise; extravagant means too costly or too much.
Wealthy means having money, not spending too much of it.

syn1.tip: Extravagant things go far beyond what is needed. Picture a party with way too much of everything.

sc1.stem: Buying a hundred-dollar cake for the dog's birthday was an _____ choice, far too costly and fancy for a pet party.

traps.why: Economical means saving money, but the cake was far too costly.
The cake may show love, but the clue is about cost and fanciness.
An ordinary choice would not be far too costly and fancy.

sc1.tip: The words "far too costly and fancy" right after the blank tell you exactly what kind of choice it was.

decoys.why: The sentence calls the choice far too costly, which has nothing to do with fairness.
The problem is the high price and fanciness, not that the choice was sudden.
Spending a hundred dollars on a dog cake shows caring a lot, not not caring.
The cake is too fancy and costly, not a sign that something bad will happen.
The sentence describes the cost of the choice, not a worried feeling.
A choice cannot move quickly and gracefully; the clue is costly and fancy.

traps.why: Modest means simple and small, the opposite of extravagant.
Extravagant parties may be festive, but extravagant means spending too much.
Stingy means spending too little, the opposite direction.

syn2.tip: Extravagant spending goes too far. Ask yourself whether the word means too much or too little, then pick the choice that means too much.

sc2.stem: Grandma's birthday party was simple, but my cousin's was _____, with a live band, a chocolate fountain, and a pony for every guest.

traps.why: Plain is like simple, but "but" says the cousin's party was different.
A thrifty party would not have a pony for every guest.
A band, a fountain, and ponies are not an affordable party.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a contrast with "simple," and the band, fountain, and ponies show the party went way over the top.

decoys.why: A band, chocolate fountain, and ponies show the party was full of things, not bare.
A pony for every guest is not careful or sensible spending.
A party with a live band was lively, not asleep or inactive.
Nothing says the party failed; the clues describe how fancy it was.
The sentence lists fancy extras, not anything about warm, damp air.
Being fair or not taking sides has nothing to do with bands and ponies.

meaning: seeming like something bad will happen
example: Ominous clouds gathered over the lake.
hook: Ominous has "omen" inside it: ominous clouds are a bad omen, a sign that trouble is on its way.

traps.why: Hopeful means expecting good things, the opposite of ominous.
Enormous sounds like ominous but means very large.
Storms can seem ominous, but ominous means warning of something bad.

syn1.tip: Find "omen" inside ominous. An omen is a sign of the future, and ominous signs point to trouble.

sc1.stem: An _____ rumble of thunder warned us that a storm was on its way, so we quickly packed up our picnic.

traps.why: An encouraging rumble would not make you rush to pack up.
Anonymous looks like ominous but means having no known name.
Amusing has the wrong feeling; the rumble warned of a storm.

sc1.tip: The rumble "warned us that a storm was on its way," and you "quickly packed up," so the sound signaled trouble.

decoys.why: Thunder warning of a storm brings rain, so a dry rumble makes no sense.
The rumble warned you of danger, so it was not uncaring or neutral.
Thunder cannot be costly or fancy; the clue is that it warned of a storm.
Thunder does not move gracefully; the sentence is about a warning sign.
Fairness has nothing to do with thunder warning you a storm is coming.

traps.why: Promising good luck is the opposite of warning of trouble.
Thunder can be loud, but ominous means it warns of danger.
Slightly unusual is too weak; ominous means something bad seems to be coming.

syn2.tip: Picture dark clouds rolling in over a picnic. They are ominous because they warn that trouble is coming.

sc2.stem: The music in the movie was cheerful at first, but when the hero opened the creaky door, it turned low and _____, so I knew danger was near.

traps.why: Joyful is like cheerful, but "but" shows the music changed.
Playful has the wrong feeling for music that signals danger.
Soothing music would calm you, not tell you danger was near.

sc2.tip: "But" shows the music changed from "cheerful," and "I knew danger was near" tells you it now sounded threatening.

decoys.why: The music changed from cheerful and told you danger was near, so it was not pretty.
Bright, impressive music would not tell you danger was near.
Music cannot be careful and sensible; the clue is that it signaled danger.
Not taking sides has nothing to do with music that warns of danger.
The sentence says the music turned low and scary, not quick and graceful.
Fancy music does not signal that danger is near behind a creaky door.

meaning: a step taken to prevent harm
example: Wearing a helmet is a smart precaution.
hook: Pre means before: a precaution is caution you take before trouble, like buckling your seatbelt before the car moves.

traps.why: A risk invites danger; a precaution guards against it.
A precaution helps prevent an accident; it is not the accident.
Pre means before, but a precaution is a safety step, not a guess.

syn1.tip: Split it: pre (before) plus caution (care). A precaution is care you take before something goes wrong.

sc1.stem: As a _____, Dad packed extra water and a first-aid kit in case anything went wrong on the hike.

traps.why: Packing supplies in case something goes wrong is smart, not a mistake.
A joke is playful; packing a first-aid kit is serious planning.
Pre means before, but Dad took an action, not made a guess.

sc1.tip: The words "in case anything went wrong" show Dad was planning ahead to keep everyone safe.

decoys.why: Dad packed supplies to prevent harm, so his action was not a threat.
Packing water and a first-aid kit is not a terrible event; it prevents one.
The sentence says he packed things in case something went wrong, which is helpful, not annoying.
Careful packing before a hike is not a complete failure.
Extra water and a first-aid kit are not a large formal meal.
Dad packed supplies ahead of time, not a small leftover piece.

traps.why: A careless mistake causes harm instead of preventing it.
A warning sign tells of danger; a precaution is what you do about it.
Pre means before, but a precaution is not just being early.

syn2.tip: Think of safety precautions like wearing goggles in science class. They are steps you take ahead of time so no one gets hurt.

sc2.stem: Our team did not take a single _____ during the camping trip, so when the storm hit, nobody had a raincoat or a flashlight.

traps.why: Taking no risks would mean being prepared, but nobody had a raincoat.
Hikes are part of camping, but skipping one would not explain missing raincoats.
Taking pictures is part of camping, but it has nothing to do with raincoats.

sc2.tip: The "so" shows a result: "nobody had a raincoat or a flashlight." That happens when no one plans ahead for safety.

decoys.why: The camping trip itself was the outing; the problem was nobody prepared for the storm.
Missing raincoats and flashlights shows a lack of preparation, not a missing beginner.
The sentence is about failing to prepare for a storm, not about an enemy.
No raincoat or flashlight means no safety step was taken, not a leftover piece.

example: The two kingdoms ended years of strife.
hook: Picture two kingdoms shaking their fists across a river for years; that long, angry quarreling is strife.

traps.why: Harmony means getting along, the opposite of strife.
Stripe looks like strife but is a band of color.
A debate is a calm discussion; strife is angry fighting.

syn1.tip: Strife often appears in phrases like "years of strife." Its feeling is angry and bitter, like fighting that goes on and on.

sc1.stem: Years of _____ between the two villages finally ended when their leaders agreed to share the river peacefully.

traps.why: Friendship would not need to end with a peace deal.
Villages may trade, but "peacefully" shows that fighting is what ended.
Fun has the wrong feeling; something ended by a peace deal was not fun.

sc1.tip: The trouble "finally ended" when leaders agreed to share "peacefully." So the blank must be the opposite of peace.

decoys.why: The years ended when leaders agreed to share peacefully, so they were fighting, not alone.
Ending with a peaceful agreement means the years before were full of conflict, not modesty.
Eagerness and energy do not need to end in a peace agreement.
A sweet smell is not something ended by agreeing to share a river.
Broken rock cannot exist between villages for years and end with an agreement.

traps.why: A peaceful agreement is what ends strife, its opposite.
Strive, meaning work hard, looks like strife, but strife means fighting.
Mild disagreement is too weak; strife is angry, bitter conflict.

syn2.tip: Picture two groups arguing and fighting for years. Strife is a strong word for angry conflict, not a small disagreement.

sc2.stem: The constant _____ over the TV remote made family movie night so unpleasant that Mom finally hid the remote in a drawer.

traps.why: Sharing the remote would make movie night pleasant, not unpleasant.
Laughter has a happy feeling, but movie night was unpleasant.
Politeness would not make Mom hide the remote.

sc2.tip: "So unpleasant that" shows a result. Something about the remote made Mom hide it, so people must have been fighting over it.

decoys.why: Mom hid the remote because of fighting, and being humble would not cause that.
Family movie night means people were together arguing, not alone.
A sweet smell would not make movie night unpleasant enough to hide the remote.
Broken rock has nothing to do with arguing over a TV remote.
A safety step would not make movie night so unpleasant that Mom hid the remote.

example: The fireworks were dazzling.
hook: Dazzle comes from daze: dazzling light is so bright it leaves you blinking and a little dazed.

traps.why: Dull means not bright, the opposite of dazzling.
Dizzy sounds a bit like dazzling but means feeling unsteady.
Visible only means able to be seen; dazzling means extremely bright.

syn1.tip: The word "daze" is inside dazzling. Something dazzling is so bright and impressive it leaves you a little dazed.

sc1.stem: The fresh snow was so _____ in the noon sun that we had to squint and shield our eyes from its sparkle.

traps.why: Dim snow would not make you squint and shield your eyes.
Snow is cold, but cold would not make you squint.
Deep snow is hard to walk in, but depth would not make you squint.

sc1.tip: "We had to squint and shield our eyes from its sparkle" tells you the snow was extremely bright.

decoys.why: You squinted because the snow was so bright, and being clean does not make you squint.
Snow that sparkles in the sun is not very ugly.
Nothing bad is coming; the sentence is about sparkle making you squint.
Pretty scenery does not make you shield your eyes; brightness does.
Snow is not dry land, and the clue is about sparkle, not rain.

traps.why: Dim and gloomy is the opposite of dazzling.
Slightly shiny is too weak; dazzling is bright enough to make you squint.
Daze is inside, but dazzling means bright, not confusing.

syn2.tip: Think of dazzling fireworks. They burst so bright you can hardly look straight at them.

sc2.stem: The old trophy had been dull and dusty, but after Grandpa polished it for an hour, it was so _____ that it seemed to light up the shelf.

traps.why: Polishing removes dirt, and a dirty trophy would not light up a shelf.
Trophies can be heavy, but weight would not light up a shelf.
Dim is like dull, but "but" shows the trophy changed.

sc2.tip: "But" signals the trophy changed from "dull and dusty," and "seemed to light up the shelf" shows it became very bright.

decoys.why: After an hour of polishing, the trophy seemed to light up the shelf, so it was not ugly.
A trophy cannot be asleep; the clue is that it seemed to light up the shelf.
Polishing makes a trophy shine, not grow extremely large.
Barren suggests dull and bare, but the polished trophy now lit up the shelf.
A shining, polished trophy does not suggest something bad will happen.

meaning: useless; having no chance of success
example: Trying to catch the bus was futile.
hook: Trying to fill a bucket that has a hole in the bottom is futile: no matter how hard you work, it never succeeds.

traps.why: Effective means it works, the opposite of futile.
Fertile looks like futile but means able to grow things.
Difficult means hard but possible; futile means no chance at all.

syn1.tip: Futile often describes "a futile attempt." If an effort has no chance of working, it is futile.

sc1.stem: Sweeping the sidewalk during the snowstorm was _____, since fresh snow covered it again the moment we finished.

traps.why: Sweeping was not worthwhile because the snow came right back.
The sweeping didn't help, since fresh snow covered it again.
Fertile looks like futile but means able to grow things.

sc1.tip: "Since fresh snow covered it again the moment we finished" tells you all the sweeping did no good.

decoys.why: Snow covered the sidewalk again right away, so the sweeping was useless, not sensible.
Fresh snow covered it again, so the sidewalk never stayed perfectly clean.
The sentence says the work was undone at once, not that it was impressive.
The clue is that snow covered it again, which shows uselessness, not graceful movement.
Sweeping cannot be honest and direct; the clue says it did no good.

traps.why: Successful means it worked, the opposite of futile.
Future sounds like futile but means the time still to come.
A lazy person doesn't try; futile means trying does no good.

syn2.tip: Picture trying to empty the ocean with a spoon. Every try fails, so the effort is hopeless, or futile.

sc2.stem: Hiding the cookies from my little brother is _____; no matter where I put them, he always finds them within five minutes.

traps.why: The hiding isn't successful, because he always finds them.
Hiding may seem needed, but the clue shows it never works.
Clever is praise, but the sentence shows the hiding always fails.

sc2.tip: "No matter where I put them, he always finds them" restates the blank: the hiding never works.

decoys.why: Hiding them sounds sensible, but he always finds them, so the effort is useless.
The sentence says your hiding never works, so it isn't clever at all.
Nothing in the sentence is costly or fancy; the clue is that he always finds them.
The sentence is about hiding never working, not about anything sudden.
Failing every time is not impressive; the sentence shows the hiding is pointless.

example: He tried to evade the question.
hook: Picture a soccer player weaving past defenders who try to grab her; she evades them by slipping away.

traps.why: To face something is to meet it head on, the opposite of evade.
Invade looks like evade but means to enter by force.
When you evade a question, you don't answer it.

syn1.tip: Think of a player who evades a tackle by darting away. To evade is to slip around something so it doesn't catch you.

sc1.stem: When Mom asked who ate the cake, Leo tried to _____ the question by quickly changing the subject to the weather.

traps.why: Changing the subject is the opposite of answering the question.
Invade looks like evade but means to enter by force.
Mom asked the question; Leo was trying to get out of it.

sc1.tip: "By quickly changing the subject" shows Leo was trying to get away from the question, not answer it.

decoys.why: Leo changed the subject, so he avoided the question instead of paying attention to it.
Changing the subject means he did not think deeply about the question at all.
Leo rushed to change the subject, so he did not enjoy the question.
Mom asked the question; Leo was trying to dodge it, not stir it up.

traps.why: Catch means to grab hold, the opposite of dodge or evade.
Evaluate starts like evade but means to judge.
Run just means move fast; evade means getting away from something.

syn2.tip: Picture dodgeball: you dodge the ball to evade it. Both mean getting out of the way.

sc2.stem: Most of the class faced the spelling bee bravely, but Tom tried to _____ it by pretending to have a stomachache that morning.

traps.why: Winning means doing well in it, but Tom pretended to be sick.
Faking a stomachache is a way to stay out, not join.
Tom wanted to stay out of the bee, not enter it.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Tom with classmates who "faced" the spelling bee. Faking a stomachache is a way to get out of it.

decoys.why: Faking a stomachache shows Tom wanted to avoid the spelling bee, not enjoy it.
Pretending to be sick would keep Tom out of the bee, not help him do better.
The stomachache trick was a way to escape the bee, not to think about it.
Tom only tried to skip it himself; a fake stomachache cannot end the whole bee.
Tom was not sad over a loss; he was trying to get out of the bee.

meaning: to slow down or get in the way
example: Snow hindered our trip to school.
hook: Hinder comes from "hind," meaning back: things that hinder you hold you back, like mud sucking at your boots.

traps.why: Help means make easier, the opposite of hinder.
Hide starts like hinder but means to keep out of sight.
Hinder comes from hind, but it doesn't mean follow behind.

syn1.tip: Hinder is related to "hind," meaning back. Something that hinders you holds you back or slows you down.

sc1.stem: Deep snow on the roads will _____ the mail carrier, slowing her down so the letters arrive late.

traps.why: Snow that slows her down is not helping her.
Delight is a happy word, but late letters are a problem.
Hide looks like hinder, but the snow slows her, not hides her.

sc1.tip: "Slowing her down so the letters arrive late" explains what the snow does: it gets in her way.

decoys.why: The sentence says the snow slows her down, so it doesn't outdo her.
The snow is in her way, slowing her down, not escaping from her.
Snow can't call the mail carrier; the sentence says it slows her down.
The snow is getting in her way, not growing or developing anything.
Snow cannot enjoy anything; the clue is that it slows her down.

traps.why: Helping something move along is the opposite of hindering it.
Stop for good is too strong; hinder means slow down or get in the way.
Hinder means slowing something else, not falling behind yourself.

syn2.tip: Think of being hindered by traffic. Traffic gets in your way and slows you down, but you still get there.

sc2.stem: Wearing a heavy backpack will _____ you in the race, so leave it at the starting line if you want to run fast.

traps.why: If the backpack helped, you wouldn't leave it behind to run fast.
A heavy backpack slows you, which is why you leave it behind.
Hinder comes from hind, but it doesn't mean follow behind.

sc2.tip: "So leave it at the starting line if you want to run fast" shows the backpack would slow you down.

decoys.why: A backpack can't beat you in the race; the sentence says it keeps you from running fast.
The backpack is on you, getting in your way, not escaping from you.
A backpack can't call you; the sentence says it would slow you down.
A backpack doesn't follow you; the sentence says it keeps you from running fast.

example: The bus came to an abrupt stop.
hook: Abrupt holds "rupt," meaning break: an abrupt stop breaks off all at once, like a song cut off mid-note.

traps.why: Gradual means little by little, the opposite of abrupt.
Rupt means break, but abrupt means sudden, not broken.
Absurd starts like abrupt but means silly or ridiculous.

syn1.tip: Abrupt holds "rupt," meaning break. Something abrupt breaks off all at once, like a car slamming its brakes.

sc1.stem: The movie came to an _____ end, cutting off in the middle of a scene without any warning at all.

traps.why: An expected end would not come without any warning at all.
An unhurried end would not cut off in the middle of a scene.
An orderly end would wrap up neatly, not cut off mid-scene.

sc1.tip: "Cutting off in the middle of a scene without any warning at all" restates the blank: the ending was sudden.

decoys.why: The clue is that it ended without warning, which means sudden, not threatening.
Cutting off mid-scene is the opposite of a fancy, showy ending.
An ending that cuts off in the middle of a scene is far from perfect.
The sentence describes a sudden stop, not an ending that doesn't care.
Taking sides has nothing to do with an ending that stops without warning.

traps.why: Slow and steady is the opposite of abrupt.
Sudden things can be loud, but abrupt is about timing, not noise.
A little early is too weak; abrupt means suddenly, with no warning.

syn2.tip: Think of an abrupt stop on a bus. Everyone lurches forward because it happened without warning.

sc2.stem: The road curved gently for miles, but then it made an _____ turn that sent our bags sliding across the back seat.

traps.why: An easy turn would not send bags sliding across the seat.
Elegant sounds graceful, but this turn jolted everything around.
An uneventful turn would not send bags sliding.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts with "curved gently," and bags "sliding across the back seat" show the turn came sharply and suddenly.

decoys.why: Agile describes graceful movers, but the clue is a sudden turn after gentle curves.
A turn can't be costly; the bags slid because the turn was so sudden.
Clean has nothing to do with it; the turn was sudden after gentle curves.
Roads don't take sides; the sentence contrasts gentle curves with a sudden turn.
Dryness doesn't explain bags sliding; the clue is a sudden turn after gentle curves.

example: A referee must be impartial.
hook: Im means not, and partial means favoring one side, so an impartial referee favors no one.

traps.why: One-sided means favoring one side, the opposite of impartial.
Not partial seems like whole, but impartial means not taking sides.
Good referees may be polite, but impartial is about not picking favorites.

syn1.tip: Break it up: im (not) plus partial (favoring one side). An impartial judge treats everyone the same.

sc1.stem: To be fair to both teams, the league chose an _____ referee who would not take sides or favor anyone.

traps.why: The league wanted to be fair, so it would not choose an unfair referee.
Impatient looks like impartial but means unable to wait calmly.
An opinionated referee might pick a side, which the league wanted to avoid.

sc1.tip: "To be fair to both teams" and "would not take sides or favor anyone" both tell you the referee had to be neutral.

decoys.why: The sentence wants a referee who won't take sides, not a sudden one.
Being quick on your feet doesn't make a referee fair to both teams.
The league wanted a fair referee, not one who seems threatening.
Having money has nothing to do with not favoring either team.
The clue is fairness to both teams, not how happy the referee is.
The sentence asks for a referee who won't take sides, not a nervous one.

traps.why: Favoring one team is exactly what impartial people don't do.
Partial can mean partly done, but impartial is about fairness.
A referee may be strict, but impartial means not picking a favorite.

syn2.tip: Think of the phrase "an impartial referee." A good ref calls the game the same way no matter which team you cheer for.

sc2.stem: Since Mia's best friend was in the contest, Mia stepped down as a judge; she knew she could not be _____ about her own friend's drawing.

traps.why: If she could not be unfair, she would have no reason to step down.
Judges should be careful, but the problem was favoring her friend.
Impatient looks like impartial but means unable to wait calmly.

sc2.tip: Mia "stepped down" because the contestant was her "best friend." She worried she would favor her friend and could not judge fairly.

decoys.why: Mia stepped down because she couldn't be fair, not because she couldn't be happy.
Mia stepped down because she might favor her friend, not because she couldn't feel worried.
The problem was fairness to her friend, not whether Mia could be tricky.
Mia's worry was taking her friend's side, not being sudden.
Judging a friend's drawing is about fairness, not about being fancy or costly.

example: Cactuses grow well in arid places.
hook: Picture the Sahara: land so arid that rain is a rare visitor and the ground cracks in the sun.

traps.why: Wet is the opposite of arid.
Deserts are often hot, but arid is about having little water.
Acid looks like arid, but it means sour or able to burn.

syn1.tip: x

sc1.stem: With less than an inch of rain all year, the Atacama Desert is an _____ region where crops cannot grow without help.

traps.why: Icy means frozen; the clue is about how little rain falls.
Urban means city; the clue is about rain, not buildings.
Aquatic means living in water, the opposite of a rainless place.

sc1.tip: The clue is 'less than an inch of rain all year.' A place with almost no rain is very dry.

decoys.why: The clue is less than an inch of rain, which means dry, not rich.
Very little rain makes the desert dry, not fancy or costly.
The sentence talks about almost no rain, which describes dryness, not cleanness.
The clue about less than an inch of rain points to dryness, not a threatening feeling.
A desert can't take sides; the clue is how little rain falls there.

traps.why: Soggy means soaked with water, the opposite of arid.
Deserts can be sandy, but arid means dry, not full of sand.
Dry places may be sunny, but arid is about lack of rain.

syn2.tip: Arid is the word scientists use for deserts. Look for the choice that means very dry, like thirsty ground.

sc2.stem: Our backyard garden stays green all summer, but my cousin's yard in Arizona is so _____ that only cactuses and a few tough weeds survive.

traps.why: Lush means thick and green, which is what 'but' sets against.
Shade helps plants grow; only cactuses surviving points to dryness.
Frozen yards are cold, but cactuses grow in dry places, not snow.

sc2.tip: 'But' sets the cousin's yard against a green garden, and 'only cactuses' survive there. That points to a very dry place.

decoys.why: Lots of room would not explain why only cactuses survive; the sentence is about dryness.
Countrylike does not explain why only tough desert plants can survive in the yard.
A huge yard could still grow anything; the clue about cactuses points to dryness, not size.
Money has nothing to do with which plants survive in the yard.
A fancy yard would not leave only cactuses and weeds alive.
A yard with only a few tough weeds is not bright and impressive.

example: A colossal statue stood in the harbor.
hook: Colossal comes from the Colossus of Rhodes, a giant ancient statue, so picture something towering over a harbor.

traps.why: Tiny is the opposite of colossal.
Big things are often heavy, but colossal is about size.
Colorful starts like colossal, but it is about colors, not size.

syn1.tip: Think of a colossal wave or a colossal mistake. Both mean something enormous, so look for the word about great size.

sc1.stem: The cruise ship was so _____ that it was taller than a twenty-story building and longer than three soccer fields.

traps.why: Cruise ships can be fancy, but the clues measure height and length.
Narrow means thin, which clashes with 'longer than three soccer fields.'
Ships can be crowded, but the clues compare the ship's size.

sc1.tip: 'Taller than a twenty-story building' and 'longer than three soccer fields' both measure size. The ship must be extremely large.

decoys.why: The sentence measures height and length, so it is about size, not cost.
Being taller than a twenty-story building describes size, not brightness.
The clues compare the ship to buildings and fields, which is about size, not cleanliness.
A ship taller than a skyscraper is described by its size, not quick movement.
Nothing in the sentence suggests something bad will happen; it only describes size.
Simple and countrylike does not explain a ship being taller than a twenty-story building.

traps.why: Miniature means very small, the opposite of colossal.
Huge things can seem important, but colossal only describes size.
The Colossus statue was old, but colossal means huge, not old.

syn2.tip: Colossal sounds like colosseum, the giant stadium in Rome. Choose the word that means extremely big.

sc2.stem: The pumpkin at the county fair was so _____ that it took six grown-ups and a forklift to lift it onto the scale.

traps.why: A tiny pumpkin would not need six adults and a forklift.
Ripe means ready to eat; ripeness does not require a forklift.
Colorful looks a bit like colossal, but color doesn't need a forklift.

sc2.tip: Ask what would make 'six grown-ups and a forklift' necessary. Only something extremely large would need that much help.

decoys.why: Needing six adults and a forklift to lift it is about size, not ugliness.
A forklift is needed because of size, not because the pumpkin is bright.
A pumpkin cannot move quickly, and the sentence is about how hard it is to lift.
Being inactive would not make a pumpkin need a forklift to lift.
Cleanliness would not explain why six grown-ups and a forklift were needed.
Countrylike fits a fair, but it does not explain why the pumpkin was so hard to lift.

example: Her kitchen was immaculate.
hook: Im- means not and macula means spot in Latin, so immaculate means not a single spot.

traps.why: Filthy means very dirty, the opposite of immaculate.
Immature looks similar but means acting younger than your age.
Clean rooms may look empty, but immaculate means having no dirt.

syn1.tip: Im- means not, and the rest comes from a word for spot. Something with not one spot is perfectly clean.

sc1.stem: Mom keeps an _____ kitchen, so perfectly clean that not a single crumb or speck of dust can be found.

traps.why: Untidy means messy, but the sentence says 'perfectly clean.'
Kitchens can be big, but the clue is about cleanness.
Empty means nothing inside; the clue is about no crumbs or dust.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank right after the comma: 'so perfectly clean that not a single crumb' remains. Choose the word meaning perfectly clean.

decoys.why: The sentence explains the word as perfectly clean, not costly or fancy.
The clue is about crumbs and dust, not about having lots of money.
No dust or crumbs means clean, not dry with little rain.
A spotless kitchen does not seem like something bad will happen.
The sentence says perfectly clean, which has nothing to do with being unsteady.
A kitchen cannot take sides; the sentence is about it being spotless.

traps.why: Very messy is the opposite of immaculate.
New paint looks nice, but immaculate means without any dirt.
Fairly neat is too weak; immaculate means perfectly clean.

syn2.tip: Immaculate is a strong word: not almost clean, but without a single speck. Pick the choice that is complete and perfect.

sc2.stem: Jake's bedroom is usually covered in socks and comic books, but the night before Grandma visited, he made it _____ from floor to ceiling.

traps.why: Cluttered is how it usually looks; 'but' signals a change.
Cozy means warm and comfy; the change is from messy to clean.
Dim means dark, but the clue is about the mess being cleared.

sc2.tip: 'Usually covered in socks' is followed by 'but,' so the room changed to the opposite of messy. That means spotless.

decoys.why: Jake was cleaning up for Grandma, so the room got better, not very poor in quality.
Picking up socks and comics makes a room clean, not costly or fancy.
Cleaning up does not make a bedroom extremely large.
The contrast is messy versus clean, not plain and countrylike.
The sentence contrasts a messy room with a clean one, not an active one with a sleeping one.
Cleaning for Grandma's visit makes the room nice, not threatening.

example: We ate in a rustic log cabin.
hook: Picture a log cabin with a creaky porch and a woodstove; that rustic look says simple country life.

traps.why: Urban means of the city, the opposite of rustic.
Rusty looks like rustic but means covered in rust.
Rustic things may look old, but rustic means countrylike.

syn1.tip: Think of a rustic cabin or a rustic barn. Rustic describes the simple style of the countryside, so look for the country word.

sc1.stem: Unlike the fancy city hotel, the _____ farmhouse had plain wooden floors, a woodstove, and chickens clucking in the yard.

traps.why: Luxurious means fancy, which 'unlike the fancy city hotel' rules out.
A woodstove and plain wooden floors are not modern.
Chickens cluck, but the clues describe simple country life, not sound.

sc1.tip: 'Unlike the fancy city hotel' tells you the farmhouse is the opposite: plain and country-style. The woodstove and chickens back that up.

decoys.why: Unlike the fancy hotel means the farmhouse was plain, and extravagant means fancy.
Plain floors and a woodstove suggest simple living, not lots of money.
Plain wooden floors and chickens are simple, not bright and impressive.
The clues describe plain country living, not perfect cleanliness.
Nothing in the sentence talks about size; it describes a plain country home.
Chickens clucking and a woodstove sound cozy, not threatening.

traps.why: Modern and stylish is the opposite of plain country style.
Rustic things are simple, not broken.
Rustic has a pleasant feeling; rough and dirty sounds bad.

syn2.tip: Rustic usually sounds charming, like a cozy farmhouse. Pick the phrase that is plain and country-style without sounding insulting.

sc2.stem: Dad wanted a break from screens and traffic, so he rented a _____ cabin in the woods with no TV, a creaky porch, and an outhouse.

traps.why: A cabin with no TV is not high-tech.
An outhouse and creaky porch are not luxurious.
Downtown is in the city, but this cabin is in the woods.

sc2.tip: Dad wanted 'a break from screens and traffic,' so he chose the opposite. 'No TV' and 'an outhouse' describe a simple country cabin.

decoys.why: A cabin with no TV and an outhouse is simple, not costly or fancy.
A creaky porch and an outhouse are plain, not bright and impressive.
The cabin is plain and simple; nothing suggests lots of money.
The clues describe simple country living, not a perfectly clean cabin.
The sentence describes how plain the cabin is, not how large.
A cabin cannot move quickly; the sentence is about simple country living.

example: They live in an affluent neighborhood.
hook: Affluent comes from a Latin word meaning to flow toward; picture money flowing freely into a rich family's bank.

traps.why: Poor is the opposite of affluent.
Rich people may be generous, but affluent only means having money.
Greedy blames someone; affluent simply means rich, with no blame.

syn1.tip: You often hear 'an affluent neighborhood' about big houses and fancy cars. Pick the word that means having lots of money.

sc1.stem: The family lived in an _____ neighborhood, where huge houses had swimming pools and three fancy cars in each driveway.

traps.why: Safety is a different topic; the clues show how rich people are.
Ancient means very old; pools and fancy cars point to wealth.
Ordinary means average, unlike huge houses with pools.

sc1.tip: Look at the details: 'huge houses,' 'swimming pools,' and 'three fancy cars in each driveway.' These all show lots of money.

decoys.why: Pools and fancy cars show wealth, not that the neighborhood was perfectly clean.
Swimming pools and fancy cars point to money, not dry weather.
Huge houses and pools describe wealth, not a feeling that something bad will happen.
A neighborhood cannot take sides; the clues point to lots of money.
The clues show wealth, not anything unsteady or irregular.
The sentence describes expensive things, not how happy anyone felt.

traps.why: Needy means lacking money, the opposite of affluent.
Rich people may be well known, but affluent is about money.
Stingy is an insult about not sharing; affluent just means rich.

syn2.tip: Think of money flowing in. The answer should describe someone doing well with money, without saying anything good or bad about them.

sc2.stem: Most families in the town struggled to pay rent, but the mill owner was so _____ that he bought a second mansion just for summer vacations.

traps.why: Poor matches the families, but 'but' sets the owner apart.
Kindness would help the families; a second mansion shows great wealth.
Laziness doesn't buy mansions; the clue is about having money.

sc2.tip: 'But' contrasts the owner with families who 'struggled to pay rent.' Buying 'a second mansion' shows he had plenty of money.

decoys.why: Buying a second mansion shows great wealth, the opposite of being very poor.
A careful, sensible person would not buy a second mansion just for vacations.
He spent money on himself, not on helping the struggling families.
Owning two mansions is the opposite of simple country living.
Buying a vacation mansion shows wealth, not watching carefully for danger.
The contrast is struggling families versus a rich owner, not active versus inactive.

example: She was ecstatic about her birthday gift.
hook: Picture yourself leaping off the couch screaming when your team wins the championship; that wild joy is ecstatic.

traps.why: Miserable is the opposite of ecstatic.
Static is hidden inside ecstatic, but it means not moving.
Content means calmly satisfied, much weaker than ecstatic.

syn1.tip: Ecstatic is a big, loud feeling of joy, like jumping and screaming. Choose the word with the most excitement and happiness.

sc1.stem: Maya was _____ when she won tickets to meet her favorite author; she jumped and screamed with happiness.

traps.why: Meeting an author could cause nerves, but she 'screamed with happiness.'
Disappointed is the opposite of screaming with happiness.
Satisfied is too calm for someone jumping and screaming.

sc1.tip: After the semicolon, the sentence tells you how she felt: 'she jumped and screamed with happiness.' That is extreme joy.

decoys.why: She jumped and screamed with happiness, so very unhappy is the opposite.
Winning tickets does not make her rich; the sentence describes her happiness.
The sentence is about how happy she felt, not about taking sides.
Jumping and screaming with happiness is not watching carefully for danger.
The clue says happiness, not failing to take proper care.
The sentence describes her joy, and a person is not sudden and unexpected.

traps.why: Deeply disappointed is the opposite of ecstatic.
Somewhat pleased is far too weak for ecstatic.
Good news can surprise you, but ecstatic is about joy.

syn2.tip: Ecstatic is happiness turned all the way up. Pick the phrase that is both happy and very strong.

sc2.stem: Leo expected to be bored at the science museum, but when he got to hold a real dinosaur bone, he was _____ and talked about it all week.

traps.why: Gloomy fits being bored, but 'but' signals his mood changed.
A bone might puzzle someone, but he talked about it all week happily.
Dinosaurs sound scary, but holding a bone thrilled him.

sc2.tip: 'Expected to be bored, but' tells you Leo felt the opposite. Talking about it 'all week' shows he was extremely happy.

decoys.why: Holding the bone thrilled him enough to talk all week, so he was not unhappy.
Nothing here is about watching for danger; the sentence describes how excited he felt.
He was not judging anything fairly; the sentence is about his strong happy feeling.
Being careful and sensible would not make him talk about the bone all week.
Nothing suggests he was careless; the sentence shows he was thrilled by the bone.
Having money has nothing to do with his reaction to holding the dinosaur bone.

meaning: very unhappy, or very poor in quality
example: I felt wretched with the flu.
hook: Picture a soaked, shivering kid with the flu; that wretched feeling is the lowest, most miserable kind of unhappy.

traps.why: Joyful is the opposite of wretched.
Wrecked looks like wretched but means smashed or ruined.
Grumpy is a mild bad mood; wretched is deep misery.

syn1.tip: You might say 'I feel wretched' when you have the flu. Choose the word for feeling truly awful and unhappy.

sc1.stem: Cold, soaked, and shivering after missing the bus in the pouring rain, Owen felt _____, as unhappy as he had ever been.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of 'as unhappy as he had ever been.'
Chilly fits the cold, but the clue is about unhappiness.
Annoyed is too mild for 'as unhappy as he had ever been.'

sc1.tip: The words after the comma restate the blank: 'as unhappy as he had ever been.' You need a word for extreme unhappiness.

decoys.why: The sentence says he was as unhappy as ever, and ecstatic means extremely happy.
Missing the bus is rushed, but the clue says he felt unhappy, not busy.
He was soaked in pouring rain, so he certainly did not feel dry.
The clue says he was deeply unhappy, not watching carefully for danger.
Being fair has nothing to do with feeling cold, soaked, and miserable.
Kindness is not a feeling of misery, and the sentence says he was unhappy.

traps.why: Full of joy is the opposite of wretched.
Slightly annoyed is much too weak for wretched.
Sick people feel sleepy, but wretched means deeply unhappy.

syn2.tip: Wretched is a strong, sad word. Look for the phrase that shows real unhappiness, not just a small bother.

sc2.stem: The food at the camp was so _____ that even my brother, who eats everything, pushed away his plate of burnt, soggy noodles.

traps.why: Delicious food would not be pushed away.
Plentiful is about amount; 'burnt, soggy' is about bad quality.
Price wouldn't make him push it away; burnt noodles show awful quality.

sc2.tip: Here wretched means very poor in quality. If a brother 'who eats everything' refused 'burnt, soggy noodles,' the food must be terrible.

decoys.why: Burnt, soggy noodles are not impressive, and the brother pushed them away.
Burnt, soggy noodles are poor food, not perfectly clean or flawless.
Fancy, costly food would not be burnt and soggy noodles.
The noodles were soggy, so they were not dry at all.
Food cannot be extremely happy; the sentence needs a word for very bad food.
Food cannot be fair or take sides; the noodles were simply terrible.

example: Her score surpassed last year's record.
hook: Picture a runner catching the leader and zooming by; to surpass is to go past and do better.

traps.why: To trail is to stay behind, the opposite of doing better.
Surprise starts like surpass but means to catch someone off guard.
To match is to tie, not to do better.

syn1.tip: Pass is inside surpass. Think of passing someone in a race: you go beyond them. Choose the word that means go beyond.

sc1.stem: With her new personal record, Kira was finally able to _____ her older sister's best time in the 100-meter dash.

traps.why: A new personal record means she beat the time, not trailed it.
She might envy her sister, but a new record means she beat her.
Measuring a time needs no new record; she did better than it.

sc1.tip: 'New personal record' and 'finally able to' show Kira did something she couldn't before: beat her sister's best time.

decoys.why: Kira set a new record to beat her sister's time, not to slow her sister down.
A new personal record means she did better, not that she gave up or lost.
Setting a record is a win, so there is nothing to feel sad about.
She did not escape her sister's time; the record shows she beat it.
You cannot follow a race time; the new record means she did better.
A race time is not a law, and she beat it rather than ended it.

traps.why: Fall behind is the opposite of surpass.
Pass is inside surpass, but surpass is not about handing things over.
Catching up only reaches someone; surpassing goes beyond them.

syn2.tip: You often hear 'surpass the record.' Breaking a record means doing better than it, not just reaching it.

sc2.stem: Last year our class collected only two hundred cans for the food drive, but this year we hope to _____ that total and bring in over five hundred.

traps.why: Repeating means two hundred again, not over five hundred.
Lowering the total clashes with bringing in over five hundred.
Counting cans is part of a drive, but the goal is beating the total.

sc2.tip: 'Only two hundred' last year, 'but' this year 'over five hundred.' The class wants to go beyond last year's number.

decoys.why: They want over five hundred cans, which means growing the total, not shrinking it.
The class hopes to collect more cans, not get in the way of the total.
Bringing in over five hundred cans means beating the total, not giving it up.
The class is hopeful about beating the total, not sad over a loss.
A can total is not a law, and they want to beat it, not end it.
They are not escaping the total; they hope to go well beyond it.

meaning: thinly spread; few and far apart
example: The grass was sparse in the shade.
hook: Picture a nearly bald head with a few lonely hairs sticking up; that sparse hair is spread thin.

traps.why: Thick is the opposite of sparse.
Spare looks like sparse but means extra, like a spare tire.
Sparse grass might be short, but sparse means spread thinly.

syn1.tip: Think of 'sparse grass' in the shade: a few blades here and there with bare dirt between. Choose the word for spread out thinly.

sc1.stem: The old dog's tail had grown _____, with only a few thin hairs scattered here and there.

traps.why: Bushy means thick and full, not 'only a few thin hairs.'
Long is about length; the clue is about how few hairs there are.
Stiff is about how hair feels, not how many hairs remain.

sc1.tip: The clue follows the comma: 'only a few thin hairs scattered here and there.' That describes something thinly spread.

decoys.why: The sentence says only a few thin hairs were left, so the tail was not huge.
A few thin hairs is the opposite of fancy or excessive.
A tail with only a few thin hairs would not be bright and impressive.
The clue is about how few hairs there were, not about cleanliness.
The clue describes how little hair was left, not how the tail moved.

traps.why: Crowded together is the opposite of sparse.
Sparse means only a little, not none at all.
Trimmed grass is cut short, but sparse means there isn't much.

syn2.tip: Sparse means some is there, but not much, with gaps between. Look for the phrase about a small number spread apart.

sc2.stem: The hiking trail was crowded with people on Saturday, but by Monday morning the hikers were _____, with only one or two passing every hour.

traps.why: Numerous means many, which 'but' and 'only one or two' rule out.
Hikers can be tired, but the clue is about how many there were.
Absent means none at all, but one or two still passed.

sc2.tip: 'Crowded' on Saturday, 'but' on Monday, so the opposite: 'only one or two' hikers. That means few and spread out.

decoys.why: Only one or two hikers an hour is quiet, the opposite of busy and rushed.
The hikers were few on Monday, so a word meaning extremely large does not fit.
The clue is about how many hikers passed, not how happy they felt.
The sentence counts hikers per hour; it says nothing about watching for danger.
Whether hikers had money has nothing to do with only one or two passing.
The clue is about how few hikers there were, not about them being unhappy.

meaning: to set on fire; to start
example: The match ignited the campfire.
hook: Ignite shares a Latin root for fire with igneous rock, which formed from fiery melted lava.

traps.why: Extinguish means put out a fire, the opposite of ignite.
Ignore starts like ignite but means to pay no attention.
Fires make smoke, but ignite means to start the fire.

syn1.tip: Think of a match that ignites a campfire. Choose the word for starting a flame.

sc1.stem: The campers struck a match to _____ the dry twigs and finally start their campfire.

traps.why: Campers gather twigs, but a struck match is for lighting them.
Soaking twigs in water would stop a fire, not start it.
Snapping twigs breaks them; a match is used to light them.

sc1.tip: 'Struck a match' and 'start their campfire' both point to setting the twigs on fire.

decoys.why: Striking a match is meant to light the twigs, not scatter them.
You do not grow dry twigs with a match; they wanted to light them.
The match was to start the fire, not to make the twigs smaller.
Caring for dry twigs as they grow does not start a campfire.
You cannot call twigs to come; the match was struck to set them burning.
They wanted to start the fire, not get in its way.

traps.why: Put out means stop a fire, the opposite of ignite.
Fire warms you, but ignite means to start the fire.
Campers pile up wood first, but igniting means lighting it.

syn2.tip: Rockets ignite at liftoff and campfires ignite from a match. Both mean flames start, so pick the phrase about starting a fire.

sc2.stem: Mr. Lopez hoped the exciting volcano video would _____ his students' interest in science, and soon everyone was begging to build their own model.

traps.why: Dampen means weaken, but students begging to build shows interest grew.
Measuring interest wouldn't make students beg to build models.
Ignore looks like ignite, but the video clearly sparked interest.

sc2.tip: Here ignite means start. The result, 'everyone was begging to build their own model,' shows the video started a burst of interest.

decoys.why: Everyone begged to build a model, so interest grew instead of shrinking.
The video got students excited, which is the opposite of getting in the way.
Students begged to build models, so the video encouraged them rather than discouraged them.
He hoped to start their interest, not put an end to it.
The sentence is about exciting students, not feeling sad over a loss.
The video was meant to spark interest, not to do better than it.

example: The fly's erratic path was hard to follow.
hook: An erratic fly zigzags around the room, and you can never guess where it will land next.

traps.why: Steady is the opposite of erratic.
Erratic looks like it has err in it, but it means unsteady, not wrong.
Erratic things may move fast, but erratic is about having no pattern.

syn1.tip: Think of an erratic fly zigzagging. Something erratic jumps around with no pattern, so you can't tell what it will do next.

sc1.stem: In the gusty wind, the kite took an _____ path, swooping, dipping, and darting in ways no one could predict.

traps.why: An even path is smooth and steady, the opposite of swooping and darting.
Orderly means neat and regular, but no one could predict this path.
Kites fly up, but this kite was also dipping and swooping.

sc1.tip: Look at "swooping, dipping, and darting in ways no one could predict." The blank must mean unpredictable.

decoys.why: The clue is that the kite moved unpredictably, not that its path was clean.
A kite's path cannot take sides; the sentence describes unpredictable movement.
A path cannot have money; the kite was swooping and darting unpredictably.
Dryness has nothing to do with a kite darting in ways no one could predict.
The clue is about unpredictable movement, not about being costly or fancy.
Nothing bad is hinted at; the sentence just says no one could predict the path.

traps.why: Following a plan is the opposite of erratic.
Erratic looks like error, but it means unsteady, not full of mistakes.
Speed is not the point; erratic means irregular and hard to predict.

syn2.tip: Picture an erratic heartbeat or erratic driving. Both mean jumping around in a way that has no steady pattern.

sc2.stem: Usually our old car's clock kept perfect time, but lately it has been _____, running fast one hour and stopping completely the next.

traps.why: Reliable fits the first part, but "but lately" signals a change.
Accurate means correct, the opposite of running fast and then stopping.
Clocks can tick loudly, but the clue is about uneven timekeeping.

sc2.tip: The word "but" shows a contrast with "kept perfect time." Then "running fast one hour and stopping completely the next" shows it is unsteady.

decoys.why: Immaculate means perfectly clean, but the clock's problem is its timing, not dirt.
Mellow means soft and gentle, which says nothing about a clock running fast then stopping.
Sparse means thinly spread, but the sentence describes a clock that keeps changing speed.
Vigilant means watching for danger, and a clock cannot be watchful.
Impartial means not taking sides, which has nothing to do with keeping time.
Colossal means huge, but the sentence is about how unevenly the clock runs.

example: The vigilant lifeguard scanned the pool.
hook: A vigilant guard keeps watch all night; a vigil is a time of staying awake to keep watch.

traps.why: Careless is the opposite of vigilant.
Violent starts like vigilant but means rough and harmful.
Guards may be brave, but vigilant means watching carefully.

syn1.tip: Vigilant contains vigil, a time of staying awake to watch. A vigilant person keeps their eyes open.

sc1.stem: The _____ meerkat stood guard on the rock, always watching carefully for hawks while the others ate.

traps.why: A lazy meerkat would not stand guard watching for hawks.
Careless is the opposite of always watching carefully.
The others were eating, but this meerkat was guarding, not wanting food.

sc1.tip: The sentence tells you the meaning: "stood guard" and "always watching carefully for hawks." Pick the word that means watchful.

decoys.why: The meerkat is watching carefully, and negligent means not taking proper care.
The meerkat is always watching, but erratic means unsteady and irregular.
Ecstatic means extremely happy, but the clue is about carefully watching for hawks.
Mellow means soft and relaxed, not alert for danger like a guard.
Colossal means extremely large, and the sentence is about watchfulness, not size.
Immaculate means perfectly clean, but the clue is about watching for hawks.

traps.why: Sleepy is the opposite of vigilant.
Nosy means snooping in a bad way; vigilant is good watching for danger.
Danger can be scary, but vigilant means watching, not feeling afraid.

syn2.tip: Think of a vigilant lifeguard scanning the pool. Vigilant is a good feeling word for someone wide awake and ready.

sc2.stem: Because a raccoon kept sneaking into our tent at night, Dad stayed _____, listening for every rustle and keeping his flashlight ready until sunrise.

traps.why: Someone asleep cannot listen for every rustle.
Careless is the opposite of keeping a flashlight ready for trouble.
Bored people don't listen closely for every rustle.

sc2.tip: "Because a raccoon kept sneaking" is the cause. The effect is "listening for every rustle" and "keeping his flashlight ready," so Dad stayed watchful.

decoys.why: Dad was listening for every rustle, the opposite of not taking proper care.
Mellow means relaxed and gentle, but Dad was alert with his flashlight ready.
Ecstatic means extremely happy, but Dad was on guard against a raccoon.
Impartial means not taking sides, but Dad was watching for the raccoon.
Immaculate means perfectly clean, which has nothing to do with listening all night.
Affluent means rich, but the sentence is about staying alert until sunrise.

meaning: kind and wanting to help others
example: A benevolent woman built a park for the town.
hook: Bene means good, and benevolent people wish others well, like a neighbor who shovels everyone's sidewalk.

traps.why: Cruel is the opposite of benevolent.
Violent looks like the end of benevolent but means harmful.
Some givers are rich, but benevolent means kind, not rich.

syn1.tip: Bene means good, as in benefit. A benevolent person wants good things for others.

sc1.stem: The _____ baker gave free bread to every hungry family in town, always wanting to help others.

traps.why: A greedy baker would not give away free bread.
Selfish is the opposite of always wanting to help others.
Frugal people save money, but this baker gave bread away free.

sc1.tip: The clue is "gave free bread" and "always wanting to help others." The blank must mean kind and generous.

decoys.why: The baker always wanted to help others, and treacherous means full of hidden dangers.
Feeding every hungry family shows care, but negligent means not taking proper care.
Vigilant means watching for danger, but the clue is about wanting to help others.
Abrupt means sudden, but the clue says the baker always wanted to help.
Colossal means extremely large, and the sentence is about kindness, not size.
Immaculate means perfectly clean, but the clue is about giving free bread to the hungry.

traps.why: Mean and selfish is the opposite of benevolent.
Rich people may give gifts, but benevolent is about kindness.
Bene means good, but benevolent means wishing good for others, not being skilled.

syn2.tip: Find bene at the start, meaning good or well. Benevolent people wish others well and help them.

sc2.stem: Unlike the grumpy king who taxed everyone, his daughter was a _____ queen who lowered taxes and built schools for poor children.

traps.why: A greedy queen would not lower taxes or build schools for the poor.
Cruel describes the grumpy king better; "Unlike" signals the opposite.
Violent looks like benevolent but means harmful, which doesn't fit building schools.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the grumpy king" tells you the queen is the opposite. "Built schools for poor children" shows she was kind.

decoys.why: She lowered taxes and built schools, so she was not full of hidden dangers.
Building schools for poor children shows care, the opposite of negligent.
Wretched means very unhappy or poor in quality, but she did kind, helpful things.
Valiant means brave, but lowering taxes and building schools show kindness, not bravery.
Dazzling means bright and impressive, but the clue is about helping poor children.
Hectic means busy and rushed, but the sentence contrasts her kindness with a grumpy king.

example: He spoke without any malice.
hook: Mal means bad, so malice is a bad wish: wanting someone to get hurt.

traps.why: Kindness is the opposite of malice.
Mal means bad, but malice is a wish to harm, not bad luck.
Mischief is playful trouble; malice is much stronger, a real wish to hurt.

syn1.tip: Mal means bad, as in malfunction. Malice is a mean, bad wish toward someone else.

sc1.stem: The prank was just for fun; there was no _____ in it, since Jay never wanted to hurt anyone's feelings.

traps.why: Saying a fun prank had no kindness doesn't fit Jay never wanting to hurt.
Pranks are funny, and this one was "just for fun," so it had humor.
A prank is mischief, so there was some; malice is the stronger, harmful wish.

sc1.tip: Read "since Jay never wanted to hurt anyone's feelings." The blank names what was missing: a wish to hurt.

decoys.why: Remorse is regret after doing wrong, but the sentence is about Jay never wanting to hurt anyone.
Zeal means great eagerness, but the clue is about not wanting to hurt feelings.
Solitude means being alone, which has nothing to do with wanting to hurt someone.
Fragrance is a sweet smell, and the sentence is about Jay's intentions.
A precaution prevents harm, but the sentence is about not wishing harm on anyone.

traps.why: A wish to help is the opposite of malice.
Mal means bad, but malice is about bad wishes, not being sick.
Malice is about harm, but it means wanting to cause it, not fearing it.

syn2.tip: You may know "without malice," meaning not meaning any harm. Malice is wanting to hurt someone.

sc2.stem: Although the two teams were fierce rivals on the field, they showed no _____ afterward, shaking hands and cheering for each other's best plays.

traps.why: Shaking hands and cheering show lots of respect, not none.
Cheering for the other team shows goodwill, so "no goodwill" doesn't fit.
Sports need skill, but the clue is about feelings toward the other team.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with "fierce rivals." Shaking hands and cheering show they had no wish to harm each other.

decoys.why: Remorse is regret for doing wrong, but the teams did nothing wrong by playing hard.
Zeal means eagerness, yet the teams were cheering, so they clearly showed energy.
Solitude means being alone, but the clue is about the teams being friendly, not unkind.
Fragrance is a sweet smell, which has nothing to do with how the rivals treated each other.

example: The negligent babysitter left the gate open.
hook: A negligent person neglects things, like forgetting the bathtub is running until water floods the floor.

traps.why: Responsible is the opposite of negligent.
Negative starts like negligent but means bad or gloomy.
Negligence can lead to danger, but negligent means not taking care.

syn1.tip: Negligent is a cousin of neglect. If you neglect your plant, you don't take care of it.

sc1.stem: The _____ pet sitter forgot to feed the goldfish for three days, failing to take proper care of them.

traps.why: A devoted sitter would never forget to feed the fish.
Watchful is the opposite of forgetting to feed the fish for days.
The fish were neglected; the sitter was the one not taking care.

sc1.tip: The sentence restates the meaning: "failing to take proper care." Choose the word that describes a careless sitter.

decoys.why: The sitter forgot to feed the fish, so the sitter was not carefully watchful.
Forgetting the goldfish for three days is not thoughtful, so considerate does not fit.
Benevolent means kind and helpful, but the sitter failed to take care of the fish.
Immaculate means perfectly clean, but the clue is about forgetting to feed the fish.
Ecstatic means extremely happy, but the sentence is about failing to take proper care.
Affluent means rich, which does not explain why the fish went unfed.

traps.why: Taking great care is the opposite of negligent.
That describes what is neglected; negligent describes the person who fails to care.
Neg can suggest no, but negligent means careless, not refusing.

syn2.tip: Hear neglect inside negligent. A negligent person is the one who neglects a job or duty.

sc2.stem: Because the _____ driver never checked his tires, one went flat on the highway, and the family missed the start of the game.

traps.why: A cautious driver would check the tires.
Careful drivers check their tires, so this word is the opposite.
Speed is about driving, but the problem came from never checking the tires.

sc2.tip: "Because" links cause and effect. He "never checked his tires," so a flat followed. The blank must mean careless.

decoys.why: The driver never checked his tires, so he was not carefully watchful.
Never checking the tires made the family late, so the driver was not thoughtful.
Valiant means brave, but the clue is that the driver never checked his tires.
Affluent means rich, which does not explain why the tire went flat.
Rustic means simple and countrylike, but the clue is about not taking proper care.
Mellow means soft and gentle, but the sentence blames the driver for skipping tire checks.

example: Mornings are hectic in our house.
hook: Picture a hectic morning: toast burning, dog barking, and everyone yelling about missing shoes.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of hectic.
Hectic times can be noisy, but hectic means rushed.
Lively is a happy word; hectic means stressfully rushed.

syn1.tip: Think of "a hectic day" when everything happens at once. It feels rushed and stressful.

sc1.stem: The morning was _____, with everyone rushing to find shoes, pack lunches, and catch the bus all at once.

traps.why: A peaceful morning wouldn't have everyone rushing.
Leisurely means slow and unhurried, the opposite of rushing.
Nobody is lazy when they're rushing to catch the bus.

sc1.tip: The examples give it away: "everyone rushing" to do three things "all at once." That is a busy, rushed morning.

decoys.why: Everyone was rushing all at once, so the morning was not soft and gentle.
Sparse means few and far apart, but everything happened at once.
Arid means very dry, but the sentence is about rushing, not weather.
Vigilant means watching for danger, but the clue is about everyone hurrying.
Impartial means not taking sides, which has nothing to do with a rushed morning.
Brittle means easily snapped, but the sentence describes a busy, rushed morning.

traps.why: Relaxed is the opposite of hectic.
A hectic house may get messy, but hectic is about rushing.
Crowded means full of people; hectic means busy and hurried.

syn2.tip: Hectic describes time, like a hectic schedule. If you're hurrying from one thing to the next, it's hectic.

sc2.stem: Saturday was slow and lazy, but Sunday was _____: we had a soccer game, a birthday party, and piano lessons, all before dinner.

traps.why: Restful fits Saturday; "but" tells you Sunday was different.
A day with three events is full, not empty.
A day packed with games and parties is not dull.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Sunday with "slow and lazy." Then the list of three events before dinner shows it was very busy.

decoys.why: Sunday was packed with a game, a party, and lessons, so it was not soft and gentle.
Sunday had many events crowded together, not just a few spread far apart.
Abrupt means sudden, but the sentence describes a day crammed with activities, not a sudden one.
The sentence is about how busy Sunday was, not about anything being perfectly clean.
Arid describes dry land with little rain, not a day full of activities.
Nobody is taking sides here; the sentence lists everything that made Sunday busy.

example: Polar bears inhabit the Arctic.
hook: Animals inhabit their habitat; both words come from a Latin word meaning to live in a place.

traps.why: Abandon means to leave, the opposite of inhabit.
Inherit looks similar but means to receive from someone who died.
Visitors stay a short while; to inhabit is to live there.

syn1.tip: Inhabit contains habit, as in habitat, the place an animal lives. To inhabit is to live in a place.

sc1.stem: Colorful fish and sea turtles _____ the coral reef, which they have made their home for many years.

traps.why: Animals don't avoid a place they've made their home.
Visiting is short; "made their home for many years" means living there.
Inhibit looks like inhabit but means to hold back.

sc1.tip: The clue is "made their home for many years." The fish and turtles live in the reef.

decoys.why: The fish have made the reef their home, so they are not escaping or avoiding it.
You abolish a law or practice, not a coral reef that animals call home.
Fish and turtles cannot set an underwater reef on fire; the clue says it is their home.
The clue is that the reef is their home, which means they live there, not think about it.
Nothing is being slowed down; the sentence says the reef is where they live.
Nothing has been lost; the sentence says the animals have happily made the reef their home.

traps.why: Moving away is the opposite of inhabiting.
Here in means in, not not, so inhabit means to live in.
Traveling through is passing by, not making a home.

syn2.tip: Think of habitat and inhabitants, the people who live somewhere. To inhabit a place is to live there.

sc2.stem: Because winters are so harsh, very few people choose to _____ the tiny island, so its houses stand empty most of the year.

traps.why: If few people left, the houses would be full, not empty.
Inherit looks like inhabit but means to receive, and doesn't explain empty houses.
Few people abandoning the island would not leave the houses empty.

sc2.tip: Follow the cause and effect: "harsh" winters, so "houses stand empty." Few people choose to live there.

decoys.why: If few people avoided the island, most would live there, but the houses stand empty.
The empty houses show people are not living there, which has nothing to do with setting fires.
You abolish a law or practice, not an island that people could live on.
The empty houses point to people not living there, not to doing better than the island.
You cannot annoy an island; the empty houses show that few people live there.
Lighting up the island does not explain why its houses stand empty most of the year.

example: Our class took an excursion to the aquarium.
hook: Ex means out, so an excursion takes you out of school or home for a short, fun trip.

traps.why: An errand is a short trip to get a task done, not for fun.
Exclusion looks similar but means leaving someone out.
A voyage is a long journey; an excursion is short.

syn1.tip: Ex means out, and outing even has out in it. An excursion is a short trip out for fun.
