Honking all night is a huge amount, not a very small amount.
An alarm honking all night and waking people is not polite.
The sentence is about honking that never stopped, not about being forgiving.
The clue is that the alarm honked all night, not that it sounded sad.

example: The stingy king kept all the gold.
hook: Picture Scrooge counting coins and refusing to give his worker even a lump of extra coal: that is stingy.

traps.why: Generous means happy to give, the opposite of stingy.
Poor means having little money; stingy people may have plenty but won't share.
Stinky looks like stingy but means smelling bad.

syn1.tip: A miser is someone who hoards money. Stingy has that same tight, unfriendly feeling of refusing to give.

sc1.stem: The _____ pirate refused to share even one gold coin with his loyal crew, hiding the whole treasure for himself.

traps.why: A giving pirate would share, but this one refused.
Pirates can be fearsome, but the clue is about refusing to share.
Stringy looks like stingy but means thin and long like string.

sc1.tip: "Refused to share even one gold coin" and "hiding the whole treasure for himself" describe someone who will not give anything away.

decoys.why: The pirate is hiding a whole treasure, so he is not poor.
A pirate who refuses to share even one coin with his crew is not warm and friendly.
Pirates in stories may be brave, but this sentence is about refusing to share gold.
Hiding all the treasure from your loyal crew is not polite or respectful.
Nobody tricks the pirate here; he simply refuses to share his gold.

traps.why: Eager to share is the opposite of stingy.
Stingy looks like sting plus -y, but it is not about stinging.
Careful with money sounds sensible and good; stingy is a selfish, negative word.

syn2.tip: Say it with a soft g, like "stin-jee." It describes people who keep everything for themselves and will not share.

sc2.stem: Grandpa always gave us extra candy on Halloween, but his neighbor was so _____ that she handed out one tiny raisin per kid and kept the big chocolate bars.

traps.why: Generous fits only if you miss "but"; she kept the chocolate.
Spooky goes with Halloween, but the clue is about not sharing.
Cheerful is a pleasant word, but keeping the treats is selfish.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the neighbor with generous Grandpa. Giving "one tiny raisin" and keeping the chocolate shows she did not want to share.

decoys.why: The one raisin was meager, but the blank describes the neighbor, who kept the chocolate bars.
She kept the big chocolate bars, so she was not too poor to share.
Giving one tiny raisin and keeping the chocolate is not warm and friendly.
The sentence is about refusing to share candy, not about being brave and noble.
She did not change her mind; she gave every kid one raisin and kept the chocolate.

example: We enjoyed the tranquility of the lake.
hook: Picture a still lake at dawn, no wind, no voices, just one bird singing: that calm is tranquility.

traps.why: Chaos means wild confusion, the opposite of tranquility.
Sleep is restful, but tranquility is a calm, quiet feeling or place.
Loneliness is quiet too, but it feels sad; tranquility feels pleasant.

syn1.tip: The word "tranquil," meaning calm, is inside tranquility. The Sea of Tranquility on the moon was named for calm.

sc1.stem: After the noisy city, the _____ of the still mountain lake, where only birds were singing, felt wonderful.

traps.why: Commotion means noisy activity, like the city, not the still lake.
Mountain lakes can be cold, but the clue contrasts noise with calm.
Emptiness feels lonely and sad, but this place felt wonderful.

sc1.tip: "After the noisy city" sets up a contrast, and "still" and "only birds were singing" describe a calm, quiet place.

decoys.why: The noisy city had commotion; the still lake where only birds sang was calm.
Wild uproar describes the noisy city, not a still lake with only birds singing.
Loud noise is what you left behind; the still lake was quiet.
A narrow crack has nothing to do with the calm, quiet lake the sentence describes.
The sentence contrasts noise with quiet, so a leftover piece does not fit.
Eager energy does not match a still lake where only birds were singing.

traps.why: Noisy confusion is the opposite of quiet calm.
Boredom is quiet but unpleasant; tranquility is a peaceful, good feeling.
Total silence goes too far; a tranquil place can still have birdsong.

syn2.tip: Tranquil means calm. Add -ity and the word names the state of being calm and peaceful.

sc2.stem: Because the baby had finally fallen asleep and the dog was napping by the fire, a sweet _____ filled the house for the first time all day.

traps.why: An uproar is loud, but everyone was sleeping.
The dog is mentioned, but it was napping, not barking.
Sadness is the wrong feeling for a sweet, restful moment.

sc2.tip: The cause is "the baby had finally fallen asleep" and "the dog was napping." That leads to a calm, quiet house.

decoys.why: The baby and dog are sleeping, so the house is calm, not full of noisy confusion.
Everyone is sleeping, so loud noise and confusion is the opposite of what filled the house.
A napping baby and dog bring quiet, not wild uproar.
Sleeping and napping suggest rest, not great eagerness and energy.

example: The drab room needed some bright paint.
hook: Drab is the color of a gray, rainy Monday: no sparkle, no brightness, just plain and dull.

traps.why: Colorful is the opposite of drab.
Dirty things can look dull, but drab means plain and colorless, not unclean.
Hideous means terribly ugly; drab is only plain and boring.

syn1.tip: Think of a drab gray sweater next to a rainbow one. Drab things lack color and brightness.

sc1.stem: Unlike her bright, sparkly sneakers, the school uniform was _____, a plain brownish gray without a speck of color.

traps.why: Dazzling is the opposite; the uniform had no color at all.
Clothes can be comfortable, but the clue is about having no color.
Uniforms have a price, but the clue describes plain brownish gray.

sc1.tip: "Unlike her bright, sparkly sneakers" signals a contrast, and "plain brownish gray without a speck of color" tells you the meaning.

decoys.why: A uniform cannot feel extremely happy, and the sentence describes its dull color.
The sentence is about color, not a small amount of something.
A uniform is not empty and lonely; the clue is its brownish gray color.
The sentence talks about color, not temperature.
A uniform cannot change its mind; the clue is that it has no color.
The sentence describes the uniform's dull color, not thinness.

traps.why: Bright and cheerful is the opposite of drab.
Old things can look drab, but drab is about color, not damage.
Drab is boring, not frightening; scary is the wrong feeling.

syn2.tip: Drab often describes clothes, walls, or weather. It means plain, colorless, and boring to look at.

sc2.stem: The old classroom walls were so _____ that the students voted to cover them with bright murals of rainbows, jungles, and planets.

traps.why: Vivid walls would already be bright, so nobody would need murals.
Walls can be sturdy, but that would not make students add bright murals.
Cheerful walls would not need fixing; the walls were dull.

sc2.tip: The result, covering the walls with "bright murals," tells you the walls were plain and lacked color.

decoys.why: Walls cannot be warm and friendly, and murals fix dullness, not friendliness.
Bright murals would not fix dangerous walls; they fix dull, colorless ones.
Painting rainbows would not warm up cold walls; the murals add color.
The bright murals show the problem was a lack of color, not a small amount.
Walls cannot change their minds; the murals point to a lack of color.

example: A spilled drink was the only mishap.
hook: Mis- means badly, and hap means luck, as in "happen" and "perhaps": a mishap is a bit of bad luck.

traps.why: A success goes well; a mishap goes wrong.
A disaster is huge; a mishap is a small accident.
Mishmash looks like mishap but means a jumbled mix.

syn1.tip: Mis- means badly or wrong, as in misspell. A mishap is something that happens badly, a small accident.

sc1.stem: Spilling a little juice on the rug was only a small _____, so Mom just laughed and grabbed a towel.

traps.why: Spilling juice is not a triumph; it is a little accident.
A catastrophe is huge, but this was "only a small" spill.
Juice can be a snack, but spilling it is an accident.

sc1.tip: "Only a small" and "Mom just laughed" tell you it was a minor bit of bad luck, nothing serious.

decoys.why: The sentence says it was small and Mom laughed, so it was not a complete failure.
A little spilled juice that makes Mom laugh is not wild uproar.
A small spill calmly wiped up is not loud noise and confusion.
Spilling juice is an accident, not a sickness.
Spilling juice is something that happened, not a funny story someone tells.
Spilling juice is an accident, not a small leftover piece.

traps.why: Good luck is the opposite of a mishap.
A tragedy is far too serious; a mishap is minor.
Hap is not "happy" here; it means luck, and a mishap is an event.

syn2.tip: Think of tripping and dropping your lunch tray. That small, unlucky moment is a mishap, not a big tragedy.

sc2.stem: The class trip went perfectly except for one _____, when Jamal's hat blew into the duck pond and he had to fish it out with a stick.

traps.why: A highlight is a best moment, but "except for" points to something going wrong.
A tragedy is too serious for a hat in a pond.
Class trips can have picnics, but the clue is the hat accident.

sc2.tip: "Except for" signals something went wrong on a perfect trip. A hat blowing into a pond is a small, unlucky accident.

decoys.why: The trip went perfectly, so a hat in a pond is not a complete failure.
Fishing out one hat with a stick is a small problem, not wild uproar.
The hat blowing away is an accident that happened, not a story being told.
A hat blowing into a pond is an accident, not a sickness.
The sentence describes an accident with a hat, not an enemy.
A hat landing in a pond is an accident, not a slight idea or hint.

example: The new girl seemed aloof at first.
hook: Picture a cat on a high shelf, watching the party below and ignoring everyone who calls its name: that cat is aloof.

traps.why: Friendly is the opposite of aloof.
Hostile means openly unfriendly and ready to fight; aloof is just cool and distant.
Lonely people are apart but wish for friends; aloof people choose distance.

syn1.tip: People say someone "kept aloof," meaning they stood apart from others. An aloof person feels cool and far away, even in the same room.

sc1.stem: Priya was not shy; she simply chose to stay _____ at the party, standing coolly apart and barely nodding when anyone said hello.

traps.why: Timid fits only if you miss "not shy"; Priya chose to stay apart.
Sociable means friendly and chatty, but she barely nodded hello.
Aloft looks like aloof but means up in the air.

sc1.tip: "Not shy" rules out fear, and "coolly apart" and "barely nodding" show she chose to keep her distance from others.

decoys.why: Priya stood coolly apart and barely nodded, which is the opposite of warm and friendly.
Barely nodding and standing apart shows no eagerness at all.
The sentence describes Priya acting cool and distant, not extremely happy.
The sentence is about Priya keeping apart from others, not being easy to handle.
Nothing in the sentence shows Priya being tricked; she is keeping her distance.
Priya chose one cool way to act all party, not changing her mind often.

traps.why: Warm and welcoming is the opposite of aloof.
Shy people stay apart from fear; aloof people stay apart by choice.
That is aloft, which looks like aloof but means up high.

syn2.tip: Aloof people keep their distance on purpose. They are not scared, just cool and uninterested in being friendly.

sc2.stem: Because the famous skater stayed _____ after the show, ignoring fans' waves and refusing to sign autographs, many kids left feeling disappointed.

traps.why: A chatty skater would talk to fans, not ignore them.
Skaters are graceful, but the clue is about ignoring fans.
Humble is a pleasant quality, but this skater disappointed the kids.

sc2.tip: "Ignoring fans' waves" and "refusing to sign autographs" show someone cool and distant, and that is why the kids felt "disappointed."

decoys.why: Ignoring fans and refusing autographs is the opposite of warm and friendly.
The skater ignored fans and disappointed kids, which shows distance, not happiness.
Ignoring waves and refusing autographs shows no eagerness toward the fans.
The sentence is about the skater ignoring fans, not being calm and easy to handle.
The skater was distant with fans; nobody was being forgiven or let off.

example: The zealous fans painted their faces.
hook: Zealous is zeal plus -ous, full of zeal, like a fan who paints their face and cheers until they lose their voice.

traps.why: Uninterested is the opposite of zealous.
Curious is too mild; zealous means extremely eager.
Zealous fans can be noisy, but the word means eager, not loud.

syn1.tip: Zeal means strong eagerness, and -ous means full of. Zealous people are full of eagerness for a cause, team, or hobby.

sc1.stem: The _____ fan arrived at the stadium five hours early, wearing face paint and cheering louder than anyone else.

traps.why: A bored fan would not arrive five hours early and cheer loudest.
A casual fan likes the team a little; this fan went all out.
Jealous sounds like zealous but means wanting what others have.

sc1.tip: "Five hours early," "face paint," and "cheering louder than anyone" are all examples of someone extremely eager.

decoys.why: A fan who arrives hours early and cheers loudest is the opposite of cool and distant.
Face paint and loud cheering show excitement, not a serious, sad mood.
A fan in face paint is not dull and colorless; the clue is his eagerness.
Showing up five hours early shows steady eagerness, not changing your mind.
Nothing in the sentence shows the fan being tricked; he is just very eager.
The sentence is about the fan's excitement, not about saving money.

traps.why: Completely bored is the opposite of zealous.
A little interested is far too weak for zealous.
Anger is a strong feeling too, but zealous means eager, not mad.

syn2.tip: Picture the most excited fan in the stadium. Zealous means full of eager energy, much more than just liking something.

sc2.stem: Most kids in the class thought the recycling project was boring, but Leo was _____, sorting bottles every recess and making posters to convince the whole school to join.

traps.why: Lazy fits only if you miss "but"; Leo worked every recess.
Grumpy is a bad mood, but Leo was excited about the project.
Projects can be confusing, but Leo clearly knew what he wanted.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts Leo with kids who found it "boring." Working "every recess" and convincing "the whole school" shows extreme eagerness.

decoys.why: Leo made posters to get the whole school involved, which is the opposite of distant.
Leo is busy and excited about the project, not sad and serious.
Recycling sounds like saving, but the sentence shows Leo's eagerness, not careful spending.
Leo works on the project every recess, so he is not changing his mind often.
The sentence contrasts bored kids with Leo's eagerness, not with being easily tricked.

example: The frigid wind stung our cheeks.
hook: Frigid and refrigerator come from the same Latin word for cold, so picture the icy inside of a freezer.

traps.why: Scorching means very hot, the opposite of frigid.
Rigid looks like frigid but means stiff, not cold.
Windy weather can feel cold, but frigid is about temperature, not wind.

syn1.tip: Frigid sounds like fridge, and both share a root meaning cold. Think of the coldest air you have felt.

sc1.stem: The mountain lake was so _____ that ice formed along the shore and our toes went numb in seconds.

traps.why: Balmy means pleasantly warm, and warm water would not make ice.
Shallow is about depth, and depth does not make ice form.
Rigid looks like frigid but means stiff, which a lake cannot be.

sc1.tip: Look at "ice formed along the shore" and "toes went numb in seconds." Only extreme cold causes both.

decoys.why: Aloof means cool toward people, but ice and numb toes describe a lake's temperature.
Ice and numb toes show the water was cold, not warm.
A lake full of water cannot be very dry; the clue is ice.
Ice and numb toes point to cold, not to the lake being empty and lonely.
Ice and numb toes describe temperature, not a dull color.
The clue is ice and numb toes, which tell you about cold, not amount.

traps.why: Pleasantly warm is the opposite of bitterly cold.
Slightly cool is too weak; frigid means extremely cold.
Rain is weather too, but frigid is about cold, not wetness.

syn2.tip: Frigid is not just a little cold. Picture a winter day so cold it hurts your face.

sc2.stem: Although the sun was shining brightly on the morning of the parade, the air was _____, so we wore thick mittens and scarves and could see our breath.

traps.why: Mild air would not call for thick mittens or show your breath.
Sunny repeats the sunshine, but "although" signals something different follows.
Humid means damp, which has nothing to do with seeing your breath.

sc2.tip: "Although" sets up a contrast with the sunshine. "Thick mittens" and "see our breath" point to very cold air.

decoys.why: Dry air would not explain thick mittens and seeing your breath; the clues point to cold.
The sentence is about temperature, shown by mittens and visible breath, not a sad or gloomy mood.
Dull color has nothing to do with mittens, scarves, and seeing your breath.
Aloof means cool in an unfriendly way, describing people, not cold air.
Empty and lonely does not explain why everyone needed thick mittens and scarves.

meaning: to give as a gift or honor
example: The queen bestowed a medal on the hero.
hook: Imagine a king placing a golden crown on a hero's head; he bestows it, giving it as an honor.

traps.why: Withhold means to keep something back, the opposite of giving it.
Stow is hidden inside bestow but means to pack something away.
Lending expects the thing back; bestowing gives it for good.

syn1.tip: Picture a queen bestowing a medal on a hero. She is giving it as a gift or honor.

sc1.stem: At the ceremony, the mayor will _____ a special award upon the girl who rescued the stranded puppy.

traps.why: Revoke means to take back, but the ceremony honors the girl.
The girl might accept the award, but the mayor is the one giving it.
Stow looks like bestow but means to pack away, not to give.

sc1.tip: The mayor is handing something "upon" the girl at a "ceremony," so you need a word for giving an honor.

decoys.why: The mayor is giving the girl an award, and hoard means keeping things for yourself.
The ceremony is meant to honor the girl, so the mayor would not leave the award out.
The award goes upon the girl, which means giving it to her, not inventing it.
The mayor is honoring the girl, not showing off the award proudly.
Emit means giving off things like light or smoke, not handing someone an honor.

traps.why: Taking something away is the opposite of giving it.
Bestow contains stow, but it does not mean packing things away.
Honors are often earned, but bestow means giving, not earning.

syn2.tip: You hear bestow at ceremonies: an award or title is bestowed upon someone. It means giving with honor.

sc2.stem: Because Ms. Rivera was so proud of how hard her class had worked all year, she decided to _____ a gold star on every single student.

traps.why: A proud teacher would not keep the stars back from her students.
Borrowing means taking for a while, not giving an honor.
Stow looks like bestow but means to pack something away.

sc2.tip: "So proud of how hard her class had worked" is the cause. A proud teacher would give an honor, not hold it back.

decoys.why: Ms. Rivera is proud and rewards every student, so she would not keep the stars to herself.
She is proud of the class, so she gives stars to every student instead of leaving them out.
She is rewarding her students, not showing off the gold stars.

example: A cold is a common ailment.
hook: When something ails you, it troubles your health; an ailment is that trouble, like a cold or a sore throat.

traps.why: A cure ends an illness, so it is the opposite of an ailment.
Element looks a bit like ailment but means a basic part of something.
Medicine treats an ailment, but it is not the sickness itself.

syn1.tip: Ailment starts with ail, as in "What ails you?" That question asks what is making you sick.

sc1.stem: Grandma's only _____ is a sore knee, a minor sickness that slows her walks but never stops them.

traps.why: A remedy fixes a sickness, but a sore knee is the problem itself.
Alignment looks similar but means lining things up, not a sickness.
You might have a doctor's appointment, but a sore knee is not one.

sc1.tip: The words "a minor sickness" right after the blank tell you exactly what the missing word means.

decoys.why: The sentence calls the sore knee a minor sickness, not an accident.
A sore knee is called a sickness here, not a leftover piece of something.
A sore knee that slows her walks is a sickness, not a natural skill.
The sentence describes a sickness, not a short funny story Grandma tells.

traps.why: Being healthy is the opposite of having an ailment.
An ailment is usually a smaller sickness, not one that kills.
You might visit a doctor for an ailment, but it is the sickness itself.

syn2.tip: A cold or a stomachache is a common ailment. Think of any everyday sickness.

sc2.stem: Mia stayed home from school for three days because of a stubborn _____ that gave her a fever and a cough.

traps.why: A cure takes away a fever; it does not give you one.
An assignment is schoolwork, and schoolwork cannot give you a fever.
Alignment looks like ailment but means lining things up.

sc2.tip: The effect is "a fever and a cough," and only a sickness causes those.

decoys.why: An accident does not give you a fever and a cough; a sickness does.
Stubborn fits a rival, but an enemy cannot give Mia a fever and a cough.
Noisy confusion does not cause a fever and a cough that keep you home.
A leftover piece does not give someone a fever and a cough.

example: Lena was elated to get a puppy.
hook: Elated comes from a Latin word meaning lifted up; picture yourself floating with joy after the best news ever.

traps.why: Miserable means very unhappy, the opposite of elated.
Related looks like elated but means connected, not happy.
Satisfied is only mildly pleased; elated is far happier.

syn1.tip: Elated is a very strong happy feeling, like jumping up and cheering when you win.

sc1.stem: Ethan let out an _____ whoop when the letter said he had made the all-star team; he had never felt so thrilled.

traps.why: Anguished means full of pain, but Ethan felt thrilled.
An angry whoop has the wrong feeling for great news.
He may have been anxious before, but the letter made him thrilled.

sc1.tip: The clues "made the all-star team" and "never felt so thrilled" show his whoop was full of joy.

decoys.why: Ethan had never felt so thrilled, and aloof means cool and distant.
The clue is about his thrilled feeling, not about a whoop that never stops.

traps.why: Gloomy means sad and dark, the opposite of elated.
Elderly starts like elated but means old.
Relieved means glad a worry is over, not bursting with joy.

syn2.tip: Think of how you feel on your birthday when you open the gift you wanted most.

sc2.stem: Lena expected to feel let down after the long drive in the rain, but she was _____ when she saw the giant waterslide at the hotel.

traps.why: Disappointed matches "let down," but "but" tells you her feeling changed.
The long drive might tire her, but the waterslide brings joy.
Elevated looks like elated but means raised up high.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a switch from "let down," and a giant waterslide would make a kid extremely happy.

decoys.why: The word but shows her mood flipped from let down to happy, so sad is wrong.
Seeing a giant waterslide after a gloomy drive would excite her, not make her distant.
The rain might suggest cold, but the sentence is about her mood changing at the waterslide.
The but signals a big burst of happiness, not just being calm and easy to handle.

example: We coaxed the cat out from under the porch.
hook: Picture holding out a treat and whispering kindly to coax a shy cat out from under the porch.

traps.why: Force means making someone act roughly, the opposite of gentle coaxing.
Coach looks like coax but means to train or teach.
Scolding is harsh; coaxing is soft and kind.

syn1.tip: You coax a scared pet with a gentle voice and a treat. It means getting someone to act by being kind.

sc1.stem: Speaking softly and patiently, Ella tried to _____ her nervous little sister out from behind the curtain before the play.

traps.why: Dragging is rough, but Ella was "speaking softly and patiently."
Scolding is harsh, which does not fit speaking softly.
Coach looks like coax but means to train someone.

sc1.tip: "Speaking softly and patiently" tells you she was gently persuading her sister, not forcing her.

decoys.why: Ella speaks softly and patiently, so she is not sharply criticizing her sister.
Ella wants her sister to come out, not to keep away from her.

traps.why: Forbidding stops someone from acting; coaxing gets them to act.
Ordering loudly is too forceful; coaxing is gentle.
Coaxing is quiet, but you are trying to get someone to move.

syn2.tip: Coaxing is soft and patient, like talking a nervous friend into trying the slide.

sc2.stem: Shouting at the frightened puppy only made it hide deeper, so Dad knelt down with a treat to _____ it out of the closet.

traps.why: Yanking is rough, but kneeling with a treat is gentle.
Chasing would scare the puppy more, just like the shouting did.
Scolding is harsh, and harshness "only made it hide deeper."

sc2.tip: Shouting "only made it hide deeper," so Dad tried a gentle way instead: kneeling down "with a treat."

decoys.why: Shouting only made the puppy hide, so Dad switched to something gentle, not criticism.
Dad kneels with a treat to bring the puppy closer, not to avoid it.

example: She persevered and finally learned to skate.
hook: Persevere has severe inside it: you keep going even when things get severe, like learning to ride a bike.

traps.why: Quit means to give up, the opposite of persevere.
Preserve looks like persevere but means to keep something safe.
Complaining about hard work is different from sticking with it.

syn1.tip: People persevere through hard times. It means you keep going and do not give up.

sc1.stem: Even after falling off her bike again and again, Hana chose to _____, and by Sunday she was riding on her own.

traps.why: If Hana quit, she would not be riding on her own by Sunday.
Complaining would not teach her to ride by Sunday.
Resting might help her body, but only practice got her riding.

sc1.tip: "Even after falling... again and again" and "by Sunday she was riding on her own" show she kept trying.

decoys.why: Hana kept going until she could ride alone, so she did not weaken or give up.
Crying out does not explain how she learned to ride by Sunday after falling.
The sentence is about not giving up after falls, not about going up.
Making things seem bigger would not help her learn to ride after falling again and again.

traps.why: Giving up is the opposite of persevering.
Persevere contains severe, but it does not mean being strict.
Persevering may lead to winning, but it means trying through difficulty.

syn2.tip: Think of a coach saying "Don't give up." That is what it means to persevere.

sc2.stem: The puzzle had a thousand tiny pieces and took weeks, but because Omar was willing to _____, the finished picture of a castle now hangs on his wall.

traps.why: If Omar surrendered, there would be no finished picture.
Preserve looks like persevere but means to keep something safe.
A puzzle that "took weeks" was not finished by hurrying.

sc2.tip: "Took weeks" shows it was hard, and the "finished picture" is the result of not giving up.

decoys.why: The puzzle took weeks and Omar finished it, so he kept going instead of weakening.
Making things seem bigger would not finish a thousand-piece puzzle; steady effort did.
Crying out suddenly has nothing to do with working on a puzzle for weeks.
The castle is only in the picture, and going up would not finish a puzzle.

example: The docile pony let kids ride it.
hook: A docile pony stands still while kids climb on; docile comes from a Latin word meaning easy to teach.

traps.why: Fierce means wild and dangerous, the opposite of docile.
A lazy animal may be still, but docile means gentle and easy to handle.
Many gentle pets are small, but docile is about behavior, not size.

syn1.tip: Picture a pony at a petting zoo that lets children brush it. That calm, gentle animal is docile.

sc1.stem: Unlike the wild, kicking colt, the old mare was _____, calm enough for even small children to lead and brush.

traps.why: Unruly means wild, which describes the colt, not the mare.
Speed is not the point; the mare was calm enough for small children.
Size does not make a horse safe for small children to lead.

sc1.tip: "Unlike the wild, kicking colt" sets up a contrast, and "calm enough for even small children" tells you the answer.

decoys.why: The mare is unlike the wild colt and calm, so rowdy is the opposite.
The clue is calm enough for children, not eager and full of energy.
Changing your mind often says nothing about being calm and easy to lead.
Old might suggest bony, but the clue is about being calm, not thin.
Being extremely happy is not what makes a horse safe for small children.
Dull color has nothing to do with being calm enough to lead and brush.

traps.why: Hard to control is the opposite of docile.
Docile animals may be calm, but docile is not about speed.
A sleepy animal is still, but docile means gentle and obedient.

syn2.tip: Docile animals do what you ask without a fuss. Think of a gentle old dog on a leash.

sc2.stem: Because the class rabbit was so _____, Mr. Kim let every student take turns holding it on their laps during reading time.

traps.why: A jumpy rabbit would leap off laps, so no one could hold it.
A teacher would never let students hold a vicious animal.
Noise is not a reason to let kids hold a rabbit.

sc2.tip: "Because" signals a reason. A teacher only lets every student hold a rabbit if it is calm and gentle.

decoys.why: A rowdy rabbit would not sit still on students' laps during reading time.
A distant, unfriendly rabbit would not be passed around for students to hold.
Changing its mind often would not make the rabbit safe to hold.
Being thin and bony is not a reason to let every student hold it.
The rabbit sits calmly on laps, so eager and full of energy does not fit.

example: He flaunted his new sneakers at recess.
hook: A peacock spreading its bright tail feathers so everyone will stare is flaunting them.

traps.why: Hide means to keep out of sight, the opposite of flaunt.
Flout looks like flaunt but means to openly ignore a rule.
Sharing gives others a turn; flaunting just shows off what you own.

syn1.tip: When people flaunt something, they wave it around so others will notice. It is showing off.

sc1.stem: Jordan liked to _____ his shiny new sneakers, strutting up and down the hallway so everyone would notice them.

traps.why: He wanted "everyone would notice them," so he was not hiding them.
Cleaning sneakers is not why someone struts up and down a hallway.
Flout looks like flaunt but means to ignore rules.

sc1.tip: "Strutting up and down" and "so everyone would notice them" show he was proudly showing off.

decoys.why: Jordan strutted so everyone would notice, not hid his sneakers away.
He wanted everyone to see the sneakers, so he was not avoiding them.
He was proud enough to strut in them, so he did not hate them.
He kept the sneakers to show off; he was not giving them as a gift.
Strutting to get attention shows them off; it does not twist their shape.

traps.why: Keeping something hidden is the opposite of flaunting it.
Giving away means losing the thing; flaunting means showing it.
Barely mentioning is far too weak; flaunting is bold and proud.

syn2.tip: Picture someone strutting in new clothes, turning so everyone sees. That is flaunting.

sc2.stem: Unlike her cousin, who loved to _____ her fancy new phone at every family dinner, Priya kept her own phone quietly tucked away in her backpack.

traps.why: Conceal means hide, which is what Priya did, not her cousin.
Charging a phone has nothing to do with the contrast to tucking it away.
Silencing a phone is quiet, much like Priya, not unlike her.

sc2.tip: "Unlike" sets up a contrast with "quietly tucked away," so the cousin must have shown her phone off.

decoys.why: Hiding the phone away describes Priya, but the cousin is unlike her.
The cousin loved her fancy phone, so she was not keeping away from it.
The cousin loved her fancy new phone, so she did not hate it.
The cousin brought the phone to every dinner instead of leaving it out.
The contrast is about showing versus tucking away, not twisting a phone's shape.

example: The stray dog looked gaunt and hungry.
hook: Picture a stray dog so thin that its ribs show and its cheeks look hollow: that bony look is gaunt.

traps.why: Plump means round and well fed, the opposite of gaunt.
Haunted rhymes with gaunt but means visited by ghosts.
Hunger can make someone gaunt, but gaunt describes how thin they look.

syn1.tip: Gaunt describes a face or body that is very thin and bony, often from hunger or illness.

sc1.stem: When the rescued horse first arrived, it looked _____, with hollow cheeks and ribs showing, but good food soon filled it out.

traps.why: A plump horse would not have ribs showing.
Sleek means smooth and healthy, not hollow and bony.
A rescued horse might be muddy, but food does not fix mud.

sc1.tip: "Hollow cheeks and ribs showing" and "good food soon filled it out" tell you the horse was very thin.

decoys.why: Hollow cheeks and showing ribs describe how thin it was, not its calm behavior.
Good food filled it out, so the problem was thinness, not thirst.
Hollow cheeks and ribs point to being thin, not to looking sad.
The clue is ribs showing and food filling it out, not dull color.
A starving horse with ribs showing would not be described as extremely happy.
The clue is about its bony body, not about being noisy and rowdy.

traps.why: Round and chubby is the opposite of gaunt.
Slim and fit sounds healthy; gaunt means unhealthily thin.
Tall and strong describes a body, but not a thin, bony one.

syn2.tip: Gaunt is a negative word. Picture hollow cheeks and showing ribs on someone who has not eaten enough.

sc2.stem: After weeks stranded on the island with almost nothing to eat, the sailor looked _____, unlike the plump, well-fed captain who had stayed safely at home.

traps.why: Chubby describes the captain, but "unlike" tells you the sailor was different.
Cheerful has the wrong feeling for weeks with almost nothing to eat.
Haunted rhymes with gaunt but means visited by ghosts.

sc2.tip: "Almost nothing to eat" and the contrast with "plump, well-fed" tell you the sailor was very thin.

decoys.why: The sailor had almost nothing to eat and is compared to a plump captain, so think thin.
A starving, stranded sailor would not look extremely happy.
The contrast is plump versus not, so pride has nothing to do with it.
Being calm and easy to handle does not contrast with a plump, well-fed captain.
Having almost nothing to eat made him thin, not careful with money.
The contrast is with plump and well-fed, so noisy and rowdy does not fit.

example: Rain nourishes the crops.
hook: Nourish is related to nutrition: think of healthy food and water helping your body and a garden grow strong.

traps.why: Starve means to go without food, the opposite of nourish.
Flourish looks like nourish but means to grow well, not to feed.
Cooking makes food, but nourishing means giving what helps you grow.

syn1.tip: Nourish sounds like nutrition. When something nourishes you, it feeds your body what it needs.

sc1.stem: Fruits, vegetables, and whole grains _____ your body, giving it the food it needs to grow strong.

traps.why: Healthy foods make your body strong, not weak.
Flourish looks like nourish, but you cannot flourish your body.
Food can upset a stomach, but these foods help you grow strong.

sc1.tip: "Giving it the food it needs to grow strong" right after the blank explains the missing word.

decoys.why: Quench is for satisfying thirst, but the sentence says these foods help your body grow.
The sentence is about giving the body food to grow, not making it comfortable.
Calming someone by giving what they want is not how food helps you grow strong.
Healthy food helps your body grow strong, not twist out of shape.
Food gives your body what it needs; it does not collect and hide your body.
Healthy foods feed your body, they do not escape or avoid it.

traps.why: Weakening is the opposite of nourishing.
Overeating is about food, but it does not mean feeding for health.
Washing keeps things clean; nourishing gives food for growth.

syn2.tip: Rain nourishes crops and milk nourishes kids. Both help living things grow healthy.

sc2.stem: Candy and soda may taste sweet, but they do little to _____ a growing body, so Coach asks us to pack fruit and milk instead.

traps.why: If candy did little harm, Coach would not ask for fruit instead.
Candy does sweeten things, so "do little to sweeten" makes no sense.
Flourish looks like nourish, but you cannot flourish a body.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts sweet taste with what candy fails to do, and "pack fruit and milk instead" points to healthy feeding.

decoys.why: Soda might quench thirst, but the sentence is about feeding a growing body.
Candy and soda fail at helping a body grow, not at showing it off.
Coach wants food that helps you grow, and twisting your body is not the point.
The sentence is about feeding a growing body, not gently persuading it.
Food does not criticize a body; the sentence is about helping it grow.

example: I had no inkling about the surprise party.
hook: Picture one tiny drop of ink on a page: an inkling is just a tiny drop of an idea.

traps.why: Certainty means knowing for sure, the opposite of a slight idea.
Inkling sounds like ink, but it has nothing to do with stains.
You may get an inkling of a secret, but the secret is something else.

syn1.tip: You often hear "I had no inkling," meaning "I had no idea at all." Think of a small clue or hint.

sc1.stem: Jamie did not have an _____ that his friends were secretly planning a surprise party for him.

traps.why: An inkwell holds ink; it looks like inkling but means something else.
Parties have invitations, but the sentence is about Jamie not knowing anything.
Outfits go with parties, but you can't have an outfit that friends are planning.

sc1.tip: The word "secretly" tells you Jamie knew nothing. You need a word meaning a slight idea of what was happening.

decoys.why: The sentence is about Jamie not suspecting a secret party, not about a sickness.
Having no home makes no sense; the sentence is about not guessing a secret.
Jamie lacked a hint about the secret, not a funny story to tell.
The friends were planning something nice, and Jamie simply did not suspect it.

traps.why: Full knowledge is knowing everything, the opposite of a slight idea.
The word looks like ink, but it means an idea, not ink.
You might get an inkling of a surprise, but the surprise is different.

syn2.tip: An inkling is a small, faint idea, like a hint you only half notice. Look for the choice that means a little bit of knowing.

example: Cold water quenched our thirst.
hook: You quench your thirst with cold lemonade, and firefighters quench a fire with water.

traps.why: To increase thirst makes it bigger, the opposite of quench.
Clench rhymes with quench, but it means to squeeze tight.
You drink to quench thirst, but drinking is the action, not satisfying.

syn1.tip: You almost always hear it as "quench your thirst." Think of what a cold drink does to thirst: it satisfies it.

sc1.stem: After the long soccer game, only a big glass of ice-cold water could _____ Malik's thirst.

traps.why: Ice-cold water makes thirst go away, not grow bigger.
You can measure water, but you can't measure thirst with a glass.
Clench sounds like quench but means to squeeze, which doesn't fit thirst.

sc1.tip: The clue is "a big glass of ice-cold water" after "the long soccer game." Water takes away thirst, so you need a word meaning satisfy.

decoys.why: Water does help the body, but nourish means feeding growth, and you would never feed a thirst.
The water should make Malik's thirst go away, not make it seem bigger.
Avert means to prevent, but Malik was already thirsty after the game.
Nobody shows off thirst; the sentence is about water satisfying it.
Twisting the shape of a thirst makes no sense; the water satisfies it.
Water cannot look carefully at a thirst; it can only satisfy it.

traps.why: To worsen thirst makes it stronger, the opposite of quench.
Wrench looks a bit like quench but means to twist hard.
Spilling is something you do with a drink, not to thirst.

syn2.tip: Quenching thirst makes the dry, thirsty feeling go away. Pick the word meaning to ease or take away a bad feeling.

sc2.stem: Sugary soda seems refreshing, but it does not really _____ your thirst; plain water does a much better job of making you feel less thirsty.

traps.why: The sentence is about making you less thirsty, not more.
Soda has flavor, but you can't flavor your thirst.
Drench sounds like quench but means to soak something completely.

sc2.tip: The part after the semicolon explains the blank: water is better at "making you feel less thirsty." So the blank means to satisfy thirst.

decoys.why: The sentence is about feeling less thirsty, and nourish means feeding growth, not satisfying thirst.
The sentence compares drinks that make you less thirsty, not ones that make thirst seem bigger.
Showing off has nothing to do with water making you feel less thirsty.
The sentence is about making thirst go away, not twisting its shape.
Coax means to gently persuade someone, and you cannot persuade a thirst.
A drink cannot look carefully at your thirst; the sentence is about satisfying it.

example: The conceited prince stared at his reflection.
hook: A conceited person is full of conceit, sure they are the best and most beautiful at everything.

traps.why: Modest people don't brag, the opposite of conceited.
Concealed looks similar but means hidden.
Confident is a good feeling about yourself; conceited is too much pride.

syn1.tip: Conceited is an insult. Think of someone who stares at the mirror and brags. Pick the word for being too proud of yourself.

sc1.stem: The _____ singer kept bragging about his own voice and admired himself in every mirror he passed.

traps.why: Humble people don't brag or admire themselves in mirrors.
Concealed means hidden, and this singer is showing off, not hiding.
Nervous singers worry about their voice; bragging shows pride, not nerves.

sc1.tip: The clues are "bragging about his own voice" and "admired himself in every mirror." Both show someone far too proud of himself.

decoys.why: Bragging and admiring himself in mirrors show too much pride, not friendliness.
Docile means calm and easy to handle, but the clues are bragging and self-admiration.
Admiring himself in every mirror is not serious and sad; it shows he is too proud.
Nothing in the sentence shows him being tricked; he brags about himself.
Drab means dull and colorless, but the clues are about bragging and pride.
Being on time has nothing to do with bragging about his voice.

traps.why: Humble people don't show off, the opposite of conceited.
Concerned starts the same way but means worried.
Popular means liked by many, not too proud of yourself.

syn2.tip: Conceited has a negative feeling, like calling someone a show-off. Choose the word that means thinking you are better than others.

sc2.stem: Even though Ava won the spelling bee, she was never _____; she thanked her coach and cheered for every other speller.

traps.why: Thanking her coach and cheering others shows she was humble, so never humble is wrong.
She thanked her coach, so saying she was never grateful makes no sense.
Concerned looks similar but means worried, which the contrast doesn't explain.

sc2.tip: "Even though" she won, she did not act a certain way, and she "thanked" and "cheered" others. The blank is how a winner might wrongly act: too proud.

decoys.why: Ava thanked her coach and cheered others, so she clearly was friendly, not never friendly.
Cheering for every speller shows Ava was warm, so never warm makes no sense.
The sentence is about Ava staying humble after winning, not about being tricked.
Being on time has nothing to do with how Ava acted after winning.
The sentence contrasts winning with staying humble, not with being dull or colorless.

example: The parched ground cracked in the sun.
hook: Picture cracked desert ground and a dry throat begging for water: that is parched.

traps.why: Soaked means full of water, the opposite of parched.
Perched differs by one letter and means sitting up high, like a bird.
Hungry is about food; parched is about needing water.

syn1.tip: You hear "my throat is parched" or "parched desert." Both are about having no water.

sc1.stem: After hiking all afternoon without any water, I was _____ and gulped down three full bottles at the trailhead.

traps.why: Refreshed people don't need three bottles of water right away.
Perched means sitting up high, not needing water.
Starving is about food, but the hiker gulped water.

sc1.tip: Look at the cause and effect: "without any water" and then "gulped down three full bottles." The blank must mean very thirsty.

decoys.why: Gulping three bottles shows you were thirsty, not thin and bony.
Hiking without water makes you thirsty, and gulping bottles does not fix being cold.
Tattered describes old torn clothes, but the clue is having no water.
Going all afternoon without water and gulping bottles points to thirst, not great happiness.
Gulping three bottles shows thirst, not eager enthusiasm.

traps.why: Fully soaked means dripping wet, the opposite of parched.
That is perched, a word that looks almost like parched.
Hunger is about food, but parched is about needing water.

syn2.tip: Think of how you feel after running on a hot day with no water. Parched is that dry, thirsty feeling.

sc2.stem: The garden was green and soggy in spring, but after a summer with no rain, the lawn was brown and _____.

traps.why: With no rain, the lawn could not be flooded.
Perched means sitting up high, which a lawn can't do.
Overgrown lawns are tall and thick, but no rain makes grass dry.

sc2.tip: The word "but" sets up a contrast with "soggy," and "no rain" explains why. The blank must mean very dry.

decoys.why: The lawn went through a summer with no rain, so it was dry, not extremely cold.
A lawn cannot be calm and easy to handle; the clue is no rain.
A lawn cannot be noisy and rowdy; the sentence contrasts soggy with dry.
Friendly describes people, and the clue is a summer with no rain.
A lawn cannot be proud; the sentence contrasts soggy spring with rainless summer.
Being on time has nothing to do with a lawn after no rain.

example: The wind subsided by evening.
hook: When a storm subsides, the wind and waves slowly die down until everything is calm again.

traps.why: Grow means get bigger, the opposite of subside.
Decide rhymes with subside but means to make a choice.
Stay means remain the same; subside means become less.

syn1.tip: Sub means under or down. When something subsides, it goes down, like pain or wind growing weaker.

sc1.stem: Once the strong winds began to _____ and grow gentle, the sailors raised their sails again.

traps.why: Winds that grow gentle are decreasing, not increasing.
Strong winds howl, but howling is not growing gentle.
Decide sounds like subside, but winds can't make choices.

sc1.tip: The words "and grow gentle" tell you what the blank means. Strong winds that grow gentle are becoming less strong.

decoys.why: The winds grew gentle, so they were weakening, not keeping on despite difficulty.
The winds grew gentle, which means they got weaker, not bigger.
Winds may howl, but the sentence says they grew gentle, so they were weakening.

traps.why: Build up means grow stronger, the opposite of subside.
Subside has side in it, but it has nothing to do with sides.
Winds can blow hard, but subside is what happens when they weaken.

syn2.tip: You often hear "the storm subsided" or "the pain subsided." Both mean the thing got weaker and quieter.

sc2.stem: My stomachache was terrible at first, but after I rested and sipped some ginger tea, the pain began to _____.

traps.why: Rest and tea help, so the pain got better, not worse.
Pain can throb, but the "but" shows it was getting better.
Spreading pain would be worse, but rest and tea made it ease.

sc2.tip: "Terrible at first, but" signals a change. After rest and tea, the pain became less strong.

decoys.why: After rest and ginger tea, the pain got better, so it did not keep going.
Rest and tea made the pain weaker, not bigger.
Pain cannot cry out; the sentence says rest and tea made it weaker.

example: Thrifty shoppers look for sales.
hook: Thrift stores sell used things cheaply, and thrifty people love them because they save money.

traps.why: Wasteful people spend carelessly, the opposite of thrifty.
Stingy is the mean, unkind way of not spending; thrifty is a compliment.
Thirsty looks like thrifty but means needing a drink.

syn1.tip: Think of a thrift store, where things cost less. Thrifty is a positive word for someone careful with money.

sc1.stem: The _____ shopper waited for the big sale, clipped coupons, and bought her son's winter boots at half price.

traps.why: Waiting for sales and clipping coupons is the opposite of wasteful.
Clipping coupons takes care, so careless does not fit.
Thirsty looks like thrifty, but the sentence is about shopping, not drinking.

sc1.tip: Look at what she did: "waited for the big sale, clipped coupons," and paid "half price." All show someone careful with money.

decoys.why: Clipping coupons and hunting for sales takes effort, not tired, slow energy.
Waiting for a sale and using coupons shows care with money, not being on time.
Nothing about clipping coupons or buying at half price shows too much pride.
The clues are sales and coupons, not being noisy and rowdy.
The sentence is about saving money, not about being cool and distant.
Dull and colorless does not explain waiting for sales and clipping coupons.

traps.why: Spending quickly is the opposite of being careful with money.
That is stingy, which sounds mean; thrifty is a good quality.
Thrifty is about saving money, not about having lots of it.

syn2.tip: Thrifty people look for sales and save. Pick the choice about using money wisely, not about how much you have.

sc2.stem: My brother spends every dollar the moment he gets it, but my sister is _____ and has saved enough allowance to buy her own bike.

traps.why: Wasteful describes the brother; "but" tells you the sister is different.
Generous means giving to others, but she saved for herself.
A spoiled kid gets things given to them, not saved for.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts the sister with her spending brother, and she "has saved enough allowance." She is careful with money.

decoys.why: Your sister saved enough to buy a bike, so she is not extremely poor.
The contrast is spending versus saving money, not being too proud.
The sentence contrasts spending and saving, not having low energy.
Being noisy and rowdy has nothing to do with saving allowance for a bike.
Being on time does not explain saving enough allowance to buy a bike.
The brother spends every dollar, so the contrast is about money, not being easy to handle.

example: The boisterous puppies tumbled in the grass.
hook: Picture a boisterous birthday party: kids shouting, laughing, and racing wildly around the room.

traps.why: Calm means quiet and still, the opposite of boisterous.
Boastful starts like boisterous but means bragging.
Angry people can be loud, but boisterous means lively, not mad.

syn1.tip: Say it out loud: boisterous sounds big and noisy. Think of a crowd of kids at recess.

sc1.stem: The _____ puppies yapped, tumbled, and chased each other around the yard, full of noisy energy.

traps.why: Sleepy puppies don't yap, tumble, and chase each other.
Boastful means bragging, and puppies can't brag.
Obedient puppies follow commands; these are wild and noisy.

sc1.tip: The sentence ends by telling you: the puppies were "full of noisy energy." The blank means loud and rowdy.

decoys.why: The puppies yapped and tumbled with noisy energy, and docile means calm and easy to handle.
The puppies are full of energy, but lethargic means tired and slow.
Yapping, tumbling puppies are playful, not dark, serious, and sad.
The puppies chase each other playfully, and aloof means cool and distant.
Nothing in the sentence suggests the puppies are sad or discouraged.
The sentence is about the puppies' noisy energy, not about being thin and bony.

traps.why: Quiet and still is the opposite of boisterous.
That describes boastful, a word that only looks like boisterous.
Boisterous is noisy fun, not unkind or cruel.

syn2.tip: Boisterous describes noisy, energetic fun, like puppies playing or fans cheering. Choose the choice with both noise and energy.

sc2.stem: The library was hushed all morning, but when the kindergarten class arrived after lunch, the room filled with _____ laughter and squeals.

traps.why: Quiet describes the morning; "but" shows the afternoon was different.
Polite laughter is soft and controlled, not squealing.
Boastful means bragging, which laughter and squeals are not.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "hushed," and "squeals" adds noise. You need a word meaning loud and wild.

decoys.why: Kindergartners squealing break the hush, so the laughter is not serious and sad.
The quiet room suddenly filled with squeals, so the laughter is not slow or tired.
The room filled with laughter, so it was not a small amount.
Laughter and squeals are happy sounds, not sad and discouraged ones.
The sentence contrasts the hushed morning with noise, and docile means calm.
Laughter cannot be cool and distant, and the clue is about noise.

example: The amiable shopkeeper knew everyone's name.
hook: An amiable person is easy to like, like a friendly neighbor who always smiles and waves hello.

traps.why: Hostile means unfriendly, the opposite of amiable.
The ending looks like -able, but amiable doesn't mean able to do things.
Friendly people may chat, but talkative just means talking a lot.

syn1.tip: Amiable has a warm, positive feeling. Think of the nicest person you know who is easy to get along with.

sc1.stem: The _____ new librarian smiled at everyone and chatted pleasantly with each student who came to her desk.

traps.why: A grumpy librarian would not smile at everyone.
Librarians can be strict, but smiling and chatting show friendliness.
Bossy is a negative word, but she chatted pleasantly.

sc1.tip: The clues "smiled at everyone" and "chatted pleasantly" describe someone warm and kind. The blank means friendly.

decoys.why: She smiled and chatted with everyone, which is the opposite of cool and distant.
A librarian who smiles at everyone is not dark, serious, and sad.
The sentence describes her being friendly, not too proud of herself.
Nothing here is about sharing or spending; she simply chats pleasantly.
Frigid can mean cold in manner, but she smiled warmly at everyone.
Smiling and chatting pleasantly do not fit someone sad and discouraged.

traps.why: Grumpy means in a bad mood, the opposite of amiable.
Amusing starts similarly but means funny.
Amiable people may be liked, but popular means liked by many.

syn2.tip: Amiable people are nice to be around. Choose the word that describes someone kind and agreeable.

sc2.stem: Our new neighbor looked serious and stern at first, but she turned out to be so _____ that she now waves and chats with every kid on our street.

traps.why: A grouchy neighbor would not wave and chat with every kid.
Strict matches her stern look, but "but" shows she was different.
Capable means skilled, which doesn't explain waving and chatting.

sc2.tip: "At first" and "but" signal a change from "serious and stern." She "waves and chats," so she is friendly.

decoys.why: She now waves and chats with every kid, so she is not distant.
Somber matches how she looked at first, but the word but signals a change.
Frigid means extremely cold, but she turned out warm enough to chat with everyone.
Waving and chatting show friendliness, not being too proud of yourself.
The sentence is about her friendliness, not about being unwilling to share.
Being on time has nothing to do with waving and chatting with kids.

example: I implored my parents for a puppy.
hook: To implore is to beg with your whole heart, like saying "please, please, please let me go."

traps.why: Commanding is giving orders, the opposite of begging.
Explore looks like implore but means to search a new place.
Ignore rhymes with implore but means to pay no attention.

syn1.tip: You implore when you want something badly and have no power to make it happen. Picture clasped hands and sad eyes.

sc1.stem: The puppy's big, sad eyes seemed to _____ us to share a bite of our sandwiches.

traps.why: Big, sad eyes ask softly; they don't give orders.
The puppy wants food, so it wouldn't forbid us from sharing.
Explore looks like implore, but you can't explore someone to share.

sc1.tip: The clue is "big, sad eyes" wanting "a bite of our sandwiches." That look begs, so the blank means beg desperately.

traps.why: Ordering tells someone what to do; imploring begs them.
You thank someone after getting something, not while begging for it.
Employ looks similar but means to hire someone.

syn2.tip: Implore is a strong, desperate way of asking. Choose the word that means to beg someone hard.

sc2.stem: Desperate to stay up for the fireworks, my little brother clasped his hands and began to _____ Mom to let him skip bedtime just once.

traps.why: Clasped hands show begging, not bossing Mom around.
You warn about danger; he was asking for something he wanted.
Daring is a challenge, but he was desperate and pleading.

sc2.tip: The words "desperate" and "clasped his hands" show how he asked. He was begging hard, so the blank means beg.

example: Be punctual for the school bus.
hook: A punctual person is right on the dot, arriving exactly when the clock says, never late.

traps.why: Late is the opposite of punctual.
Punctured looks similar but means poked with a hole.
Patient people wait calmly; punctual people arrive on time.

syn1.tip: You might hear "please be punctual." It is about time, meaning showing up right when you should.

sc1.stem: Mr. Diaz arrives at exactly 7:55 every morning, never even a minute late; he is the most _____ teacher at school.

traps.why: Tardy means late, but he is "never even a minute late."
Teachers can be strict, but the sentence is about arriving on time.
Patient means waiting calmly, not arriving at exactly the right time.

sc1.tip: The clues "exactly 7:55 every morning" and "never even a minute late" both describe someone always on time.

decoys.why: He is never even a minute late, and lethargic means slow and lacking energy.
The sentence is about arriving on time, not about being cheerful.
Arriving at exactly 7:55 is about time, not being careful with money.
Nothing in the sentence says he is distant; it says he is never late.
The clue is his exact arrival time, not being too proud of himself.
Frigid means extremely cold, but the sentence is about never being late.

traps.why: Always late is the opposite of punctual.
Punctual and punctuation share a root, but punctual is about time.
Rushing is different from simply arriving when you should.

syn2.tip: Punctual is about the clock. A punctual student is in the seat when the bell rings.

sc2.stem: My cousin is usually late for everything, but on the day of the class trip she was _____ and stood at the bus door ten minutes before it left.

traps.why: Tardy matches "usually late," but "but" shows this day was different.
She stood at the bus door, so she wasn't absent.
Punctured means poked with a hole, which doesn't describe a person.

sc2.tip: The word "but" contrasts with "usually late," and she arrived "ten minutes before." The blank means on time.

decoys.why: She arrived ten minutes early, which does not fit someone slow and lacking energy.
The sentence is about her arriving early, not about being sad and discouraged.
Standing at the bus door early is about time, not being cool and distant.
Being early for the bus has nothing to do with being careful with money.
The clue is that she came ten minutes early, not that she was thin.
Nothing in the sentence is about thirst; it is about being on time.

example: The pirate flag was tattered.
hook: Picture a pirate flag flapping after years at sea, full of holes and ragged strips: that flag is tattered.

traps.why: New is the opposite of tattered, which means old and torn.
Tattooed looks similar but means marked with ink pictures.
Old things can be dirty, but tattered is about being torn.

syn1.tip: Think of a tattered flag or a tattered old book: worn out and falling apart in strips. Look for the choice that means torn up.

sc1.stem: After years of hugs and adventures, the teddy bear was _____, its ears ripped and its fur torn in several spots.

traps.why: Spotless means perfect, but the bear has ripped ears and torn fur.
Hugs suggest love, but the clue describes damage, not feelings.
Teddy bears are often fluffy, but this one's fur is torn.

sc1.tip: Read past the blank: "its ears ripped and its fur torn." The missing word has to mean the same thing as ripped and torn.

decoys.why: Drab means dull in color, but the clue is ripped ears and torn fur.
Gaunt means thin and bony, but the bear's fur is torn, not thin.
The sentence describes rips and tears, not a bear full of sadness.
Ripped ears and torn fur describe damage, not feeling sad and discouraged.
Nothing in the sentence is about cold; it describes ripped and torn spots.
The bear is ripped and torn, not dry or thirsty.

traps.why: Neat and whole is the opposite of tattered.
Wrinkled is too mild; tattered things are actually ripped.
Old clothes may be out of style, but tattered means damaged.

syn2.tip: Tattered has the word "tatter" in it, which means a torn scrap. Something tattered is in scraps and rips.

sc2.stem: Unlike the crisp new flag the school raised on Monday, the old one had been whipped by storms for years and was _____ at every edge.

traps.why: Flawless describes the new flag, not the storm-beaten old one.
Flags get folded, but storms rip flags rather than fold them.
Flags are colorful, but the clue is about storm damage.

sc2.tip: "Unlike the crisp new flag" tells you the old flag is the opposite of new. "Whipped by storms for years" shows it is ripped and worn.

decoys.why: Whipped by storms for years means torn edges, not just dull color.
Gaunt means thin and bony, which does not describe a flag's edges.
Storms might be cold, but the contrast with a crisp new flag points to wear.
A flag whipped by storms is worn and torn, not dry or thirsty.
A flag cannot feel discouraged; the sentence describes its worn edges.
The clue is years of storm damage, not sadness.

example: "Look, a rainbow!" she exclaimed.
hook: When you exclaim, words burst out of you; that is why the mark after a shout is called an exclamation mark.

traps.why: Whisper is the opposite of exclaim, which means cry out loudly.
Explain looks like exclaim but means to make something clear.
Complain rhymes with exclaim but means to say you are unhappy.

syn1.tip: Exclaim is inside "exclamation mark," the mark you put after a sudden shout. Ex- means out: words cried out.

sc1.stem: Opening the box to find a puppy inside, Lily could not help but _____ "Wow!" at the top of her lungs.

traps.why: You cannot whisper "at the top of her lungs."
Explain looks like exclaim, but nobody explains a single surprised "Wow."
A sigh is too soft for "at the top of her lungs."

sc1.tip: The clues are "could not help but" and "at the top of her lungs." Lily cries out suddenly and loudly.

decoys.why: Lily is thrilled by a puppy, not begging anyone for something.
Finding a puppy made Lily happy, so she would not sharply criticize anyone.
She said "Wow!" at the top of her lungs, so she did not leave it out.
You show off things you own; Lily is crying out in surprise, not showing off.
The sentence is about shouting "Wow!" loudly, not looking at something carefully.

traps.why: Murmuring quietly is the opposite of crying out.
Ex- means out, but exclaim is about words coming out, not you.
Chatting is talking, but exclaiming is a sudden burst, not a long talk.

syn2.tip: Think of the exclamation mark. Someone who exclaims says something loudly and all at once because they are surprised or excited.

sc2.stem: Grandpa usually speaks in a slow, quiet voice, but when his team scored in the final second, he leaped up to _____ loudly that it was the best game ever.

traps.why: Whispering is quiet, but the sentence says loudly and he leaped up.
Complain is unhappy, but Grandpa is thrilled about the best game ever.
Mumbling is too weak for someone leaping up and speaking loudly.

sc2.tip: "Usually...quiet...but" signals a change. "Leaped up," "loudly," and "best game ever" show a sudden excited cry.

decoys.why: Grandpa is cheering about a great game, not begging anyone for help.

example: His voice faltered during the speech.
hook: A runner's legs falter near the finish; a speaker's voice falters when nervous. Both wobble and start to give out.

traps.why: Strengthen is the opposite of falter, which means to lose strength.
Alter is hiding inside falter, but it means to change.
Collapse is too strong; faltering is wobbling, not falling down completely.

syn1.tip: Think of the phrase "his voice faltered." It got shaky and unsteady. Pick the word for wobbling or becoming unsure.

sc1.stem: Near the end of the long race, Jada's tired legs began to _____, but she found new strength and pushed on.

traps.why: Sprint ignores "but she found new strength," which means her legs had weakened.
Runners stretch, but the clue is about legs losing strength.
Alter looks like falter but means change, which does not fit tired legs.

sc1.tip: Look at "tired legs" and "but she found new strength." The "but" means her legs had been losing strength first.

decoys.why: Her legs were tired and she then found new strength, so they were not pushing on yet.
Legs cannot put off a task; the sentence is about tired legs losing strength.
Her legs did not move back or away; they were tired and weakening.
Legs cannot cry out; the clue is that they were tired near the end.

traps.why: Gaining power is the opposite of losing strength.
Faltering is weakening for a moment, not giving up forever.
Losing a game is about the score, not about getting weaker.

syn2.tip: When something falters, it starts to slip or weaken, like a candle flame flickering. It may recover, as Jada does.

sc2.stem: When the lights went out in the middle of the school play, Mia's voice began to _____, so she paused, took a breath, and started her lines again.

traps.why: If her voice grew stronger, she would not need to pause and restart.
Filter looks a bit like falter but means to strain something.
Lines in a play can rhyme, but that would not make her stop.

sc2.tip: Cause and effect: the lights going out shook her, and "so she paused...and started her lines again" shows her voice got shaky.

decoys.why: She had to pause and breathe, so her voice was weakening, not crying out loudly.
She stopped and started over, so her voice was not steadily keeping on.
A voice cannot put off a task; the sentence shows her voice wobbling in the dark.
Mia was saying her lines in a play, not begging anyone for something.

example: The industrious ants built a huge hill.
hook: Picture busy ants carrying crumbs all day without a break: industrious workers who never stop.

traps.why: Lazy is the opposite of industrious.
Industrial looks similar but means having to do with factories.
Skillful means good at something, not willing to work hard.

syn1.tip: Industrious is related to industry, meaning hard work. The ending -ous means full of, so it means full of hard work.

sc1.stem: Like a busy beaver building its dam, Carla was an _____ worker who kept working hard from morning until night.

traps.why: An idle worker does nothing, but Carla worked from morning until night.
Industrial means about factories, not describing a person who works hard.
An occasional worker works only sometimes, not "from morning until night."

sc1.tip: Two clues: "like a busy beaver" and "kept working hard from morning until night." The blank means always working hard.

decoys.why: The beaver clue and working from morning until night are about hard work, not friendliness.
The sentence describes how hard Carla worked, not how happy she felt.
Nothing says Carla was distant; the clue is that she worked hard all day.
The busy beaver clue points to hard work, not stubbornly refusing to change.

traps.why: Idle and slow is the opposite of always working hard.
Industry can mean factories, but industrious describes a hard worker.
Hard workers may get tired, but industrious means working, not tired.

syn2.tip: Think of the example: industrious ants building a huge hill. They keep busy, steady, and working all day.

sc2.stem: While his brother napped on the couch all Saturday, Omar was _____, raking leaves, washing the car, and helping Dad fix the fence before dinner.

traps.why: Lazy describes his napping brother, not Omar doing chore after chore.
Industrial means about factories, not a busy person.
Talented is about skill, but the list shows effort, not skill.

sc2.tip: "While his brother napped" sets up a contrast. Then the list of chores shows Omar kept working hard all day.

decoys.why: His brother was the lazy one napping; Omar was busy doing chores all day.
Raking, washing, and fixing show hard work, not being careful with money.
The list of chores shows Omar working hard, not arriving on time.
Omar was doing chores, not being noisy and rowdy.

example: I felt lethargic after the big lunch.
hook: After a giant Thanksgiving dinner, you feel lethargic: heavy, slow, and too sleepy to get off the couch.

traps.why: Energetic is the opposite of lethargic.
Allergic rhymes with lethargic but means your body reacts badly to something.
Lethargic people are awake, just tired and slow.

syn1.tip: Lethargic is how you feel after a big lunch: no energy, moving slowly. Pick the word that means slow and heavy.

sc1.stem: With a high fever, our usually playful puppy was _____ all day, too tired and slow to even lift his head.

traps.why: The puppy is "usually playful," but today he is too tired to lift his head.
Puppies are curious, but the clue says tired and slow.
Allergic sounds like lethargic but the puppy has a fever, not an allergy.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank right after it: "too tired and slow to even lift his head." The word means tired and slow.

decoys.why: The puppy was too tired to lift his head, so he was not noisy and rowdy.
A puppy too tired to lift his head is not eager and enthusiastic.
A sick puppy with a high fever would not be extremely happy.
The puppy was too tired and slow to move, so he was not working hard.
The word usually tells you the puppy was not his playful, cheerful self that day.

traps.why: Full of pep means lively, the opposite of lethargic.
That is lethal, which looks like lethargic but means deadly.
Fast asleep goes too far; lethargic people are awake but slow.

syn2.tip: Lethargic is a negative word about energy. A lethargic puppy just lies around. Look for the phrase that means having little energy.

sc2.stem: On the first warm day of spring, the kids raced around the playground, but the old cat stayed _____ on the porch, barely blinking as the hours drifted by.

traps.why: Lively fits the racing kids, but the "but" says the cat was different.
Lethal looks like lethargic but means deadly.
Cats are curious, but this one is "barely blinking."

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the cat with the racing kids. "Barely blinking as the hours drifted by" shows it had almost no energy.

decoys.why: The kids were the rowdy ones; the cat barely blinked.
A cat barely blinking for hours is not working hard.
The cat barely blinked as hours drifted by, so it was not eager or excited.
It was the first warm day of spring, so the cat was not extremely cold.
The sentence shows a slow, sleepy cat, not a cheerful, friendly one.

example: The mouse eluded the cat again.
hook: A slippery fish eludes your hands in the creek; a word on the tip of your tongue eludes your memory.

traps.why: Capture is the opposite of elude, which means to get away.
Include rhymes with elude but means to make part of a group.
Chasing is what the hunter does; eluding is what the escaper does.

syn1.tip: Think of a mouse eluding a cat by slipping away every time. Pick the word that means getting away.

sc1.stem: The answer to the riddle continued to _____ Sam; no matter how hard he thought, it slipped out of his reach.

traps.why: Amuse is happy, but Sam is struggling and the answer slips away.
Include sounds like elude, but it makes no sense with a riddle's answer.
Following stays close, but the answer "slipped out of his reach."

sc1.tip: After the semicolon, the sentence explains the blank: "it slipped out of his reach." The answer kept escaping Sam.

decoys.why: The answer kept slipping out of reach, which is escaping Sam, not persuading him.
An answer slipping out of reach does not feed Sam; it escapes him.
The answer was not criticizing Sam; it kept slipping away from him.
Sam was the one thinking hard; the answer was escaping him, not studying him.
Nothing about thirst here; the answer kept slipping out of Sam's reach.

traps.why: Getting caught is the opposite of eluding.
Hiding can help you escape, but elude means getting away, not where you hide.
Elude comes from a word for play, but it means escape, not play.

syn2.tip: Elude sounds like a cousin of escape. Things that elude you keep slipping out of reach, like a word you cannot remember.

sc2.stem: Because the rabbit was so quick and clever, it managed to _____ the fox every time, darting into its burrow just before those sharp teeth could snap.

traps.why: Approaching the fox is moving toward it, not darting away.
Befriend is friendly, but the fox is trying to bite the rabbit.
Chasing is the fox's job; the rabbit is running away.

sc2.tip: "Because...quick and clever" gives the cause. "Darting into its burrow just before those sharp teeth could snap" shows it escaped.

decoys.why: The rabbit darted into its burrow to escape, not to gently persuade the fox.
The rabbit escaped those sharp teeth, so it did not feed the fox.
The rabbit was running away from the fox, not scolding it.
The clue is darting away quickly, not looking carefully at the fox.
The rabbit used speed and cleverness to escape, not begging the fox.

example: He felt dejected after missing the goal.
hook: De- means down and ject means throw: a dejected person feels thrown down, head hanging, shoulders slumped.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of dejected.
Rejected looks similar but means turned down by someone.
Angry is a different bad feeling; dejected means sad and discouraged.

syn1.tip: De- means down. A dejected person feels down, like their spirits were knocked to the ground. Look for a word with the same down feeling.

sc1.stem: After missing the winning shot, Marcus felt _____, slumping on the bench, sad and discouraged.

traps.why: Nobody feels proud after missing the winning shot and slumping.
Relieved is a good feeling, but Marcus is sad and discouraged.
Injected looks like dejected but means given a shot with a needle.

sc1.tip: The sentence defines the blank at the end: "sad and discouraged." Slumping on the bench is another clue.

decoys.why: The sentence says Marcus was sad and discouraged, and elated means extremely happy.
Marcus missed the winning shot and felt sad, not cheerful and friendly.
Slumping on the bench is quiet and low, not noisy and rowdy.
Missing the winning shot made Marcus feel sad, not too proud of himself.
The sentence describes Marcus as discouraged, the opposite of eager and enthusiastic.
The sentence is about Marcus feeling sad, not thirsty.

traps.why: Hopeful is the opposite of discouraged.
Ject means throw, but dejected describes a sad feeling, not tossing.
Heartbroken is much stronger; dejected is sad and discouraged, not crushed.

syn2.tip: Picture someone after losing a big game, slumped and quiet. Dejected is a negative feeling of sadness and lost hope.

sc2.stem: Ana had expected to win the spelling bee, so when she misspelled an easy word in the first round, she walked off the stage looking _____.

traps.why: She lost in the first round, so she could not look victorious.
Bored means uninterested, but Ana cared a lot about winning.
Amused is a happy feeling, wrong for someone who lost unexpectedly.

sc2.tip: Cause and effect: she "expected to win" but "misspelled an easy word in the first round." That would leave her sad and discouraged.

decoys.why: Ana expected to win but lost early, so she would not look extremely happy.
She expected to win, but after missing an easy word she would not look too proud.
Losing in the first round would not leave Ana looking cheerful.
Walking off after a mistake suggests sadness, not noisy, rowdy energy.
Ana just lost, so she would look discouraged, not eager and enthusiastic.
The clue is her disappointing loss, which points to sadness, not friendliness.

example: The ravenous bear ate all the berries.
hook: After soccer practice you are so ravenous you could eat a whole pizza by yourself.

traps.why: Stuffed means completely full, the opposite of ravenous.
Ravenous looks like raven, but it has nothing to do with birds.
Thirsty means needing a drink; ravenous means needing food.

syn1.tip: Think of a ravenous bear gobbling every berry. Ravenous means so hungry you want to eat everything in sight.

sc1.stem: After a long winter's sleep, the _____ bear gobbled up every berry and fish it could find.

traps.why: The bear just woke up, but gobbling food shows hunger, not sleepiness.
A satisfied bear is full and would not gobble every berry.
A picky bear would not eat every berry and fish it found.

sc1.tip: Cause and effect: "a long winter's sleep" means no food for months, and "gobbled up every berry and fish" shows huge hunger.

decoys.why: The bear gobbled berries and fish, which shows hunger, not thirst.
The bear just woke, but gobbling up every bite shows eager hunger, not sluggishness.
Winter is mentioned, but the bear gobbling food shows it was hungry, not cold.
A bear that ate every berry and fish it found was not saving anything.
The sentence is about the bear eating everything, not about being on time.

traps.why: Completely full is the opposite of extremely hungry.
Slightly is too weak; ravenous means extremely hungry.
Picky eaters are choosy; ravenous eaters will eat almost anything.
