syn2.tip: Ravenous is a strong word. It is not a little hungry but starving, the kind of hunger that makes you gobble food.

sc2.stem: Usually a slow, picky eater, my little brother came home from soccer camp so _____ that he finished two sandwiches and asked for more.

traps.why: Someone stuffed would not finish two sandwiches and ask for more.
Thirsty would make him want drinks, not two sandwiches.
Camp can make you tired, but being tired does not explain eating so much.

sc2.tip: "Usually a slow, picky eater" sets up a contrast, and "so _____ that he finished two sandwiches and asked for more" shows extreme hunger.

decoys.why: He is usually slow, but finishing two sandwiches and asking for more shows hunger.
He ate two sandwiches, which shows he was hungry, not thirsty.
The sentence is about how much he ate, not about being careful with money.
Being thin does not explain why he finished two sandwiches; being hungry does.
Eating two sandwiches shows hunger, not being on time.
Nothing in the sentence suggests sadness; eating so much shows he was very hungry.

example: The jeweler scrutinized the tiny diamond.
hook: Picture a detective with a magnifying glass, scrutinizing every fingerprint so no tiny detail is missed.

traps.why: Ignore is the opposite of looking at something very carefully.
Criticize sounds similar but means to point out faults.
A glance is a quick look; scrutinize means a long, careful look.

syn1.tip: Think of a jeweler scrutinizing a tiny diamond under a lens. The word means to look at something very closely.

sc1.stem: Detectives _____ every tiny clue, studying fingerprints under a magnifying glass so nothing is missed.

traps.why: Overlook means miss, but the detectives make sure "nothing is missed."
Skimming is quick; a magnifying glass means slow, careful looking.
Criticize sounds like scrutinize, but detectives study clues, not judge them.

sc1.tip: The clues are "studying fingerprints under a magnifying glass" and "so nothing is missed." The blank means look at very carefully.

decoys.why: The sentence says nothing is missed, so detectives do not leave clues out.
Detectives study clues under a magnifying glass; they do not avoid them.
Clues might confuse detectives, but detectives do not confuse clues.
Detectives study fingerprints carefully to see them truly, not twist them out of shape.
Making sure nothing is missed is the opposite of wasting clues.
Studying under a magnifying glass means looking closely, not showing off.

traps.why: Barely noticing is the opposite of studying closely.
A peek is too quick; scrutinizing takes a long, careful look.
You might find faults while looking, but scrutinize just means look carefully.

syn2.tip: You may have heard of something being "under scrutiny," meaning watched very closely. To scrutinize is to give that close look.

sc2.stem: My little sister glanced at the puzzle box for one second, but Grandpa sat down to _____ each piece, turning it slowly and checking every edge before placing it.

traps.why: Neglecting pieces means ignoring them, but Grandpa checks every edge.
A glimpse is a quick look, like the sister's, not Grandpa's slow study.
Puzzle pieces get lost, but Grandpa is carefully handling each one.

sc2.tip: "Glanced...for one second, but" signals the opposite. "Turning it slowly and checking every edge" shows Grandpa looks very carefully.

decoys.why: Grandpa checked every edge of each piece, so he did not leave any out.
A puzzle might confuse Grandpa, but he cannot confuse the pieces.
Grandpa was turning and checking pieces carefully, not twisting them out of shape.
Turning a piece slowly to check edges is careful looking, not showing off.
Grandpa used each piece carefully, the opposite of wasting it.

example: She wavered between the two choices.
hook: When you waver, your choice sways back and forth like a wave: chocolate, no, vanilla, no, chocolate.

traps.why: Decide is the opposite of waver, which means being unsure.
Wander looks like waver but means to roam around.
Arguing means disagreeing with someone, not being unsure yourself.

syn1.tip: Picture someone who wavers between two choices, swinging back and forth. Pick the word that means pausing because you are unsure.

sc1.stem: Standing at the ice-cream counter, Sam began to _____ between chocolate and vanilla, unable to make up his mind.

traps.why: Sam is "unable to make up his mind," so he cannot decide.
Wander looks like waver but means walk around, not choose.
Wave looks like waver, but waving has nothing to do with choosing flavors.

sc1.tip: The sentence ends with "unable to make up his mind." Going back and forth "between" two flavors means being unsure.

decoys.why: Sam was unable to make up his mind, not pushing on despite difficulty.
The sentence is about Sam being unsure, not something becoming less strong.
Sam was not moving back; he was unable to choose a flavor.
Sam was undecided between flavors, not getting smaller little by little.
Unable to make up his mind suggests quiet doubt, not crying out suddenly.

traps.why: Feeling certain is the opposite of wavering.
Waver looks like wave, but it has nothing to do with waving goodbye.
Wavering is going back and forth, not quitting entirely.

syn2.tip: Think of "she wavered between the two choices." Her mind went back and forth and she could not settle on one.

sc2.stem: Ben had practiced his speech so many times that his voice did not _____ even once; he spoke clearly and calmly from the first line to the last.

traps.why: If his voice did not succeed, he could not speak clearly and calmly.
Wander looks like waver but means roam, which voices do not do.
Speeches can rhyme, but the clue is about speaking steadily.

sc2.tip: Cause and effect: lots of practice made him steady. After the semicolon, "clearly and calmly" tells you his voice never got shaky.

decoys.why: Ben spoke clearly to the end, so saying his voice did not keep trying makes no sense.
The sentence is about his voice staying steady and calm, not about crying out.
He practiced many times, but the blank is about his voice staying steady, not delaying.
The clue is that he spoke clearly and calmly, meaning his voice was steady, not moving away.

example: Our jovial mail carrier always waves.
hook: Jovial comes from Jove, another name for Jupiter, the planet once thought to make people cheerful.

traps.why: Gloomy is the opposite of jovial.
Juvenile looks a little like jovial, but it means young or childish.
Jovial people may laugh loudly, but jovial means cheerful, not noisy.

syn1.tip: Jovial and jolly both start with jo and mean the same thing. Picture a jovial Santa laughing with everyone.

sc1.stem: Our _____ bus driver laughs at every joke, waves to everyone on her route, and greets each rider with a cheerful grin.

traps.why: Grouchy is the opposite; a grouchy driver would not grin and wave.
Jittery starts like jovial, but it means nervous, not cheerful.
A solemn person is serious, not someone who laughs at every joke.

sc1.tip: The clues "laughs at every joke," "waves to everyone," and "cheerful grin" all describe someone happy and friendly.

decoys.why: A driver who laughs and grins cheerfully is not quietly angry and gloomy.
Laughing at every joke shows she is cheerful, not sad and discouraged.
Waving to everyone and greeting riders warmly is friendly, not looking down on others.
Her cheerful grin shows happiness, not sadness.
Bus drivers should be on time, but the clues describe her cheerful, friendly manner.
Laughing, waving, and grinning show lively cheer, not tiredness and low energy.

traps.why: Grumpy and cold is the opposite of jovial.
Jovial is a compliment, but silly and foolish sounds like an insult.
Loud and wild goes too far; jovial just means pleasantly cheerful.

syn2.tip: Jovial has a warm, happy feeling. Think of a jovial mail carrier who smiles and waves at everyone.

sc2.stem: Although the weather on our camping trip was cold and rainy, Uncle Ray stayed _____, telling funny stories and making everyone laugh around the fire.

traps.why: Gloomy matches the weather, but Ray was making everyone laugh.
Chilly describes the cold weather, not Ray's happy mood.
Soggy fits the rain, but the sentence is about Ray's cheerful mood.

sc2.tip: "Although" signals a contrast with the bad weather. "Telling funny stories and making everyone laugh" shows Ray was cheerful.

decoys.why: Uncle Ray told funny stories and made everyone laugh, so he was not gloomy.
Although means he stayed cheerful despite the rain, not sad and discouraged.
The weather was cold, but the blank describes his mood while telling funny stories.
The rain was bad, but Uncle Ray was making everyone laugh, not feeling very sad.
Making everyone laugh around the fire is friendly, not looking down on others.
Telling funny stories and making people laugh takes energy, not tiredness.

example: Don't squander your allowance on junk.
hook: Picture someone tossing coins into a fountain until the piggy bank is empty: that money was squandered.

traps.why: Save is the opposite of squander.
Wander rhymes with squander, but it means to walk around aimlessly.
Squandering often involves money, but buying is not always foolish.

syn1.tip: Squander is usually about money, time, or chances, and it has a bad feeling. Think of "squander your allowance on junk."

sc1.stem: Instead of saving his birthday money, Jake chose to _____ it all on candy he did not even want.

traps.why: The sentence says Jake did this instead of saving, so save cannot fit.
Budget is a money word, but it means planning carefully, not wasting.
Investing is a smart use of money, not spending on unwanted candy.

sc1.tip: "Instead of saving" and "candy he did not even want" show Jake used his money foolishly.

decoys.why: Bestow means to give as an honor, but Jake just wasted his money on unwanted candy.
Flaunt means to show off, but the sentence is about wasting money, not showing it off.
Scrutinize means to look at carefully, which does not match spending money on candy he did not want.

traps.why: Saving up carefully is the opposite of squandering.
That means wander, which only sounds like squander.
Squander is negative; spending wisely is a good thing.

syn2.tip: Squander has a bad feeling. If you squander something, you lose it on things that do not matter.

sc2.stem: Our coach warned us not to _____ our short practice time chatting, because the big game was only two days away.

traps.why: Treasuring time means valuing it, the opposite of wasting it chatting.
Schedule is about planning time, but the coach warns against wasting it.
Guarding time means protecting it, not wasting it on chatter.

sc2.tip: The coach gives a warning "because the big game" is near, so chatting would waste precious practice time.

decoys.why: Scrutinize means to examine closely, but the coach is worried about time being wasted on chatting.
Flaunt means to show off, but the coach warns against wasting practice time, not showing it off.
Bestow means to give as a gift, but chatting away practice time is wasting it.
Nourish means to help something grow, but chatting would waste the short practice time.

example: The dog let out a mournful howl.
hook: Mournful is mourn plus -ful: full of the sadness people feel when they mourn a loss.

traps.why: Joyful is the opposite of mournful.
Fearful is another strong feeling, but it means scared, not sad.
Angry is a strong feeling too, but mournful is about sadness.

syn1.tip: Find the word mourn inside. People mourn when someone dies, and -ful means full of, so mournful means full of sadness.

sc1.stem: The violin played a _____ tune, slow and full of sorrow, that made the whole audience want to cry.

traps.why: A cheerful tune would not be full of sorrow.
Bouncy means quick and happy, but the tune was slow and sad.
A silly tune makes people laugh, not want to cry.

sc1.tip: The words right after the blank, "slow and full of sorrow," tell you the tune was sad.

decoys.why: The tune is full of sorrow and makes people cry, and jovial means cheerful.
The sentence says the tune is slow and sad, but boisterous means noisy and rowdy.
Haughty means proud and snobbish, but the tune is full of sorrow.

traps.why: Very happy is the opposite of mournful.
Mourning sounds like morning, but mournful has nothing to do with time.
A mournful howl may be loud, but mournful means sad.

syn2.tip: Think of "a mournful howl" from a lonely dog. The word mourn inside tells you it is about sadness.

sc2.stem: When our old cat Whiskers ran away, my sister sat by the window for hours, humming a _____ song as she waited for him to come home.

traps.why: Your sister had just lost her cat, so she would not feel cheerful.
Morning sounds like mourning, but the song's time of day is not the point.
A triumphant song celebrates a win, not a lost pet.

sc2.tip: The cause is in the first part: "our old cat Whiskers ran away." Losing a pet makes you sad.

decoys.why: Her cat ran away and she waited for hours, so a cheerful song does not fit.
She was quietly humming while sad and waiting, not making a noisy, rowdy song.
Haughty means looking down on others, but she is sad that Whiskers ran away.
Conceited means too proud of yourself, which has nothing to do with missing a lost cat.

example: The obstinate toddler would not wear shoes.
hook: Picture a mule planting its hooves and refusing to budge no matter how hard you pull: that mule is obstinate.

traps.why: Flexible people change easily, the opposite of obstinate.
Obedient starts like obstinate, but it means doing what you are told.
Obstinate people may seem angry, but obstinate means refusing to change.

syn1.tip: Obstinate people refuse to change, no matter what. Think of an obstinate toddler who will not put on shoes.

sc1.stem: Like an _____ mule, my brother stubbornly refused to change his mind, no matter what anyone said to him.

traps.why: Obedient looks like obstinate, but an obedient mule would do as told.
Agreeable is the opposite; the brother refused to change his mind.
He may have been angry, but the clue is about refusing to change.

sc1.tip: The sentence says your brother "stubbornly refused to change his mind," and mules are famous for refusing to move.

decoys.why: The brother stubbornly refused to change his mind, and amiable means friendly and pleasant.
Mules can work hard, but the sentence is about being stubborn, not hardworking.

traps.why: Easy to persuade is the opposite of obstinate.
That means obvious, which only looks a bit like obstinate.
An obstinate person might be rude, but the word means refusing to change.

syn2.tip: Obstinate has a stuck, stubborn feeling. Picture someone with arms crossed saying "No" over and over.

sc2.stem: Most of the team agreed to try the new plan, but Ava remained _____, insisting on doing things her old way even after the coach explained why.

traps.why: The rest of the team was cooperative; "but" shows Ava was different.
The coach explained, but Ava was not confused; she simply refused to change.
Obvious looks a bit like obstinate, but it means easy to see.

sc2.tip: "But" sets Ava against the team that "agreed," and "insisting on doing things her old way" shows she refused to change.

decoys.why: Ava kept insisting on her own way, which is stubborn, not friendly and pleasant.
Jovial means cheerful, but the sentence is about Ava refusing to change her ways.
Pensive means deep in thought, but Ava was refusing to change, not quietly thinking.
Industrious means hardworking, but the clue is that Ava insisted on her old way.
Punctual means on time, which has nothing to do with refusing to try the new plan.

example: The magic trick baffled everyone.
hook: When a magic trick leaves everyone scratching their heads, asking how it worked, the trick has baffled them.

traps.why: Explaining makes things clear, the opposite of baffling.
Battle looks like baffle, but it means to fight.
A magic trick may amuse you, but baffle means confuse.

syn1.tip: Picture a riddle nobody can solve. People say "I'm baffled" when a mystery makes no sense to them.

sc1.stem: The tricky riddle continued to _____ the whole class; not one student could figure out the answer all week.

traps.why: Riddles happen in class, but nobody learned the answer, so it did not teach.
A boring riddle is dull; this one was too hard to solve.
Battle looks like baffle, but a riddle does not fight anyone.

sc1.tip: The part after the semicolon is the effect: "not one student could figure out the answer." So the riddle confused them.

decoys.why: The students would scrutinize the riddle; a riddle cannot look carefully at a class.
Coax means to gently persuade, but the riddle left everyone unable to find the answer.
Nourish means to feed, but the riddle confused the class so no one could solve it.
Implore means to beg, but a riddle that nobody can solve confuses people.
Quench means to satisfy thirst, which has nothing to do with a riddle nobody solved.

traps.why: Making something clear is the opposite of baffling.
Fighting hard means battle, which only looks like baffle.
Baffle is stronger; it means confusing someone completely.

syn2.tip: If something baffles you, you have no idea at all how it works, like a great magic trick.

sc2.stem: Long division used to _____ my little brother, but after Grandpa showed him an easy trick, the problems finally made sense to him.

traps.why: "But" shows the problems did not make sense before, so they did not satisfy him.
Delight is a happy feeling, but the problems used to confuse him.
Long division is a lesson, but the problems did not make sense at first.

sc2.tip: "But" signals a change: the problems "finally made sense." So before, they did not make sense, which means they confused him.

decoys.why: Your brother might scrutinize problems, but the sentence says long division confused him until the trick.
Nourish means to feed, but the problems confused him before they finally made sense.
Coax means to gently persuade, but long division did not make sense to him at first.
Implore means to beg, but the clue is that the problems once confused him.
Quench means to satisfy thirst, which does not fit math problems that confused him.

example: He gave a sullen shrug.
hook: A sullen kid slumps in his chair, arms crossed, saying nothing, like a little storm cloud at the table.

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of sullen.
Swollen sounds like sullen, but it means puffed up.
Furious is too strong; sullen is a quiet, gloomy anger.

syn1.tip: Sullen and sulky both start with su and describe a quiet, grumpy mood, like a pouting child.

sc1.stem: Angry about losing his video game time, Leo sat silently at dinner, _____ and scowling, refusing to say a word.

traps.why: Leo was angry and scowling, so he was not cheerful.
Leo refused to say a word, the opposite of chatty.
The scene is at dinner, but the clues are about Leo's angry mood.

sc1.tip: Look at the clues "angry," "sat silently," and "scowling." The missing word must describe a quiet, angry mood.

decoys.why: Leo is angry and scowling, so cheerful and friendly does not fit.
Leo just lost his video game time and is scowling, not joyful and celebrating.
Leo refuses to say a word and scowls, which is the opposite of friendly.
Leo sat silently, but boisterous means noisy and rowdy.
Tactful means careful of feelings, but the sentence describes Leo being angry and silent.
The scene is at dinner, but the clue is that Leo is angry, not hungry.

traps.why: Sunny and chatty is the opposite of sullen.
Puffed up means swollen, a word that only sounds like sullen.
Loud and raging is too strong; sullen anger stays quiet.

syn2.tip: Think of "a sullen shrug": someone too grumpy even to answer. Sullen anger is quiet, not shouting.

sc2.stem: Usually Maya bounces into class laughing and chatting with friends, but today she slumped into her seat looking _____ and would not speak to anyone.

traps.why: That is how Maya usually looks; "but today" signals a change.
Swollen sounds like sullen, but it means puffed up.
Giggly fits her usual mood, not someone who would not speak.

sc2.tip: "Usually" and "but today" signal a change from her happy self. "Slumped" and "would not speak" show a gloomy mood.

decoys.why: The word but shows today was different from her usual cheerful self, so jovial is wrong.
She slumped and would not speak, so she was not joyful and celebrating.
Boisterous describes how she usually acts, but today she slumped and stayed silent.
She would not speak to anyone, so she was not friendly and pleasant today.
Tactful means careful not to hurt feelings, but the sentence shows her slumped and gloomy.

example: The scrawny kitten grew strong with care.
hook: Scrawny rhymes with brawny, its opposite: brawny means muscular, while scrawny means all skin and bones.

traps.why: Brawny means muscular, the opposite of scrawny.
Scratchy looks like scrawny, but it means rough or itchy.
Scrawny is about being thin, not about height.

syn1.tip: Scrawny rhymes with its opposite, brawny. Think of a scrawny kitten that needs food to grow strong.

sc1.stem: The runt of the litter was a _____ little pup, all skinny legs and bony ribs, but she grew strong with care.

traps.why: A plump pup would not have skinny legs and bony ribs.
Puppies can be fluffy, but the clue is about being thin and bony.
Scratchy looks like scrawny, but it means rough or itchy.

sc1.tip: Right after the blank you read "all skinny legs and bony ribs." That describes a pup who is thin and bony.

decoys.why: Tattered describes torn old things like clothes, not a pup with skinny legs and bony ribs.
The clue describes the pup's skinny body, not a cheerful mood.
Skinny legs and bony ribs describe a thin body, not a proud attitude.
Being on time has nothing to do with skinny legs and bony ribs.
A pup cannot be careful with money, and the clue is about being thin.

traps.why: Strong and muscular is the opposite of scrawny.
Scrawny animals are often young, but scrawny means thin and bony.
Rough and itchy means scratchy, which only looks like scrawny.

syn2.tip: Picture a scrawny stray cat with ribs you can see. Scrawny is an unflattering way to say very thin.

sc2.stem: After a summer of swimming and lifting hay bales on the farm, my cousin was no longer the _____ boy we remembered; his arms had grown thick and strong.

traps.why: He is muscular now; "no longer" means he used to be the opposite.
Sturdy describes him after the summer, not the boy he used to be.
Summer swimming fits tanned, but the clue is about thick, strong arms.

sc2.tip: "No longer" signals contrast with arms that grew "thick and strong." Before the summer, he must have been thin and bony.

decoys.why: He worked hard all summer, so saying he is no longer hardworking makes no sense.
Tattered fits torn clothes, but the contrast is with arms grown thick and strong.
The sentence contrasts his body with strong arms, not whether he arrives on time.
Thick, strong arms contrast with a thin body, not with being careful with money.
The change described is in his arms, not in how carefully he speaks.

example: Don't procrastinate on your project.
hook: Procrastinate contains the Latin word cras, meaning tomorrow, so procrastinators keep putting things off until tomorrow.

traps.why: Hurry is the opposite of procrastinate.
Protest starts like procrastinate, but it means to object.
People may relax instead of working, but procrastinate means putting tasks off.

syn1.tip: Inside procrastinate is cras, Latin for tomorrow. A procrastinator always says "I'll do it tomorrow."

sc1.stem: Instead of starting his science project early, Diego chose to _____, waiting until the night before it was due.

traps.why: Preparing means getting ready early, but Diego waited until the last night.
Hurry means acting fast, but Diego waited until the night before.
Experiments go with science projects, but the clue is about waiting.

sc1.tip: "Instead of starting his science project early" and "waiting until the night before" show that Diego put off his work.

decoys.why: Waiting until the night before is putting work off, the opposite of keeping at it.
Diego waited instead of starting early, which is not looking carefully at something.
Nothing in the sentence is about showing off; it is about waiting too long.
Diego is not arguing with anyone; he is delaying his project.
Waiting until the night before has nothing to do with crying out suddenly.

traps.why: Starting right away is the opposite of procrastinating.
Procrastinating is not starting at all, not working slowly.
That means protest, which only looks like procrastinate.

syn2.tip: Think of a project you left until the night before. Waiting and waiting to start is procrastinating.

sc2.stem: Because Mia tends to _____, she ended up rushing to finish her book report at breakfast and could not remember how the story ended.

traps.why: Preparing would have prevented the last-minute rush at breakfast.
Book reports involve reading, but reading would not cause rushing at breakfast.
Protest looks like procrastinate, but objecting does not cause a rush.

sc2.tip: This is cause and effect: her habit caused the last-minute "rushing to finish." That habit is putting things off.

decoys.why: Rushing at breakfast shows Mia put the work off, not that she kept trying.
If she read carefully, she would remember the ending instead of rushing at breakfast.
Arguing about small things would not explain rushing a report at breakfast.
Showing off does not explain why she rushed her report at the last minute.
Crouching in fear does not explain finishing a report late at breakfast.

example: The floodwaters receded after a week.
hook: Recede joins re- (back) with a Latin word meaning go: picture waves going back out to sea.

traps.why: Advance means move forward, the opposite of recede.
Recite looks like recede, but it means say aloud from memory.
Re- can mean again, but in recede it means back.

syn1.tip: Re- here means back. Picture floodwaters that recede, going back away from the houses.

sc1.stem: As the tide began to _____, moving back from the shore, the children found starfish in the wet sand.

traps.why: A rising tide comes in; this one was moving back from the shore.
Re- can mean again, but the clue says the tide moved back.
Water may sparkle, but the clue is about the tide moving back.

sc1.tip: The phrase right after the blank, "moving back from the shore," tells you exactly what the tide did.

decoys.why: The sentence says the tide is moving back from shore, not winding slowly along.
Beckon means to call someone closer, but the tide is moving back from the shore.
Tides do not walk heavily; the clue says the water is moving back.
The tide is moving back from shore, not showing off.
The clue says moving back from the shore, which has nothing to do with trying hard.

traps.why: Moving forward is the opposite of receding.
Re- can mean again, but in recede it means back.
Water can rise, but receding water goes down and away.

syn2.tip: Think of a tide going out or a hairline that recedes. Both move back from where they were.

sc2.stem: Once the long storm finally ended and the sun came out, the floodwaters began to _____, and soon the soccer field was dry enough to play on.

traps.why: Rising water would cover the field, not leave it dry.
Spreading water would flood more ground, not dry the field.
Water can freeze, but frozen water would not leave the field dry to play.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: "soon the soccer field was dry." For that to happen, the water had to move back away.

decoys.why: Water feeding the field would not make it dry enough to play on.
Water winding around would not leave the field dry; it has to go away.
Floodwaters that kept going would not let the field dry out.
Water cannot signal anyone to come, and the field got dry because water left.
Water cannot argue, and the sentence is about the field drying out.

example: The tumult of the parade filled the street.
hook: Picture a stadium right after a winning goal: shouting, stomping, horns blaring everywhere. That noisy confusion is a tumult.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of tumult.
Tumble looks like tumult, but it means a fall.
Crowds often cause a tumult, but tumult means the noise and confusion.

syn1.tip: Think of "the tumult of the parade": drums, cheering, and people everywhere. Tumult means loud noise and confusion.

sc1.stem: The _____ of the cheering crowd, full of stomping and whistling, was so loud we could not hear the announcer.

traps.why: Silence is the opposite; the crowd was so loud you could not hear.
Crowds have a size, but the clue is about noise, not how many people.
Tumble looks like tumult, but it means a fall.

sc1.tip: The clues "cheering," "stomping and whistling," and "so loud we could not hear" point to loud noise and confusion.

decoys.why: Stomping and whistling so loud you cannot hear is the opposite of calm and quiet.
Deep respect is quiet, but this crowd was stomping and whistling loudly.
Eagerness is a feeling, but the sentence needs a noise that was so loud.
Radiance is glowing light, and light cannot be too loud to hear the announcer.
A crowd stomping and whistling is making noise, not telling a short story.

traps.why: Peaceful quiet is the opposite of tumult.
A sudden fall is a tumble, which only looks like tumult.
A large crowd can make a tumult, but it is not the tumult itself.

syn2.tip: Tumult has a wild, noisy feeling. Picture a cafeteria when the fire alarm goes off and everyone talks at once.

sc2.stem: The library was peaceful all morning, but when the kindergarten class burst in at noon, the room filled with a _____ of shouts, giggles, and scattered books.

traps.why: A hush is quiet, but shouts and giggles are noisy.
A whisper is far too soft for shouts and scattered books.
Classes have lectures, but the clue describes wild noise, not a talk.

sc2.tip: "But" contrasts the "peaceful" morning with what came next: "shouts, giggles, and scattered books." That is noisy confusion.

decoys.why: The library was peaceful before; shouts and giggles ended that calm.
Shouts, giggles, and scattered books are noisy confusion, not one small accident.
Shouts and scattered books are a noisy mess, not great beauty.
The room filled with noise and mess, not glowing light.
A natural skill makes no sense with shouts, giggles, and scattered books.

example: The lost puppy gave a woeful whimper.
hook: Woeful means full of woe, the deep sadness in the old saying 'woe is me.'

traps.why: Cheerful is the opposite of woeful.
Wakeful looks similar but means unable to sleep.
Lonely people may be sad, but lonely means being alone.

syn1.tip: Find the word woe inside, plus -ful, meaning full of. Woeful is full of woe, or deep sadness.

sc1.stem: After the rainstorm ruined the bake sale, the cookie table was a _____ sight, soggy and very sad to see.

traps.why: Delightful is the opposite of a soggy, sad sight.
Cookies are tempting, but soggy ruined ones are not.
Bake sales can be crowded, but the clue is about sadness.

sc1.tip: The sentence explains the blank right after it: 'soggy and very sad to see.' You need a word meaning very sad.

decoys.why: The sentence says the soggy table was very sad to see, not cheerful.
A ruined, soggy bake sale is very sad to see, not joyful.
The clue says very sad to see, which is the opposite of happy delight.
A soggy cookie table is quiet and sad, not noisy and rowdy.
A table cannot be on time, and the clue says the sight was very sad.
A soggy cookie table cannot be proud; the clue says it was sad to see.

traps.why: Very happy is the opposite of woeful.
Slightly bothered is much too weak; woeful is very sad.
That fits whoa, which sounds like woe but means stop.

syn2.tip: Woe is a big sadness, as in 'woe is me.' Add -ful and you get full of sadness.

sc2.stem: Our soccer team usually plays well, but last Saturday's game was _____: we missed every shot and lost by six goals.

traps.why: Excellent fits 'plays well,' but 'but' flips it to a bad game.
Games can be exciting, but the clue says it went badly.
Average is too mild; missing every shot is very bad.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' sets up a contrast with 'usually plays well.' Then 'missed every shot and lost by six' shows the game was very bad.

decoys.why: Missing every shot and losing by six goals is nothing to celebrate.
Losing by six goals means the game went badly, not happily.
The sentence is about how badly the team played, not about being on time.
Illegible describes messy writing, not a game where every shot missed.
A game cannot be careful with money; the clue is that it went very badly.
Missing every shot shows a very bad game, not care about people's feelings.

example: The stream meanders through the meadow.
hook: An ancient river in Turkey, the Maeander, curved so much that its name became our word meander.

traps.why: Hurry is the opposite of meander, which is slow.
Move is too general; meander is a slow, winding kind of moving.
Marching is walking, but in straight, steady steps.

syn1.tip: Think of a stream in a meadow that loops slowly this way and that. Meander describes that slow, winding path.

sc1.stem: The lazy river seemed to _____ through the valley, curving slowly back and forth like a ribbon.

traps.why: Rush is fast, but the river is lazy and slow.
Rivers can flood, but the clue is about curving back and forth.
Rivers sparkle, but sparkling is not curving slowly.

sc1.tip: Look at 'lazy' and 'curving slowly back and forth like a ribbon.' The blank must mean winding slowly.

decoys.why: The river is lazy and moves slowly, but scamper means to run quickly.
The river curves back and forth; recede means to move back or away.
Nothing says the river gets smaller; the clue is about curving back and forth.
Subside means to become less strong, but the sentence describes the river's curving path.
Falter means to lose strength, which says nothing about curving like a ribbon.
A river cannot crouch in fear; the sentence describes slow curving.

traps.why: Going straight is the opposite of winding along.
Meander starts with mean, but it has nothing to do with unkindness.
Rivers can flow fast, but meandering is slow.

syn2.tip: Picture a lazy river curving across a map. Meandering is slow and winding, never fast or straight.

sc2.stem: On school mornings Dad rushes us straight to the bus, but on Sundays we _____ through the park, taking the long, looping way past the duck pond.

traps.why: Race matches school mornings, but 'but' signals Sundays are different.
Marching is walking in straight lines, not a looping path.
Stomp is angry walking, but this Sunday stroll is relaxed.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' contrasts with 'rushes us straight.' Then 'the long, looping way' tells you the walk is slow and winding.

decoys.why: Sundays are the slow, looping walk, but scamper means running quickly like the rushed mornings.
Trudge means walking heavily and tiredly, not wandering a relaxed, looping way past the pond.
Nobody is afraid in this sentence, so crouching in fear makes no sense.
Recede means to move back or away, not to wander on a looping path.
Procrastinate means putting off a task, not taking a slow, winding walk.

example: Pandemonium broke out when the bell rang.
hook: The poet John Milton made up pandemonium as the name for the demons' noisy capital city.

traps.why: Calm is the opposite of pandemonium.
Pandemic looks similar but means a sickness spreading everywhere.
Crowds can cause uproar, but a crowd is just many people.

syn1.tip: Hear the word demon inside? Picture a city full of wild demons yelling and running everywhere. That noisy mess is pandemonium.

sc1.stem: When the winning goal was scored, _____ broke out as fans screamed, jumped on seats, and hugged in a wild uproar.

traps.why: Silence is the opposite of fans screaming and jumping.
Applause is too mild for screaming and jumping on seats.
Sorrow is sad, but these fans just won.

sc1.tip: The sentence ends with the clue: 'in a wild uproar.' Screaming, jumping on seats, and hugging all describe wild, noisy confusion.

decoys.why: Fans screamed and jumped in a wild uproar, and tranquility means calm and quiet.
Reverence is deep respect, but the fans are screaming and jumping wildly.
Splendor means great beauty, but the sentence describes a wild, noisy uproar.
Radiance is glowing light, not the screaming and jumping the sentence describes.
Valor means courage, but the fans are just celebrating wildly.
Tact is skill at not upsetting people, which has nothing to do with a wild uproar.

traps.why: Peaceful order is the opposite of pandemonium.
Mild disagreement is far too weak; pandemonium is wild.
Celebrations can get loud, but pandemonium means uproar and confusion.

syn2.tip: Pandemonium is what happens when a classroom goes wild: shouting, running, nobody in control. Look for noise and confusion.

sc2.stem: The classroom was quiet while the teacher read aloud, but when a frog leaped out of Max's backpack, _____ followed, with kids shrieking and climbing onto desks.

traps.why: Calm fits 'quiet,' but 'but' signals a change to wildness.
Order is the opposite of kids climbing on desks.
Curiosity is too mild for shrieking and climbing onto desks.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' contrasts with 'quiet.' Then 'shrieking and climbing onto desks' shows wild uproar.

decoys.why: The room was quiet before the frog, and tranquility means calm, not shrieking kids.
Reverence is deep respect, but kids were shrieking and climbing onto desks.
Tact means not upsetting people, but the sentence describes wild shrieking and chaos.
Splendor means great beauty, not kids shrieking and climbing onto desks.
Valor is great courage, but the kids were shrieking and fleeing the frog.
Radiance is glowing light, which does not describe the noisy chaos after the frog.

meaning: proud and looking down on others
example: The haughty queen ignored the servants.
hook: Haughty comes from an old French word for high: a haughty person holds their nose high above everyone.

traps.why: Humble is the opposite of haughty.
Naughty looks and sounds alike but means badly behaved.
Confident is a good feeling; haughty is unpleasant pride.

syn1.tip: Picture someone with their nose high in the air, looking down on people. Haughty is a negative word for snobby pride.

sc1.stem: The _____ princess looked down her nose at the servants, acting as if she were far better than everyone else.

traps.why: A humble princess would not act better than everyone.
Princesses are royal, but royal doesn't mean looking down on others.
Naughty rhymes with haughty but means misbehaving, not acting superior.

sc1.tip: The clue is 'looked down her nose' and 'acting as if she were far better than everyone else.' You need a word for snobby pride.

decoys.why: She looked down on the servants, so she was not friendly and pleasant.
Acting better than everyone is rude, not careful about others' feelings.
Looking down her nose at servants is not cheerful and friendly.
The princess feels superior, not sad and discouraged.
Tattered describes old, torn things, but the clue is about her proud attitude.
Scrawny describes a thin body, but the sentence is about acting superior.

traps.why: Modest and kind is the opposite of haughty.
Haughty comes from high, but it means high pride, not height.
That describes naughty, which only rhymes with haughty.

syn2.tip: A haughty person acts 'high' above everyone. Think of the phrase 'looking down your nose' at people.

sc2.stem: Most of the new students were friendly, but one _____ girl refused to sit with us, saying our lunch table wasn't good enough for her.

traps.why: Cheerful fits 'friendly,' but 'but' signals this girl is different.
Shy kids might not sit with you, but not because you're not good enough.
A humble girl would never say a table isn't good enough.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' contrasts her with the friendly students. Her reason, 'wasn't good enough for her,' shows she thinks she is better.

decoys.why: The sentence contrasts her with the friendly students, and amiable means friendly.
She refused to sit with you, so she was not cheerful and friendly.
Saying your table wasn't good enough is hurtful, the opposite of tactful.
Punctual means on time, which has nothing to do with thinking she is better.
The lunch table is mentioned, but the clue is her feeling too good for you.
Scrawny describes how thin someone is, not her proud, snobby attitude.

example: She looked pensive as she stared outside.
hook: Picture the famous statue The Thinker, chin resting on his hand, lost in thought: that is a pensive pose.

traps.why: Giddy means silly and excited, the opposite of quiet thought.
Pensive hides inside expensive, but expensive means costing a lot.
A quiet person might look sleepy, but pensive means thinking.

syn1.tip: Picture someone gazing out a window, chin in hand, thinking quietly. Pensive is that deep, calm thinking look.

sc1.stem: Sitting by the rainy window in quiet thought, Kenji looked _____ as he wondered what middle school would be like.

traps.why: Giggly is the opposite of sitting in quiet thought.
Rainy days can be boring, but Kenji is busy thinking.
Terrified is far too strong for quiet wondering.

sc1.tip: The sentence tells you directly: 'in quiet thought' and 'wondered.' The blank must describe someone deep in calm thinking.

decoys.why: Kenji sits in quiet thought, not acting cheerful and friendly.
The sentence describes quiet wondering by a rainy window, not happy delight.
Kenji is quietly thinking, not joyfully celebrating.
Nobody is being looked down on; Kenji is just quietly wondering.
Kenji is sitting and wondering, not working hard.
Nothing mentions food; the clue is that he sits in quiet thought.

traps.why: Full of energy is the opposite of quietly thinking.
Pensive starts with pen, but it has nothing to do with writing.
Worried is anxious; pensive is calm, quiet thinking.

syn2.tip: Pensive comes from an old French word meaning to think. Imagine a person so deep in thought they don't hear you.

sc2.stem: Usually Maya chatters all through dinner, but tonight she was _____, quietly stirring her soup and thinking hard about her friend's surprising news.

traps.why: Talkative fits 'chatters,' but 'but' signals tonight was different.
Dinner suggests hunger, but she is stirring, not eating, while thinking.
Noisy is the opposite of quietly stirring her soup.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' contrasts with 'chatters.' Then 'quietly' and 'thinking hard' tell you she was lost in thought.

decoys.why: Chatty and cheerful is how Maya usually is; tonight she is quiet and thinking.
Maya is quietly thinking hard, not full of happy delight.
She is quietly stirring her soup, not celebrating.
Maya is thinking about news, not looking down on anyone.
She only stirs her soup, so she is not acting extremely hungry.
Being on time has nothing to do with her thinking hard at dinner.

example: The jubilant team lifted the trophy.
hook: Picture a jubilant crowd after the big win: arms in the air, horns honking, confetti falling everywhere.

traps.why: Gloomy is the opposite of jubilant.
Content is quietly satisfied, much too calm for jubilant.
Celebrations are noisy, but noisy doesn't mean happy.

syn1.tip: Jubilant is a big, happy, celebrating word. Picture a team jumping around with a trophy.

sc1.stem: The _____ fans danced in the streets and waved flags, celebrating the team's first championship in fifty years.

traps.why: Disappointed fans would not dance and celebrate.
Fans are loyal, but loyal doesn't explain dancing in the streets.
Nervous is an uneasy feeling, not a celebrating one.

sc1.tip: Look at what the fans do: 'danced in the streets,' 'waved flags,' 'celebrating.' The blank must mean joyful and celebrating.

decoys.why: The fans are dancing and celebrating, not full of sadness.
Fans waving flags after a championship are not sad and discouraged.
A first championship in fifty years brings joy, not woe.
Dancing in the streets is not quietly angry and gloomy.
The fans are loudly dancing, not deep in quiet thought.
Dancing and waving flags takes energy, so the fans are not lethargic.

traps.why: Deeply upset is the opposite of jubilant.
Mildly pleased is far too weak; jubilant is bursting with joy.
Complaining is loud too, but it has an unhappy feeling.

syn2.tip: Jubilant sounds a bit like jubilee, a big celebration. Think cheering, dancing, and shouting for joy.

sc2.stem: Yesterday Coach looked gloomy after our loss, but today he was _____, grinning and high-fiving every player after we finally won the championship.

traps.why: Miserable fits yesterday, but 'but today' signals a change.
Coaches can be strict, but strict doesn't fit grinning and high-fiving.
Sleepy doesn't fit someone grinning and high-fiving everyone.

sc2.tip: The words 'but today' contrast with 'gloomy.' Then 'grinning and high-fiving' after a championship shows great joy.

decoys.why: Sullen matches yesterday's gloom, but today Coach is grinning after a win.
Dejected fits after a loss, but the sentence says today you won the championship.
Coach is grinning and high-fiving, which is not full of sadness.
The word but signals a change from gloomy, so woeful is backward.
Grinning and high-fiving every player is celebrating, not quiet thinking.
High-fiving every player shows energy, not tiredness.

example: A lizard hid in a crevice in the wall.
hook: A crevice is a crack just wide enough for a lizard, a coin, or a lost crayon to slip into.

traps.why: A bump sticks out; a crevice goes in.
Device looks similar but means a gadget or tool.
Crevices are found in rocks, but a boulder is the rock itself.

syn1.tip: Think of a lizard hiding in a rock wall. It squeezes into a thin gap called a crevice.

sc1.stem: The tiny lizard squeezed into a narrow _____ between two rocks to stay cool in the shade.

traps.why: A lizard can't squeeze into a boulder; it sits on one.
Device looks like crevice but means a gadget.
Lizards climb branches, but a branch isn't between two rocks.

sc1.tip: The clues are 'squeezed into,' 'narrow,' and 'between two rocks.' Something narrow you squeeze into between rocks is a thin crack.

decoys.why: A commotion is noisy confusion, not a crack a lizard could squeeze into between rocks.
The lizard squeezes into a narrow space between rocks, and a mishap is an accident, not a space.
An ailment is a sickness, and you cannot squeeze into a sickness between two rocks.
An anecdote is a short story, not a narrow opening between two rocks.
An inkling is a slight idea, not a physical gap where a lizard can hide.

traps.why: A wide field is the opposite of a narrow opening.
A cave is far too big; a crevice is a thin crack.
Crevices are in stone, but a crevice is the gap, not the stone.

syn2.tip: A crevice is small and thin, like the gap between two rocks or between floorboards. Look for an answer meaning a narrow gap.

sc2.stem: My earring slipped off and fell into a _____ between the floorboards, and the gap was so thin that not even my finger could reach it.

traps.why: Things fall into buckets, but buckets aren't between floorboards.
A canyon is huge; this gap is too thin for a finger.
Device looks like crevice but means a gadget.

sc2.tip: The sentence restates the blank: 'the gap was so thin.' A thin gap between floorboards is a narrow crack.

decoys.why: Losing the earring was unlucky, but the sentence describes a thin gap between floorboards, not an accident.
The sentence describes a thin gap in the floor, and a commotion is noisy confusion.
An ailment is a sickness, and an earring cannot fall into a sickness between floorboards.
An inkling is a slight idea, not a gap too thin for a finger.
An anecdote is a story, not a narrow space between floorboards.

meaning: to get smaller little by little
example: Our cookie supply dwindled by Friday.
hook: Picture a candle dwindling: hour by hour it burns a little lower until only a tiny stub is left.

traps.why: Grow is the opposite of dwindle.
Swindle looks similar but means to cheat someone.
Vanish is all at once; dwindle is little by little.

syn1.tip: Think of a cookie jar that gets emptier each day. When something dwindles, it gets smaller bit by bit.

sc1.stem: All week our supply of snacks continued to _____ down, little by little, until only one cracker was left.

traps.why: You might count down the snacks, but a supply can't count.
Settle down means calm down, not get smaller.
Cool down is about temperature, not a shrinking supply.

sc1.tip: The clues are 'little by little' and 'until only one cracker was left.' The supply was getting smaller slowly.

decoys.why: People squander things, but a supply cannot waste itself; the sentence says it got smaller bit by bit.
To meander is to wander slowly, but a snack supply shrinking to one cracker does not wander.
To scamper is to run quickly, and the sentence says the supply shrank little by little.
To trudge is to walk heavily, but a supply of snacks does not walk; it shrinks.
To glisten is to shine, which has nothing to do with snacks running out.

traps.why: Increasing is the opposite of dwindling.
That is dawdle, which looks similar but means wasting time.
All at once is too sudden; dwindling happens gradually.

syn2.tip: Dwindle is about getting smaller slowly, like a pile of snacks shrinking through the week.

sc2.stem: At first, hundreds of fans waited outside the stadium for autographs, but as the cold night went on, the crowd began to _____ until only a few were left.

traps.why: Grow is the opposite; the crowd ends with only a few.
Fans cheer, but cheering doesn't leave only a few people.
The night was cold, but shivering doesn't make a crowd smaller.

sc2.tip: Notice the contrast: 'hundreds' at first, 'but' later 'only a few were left.' The crowd got smaller over time.

decoys.why: Arguing would not make hundreds of fans shrink down to only a few.
The cold might make fans huddle, but the sentence says the crowd got smaller until few remained.
Putting off leaving would keep the crowd large, but the sentence says only a few were left.
Crying out does not explain how hundreds of fans became only a few.
To glisten is to shine, and the sentence is about the crowd getting smaller.

example: She gave a tactful answer about the ugly hat.
hook: Tactful means full of tact, the skill of saying hard things gently, like politely thanking someone for a gift you dislike.

traps.why: Rude is the opposite of tactful.
Tasteful looks similar but means having good style.
Tact is about how you tell the truth, not whether you do.

syn1.tip: Tactful ends in -ful, so it means full of tact. Tact is the skill of being careful with other people's feelings.

sc1.stem: Not wanting to hurt Grandma's feelings, Lily gave a _____ answer about the itchy sweater Grandma had knitted for her.

traps.why: A blunt answer might hurt Grandma's feelings.
Answers can be quick, but quick has nothing to do with feelings.
The sweater is scratchy, but an answer can't be.

sc1.tip: The sentence begins with the reason: 'Not wanting to hurt Grandma's feelings.' So Lily's answer was careful and kind.

decoys.why: Lily did not want to hurt Grandma's feelings, and a haughty answer would be proud and rude.
A gloomy, angry answer would hurt Grandma, which is exactly what Lily wanted to avoid.
A very sad answer would not protect Grandma's feelings about the sweater she knitted.
A sorrowful answer would make Grandma feel bad, but Lily wanted to spare her feelings.
Sounding discouraged would hurt Grandma, and the sentence says Lily wanted to avoid that.
Scrawny means thin and bony, which describes a body, not a kind answer.

traps.why: Blunt and hurtful is the opposite of tactful.
Tactful sounds like tack plus -ful, but tacks have nothing to do with it.
That describes tactical, which looks similar but means clever planning.

syn2.tip: Someone tactful chooses gentle words so nobody gets hurt. Think of the opposite, tactless, which means hurting feelings without meaning to.

sc2.stem: Instead of laughing at Ben's terrible haircut like the others did, Ana was _____ and said only that it would grow back soon.

traps.why: Rude fits the laughing kids, but 'instead of' shows Ana was different.
Stylish is about hair, but the clue is about Ana's kind words.
Mocking is what the others did, not Ana.

sc2.tip: The words 'Instead of laughing' contrast Ana with the others. Saying 'it would grow back soon' is a gentle, kind response.

decoys.why: Ana avoided mocking Ben and spoke kindly, so she was not proud and looking down on him.
The others were laughing gleefully, but the sentence says Ana did not join them.
Nothing was being celebrated; Ana was gently trying not to hurt Ben's feelings.
Ana spoke kindly about the haircut growing back, not in a gloomy, angry way.
Being very hungry has nothing to do with how Ana responded to Ben's haircut.

example: The twins bicker over the front seat.
hook: Picture two kids in the backseat: 'My side.' 'No, my side.' That endless small arguing is bickering.

traps.why: Agree is the opposite of bicker.
Flicker looks similar but means to flash on and off.
Battle is far too strong; bickering is small, petty arguing.

syn1.tip: Think of brothers and sisters arguing over who gets the front seat. Bicker means arguing about small, silly things.

sc1.stem: The twins always _____ over silly things, like who gets the window seat or the bigger slice of pizza.

traps.why: Agreeing doesn't fit fights over who gets the window seat.
The things are silly, but fighting over seats isn't laughing.
Worry is a feeling inside; the twins are clashing with each other.

sc1.tip: Look at the examples: 'who gets the window seat or the bigger slice.' Those are small things kids argue about.

decoys.why: The twins fight over seats and pizza, which is arguing, not just crying out suddenly.
Putting things off does not fit fighting over who gets the window seat.
To scamper is to run lightly, but the twins are fighting over seats and pizza slices.
To glisten is to shine, which has nothing to do with fighting over pizza.
The twins are not getting smaller; they are arguing over silly things.

traps.why: Getting along well is the opposite of bickering.
Bicker starts with bi like bicycle, but has nothing to do with bikes.
Fighting with fists is too strong; bickering is only words.

syn2.tip: Bickering is petty arguing, the kind of back-and-forth over tiny things that siblings do on long car rides.

sc2.stem: At school, Leo and Sam are best friends who share everything, but at home the brothers _____ about whose turn it is to feed the dog.

traps.why: Agree fits best friends, but 'but at home' signals the opposite.
Friends joke, but 'but' shows home is less friendly.
Forgetting is not something that contrasts with being best friends.

sc2.tip: The word 'but' contrasts 'best friends who share everything' with home. Arguing about a small chore like feeding the dog is bickering.

decoys.why: The word but shows the brothers stop getting along at home, so they argue, not just cry out.
Running around does not contrast with being best friends; arguing about the dog does.
Wandering slowly does not show the brothers disagreeing about whose turn it is.
Walking heavily does not fit a disagreement about whose turn it is to feed the dog.

example: My brother's handwriting is illegible.
hook: Legible means readable, so il-legible means not readable, like a doctor's scribbled note.

traps.why: Neat writing is easy to read, the opposite of illegible.
Illegal looks similar but means against the law.
Misspelled words are a writing problem, but you can still read them.

syn1.tip: Legible means clear enough to read. The il- at the start means not, so illegible means not readable.

sc1.stem: Dr. Patel's handwriting was so _____ that the pharmacist could not read a single word on the note.

traps.why: Legible means readable, but the pharmacist could not read it.
Eligible looks similar but means allowed to take part.
A doctor's note is important, but importance doesn't stop someone reading it.

sc1.tip: The clue is "could not read a single word." Handwriting that nobody can read is illegible.

decoys.why: Scrawny sounds like scrawl but means thin and bony, not too messy to read.
Handwriting cannot be careful about feelings; the pharmacist simply could not read it.
Lethargic means tired and slow, but the clue is that no word could be read.
Cheerful handwriting would not stop the pharmacist from reading a single word.
Handwriting cannot be proud; the sentence says the note was impossible to read.

traps.why: Easy to read is the opposite of illegible.
Against the law means illegal, a word that only looks like illegible.
Pencil writing can be perfectly clear; illegible is about being unreadable.

syn2.tip: Find the word legible inside, which means readable. Adding il- flips it to not readable.

sc2.stem: Unlike her neat, careful printing in third grade, Maya's rushed notes this year were so _____ that even she couldn't figure out what she had written.

traps.why: Tidy matches her old printing, but "unlike" signals the notes changed.
Illegal looks similar but means against the law, not messy.
Colorful notes can still be read; she couldn't read hers.

sc2.tip: "Unlike her neat, careful printing" signals a contrast. If even she "couldn't figure out" her notes, they were illegible.

decoys.why: Scrawny sounds like scrawl but means thin and bony, not too messy to read.
Hardworking notes would not be impossible to read; the sentence says Maya could not read them.
Notes cannot be careful about feelings; the problem is that Maya could not read them.
Thoughtful notes would not explain why Maya could not figure out her own writing.
The notes were rushed, not slow and tired, and the clue is that they were unreadable.

example: The puppy cowered during the thunderstorm.
hook: Picture a scared puppy shrinking low under the table during a thunderstorm; that is cowering.

traps.why: To strut is to walk proudly, the opposite of shrinking in fear.
Cover looks like cower but means to put something over.
A growl shows anger at a threat, not shrinking away in fear.

syn1.tip: Picture a frightened animal making itself small. Cower is a fear word, so look for shrinking back.

sc1.stem: During thunderstorms, our puppy would _____ under the kitchen table, crouching low with its tail tucked between its legs.

traps.why: Strutting is proud walking, but the puppy crouched with its tail tucked.
A napping puppy is relaxed, not crouching low with a tucked tail.
Barking is a puppy sound, but the clue describes a scared posture.

sc1.tip: Look at "crouching low with its tail tucked between its legs" during "thunderstorms." That is a scared puppy cowering.

decoys.why: The puppy is crouching low in one spot, not wandering slowly around.
A puppy with its tail tucked is scared, not rudely making fun of anyone.
The puppy is hiding from the storm in fear, not wasting time.
Nobody is arguing here; the puppy is crouching alone in fear.
The sentence is about the puppy's fear of thunder, not shining.
The puppy is crouching low under the table, not walking heavily.

traps.why: Standing proudly is the opposite of crouching in fear.
That is what cover means, a word that only looks like cower.
Bowing is bending down with respect, not with fear.

syn2.tip: Cower always has fear in it. Think of someone hunched and trembling, trying to hide from danger.

sc2.stem: My little brother acts brave all day, but when the lights go out, he will _____ under his blanket until Dad checks the closet for monsters.

traps.why: Relaxing is calm, but "but" shows he stops acting brave.
Giggling is happy, but he is afraid of monsters.
Snoring happens under blankets, but he's awake and scared, waiting for Dad.

sc2.tip: "Acts brave all day, but" signals a change. Waiting for Dad to check for "monsters" shows fear, so he cowers.

decoys.why: The brother is scared of the dark, not making fun of anyone.
He is hiding alone under his blanket, not arguing with anyone.
The word but shows his bravery disappears; he is scared, not wasting time.
He stays hidden under his blanket, so he is not wandering anywhere.
He is quietly hiding in fear, not crying out suddenly.
The sentence is about being afraid of monsters, not shining.

example: The gleeful kids splashed in puddles.
hook: Glee is great delight, and -ful means full of, so gleeful means full of happy delight.

traps.why: Gloomy means sad, the opposite of gleeful.
Gleaming looks similar but means shining brightly.
Gleeful kids may be loud, but gleeful is about a happy feeling.

syn1.tip: Glee means great delight, and -ful means full of. A gleeful person is full of happy delight.

sc1.stem: With a _____ giggle, Toby watched his snowball sail over the fence and land right on his big brother's hat.

traps.why: A gloomy giggle makes no sense; Toby is delighted by his shot.
Nervous has the wrong feeling; Toby is enjoying his perfect throw.
Grateful looks similar but means thankful, which doesn't fit this moment.

sc1.tip: The snowball landed "right on his big brother's hat," and Toby let out a "giggle." That shows playful delight, so gleeful fits.

decoys.why: Toby's snowball hit its target, so his giggle is happy, not sad.
A giggle at a perfect snowball throw is delighted, not gloomy and angry.
Toby succeeded with his snowball, so he is not discouraged.
Landing a snowball on his brother's hat makes Toby happy, not sad.
A giggle is playful, not quiet and deep in thought.
Toby is giggling and throwing snowballs, so he is not tired and slow.

traps.why: Sorrow is sadness, the opposite of glee.
Slightly pleased is too weak; gleeful means bursting with delight.
Gleeful people may be energetic, but the word means delighted.

syn2.tip: You may know the word glee from "shouting with glee." Add -ful, meaning full of, and you get full of delight.

sc2.stem: When the principal announced that summer vacation would start a day early, the _____ students cheered, hugged, and danced right out the classroom door.

traps.why: Disappointed students wouldn't cheer and dance about extra vacation.
Anxious means worried, the wrong feeling for cheering and dancing.
Tardy is a school word meaning late, not a feeling of joy.

sc2.tip: The cause is vacation starting "a day early"; the effect is students who "cheered, hugged, and danced." That joy means gleeful.

decoys.why: The students cheered and danced, so they were happy, not discouraged.
Students who cheer and hug are delighted, not quietly angry.
An early vacation made them cheer, so they were not full of sadness.
Students who danced out the door had lots of energy.
Cheering and dancing show joy, not sadness.
Students who cheer and dance are not quietly lost in thought.

example: We trudged home through the deep snow.
hook: Imagine dragging heavy boots through deep snow, step after tired step; that slow, heavy walk is a trudge.

traps.why: Skipping is light and bouncy, the opposite of trudging.
Nudge rhymes with trudge but means to push gently.
Travel is too general; trudge means walking slowly and heavily.

syn1.tip: Picture tired hikers dragging their feet through mud. Trudge has a heavy, worn-out feeling, so look for slow, heavy walking.

sc1.stem: Tired after school, the kids had to _____ home through the deep, wet snow, their heavy boots dragging with each step.

traps.why: Skipping is bouncy, but their boots were dragging with each step.
Zooming is fast, but the kids were tired and slow.
Skating is a snow and ice activity, but they were walking in boots.

sc1.tip: Look at "tired," "deep, wet snow," and "heavy boots dragging." Those all describe slow, heavy walking, which is trudging.

decoys.why: Tired kids with dragging boots move slowly and heavily, not quickly and lightly.
The wet snow might shine, but the sentence is about how the kids walked.

traps.why: Running lightly is the opposite of walking slowly and heavily.
Push gently is what nudge means; nudge only sounds like trudge.
Go somewhere is too general; trudging is a slow, heavy walk.

syn2.tip: Say trudge slowly; it even sounds heavy. It describes tired feet dragging, like walking home through deep snow.

sc2.stem: In the morning we raced to the beach, but after a long afternoon in the hot sun, we had to _____ back to the car with our heavy bags.

traps.why: Race fits the morning, but "but" shows the trip back was different.
Swimming is a beach activity, but you can't swim to a parked car.
Skipping is cheerful and light, but they were tired and carrying heavy bags.

sc2.tip: "We raced to the beach, but" signals a contrast. After "a long afternoon" with "heavy bags," they walked slowly and heavily.

decoys.why: The word but shows they slowed down; heavy bags rule out running lightly.

example: After soccer, I was famished.
hook: Famished and famine both come from an old Latin word for hunger, so famished means extremely hungry.

traps.why: Full means you've had enough to eat, the opposite of famished.
Famous looks similar but means well known.
Thirsty is needing a drink; famished is needing food.

syn1.tip: Famine means a time when there is no food, and famished comes from the same idea. Think of being so hungry you could eat anything.

sc1.stem: Having skipped lunch to finish his art project, Diego felt _____ by dinner and wolfed down three plates of pasta.

traps.why: Someone stuffed wouldn't wolf down three plates of pasta.
He may be proud of his art project, but the clue is about eating.
Finished looks a bit like famished but means done.

sc1.tip: The cause is "skipped lunch"; the effect is he "wolfed down three plates of pasta." Skipping a meal and eating lots shows extreme hunger.

decoys.why: Wolfing down three plates after skipping lunch shows hunger, not celebration.
The clue is skipping lunch, which makes him hungry, not delighted.
Eating three plates of pasta shows hunger, not quiet thinking.
Nothing here shows pride; skipping lunch made Diego hungry.
The sentence is about skipping lunch and eating a lot, not being polite.
Diego wolfed down pasta because he was hungry, not because he was stubborn.

traps.why: Very full is the opposite of very hungry.
That means famous, a word that only looks like famished.
You might be tired after skipping meals, but famished is about hunger.

syn2.tip: Think of famine, a time without food. Famished is how your stomach feels after a long day with nothing to eat.

sc2.stem: Although Mia had eaten a huge breakfast, by the end of the long hike she was so _____ that she ate two sandwiches and a whole bag of apples.

traps.why: Satisfied fits the big breakfast, but "although" shows she got hungry again.
Hikers can get sunburned, but that wouldn't make her eat so much.
Famous looks like famished but means well known.

sc2.tip: "Although" means the breakfast didn't last. Eating "two sandwiches and a whole bag of apples" shows she was extremely hungry.

decoys.why: Being thin is not why she ate so much; the long hike made her hungry.
Eating two sandwiches and a bag of apples shows hunger, not cheerfulness.
Being delighted would not make her eat so much food after a hike.
Thinking deeply does not explain eating two sandwiches and a bag of apples.
Being polite has nothing to do with eating a huge amount after a hike.
Pride does not explain eating so much; the long hike made her hungry.

example: The teacher beckoned me to her desk.
hook: When a friend curls a finger toward you to mean come here, they beckon you.

traps.why: To dismiss is to send someone away, the opposite of beckon.
Reckon rhymes with beckon but means to think or guess.
Whispering uses your voice; beckoning is a gesture saying come here.

syn1.tip: Picture someone waving you over with their hand. That silent come-here gesture is a beckon, a kind of signal.

sc1.stem: From across the playground, Grandpa gave a little wave of his hand to _____ us over for lunch.

traps.why: To shoo is to wave someone away, not call them over.
Chasing is rough, but Grandpa gave a gentle little wave for lunch.
Grandpa can't carry kids across a playground with a wave.

sc1.tip: The clue is "a little wave of his hand" to get you "over for lunch." A hand gesture asking you to come is a beckon.

traps.why: Send away is the opposite of calling someone closer.
Waving goodbye is a hand gesture, but it means leave, not come.
That is what reckon means; reckon only looks like beckon.

syn2.tip: Beckon is always about getting someone to come closer. Think of a hand gesture that says come over here.

sc2.stem: When the lifeguard spotted us swimming too far out, she began to _____ us back toward shore, waving her arms until we swam closer.

traps.why: Dismiss means send away, but she wanted them to swim closer.
Splashing happens in water, but waving arms called them back.
Towing means pulling with a rope or boat, but they swam back themselves.

sc2.tip: The effect tells you: she waved her arms "until we swam closer." Her gesture made them come, so she beckoned them.

example: The chipmunk scampered up the tree.
hook: Picture a squirrel scampering up a tree trunk on quick, light little feet.

traps.why: Crawling is slow, the opposite of quick, light scampering.
Scatter looks similar but means to spread out in all directions.
Move is too general; scamper means running quickly and lightly.

syn1.tip: Picture a mouse dashing off on tiny feet. Scamper is quick, light running, so look for the fast, small-step word.

sc1.stem: Quick and light on their tiny feet, the chipmunks would _____ across the path before disappearing under a log.

traps.why: Plodding is slow and heavy, not quick and light.
Stomping is heavy, but the chipmunks were light on their feet.
Animals swim, but chipmunks cross a path on their feet.

sc1.tip: The clue is "quick and light on their tiny feet." Running that way is scampering.

decoys.why: The chipmunks are quick and light on their feet, and trudge means walking slowly and heavily.
Meander means wandering slowly, but the sentence says the chipmunks are quick.
The chipmunks are quick, and dawdle means being slow.

traps.why: Walking heavily is the opposite of running lightly.
Animals that scamper may climb, but scamper means running quickly.
Small animals often hide, but scampering is quick running.

syn2.tip: Scamper is how small, playful animals move, like chipmunks or kittens. It is quick, light, and a little bouncy.

sc2.stem: The old dog lumbered slowly across the yard, but the new kitten would _____ past him in a quick blur of tiny paws.

traps.why: Trudge matches the slow old dog, but "but" shows the kitten is different.
Crawling is slow, but the kitten moved in a quick blur.
Kittens stare, but a stare can't move past him in a blur.

sc2.tip: "Lumbered slowly... but" sets up a contrast. The kitten moves in "a quick blur of tiny paws," which means it scampers.

decoys.why: The old dog is the slow, heavy walker; the kitten moves in a quick blur.
The kitten moves in a quick blur, not a slow, winding wander.
The word but contrasts the kitten with the slow dog, so it cannot be slow.

example: Dew glistened on the grass.
hook: Picture dew on morning grass glistening in the sun, shining because it is wet.

traps.why: Fading means growing dim, the opposite of shining.
Listen is hiding inside glisten, but it means to hear.
Wet things drip, but glisten is about shining, not falling drops.

syn1.tip: Glisten looks like listen with a g, but it is about light. Think of wet streets or dewy grass shining in the sun.

sc1.stem: After the morning rain, the wet leaves seemed to _____ in the sunlight like tiny jewels.

traps.why: Darkening is the opposite of shining like jewels.
Leaves rustle, but that's a sound, and jewels are about shine.
Listen looks like glisten but means to hear.

sc1.tip: Look for "wet leaves," "in the sunlight," and "like tiny jewels." Wet things shining in the sun glisten.

decoys.why: Leaves shining like tiny jewels are not getting smaller little by little.
Leaves cannot crouch in fear, and like tiny jewels points to shining.
Jewels do not run; the clue like tiny jewels tells you the leaves shine.

traps.why: Growing dim is the opposite of shining.
Hear carefully means listen, a word that only looks like glisten.
Glistening things are often wet, but glisten means shine.

syn2.tip: Glisten is a light word. Picture raindrops on a car or sweat on a runner catching the sunlight.

sc2.stem: The old copper penny looked dull in my pocket, but after I washed it and set it on the wet sink, it began to _____ under the bathroom light.

traps.why: Fade matches "dull," but "but" shows the penny changed after washing.
Wet metal can rust, but that makes it duller, not brighter.
Coins jingle, but the clue is about how it looked under the light.

sc2.tip: "Looked dull... but" signals a contrast. After washing, the wet penny caught the light, so it began to glisten.

decoys.why: The penny went from dull to shiny; it did not get smaller.
The word but contrasts dull with shiny, not with moving away.
A penny cannot crouch in fear; the contrast with dull means it shines.

example: It is unkind to jeer at the other team.
hook: Jeer rhymes with cheer but means nearly the opposite: rude shouting that makes fun of someone.

traps.why: Praising someone is saying nice things, the opposite of jeering.
Peer looks like jeer but means to look closely.
Complaining is grumbling about something, not making fun of someone.

syn1.tip: Picture a rude crowd booing and shouting insults. Jeer is a mean word, so pick the choice about making fun of someone.

sc1.stem: Good sports never _____ at the other team, even when a player misses an easy shot.

traps.why: Good sports do cheer, so "never cheer" makes no sense here.
Smiling is friendly, and good sports often smile at opponents.
Peer looks like jeer but means look closely.

sc1.tip: "Good sports never" do something rude when a player "misses an easy shot." Making fun of a mistake is jeering.

decoys.why: The missed easy shot hints at mocking the other team, not crouching in fear.

traps.why: Cheering someone on is supportive, the opposite of jeering.
Look closely at means peer, a word that only looks like jeer.
Laughing along is friendly; jeering is rude laughing at someone.

syn2.tip: Jeer has a nasty feeling. You jeer at someone when you shout rude things to make them feel bad.

sc2.stem: Because some fans began to _____ at our goalie whenever she missed, the referee warned them that poor sportsmanship would get them sent home.

traps.why: Cheering is good sportsmanship, so no referee would warn them for it.
Waving is friendly, not poor sportsmanship.
Glancing at a goalie is harmless; it wouldn't get fans sent home.

sc2.tip: Look at the effect: the referee warned them about "poor sportsmanship." Rude behavior "whenever she missed" means they jeered.

decoys.why: The referee warned about poor sportsmanship, which means rude mocking, not crouching in fear.

meaning: to be slow; to waste time
example: Don't dawdle on the way to school.
hook: A kid who dawdles pokes along, stopping at every bug and puddle on the way.

traps.why: Hurrying is moving fast, the opposite of dawdling.
Doodle sounds like dawdle but means to draw little pictures.
Slow kids may complain, but dawdle is about taking too long.

syn1.tip: Picture a kid poking at every bug on the way to school. Dawdle has a slow, time-wasting feeling.

sc1.stem: Mom warned Theo not to _____ on the walk to school, moving at a snail's pace and poking at every bug.

traps.why: Theo was moving at a snail's pace, not hurrying.
Doodle sounds like dawdle but means drawing, not moving slowly.
Shouting is noisy, but the clue is about moving slowly.

sc1.tip: The clue is "moving at a snail's pace and poking at every bug." Going that slowly is dawdling.

decoys.why: Theo moves at a snail's pace, and scamper means running quickly.
The sentence describes moving slowly and poking at bugs, not arguing.
Poking at every bug shows Theo is slow and curious, not afraid.
Nothing in the sentence is about making fun of anyone; it is about going slowly.

traps.why: Rushing ahead is the opposite of being slow.
That means doodle, which only sounds like dawdle.
Dawdling can make you late, but it means being slow, not arriving.

syn2.tip: Parents often say "Don't dawdle" when you are taking forever. It means being slow and wasting time.

sc2.stem: Kayla usually rushes through breakfast, but on lazy Saturday mornings she likes to _____ over her pancakes for nearly an hour.

traps.why: Hurry matches "usually rushes," but "but" shows Saturdays are different.
People argue over things, but nothing in the sentence suggests a fight.
Panic is a worried feeling, wrong for a lazy, relaxed morning.

sc2.tip: "Usually rushes... but" signals a contrast. On "lazy" mornings she takes "nearly an hour," so she dawdles.

decoys.why: The contrast with rushing means she eats slowly, not that she argues over pancakes.
